FRIDAY, 22 JULY 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 9 a.m.
Prayers.
ADJOURNMENT
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): As is customary, it is proposed to meet at
7.30 p.m. on Tuesday next when, normally, the Leader of the Opposition would speak in the
Budget debate. Therefore, I move, That this House do, at its rising, adjourn until 7.30 p.m.
on Tuesday next, and proceed at that hour to the Order of the Day set down.
Motion agreed to.
SELECT COMMITTEE
Mr HARRISON (Hawke's Bay): With the leave of the House, I move, That a select
committee be appointed, consisting of five members, to inquire into the character of every Bill
which may be referred to it by Mr Speaker during its progress and to report its opinion to the
House as to whether it is a public, local, or private Bill; the committee to consist of Mr McLay,
Mr Prebble, Mr Reweti, the Hon. Mr Thomson, and the mover.
Motion agreed to.
PRIVILEGE
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I give notice of my intention to move next sitting
day, That this House notes with very great concern that the Dominion on the morning of
the Budget in its front page story correctly predicted that the tax on cigarettes and liquor
would be increased in the Budget, and notes that the Dominion stated that the story was
revealed by political sources; and that this House concludes that it appears that there has
been a serious leak of Budget taxing proposals, and calls upon the Government to explain
this leak from the Budget, and to hold an inquiry to discover who leaked the Budget
information and whether any persons have benefited from the premature disclosure of
Budget secrets.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I am astonished that the member has
given this notice of motion, which I must treat seriously and assume is not an attempt to
score a political point. This is very serious charge indeed, and, if the member has any
evidence, he should bring it forward and move that what has happened constitutes a breach
of privilege of this House.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): The notice of motion
explained the evidence-a flat statement in a newspaper. The honourable member has
drawn the attention of this House to the wording of an article in yesterday's newspaper, that
the Budget "will contain" something-no "may", "is expected to", or anything else. The
article also states that the information came from political sources. The member has drawn
attention, as he is entitled to do, to what appears to be evidence of a leak. He is not privy to
any leak, nor is he aware of the political source that, allegedly, is quoted.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): In that case, Mr Speaker, I suggest that
you rule on whether a prima facie breach of privilege has occurred. I would have no
hesitation whatever in moving that the matter be referred to the Privileges Committee.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I confess to no less surprise than that which
assails the Prime Minister, but my surprise is that he has not himself taken action in the face
of what seems to be an accurate and reliable report anticipating part of the contents of the
Budget; a situation that normally calls for inquiry. I should have thought that the Prime
Minister would institute an inquiry of his own immediately, whether or not invoking the aid
of the House, but, if he considered it necessary to do so, the initiative should have come
from him, not from a private member.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I suggest that the House should not
resolve this matter on a basis of conviction by allegation, which it is in danger of doing.
Standing Order 103, headed "Certain notices not allowed", states, "Notices of motion shall

Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I shall deal first with the point raised by the
Minister of Justice. My notice of motion does not contravene the Standing Orders because
what is stated is factual. I pointed out that a front page newspaper article correctly set out
what would be in the Budget. The headline reads, "Budget lines up smokers and drinkers to
pay more". It then states, "Higher excise duty on cigarettes and liquor will be announced in
the Budget tonight. Political sources revealed last night that Parliament will take urgency to
pass a special Customs Bill increasing the Government's bite on tobacco and alcoholic
products. The extra revenue will be aimed at public health finance." When the Budget was
read, that statement proved to be factual.
In my notice of motion I said that there appears to have been a serious leak of Budget
taxing proposals, and I have called on the Government to explain this leak. If the Prime
Minister considers another course of action should have been taken, that is his prerogative,
but he should explain to the House at some stage how the Dominion came to give such a
correct forecast of the contents of the Budget. I submit that my notice of motion is in order,
and that the initiative is now with the Government to take what action it thinks fit.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Judging from the expression of a certain
member of the Opposition while that extract was being read I am of the opinion that this is a
political move. Nevertheless, I treat it seriously. I read that statement very carefully
yesterday morning, and with a great deal of concern. My overall impression was that it was a
style of journalism, and nothing more, and I took no further steps. I ask you, Mr Speaker, to
rule on whether this is a breach of privilege, and if you rule it is not I would be perfectly
happy and indeed keen, with the agreement of the Leader of the Opposition, to set up a
special select committee to investigate.
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I have one small point to contribute. I
concur wholeheartedly with the Prime Minister's suggestion that the house should take this
seriously, but I believe that if you examine the article you will see that it is exactly what the
Prime Minister has said it is, a style of journalism. Unfortunately, the member for Auckland
Central did not read far enough into the article. I do not have the article with me but I clearly
remember a statement in it that there would be no increase in the standard tertiary bursary.
That was a categorical statement in that article. In fact, the standard tertiary bursary was
increased by $2 a week in last night's Budget. I suggest that there are some items which were
good guesses and some which were bad guesses. All such allegations should be taken
seriously, and if you rule that the matter be examined I am sure it will be shown to be what I
believe it is, a piece of journalism. However, such innuendoes should not be allowed without
thorough examination.
Mr SPEAKER: Attention has been drawn to the fact that part of the article, which is not
in front of me, is plainly wrong in that the statement given is categorical and not something
saying, "My guess is so and so." Two cases have been mentioned as categorical statements
that appear to have been right, while one has been wrong. I feel I should not rule on whether
there is a prima facie breach of privilege until I have had an opportunity to look at the
article, and I accordingly hold over my ruling on that point.
On the earlier question of whether the notice of motion is unacceptable, I feel there is
nothing in our procedures or rules that precludes notice of intention to move a motion like
this, even though, if the matter is as suggested in the motion, it is correct to say that the
question of privilege could well have been raised. I do not think the two are mutually
exclusive. In the meantime, the notice that has been given should be treated in the ordinary
way. I shall consider the question of a prima facie breach of privilege when I have an
opportunity to examine the article in the light of the matters raised this morning.
POTATO GROWING INDUSTRY BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Potato
Growing Industry Bill be introduced. This Bill replaces the Potato Growing Industry Act of
1950, which established the New Zealand Potato Board, defined its powers and functions,
and provided for the regulation of the potato growing industry. While the Potato Board has
done a very worth-while job since its inception 27 years ago, the Act under which it was


## p. 1555 (#11) ############################################

22 July
1555
Potato Growing Industry Bill
established has one major limitation in that it covers only potatoes planted after 1 August
and delivered for marketing between 1 March and 30 November the following year—the so-
called “main_crop" potatoes. Under the present Act the only growers represented on the
Potato Board are the main crop producers.
While this situation reflected the dominant role of those growers in the industry as it was
in 1950, nearly half the potatoes grown in New Zealand now come within the category
known as "early crop". These are the potatoes produced from seed planted between 1
January and the end of February in any year. Under the existing legislation early crop
growers are not represented on the board, and this limitation has severely affected the
board's ability to supervise the supply of potatoes on the New Zealand market throughout
the year.
For the last 10 years or so early and main crop potato growers have sought ways of co-
operating through a reconstituted Potato Board with responsibility for all potatoes grown in
New Zealand. However, under successive Governments and successive Ministers the
growers have been unable to reach agreement, and there have been some quite deep
divisions in the attitudes adopted by the two sectors of the industry. Consultations to resolve
the divisions have been held over many years with the existing Potato Board, the Potato
Growers Federation, the Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation, the Agricultural
Merchants Federation, the Fruit and Produce Merchants and Auctioneers Federation, the
South Auckland Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation, Federated Farmers, and local
branches of all those organisations. One can see from that list that there have been very
wide-ranging consultations within the industry for a long time before the Bill was introduced
today.
While the new Bill still maintains the old definitions of early and main crop potatoes,
one of the major clauses provides for an expanded board of nine members. This board will
comprise three main crop growers, three early crop growers, and one representative each
from the Agricultural Merchants Federation, the Fruit and Produce Merchants and
Auctioneers Federation, and the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. The ministry's
representative will have full voting rights under the new Act and will be responsible for
representing consumer interests on the board. The composition of the new board gives a
clear majority to potato producers, and that was one of my intentions in promoting the Bill.
This is an improvement on the existing situation in which growers have only equal
representation with potato merchants, and it is in line with precedents set with other similar
organisations, such as the major primary producer boards.
The new board will be responsible for all potatoes grown in New Zealand and for
operating a registration scheme for potato plantings. In addition the board will be respons-
ible for establishing and maintaining minimum quality standards for all potatoes sold in this
country for human consumption. It will also be charged with the responsibility of ensuring an
adequate supply of potatoes to local consumers throughout the year, and to this end will
administer, subject to ministerial supervision, schemes for potato imports and exports as
required. Consultation has been widespread. The most contentious matter has been that of
grower representation on the reconstituted board, and while agreement on this issue was
reached at a meeting in November 1976, I understand there is still dissatisfaction in some
quarters. However, I believe that the procedure set down under the Act to recommend three
producer members from the two main groups will be satisfactory-in other words, the
nominees of the Potato Growers Federation and the Vegetable and Produce Growers
Federation will be a method of overcoming the stalemate about representation on the board
that has existed for upwards of 10 years. It is my intention to recommend that the Bill be
referred to the Lands and Agriculture Committee for further study so that all viewpoints
may be heard.
Squadron Leader DRAYTON (St. Albans): The Opposition is in general agreement
with the Bill, and I have only one or two questions for the Minister. Within the St. Albans,
Rangiora, and Avon electorates is the South Island's second largest potato growing area,
producing about 15 000 tonnes a year. That area has been infected on many occasions with
nematode potato cyst, and the growers have been flooded five times in the last 3 years. Will
the board be able to appoint disaster committees to look at flooding or nematode potato cyst
outbreaks, and will it have the power to grant loans to growers who have faced such
disasters, and to allocate money to research to help overcome outbreaks of nematode potato
cyst? I should also like to know whether the Bill has been referred to the various potato
wards for their comments.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): My reaction to the Bill is similar to that of the

## p. 1556 (#12) ############################################

1556
22 July
Potato Growing Industry Bill
member for St. Albans, but I too have one or two questions for the Minister. Clause 13 sets
out the functions of the board, one of which is to foster research and development in the
potato growing industry. This is the Potato Growing Industry Bill but there is no provision in
the board's constitution for a representative from the potato processing industry. However,
more potato processing is being done now than in the past, and I think it would be desirable
to have liaison between the processers and growers to ensure that the type of potato most
suitable for processing is planted.
Provision is made for registration of potato planting and marketing. Is this an attempt to
interfere with direct sales to consumers from stalls or at the gate? While marketing control is
desirable to ensure high standards, too much interference is undesirable, and any moves
made should not interfere with the consumers' ability to go directly to the grower and
purchase at a more advantageous price.
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson): I should like to know whether the main crop producers or
the early crop producers asked for the Bill, and what their reasons were. I should also like to
know whether consumers will get a better price, or whether the Bill will mean consumers will
pay higher prices. For some time the main crop growers have been expressing to the Minister
their displeasure at the march stolen by the early crop growers on the South Island market
and the potato market generally at the beginning of the season. What effects will the Bill
have on the early potatoes received by the South Island? I should like to see an export
market developed for our potatoes, and I wonder how the Bill will assist in that direction.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: (Associate Minister of Agriculture): The member for St. Albans
mentioned nematode cyst, and the problems associated with that disease. He would be
aware that considerable work has been done on this subject, and it will be continued. The
board will assist in the promotion of that work, but there is no suggestion that the total
research work will be left entirely to the board. This will continue as at present under the
auspices of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. Loans to assist growers who have been
hit by disasters are not covered by the Bill, but would be by direct Government involvement.
The member for Timaru asked whether the processing industry should be represented
on the board. He would be aware that some of the major growers are also processers.
Therefore, there is no provision for a processing representative on the board, but the two
federations represented do have links with the processing industry. The Bill will not interfere
with the sale of potatoes at the gate. The provision for registration of planting is to enable an
accurate assessment of the number of potatoes planted to be obtained. As members will
know, the industry is notorious for having annual cycles of one good year then one bad year,
and this provision will give a better indication to the people marketing the product of just
what the production is likely to be.
The new board will have the additional responsibility of providing consumer protection
by quality standards. The Bill makes provision for quality control by the board. Potatoes
below a certain standard will not be permitted to be sold for human consumption. The Bill
assists the New Zealand consumer by the production of a better quality product, and this is a
logical and worth-while development. The member for Nelson was more optimistic, and
wanted an assurance on price. I assure him that every potato producer would like an
assurance on price, particularly the producers of large quantities of potatoes, who experi-
enced very depressed prices this year. I cannot give the honourable member an assurance on
price, and I do not believe he expects me to. The potato industry moves up and down, and I
think more additional costs are put on by the retail sector, with which he is more familiar,
than by the producing sector. I should welcome an assurance from the member for Nelson
that the retailers will be conscious of the cost that the consumer bears.
The member also raised the question of exports. He would be aware that New Zealand
has only a limited opportunity to export, because we are a long way from major markets.
Last year New Zealand successfully exported potatoes, but this year we were not so
successful because of the lack of sufficient quality control at this end. The board will address
itself to the question of exports, but I cannot give the member an assurance that the board
can give him a stable price at all times. The objects are to produce a better quality potato, to
have a better system of monitoring production volumes, and to ensure that the product is
marketed in a satisfactory manner.

Government on a morning after an important event like a Budget. As the member for

congratulate my colleague the member for Nelson on rightly calling attention to the all-

Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: A point of order, Mr Speaker. When the Standing Orders

be relatively short and devoted to asking questions of the Minister in charge of the Bill, but
that there could be exceptions to this. Successive Speakers have taken note of that over the
years. This is an administrative Bill with a relatively small policy content. It was requested by
the industry and it has been thoroughly discussed with the industry. It will go to a select
committee where submissions will be heard from interested parties. It will then come back to
the House in its present form or with amendments and be subject to a second reading debate
and a Committee stage. I am not sure what the member for New Lynn has in mind this
morning, but I suggest that it is not conducive to the smooth and orderly running of the
House for the member to perform in the manner he is on the introduction of a Bill. We saw
this happen last year and we all know the consequences. I suggest to the Leader of the
Opposition that the best interests of Parliament will be served by not doing that again this
year.

adverted to by the Prime Minister, a time limit was imposed for the introductory stage of a

by the provisions of clause 13?

MINISTERIAL STATEMENT-RELATIONS WITH FIJI
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): With the leave of the House, I want to
make a statement about New Zealand's relations with Fiji. We have all watched with
concern and some anxiety recent events in Fiji in which New Zealand trade unionists have
been involved in a domestic industrial dispute in that country. From private communications
with the Prime Minister of Fiji, and from his public statements, I am aware how deeply the
Fijian people resent what is considered to be interference in Fiji's internal affairs by
nationals of other countries-particularly of those countries which enjoy the closest and
most friendly relations with Fiji.
In this context I am confident that the Prime Minister of Fiji would share with me the
belief that this unfortunate incident need not, and must not, in any way be allowed to impair
the long-term relationship between our countries. I have already offered to him my best
offices in working towards that end. All New Zealanders-and I include the responsible New
Zealand trade union movement-share the Government's desire to foster and enhance the
intimate and long-standing relationships, which we so highly value, with our neighbours in
the South Pacific.
We in New Zealand respect and acknowledge the constructive role that responsible
trade unions can and do play in a democratic society such as ours. Although my Government
has differences of opinion with them from time to time, I believe that, generally, trade
unionists and trade union leaders in New Zealand are responsible. Nevertheless, I feel
bound to point out that the best intentions can be frustrated by the actions of a small group
of people whose allegiances lie elsewhere than to the country of which they happen to be
citizens. The plain fact is that, in the incident in Fiji to which I am referring, some—and, I
readily concede, only a small number- of the protagonists from the New Zealand side have
ideological affinities with great powers whose interests lie outside the welfare of either Fiji or
New Zealand.
Let me be specific. Among the crew of the Ngahere, and playing a prominent part in the
incident, was a man who is known to have been a member of the New Zealand Communist
Party. In addition, shortly after the incident. one known member of the New Zealand
Communist Party, and another man who has had close associations with that party in the
past, travelled to Fiji to stir things along. The identities of those people will be well known to
their fellow trade unionists. The essentially destructive approach of these men to the
situation that arose in Fiji should in no way be constructed as a reflection of the attitudes of
the New Zealand Government or the people of this country to our relationship with Fiji. Nor
do I believe they characterise the views of most responsible New Zealand trade unionists.

Ministry of Energy Bill
MINISTRY OF ENERGY BILL
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I move, That the Ministry of Energy
Bill be introduced. This Bill provides for the establishment of one department of State that
will be responsible for formulating energy policies and ensuring they are implemented. The
operations of the New Zealand Electricity Department and the Mines Department are to be
part of the new ministry's responsibilities, as are the functions of the Ministry of Energy
Resources. The Government's interests in petroleum exploration and development will also
be brought closer together through the absorption of the Natural Gas Corporation by a
company wholly owned by the Government, which is concerned to ensure that New
Zealand's future is not placed at risk through unco-ordinated energy policies.
In establishing this new ministry, the Government is ensuring that New Zealand's
energy resources will be properly developed and used. We need to know much more about
our energy resources. We also need to be quite sure that New Zealand and New Zealanders
obtain the greatest benefits from the ways we use energy. By bringing together the
responsibilities for producing energy and for anticipating the energy needs of the future, the
Government will be able to ensure that development proposals are fully co-ordinated among
all sources and types of energy. The New Zealand Planning Council, the Commission for the
Future, and the New Zealand Energy Research and Development Committee have all
indicated the advantages New Zealand could expect from a careful consideration of our
resources, the options available in the future, and the choices that should be made now.
These advantages apply equally to the energy needs of our industries, primary producers,
and all consumers; they affect almost every aspect of New Zealand's way of life. I am sure
that the formation of a single ministry has the support of both sides of the House and of the
many others who are concerned about the present and future use of energy in New Zealand.
The major features of the Bill are: the establishment of a new Ministry of Energy, which
is to absorb the Ministry of Energy Resources, the New Zealand Electricity Department,
and the Mines Department; the prescription of the functions of the ministry, which concern
energy, in particular, but also draw attention to its mineral responsibilities; the provision of
power for the Government to form or participate in companies undertaking activities related
to energy or minerals; the transfer of the responsibility for pricing petroleum and coal from
the Department of Trade and Industry to the Ministry of Energy; the transfer of the
responsibility for geothermal energy licensing and related matters from the Ministry of
Works and Development to the Ministry of Energy; and the transfer of the assets and
liabilities, and rights and responsibilities, of the Natural Gas Corporation to a company
wholly owned by the Government, on a date to be appointed by the Governor-General.
These provisions will enable the new ministry and the Government to develop a range
of co-ordinated policies, and to ensure that they are followed. Consultation with electricity
and gas distribution authorities and with private sector producers and distributors of other
forms of energy will, of course, be continued. The Bill does not introduce new policy, but
provides the authority necessary for the development of a new Ministry of Energy and a
merger of the Government's petroleum and gas operations. The new organisation will
enable the Government to ensure that the policies needed in the future are developed
quickly and soundly and put fully into effect. It is not proposed to send the Bill to a select
committee. Neither the Bill that created the Ministry of Transport, nor that which dealt with
social welfare-the nearest precedents for this-was referred to select committees. There is
no need for this Bill to be dealt with any differently; it repeats powers that already exist
under other provisions.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): This important Bill will have far-reaching consequ-
ences on the energy scene. It disestablishes as we have customarily known them three
important Government departments: the Mines Department, which is something like 80
years old and which will be drastically reorganised; the New Zealand Electricity Depart-
ment, a very important Government department that has operated since 1946; and the
Ministry of Energy Resources, which is of more recent origin. The new ministry can pretty
well establish a new ball game in the administration of the various departments and interests
that handle energy. In view of the energy crisis that hit the world very hard in mid-1973, to
rationalise and reorganise is a logical development. The Bill was forecast 2 months ago, and
it is surprising that it has taken so long to appear in Parliament. The Government has
professed a sense of urgency in energy matters, but the country has been waiting 20 months,
ever since the Government came into office, for an overall energy policy. We have had two

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I think it is appropriate that I reply to
some of the many points raised by the Opposition spokesman on energy before the debate is
extended. Naturally, I welcome his indication that the Opposition supports the Bill, but I
should have been very surprised indeed if it had not done so. The proposal to amalgamate or
merge the three departments into one featured in the 1972 policy of the Labour Party, but it
was conspicuous by its absence in the party's 1975 policy. However, the member for Petone
reminded us that this policy was reactivated at the recent Labour Party conference; so
obviously this move has the support of both sides of the House, at least in broad principle.
It is true that the proposed merger was forecast 2 months ago. The announcement was
made immediately after the Cabinet meeting at which the final decision was made, and in my
judgment it was most important that the people concerned and the people generally should
be told about it as soon as possible. It has taken a little longer to put the Bill together than I
expected, but it is not a matter of life or death as long as the Bill is passed within the next few
weeks, as I am sure it will be. The member for Petone suggested that a sense of urgency had
been professed, and he wondered why so much time had been taken to bring the Bill
forward. He must appreciate the time it takes to do these things. He was a Minister for 3
years, and I recall that things sometimes moved pretty slowly in immigration when he was in
charge of that portfolio. It is also a fact that we waited 3 years, between 1972 and 1975, for
the Labour Government to honour the energy part of its policy. Not only did it not merge
the three departments into one, it actually preserved the separation more securely than ever
by involving three separate Ministers.
The member for Petone also asked when the new ministry would become fully
operational. It is important that the steps be taken carefully and that the work be done

appointment of the new Secretary of Energy cannot be made until the Bill is passed. When
an appointment is made, the length of time of which the person selected must give notice in
his present position will determine the time taken to establish the new order. It is important
that the new man is fully consulted in the restructuring of the department, and I am not
anxious to anticipate or pre-empt the moves he may like to advise the Government to make.

Gas Corporation and Off-shore Mining will both be brought within the ambit of the new

companies responsible to the Minister of Energy, and obviously working closely with the
Ministry of Energy. If the honourable member would like an example of what can be done

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): There are two or three points which,
I think, should be replied to straight away. I realise that the member for Mt. Albert has not
had the opportunity to read the whole Bill, and has seen just a small portion of it. I assure
him he has misread what the Bill in fact will do. No additional powers are being taken by a
Government official. There are no fewer responsibilities, nor are there fewer opportunities
or channels for appeal. All that is suggested-in other words, the alteration of the law as it
now stands under the Commerce Act-is that the control of energy pricing will be moved
from the Secretary of Trade and Industry to the Secretary of Energy, or from the Minister of
Trade and Industry to the Minister of Energy, as the case may be. The appeal provisions
stand as they exist today in the Commerce Act.
I also point out that not all energy is related to oil prices; electricity costs are not so
related. The honourable member, as a former Minister of Energy Resources, will appreciate
the importance of the relative position of one energy cost against another energy cost in the
impact it has upon demand. Clause 12(5) specifically refers to consultation between the
Secretary of Energy and the Secretary of Trade and Industry about retail margins for
petroleum products, but a close association between the two departments in thinking and
planning and in decision-making must continue in the future, in any case. As the honourable
member will appreciate, the Ministry of Energy Resources has been closely involved in the
past with the Department of Trade and Industry, and has provided the background
information upon which the Department of Trade and Industry has made its formal price
pronouncements. There has been no lack of consultation in the past, and I can assure the

its own sake, but to make sure that the supply of electricity is sufficient to meet the electrical
needs of the country. The Ministry of Energy or the present Department of Electricity would
be clearly failing in their duty if they did not arrange this.

provisions set out in the first clause are in any case subject to section 11 of this same
measure. Section 11 makes clear that, among the considerations, the Minister shall in
particular "promote, encourage, and stimulate efficient, economical, and co-ordinated
methods in activities relating to energy; promote, encourage, and stimulate efficient and
economical uses of energy and sources of energy; formulate methods of influencing and
promoting the conservation of energy". All those provisions, which the new ministry must
have regard to, bear very strongly on conservation and efficiency.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONSS
Unemployed-Special Workers for Tree Planting
1. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa) asked the Minister of Labour: How many unemployed are
planned to be used this season on special work for tree planting, and how does this number
compare with that for the past 2 years?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): There is no analysis of the number of special
workers engaged on tree planting in the New Zealand Forest Service. However, the Forest
Service expects to employ up to 1500 special workers this year, and all of those will be
employed on work either directly or indirectly related to planting trees. The maximum
number employed by the New Zealand Forest Service in 1976 was 1510, and in 1975, 1242.
Mr Hunt: Why is it that although there are still a large number of people on special work
for tree planting the amount of money put aside by the Forest Service for the planting of new
forests has gone down quite considerably since the Labour Government was in power?
Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: I cannot allow that question. It is not in elucidation of the
answer given. The question asked how many unemployed will be used on special work for
tree planting, and how that number compares with the figures for the last 2 years. It is a
matter of numbers, not money, and is not in my opinion relevant.
Mr Hunt: Could I rephrase the question?
Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: Certainly.
Mr Hunt: As the Minister's answer indicated that over 1000 people are still involved in
tree planting, can he indidate whether there will be trees for them to plant?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The member has his figures wrong. There are more than 1500
special workers; the member referred to 1000. The original answer indicated that it had risen
from 1242 under the Labour Government to 1510 under the National Government, and that
it was proposed to have more than 1500 special workers, in addition to the permanent Forest
Service staff, planting trees this year. We have planted more trees in the last 2 years than in
the preceding 2 years under both programmes-Forest Service planting plus special work.
There is no shortage of trees this year for all the special workers, but we must have
contingency plans, depending on the number of unemployed.
Mr Bell: Can the Minister confirm that the employment of these special workers has not
resulted in a reduction of permanent staff for this purpose in the Forest Service?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The permanent Forest Service staff supervise. One or perhaps
two staff members go right into the area in Defence Department four-wheel-drive vehicles.

Masterton Gas Company
4. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: Will he
confirm the report in the June issue of Gas News that, "substitute natural gas (SNG) has
been produced in an eleventh-hour attempt to save the Masterton gas undertaking from
extinction", and the further quote of Mr D. Craven, commercial manager of the Natural Gas
Corporation that, "We have proved the system: all that remains is the political decision as to
whether the Masterton gas undertaking should be rescued"; and, if this is the case, will the
political decision be taken and conveyed to the Masterton undertaking before 31 October,
when the gasworks is due to close?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): An experimental unit using propane
as a feedstock has shown that technically a substitute natural gas can be produced success-
fully by this method. However, as far as I am aware, the Masterton Borough Council is not
intending to reconsider its decision to close the gasworks.
Hon. F. M. Colman: In view of the Minister's reply and the claim by the commercial
manager of the Natural Gas Corporation that it is a viable proposition, and also in view of
the need to make the best possible utilisation of energy resources, will the Minister not
impress upon those who make the decision that the proposal should be undertaken?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: Perhaps it would be appropriate to give the honourable member a
little more background to this project. An experimental propane air carburettor for
producing substitute natural gas has been operated successfully at the Masterton gasworks.
Although the technical aspects of this method of producing gas are well known, other
matters need to be taken into account in determining whether such a system is feasible,
including the cost of propane or butane as a feedstock, the state of the reticulation system,
and the cost of converting gas appliances. It is by no means obvious that in the situation at
Masterton a system based on SNG from propane air would be an economic proposition. It is
clear that, even if the economic viability of the system were established, arrangements for
the financing and installation of the plant required for upgrading reticulation and for
appliance conversion to be completed would take some time-time which, given the present
state of the operation and the costs being incurred, is not available.
Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: Perhaps I could draw the attention of honourable members
and Ministers to the fact that questions and replies should be concise.
Mr Friedlander: Can the Minister confirm that the Government is currently giving
consideration to establishing an LPG plant which would supply New Zealand's needs,
including those of Masterton, and that this would therefore be a factor to be taken into
consideration?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I can confirm that the Government has a major LPG study under
review at the moment. Some of the implications will need to be discussed with the partners in
the oil industry, but I am hopeful that in time—and I fear it may be some months—a very
useful new development in the field will be announced.

Wanganui Education Board—Administrative Grant
8. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: Has he seen the

"despite submission of a realistic budget to the department early in 1976 the board was not
formally notified until 7 January 1977 of the amount of the administration grant which was
approved for the financial year which ended 3 weeks later", and, if so, can he explain this
lengthy delay?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I have seen the report referred to and,
although it is true that approved grants for 1976-77 were not notified until 7 January 1977, I
am sure the board will know, through its membership of the Education Boards Assocation,
the reasons for the apparent delay. There are 10 education boards, and their grants are
considered on a national basis and have regard to the provisions made in the annual
estimates of expenditure of my department. Discussion was held with representatives of the
Education Boards Association as to the levels considered reasonable for each board, bearing
in mind the results of operations in the previous year. Two boards did not supply the latter
information until August 1976, despite repeated reminders. An additional factor contribut-
ing to the apparent delay was the need to take account of increases of salaries, which
comprise 80 percent of boards' administrative costs. The Wanganui Education Board and
others did not supply the estimated cost of the 25 June 1976 salary order until October 1976.
A further point worth recording is that the total amount shown in the Budget announced on
29 July 1976 for the administration grant for all boards was $5.84 million. This was an
increase of nearly 25 percent over the 1975-76 expenditure, and I believe it would have been
reasonable, because of the national picture, for boards generally to expect an increase of this
size.
Mr Marshall: Can the Minister say when the boards will be notified of their final
administration grants for 1977-78?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I know we are fairly close to being able to give a satisfactory
answer, but I would point out that in last night's Budget there was an indication that the
amount for the year will be $6.8 million, representing an increase of 18 percent, so boards
can do the same sort of estimating they could have done last year and assume that that will be
about the order of the increase this year.
Mr Wellington: Is the determination of administration grants for education boards not a
very protracted exercise in any event, and has the Minister received this year, although he is
probably reluctant to say so, a letter from the Education Boards Association congratulating
him on the speed with which grants have been announced and made available?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: That is correct in respect of incidental grants. The administra-
tion grant is more complex, but the Government undertakes to see that education boards
carry out efficient administration. Some of the restraints imposed upon the Government
itself are being imposed on education boards, and this makes for some complicated
discussions.
Mr Marshall: Would the Minister not agree with the further contention in the Wanganui
Education Board's annual report that if the grants cannot be announced until January it is
rather futile for his department to send letters to the education boards on 12 May-8 months
before-instructing them that "financial allocations must not be overspent”?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I do not see any discrepancy in that. As the member has quoted
from the Wanganui Education Board's report, I would remind him that the report also
states, in respect of the board's administration grant, that early predictions on severe
financial cutback proved to be overstated, and there was no requirement to restrict activity
to the point where essential services to the schools would have been seriously impaired.

Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: I am quite aware of the content of the Minister's reply and of
the member's supplementary question, the repetition of which makes no difference to my
original ruling that it was not in elucidation of the original answer. Some members are
getting into a bad habit of questioning rulings. A lot of time could be spent doing that, but in

Nuclear Bomb Testing at Muraroa
12. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What steps
has the New Zealand Government taken to indicate New Zealand's opposition to the
conducting of nuclear bomb tests in the South Pacific by the French Government at
Muraroa?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): Since the
French Government commenced underground testing in 1975, following the cessation of
atmospheric tests, the New Zealand Government has viewed the conducting of each test
with the same regret with which it has witnessed underground tests carried out by each of the
other four nuclear weapon states. There is a difference between atmospheric tests, which
pose greater environmental hazards—which a multilateral treaty, the partial test ban treaty,
was designed to prohibit-and underground tests which every nuclear weapon state has
continued to conduct in the absence of any proscriptive multilateral treaty. New Zealand
does not, therefore, single out France for condemnation, but rather condemns all nuclear
testing by all states in all environments—
Mr Hunt: What about the Pacific Ocean?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: In reply to the interjection I was saying, but rather
condemns all nuclear testing by all states in all environments-and that includes the Pacific
Ocean-and has urged the nuclear weapon states to conclude a comprehensive test ban
treaty as a matter of urgency. I shall arrange for the honourable member to receive a copy of


## p. 1580 (#36) ############################################

22 July

the Government's latest statement on the subject of a comprehensive test ban treaty as soon
as it is available at an early date.

tests in the South Pacific, have National Ministers taken the opportunity, when they have
been in France, to indicate New Zealand's opposition to the nuclear tests still being

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The French Government has been made well aware

CITIZENS AND ALIENS BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Citizens and Aliens Bill. The committee recommends
that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
The Bill was introduced at the beginning of the present session, and consolidates and amends
the British Nationality and New Zealand Citizenship Act 1948 and the Aliens Act of that
same year. The Statutes Revision Committee received six submissions, all of which
supported, and in some cases warmly applauded, the Bill. However, several matters
emerged, either from the submissions or from consideration of the Bill, and I comment upon
those that were of some substance and particularly those on which the committee recom-
mends some amendment.
First, clause 8(1) authorises the Minister of Internal Affairs to grant New Zealand
citizenship to any person who has attained the age of 16 years. Both the National Council of
Women and the Committee on Women suggested in their submissions that a change of
citizenship is something too important for a 16-year-old to be able to undertake on his or her
own, bearing in mind that there are still special provisions for an application by or on behalf
of a minor contained in clause 9 of the Bill. Both organisations recommended that the age
should be increased to 18 years. After careful consideration, and particularly bearing in mind
the provisions of the Guardianship Act, which provides some jurisdiction in respect of
minors up to the age of 18 years, the committee agrees with this view and, with respect to
clause 8(1), and in all other cases except one in the Bill, recommends that references to the
age of 16 years be amended to 18 years.
Secondly, the Bill as introduced provided that citizenship by descent should be available
only to members of a first generation born outside New Zealand. Clause 9(1)(c) permits the
Minister to grant a certificate of citizenship if, because of exceptional circumstances of a
humanitarian or other nature relating to the applicant, he-the Minister-is satisfied that
granting a certificate of New Zealand citizenship would be in the public interest. The
Salvation Army suggested to the committee that this "first generation only" rule might be
unfair to the families of missionaries, and the committee is equally satisfied that this might
apply to the families of academics, who spend much of their lives outside New Zealand,
where they have citizenship, and could apply to other groups as well. It was originally
suggested to the committee that clause 9(1)(c) gave sufficient discretion to the Minister to
deal with this particular problem, but the committee was not satisfied that this was so. The


## p. 1583 (#39) ############################################

22 July
1583
Citizens and Aliens Bill
committee therefore proposes an amendment to permit persons claiming citizenship by
descent to perfect their citizenship and also to allow the Minister to deal with second
generation cases on criteria that are not as rigid as the exceptional circumstances of a
humanitarian nature contemplated by clause 9(1)(c). Consequential amendments are also
proposed to clause 8 to give effect to this particular amendment.
Thirdly, in the transitional provisions of the Bill—that is, clause 12 (c)—provision was
originally made that every person born outside New Zealand on or after 1 January 1949, but
before 1 January 1978, should be a New Zealand citizen by descent if either the father was a
New Zealand citizen at the time of the child's birth, or, in the case of a person born after 1
January 1970-which was the commencement date of the Status of Children's Act 1969-the
mother was a New Zealand citizen at the time of the child's birth. Although this provision,
on the face of it, might appear to be discriminatory, the committee did recognise that it did
nothing more than restate existing New Zealand law. Nonetheless, both the National
Council of Women and the Committee on Women drew attention to the clause, and
suggested that the two subclauses of clause 12(3) should be amalgamated. The effect of this
would be to make all children born outside New Zealand between 1 January 1949 and 1
January 1978 New Zealand citizens, if either parent was himself or herself a New Zealand
citizen. Although such a change would be retrospective in its effect, the committee did not
find this in itself objectionable, because it would in no way be detrimental to the rights of a
potential citizen; in fact, it conferred a right rather than taking it away.
However, the proposal would give rise to certain problems unless it was made without
some qualifications. Persons with citizenship in another country could well find themselves,
as a result of the proposal put forward by the two women's organisations, in a situation of
dual citizenship that might well be illegal in another country. The committee therefore
proposes an amendment not to amalgamate the two sublcauses, but rather to permit a grant
of citizenship to be made as of right-that is, without any ministerial discretion-on
application from any person born outside New Zealand before 1 January 1978, if either
parent was a New Zealand citizen. That proposed amendment removes the discrimination
that is inherent in clause 12(3) as far as that is possible. The new clause will become clause
9A.
Finally, the Minister of Internal Affairs has advised the committee of possible changes
to the law relating to aliens, which are at present contained principally in Part III of the Bill.
The committee was originally invited by the Minister to delete all provisions in the Bill that
might refer to aliens, but after further consultation with the Minister of Internal Affairs it
decided this action was not appropriate as a final policy decision has yet to be made. The
matter can, if necessary, be dealt with by a Supplementary Order Paper during the course of
the Committee stage of the Bill, in which case the Bill would become a Citizens Bill rather
than a Citizens and Aliens Bill.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): The Opposition agrees that reforms are needed for
the registration of citizens and aliens. When the Opposition examined the Bill it found it
unsatisfactory in many ways. The law relating to citizenship and aliens is complex and
changes can have a very wide effect, because the law of other countries must be taken into
consideration. I draw the attention of the House to the fact that there was disagreement
between the committee members about many aspects of the Bill. Citizenship is a very
important right, governed by many international laws, and to lose one's citizenship can have
a disastrous effect upon a person and his family. No country should lightly make any person
stateless. The United Nations has passed a resolution about this.
For many people this is probably one of the most important pieces of legislation that will
ever be put through Parliament. I draw the attention of the House to the fact that rights held
by citizens are normally protected by our courts or by some special tribunal, and that
Parliament has recognised that a politician, even though he may be acting in good faith,
should not have absolute discretion over the rights and liberties of the citizens of New
Zealand. However, clauses 8 and 9 give the Minister, in a number of instances, absolute
discretion on whether or not to grant citizenship. We made it very clear at the committee,
and we divided on the matter, that the Minister should not have this absolute discretion,
because there is no obligation on him to give his reasons. In fact, a Minister could properly
refuse the status of citizenship to a person who should be granted New Zealand citizenship,
and that person would be left without any recourse. That is wrong. We made it clear at the
committee that it is wrong, and advocated as strongly as we could that there should be a right
of appeal.
Appeal rights for citizens have been established in other countries, and have worked

TUESDAY, 26 JULY 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 7.30 p.m.
Prayers.
PRIVILEGE
Mr SPEAKER: This might be a convenient moment to refer to a matter of privilege
raised on Friday of last week. At that time, notice was given of intention to move a motion
expressing concern at what was suggested had been a leak of the contents of the Budget.
Thereupon, the question was raised by the Prime Minister whether the newspaper article in
question, which appeared on the front page of the Dominion of 21 July, might constitute a
breach of privilege. This I have now to decide.
First, I should state that the well established principle of the inviolability of the Budget
in our British type of parliamentary and Executive government is a Cabinet or Executive
matter as opposed to one of parliamentary privilege, or its converse, contempt. In
November 1947, the then Chancellor of the Exchequer in Great Britain admitted having
indiscreetly mentioned to a pressman an important matter in the Budget about to be
delivered; he thereupon resigned. But the question of privilege was not even raised at that
time in the House of Commons, or in connection with the affair. The reason for the principle
of inviolability is, of course, concern lest prior knowledge of intended changes in such things
as tax rates might lead to improper buying and selling of shares or of commodities, with
improper gains to those in the know; but, as I have said, this is distinct from the question of
parliamentary privilege.
If, however, it happened that a document or statement intended for first promulgation
in Parliament was improperly obtained or intercepted and then published before its
promulgation in Parliament, or if an embargo were broken with similar effect, then it might
well be argued that there had been a breach of parliamentary privilege. The only document
in the present case that could be affected is the Budget, or, as it is more correctly called, the
Financial Statement, but the newspaper article in question seemed to make it clear that its
writers were not in possession of the Budget.
This seems an instance of the usual pre-Budget guessing game, and, in this instance, it
appears to have been mostly well done; but the presence of bad as well as good guesses and
the complete omission of allusion to various matters that might have been assumed to be of
public or news interest-such as energy policy and on-shore drilling, changes in nursing
training, and the establishment of certain community colleges-make it virtually certain that
the gentlemen making the guesses were not in premature possession of a copy of the Budget,
even though the categorical style used in lieu of some such expression as "it is expected"
gives the superficial impression of a leakage when the guesses happen to be good ones.
The statement in the opening sentence turned out to be correct, but the opening words
of the fifth sentence are, "More novel announcements involve subsidies for maraes. . .".
This though stated categorically, turned out to be a bad guess, because, as far as I have been
able to glean, there is no announcement or reference in the Budget about subsidies to
maraes. Moreover, if there had been, the statement would have been off beam in that there
would have been no novelty. There are two relevant items in the estimates, one for subsidies
for Polynesian community centres and the other for subsidies under the Maori Welfare Act
which are doubtless related to maraes, but these items also appeared in last year's estimates.
The proposed votes are an increase on last year's figures, these having been lower than those
in the previous year.
Next, there is reference to an increased budget for pre-school education. This turned
out to be correct, but the following sentence states, "but it is understood tertiary student
bursaries will not be increased". This turned out to be a bad guess, in that tertiary student
bursaries are, according to the Budget provisions, to be increased by $2 a week next
academic year.
I am therefore satisfied that there is no case to answer based on the improper or
premature obtaining of the Budget document by the writers of the article. I therefore
conclude that there is no case to answer in regard to a breach of parliamentary privilege.
I have two observations to make. The second sentence of the article states: "Political
sources revealed last night that Parliament will take urgency to pass a special Customs Bill
2.


## p. 1588 (#44) ############################################

1588
26 July
Privilege
increasing the Government's bite on tobacco and alcoholic products." A political source is
difficult to define and might easily consist of a member of Parliament, a member of the staff
of Parliament, or even a member of the press gallery. Every experienced member of
Parliament, staff member, or parliamentary reporter knows that, if changes in customs or
excise duties are to be announced in the Budget, it is certain that the Government will seek
urgency to pass the legislation the same evening. However, one can be certain that incorrect
statements were bad guesses, even though categorically expressed. As to statements that
turned out to be correct, one can say only that they might have been based on good guesses
or on information garnered somewhere.
I conclude by saying that there can be no doubt about the importance of avoiding
Budget leaks, and it may well be desired that some inquiry be conducted into the
implications of the words "political sources revealed" and into the question of whether
correct forecasts were the result of some leak or merely the overconfident expression of what
turned out to be good guesses; but I am of the opinion that parliamentary privilege would
not be the appropriate vehicle for such an inquiry.

Even the pieces of verbiage to which people might cling for some hope apparently do

sacrificed and what it has not. It is bewildered by its inability to come to grips with the
problems.
The Government lacks a sense of direction and purpose, yet it still tries to blame others.
The public has had enough of that. People's memories are not short, and they remember the
irresponsible Budget of 1972 and the loud proclamation made by the Minister of Finance
that he had spent it all. They find, 5 years later, that the Minister of Finance is still as
irresponsible as he was then. He likes to hark back to the boom of 1973, and then very
conveniently forgets the international recession of 1974 and 1975 and the massive export
boom his Government inherited in 1976. The National Government inherited a 50 percent
increase in export earnings, which represented an extra $1,000 million. The Labour
Government had planned and worked for that, but the benefits have been destroyed by this
Tory Government. As the market falters, there is little room for manoeuvre. The Prime
Minister and his Cabinet are just like so many sailors in a lifeboat partly filled with water;
they think that all they have to do to let the water out is drill a few more holes in the bottom.
I shall now look at some of the issues before us. I turn first to taxation, because it
concerns every New Zealander. The Minister of Finance has allowed the beneficiaries to be
brought into the tax net. I shall be surprised if he has not received mail from them, because I
have received many dozens of complaining letters. People from one end of the country to the
other, no matter what their political opinion, consider that the whole tax structure should be
pulled apart and rebuilt to cater for two significant objectives: incentives for the people, and
proper protection for the family budget. It is fair to say that, until the 1977 Budget appeared,
many people believed that the Minister of Finance would have the gumption at least to have
a go. Now they have their answer-plenty of blow, but no go.

Against that background of failure, I shall quote from the 1976 Budget. On page 33 we
read: "Whereas the previous Government increased State participation in the housing
sector, thus driving out private investment, our aim is to restore to the private sector the
dominant role in the new housing market. We are now moving towards this objective in an

an orderly fashion, while still ensuring that housing construction is maintained at an

This time, we have the same Minister of Finance talking about easing demand on home
building. I have not the slightest doubt that he can support his argument by turning to the
permit statistics, so we shall help him out. The number of permits has fallen. The average
monthly number of permits issued for the 3 months ended June 1976 is 2488, while the
average number of permits for the 3 months ended June 1977 is 2008, an average decline of
480. Of course, that argument can be taken to its logical conclusion, and I do not doubt that
the Prime Minister will do so; if he does, he will find that fewer than 23 000 units were built
in the last year. He said that the demand for housing had eased. The truth is that people are
not bothering to apply for permits, because they know that the likelihood of obtaining
mortgage finance is pretty remote, and that even if they could get it there is no possibility
that a single-income wage or salary earner can meet a second mortgage commitment of 23
percent. That is the present state of affairs under the Government's housing policy.
On the other side of the coin, the further easing of the savings banks' security ratios can
offer some relief in the sale of existing homes. In fact, I advocated that very strongly in the
Address in Reply debate, and my colleagues have advocated it since. However, that can
hapen only if savings levels can be maintained, and, with the small savers up against the wall
as they now are, there is a very real question mark against that one. I agree with the abolition
of stamp duty on the purchase of a first section or a first home, but neither of those moves
will build one more house or provide one more section at a reasonable cost to young New
Zealanders.
It is therefore essential that a number of steps be taken-and these steps will certainly
be included in the Labour Party's policy. First and foremost, there must be a reactivation
and an expansion of the land bank. Secondly, funds for refinancing must be provided for
genuine home owners who find themselves in short-term mortgage difficulties. At present
they are ignored by the Minister of Housing. Thirdly, a proper degree of control over
interest rates must be exercised. Fourthly, funds must be provided to enable the Housing
Corporation adequately to supplement reasonable cost finance from the private sector, in
order to sustain the building industry to its full commitment. Fifthly, the corporation must be
authorised to advance mortgages at a reasonable level. None of those factors is being
properly accommodated at present.
The tax rebate on rates is essentially an election sop. It will clearly be overwhelmed by
inflation. A number of people have already told me that their rates in the last year have risen
more than the Budget concession. In the Budget itself we are told that local bodies will have
to pay 10.5 percent for their loan funds. Once again, the ratepayers will be called upon to
foot the bill.
In summary, the housing section of the Budget offers some concessions to the lender,
but very little of real consequence to the purchaser. For a National Government that is about
par for the course.

It might not be a bad idea to illustrate what is happening in welfare. I shall take the
hypothetical example of three brothers-any three New Zealanders known to any member.
They are all in their fifties, or they were last week. They were then all in jobs that gave them
an income of $8,600 each. Yesterday one of the brothers turned 60, and for passing "go" he
gets an added gross income of $4,300, and up he goes to $12,900. The second brother was
involved in a serious automobile accident on his way to work, and was injured so badly that
he will not be able to work again. Because it was an accident, he is entitled to accident
compensation of 80 percent of his former income, so he will drop back by about $1,700. The
third brother, the youngest, with children still at secondary school, had a coronary that was
so severe that the doctor said he would never work again. He cannot claim accident
compensation, because it was not an accident, and he cannot get in on the Government's
superannuation act, because he is far too young; and so he goes back about $5,000 and winds
up on a sickness benefit of $3,600. Last Friday we had three men each on $8,600 a year; on
Monday the youngest, who still has dependants, has an income of $3,600, the second has an
income of $6,900, and the only one who is fit and well and able to continue to work has an
income of $12,900. What kind of a crazy mess are we getting into when we get to a
circumstance like this?

dearly, in both economic and social terms. The people of the regions were keen, and the
Labour Government, with great assistance from the Development Finance Corporation,
provided $50 million in less than 3 years. The results began to show at an early stage.
Population drifts were slowed or were halted, and in some areas they were even reversed.
More important, there was a new spirit and a sense of purpose and dedication in many areas.
But, tragically, there was a change of Government, and that spirit has been trampled on.
Once again, the Tory Government has set the clock back years. The Budget does little
to undo the damage already done; the Government's half-hearted approach is probably best
expressed by a couple of lines from the Budget, which states that a number of restrictions
that were imposed on the existing programme last year will be relaxed. Not all of
them-some of them. It is a bit of a gesture from the Government, which could not care less.

the regions who are keen to weigh in and help themselves that the incoming Labour

Since March 1976 the Government has been endeavouring to reshape and free up the
money system. To continue that, this Budget is vital. The Government wants to free up the
money system and develop more realistic interest rates, thereby stimulating more savings
and expanding the role of the financial institutions. The Government also wants to ensure
better central management of credit. Tactically these are all highly desirable as part of an
overall monetary strategy. Without them the development of a modern economy cannot be
sustained. This policy will allow for a closer monitoring of future development and a more
even flow of money for housing and for local bodies, but not so much as to fuel inflation.

Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): It is obvious that the Associate Minister of Finance
had a major part in writing the Budget. His speech proved as boring as the Budget, and

This evening the Leader of the Opposition outlined some positive policy points about
housing. I shall expand on one or two of those points. The Prime Minister, in one of his more
incredible statements, recently said that growing public concern about housing was against
the facts. He went on to say that everything was rosy, because house sale prices had risen by
only X percent and thousands of people had fled the country, so there was little demand for
housing. He ignored the fact that first home owners do not have the opportunity to buy
existing houses. The Prime Minister's statement is an incredible example of using half a
statistic-he is ignoring the quite tragic situation that really exists. Housing is one of New
Zealand's most serious problems, The Budget does nothing to help solve that problem, and
therefore tonight I intend to look at housing and to offer some solutions to the problems.
All New Zealanders grow up in the expectation that they will get a home of their own.
They look, as a fundamental right, to a home that provides a stable base for a growing
family, and is paid for over a working lifespan. The Labour Party agrees with them and
acknowledges that the fulfilment of that right is one of the most important responsibilities of
any Government. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Housing may not care to know
about it, but there is a generation of young families who now have no hope of owning their
own homes. Why is there a generation of young families with no hope of owning homes of
their own? For a start, how can an average working couple save for a home? Look at any
"To let" column in the newspapers and see if you can find a one-bedroomed flat for under
$30 a week? Then think of what families with three and four children must be paying. Any
family coping with 20 percent inflation, controlled wages, crippling taxes, rates, and
uncontrolled rents, has little hope of extricating itself from such a situation. It is forced into a
poverty trap not of its making.
Housing Corporation tenants also are trapped. Increases in income over $100 a week
are taxed at an effective rate of more than 80c in the dollar. We are putting families that rent
into a poverty trap, ensuring that they stay there, and then we wonder when a man in that
situation reacts in despair. The problem is clear. What then should we do? Rents should be
frozen for at least 2 years, with only increased costs allowed. Speculators and rent racketeers
have made their piles, and it is time to call a halt. A rent freeze would stabilise the rental
market and provide a breathing space until costs could be brought under control. It would
give families hope and enable them to save money towards their own homes. To this end the
home ownership scheme introduced by the Labour Government should be promoted
vigorously.
The second item I want to deal with is the deposit gap. Three years ago a builder could
provide a home for a young family for a deposit of between $700 and $5,000. Today, a
deposit of between $8,000 and $13,000 is needed, and costs are going up all the time. This
tragic situation was not brought about by a shortage of mortgage finance-although I shall
have something to say about the cost later-but because lending rules are not suited to the
current relationship between incomes and house prices. It is arguable whether the money is
available. For all its proud words the Government's measures have done little to stimulate
the flow of funds from the private sector so confidently promised by the Minister of Energy
Resources during 1975. There is a deposit gap, and it is widening every day.
In October 1975, under Labour, a typical married man, with three children, receiving
the average wage was eligible-on a house costing $25,000-for a basic loan of $14,000, a
low-income supplement of $2,000, a dollar-for-dollar subsidy of $2,000, and a section loan of
$4,800, all at an initial interest rate of 3 percent, giving weekly repayments of about $22.30 a
week. Taking his family benefit capitalisation of $2,000 into account, in 1975 this young man
had to raise less than $1,000 for a deposit on a home. What is the situation of that same man
today? With no section loan, no low-income supplement, and no capitalisation, the most he
can expect from the Housing Corporation is a loan of $14,000. His weekly repayments at the

new interest rate will be about $27.30, since he is no longer eligible for the concessional

The Housing Corporation, as one would expect, has an answer to the problem-on a
typical package like the one I have outlined it will lend only if the weekly income of the
couple buying the home is more than $240. If you earn less than $240 a week, do not bother
to apply. Is that really housing the way the family man on the low or single income wants it?
The problem is clear, and so is the answer. As the Prime Minister said on 8 January 1975
from his cottage at Hatfield's Beach, mortgage finance available from the Housing Corpora-

even a cottage, but that was what the Prime Minister said in 1975.
The first step, therefore, must surely be to provide more finance from the Housing
Corporation. The second step must be to provide that finance on a first-mortgage basis-that
is, 80 percent of the cost of a reasonably priced home. I shall not say 85 percent as promised
in the Government's manifesto, but 80 percent. That policy should be implemented
immediately, and it could be done in the following manner. First, as loans would be on an 80
percent one-mortgage basis, the demand for Housing Corporation finance would increase
dramatically and some queueing would be essential. Priority should be given to those who
have saved through the home ownership account system, those who have saved a substantial
deposit of their own, or those with an urgent housing need.
I am sure that first home owners would be prepared to wait for up to, say 2 years for a
one-mortgage loan rather than be burdened with the present system, which lets thousands of
young couples scramble into homes only to cripple their marriages and their personal lives
with exorbitant interest rates forced on them by this Government's policy. There are many
young couples whose loan repayments are between $60 and $90 a week. These payments are
crippling their marriages and their personal lives, and they would be quite happy to wait a
little longer for a loan if they could get it on a one-mortgage basis, with repayments of
between $25 and $35 a week.

mere drop in the bucket. The Government's monetary policies have allowed open slather in

I suggest that the inquiry set up by the Labour Government into the financial structure
of the mortgage market should be completed. Although not appearing to have completely
shelved it, the present Government is doing little to push the inquiry to a satisfactory
completion. The National Housing Commission stated in its 1976 report: "The commission
remains deeply concerned over the provision of adequate mortgage finance for housing. In

adds about $10,000 to the interest charge during the term of the average corporation loan. I
suggest that this action is irresponsible in present circumstances, when one considers the
interest rates that people are having to pay in the private sector. People should be given a
mortgage at an interest rate of not more than 5.5 percent for the first 5 years of the
mortgage. That would allow young couples to get on their feet. The rate could be revised at
the end of the 5 years, and increased as circumstances permit and according to the
circumstances of the borrower.
The fourth area I want to deal with is the refinancing of existing mortgages. Thousands
of hardworking families are now faced with the prospect of having their homes sold over
their heads-in fact, of losing their homes and the equity they have built up-because they
cannot find money in the private sector to refinance their existing loans. Unless people in

possible for them to do so, or, at best, very difficult. Solicitors will endeavour to help, but

tragic. What should be done?
The first thing is to recognise the problem, and not to turn a blind eye to it as the
National Government is doing. The second point is to recognise that, if the correct overall
housing policies are adopted, the problem of refinancing existing mortgages should be of a
short-term nature only. In these circumstances the Government should release the Housing
Corporation from its commitment, say for the next 2 years, to pay interest on Government
loans. The money so released-more than $20 million a year-could be used by the Housing
Corporation to refinance existing mortgages. I make that suggestion only as a short-term
measure, because of the difficult position in which we find ourselves at present.
The Government should simultaneously instruct other institutions, such as the trustee
savings bank and insurance companies, to refinance loans for the next 12 months on the
same basis as they consider new loan applications. With the present problems of refinancing,
