us with an impossible debt load. Fortunately the people saw the problem and tossed the
former Labour Government out. The National Government has not relished the task of
imposing restraints to live within our income, but it has courageously shaped up to its
responsibilities in a manner that I know is understood and accepted by most New Zealan-
ders. We have applied restraints that are tidying up the economy and checking inflation
without increasing unemployment and without drastic taxation measures. This has been
described by an economist of world standing as an economic miracle-and it certainly is.
On the subject of taxation, the House should be reminded that if a Labour Government
had been returned to office those covered by Labour's superannuation scheme would have
been paying 2.5 percent of their wages as a special tax in addition to the present tax rate—$3
a week extra on the average weekly wage, or $150 a year. The Prime Minister, the Minister
of Finance, has relieved the people of that taxation burden, which would have provided for
an inadequate superannuation scheme. Under Labour, employers also would have had to
pay a similar amount—a multi-million-dollar tax rip-off for an interior selective superannua-
tion scheme, typical of the member for Manukau when he was in Government. His speech
tonight sounded good in the first instance, but his promises prove pretty bitter pill to
swallow. The comprehensive national superannuation scheme has been funded without any
special tax.
The Budget is an imaginative document containing the ingredients for progress. It is a
realistic document. Our energy policy is a comprehensive approach, grappling with the
assurance of energy for the future on a broad basis and with the objective of reducing
dependence on overseas supplies, which, apart from their ever-increasing cost, have a
measure of unrealiability. Apart from the continuation of hydro development this Budget
provides for an accelerated programme of investigation and development of alternative
energy sources. I particularly welcome the expanded geothermal investigation programme,
which will mean a trebling of investigative drilling programmes. This will place a heavy
demand on the Ministry of Works and Development, but I am sure my department can rise
to the occasion.
I mentioned the comprehensive approach to energy, and it is significant that, as part of
the Budget package, in addition to encouraging development of our resources, emphasis is
placed on and there are inducements for the more efficient use of available resources;
financial encouragement for the use of natural gas; and interest-free loans for home
insulation. One would have expected the wholehearted support of the Opposition for our
Budget energy package, but probably it was so imaginative and practical as to be beyond the
comprehension of the Opposition.
The provision for water and soil development, which is within my portfolio, gives me
much satisfaction. The statement under Land Settlement and Development on page 13 of
the Budget that, "The Government is increasing its funding for water and soil projects,
including the provision of an additional $2.9 million in the current financial year to
commence new projects with high economic potential", has a welcome and much greater
significance than that simple sentence conveys. The total expenditure for water and soil
conservation has been increased from $20 million to $27 million for the 1977-78 year. The
significance of an increase of more than one third is most important. It is good news for many
farmers, who have been awaiting an assurance of Government financial support for
approved rural water schemes. Those with technically approved schemes, 11 in number,
have the go-ahead. Further schemes will be approved if they meet productivity and
engineering criteria. Likewise, approved catchment schemes can go ahead provided they
meet appropriate criteria.
This massive increase of funds from the Government, together with finance from the
local communities, will see a level of finance and activity in the water and soil sector never
previously attained. For example, funding for the Hikurangi Swamp scheme in the North
and additional work on the stopbanking of the Waihou River on the Hauraki Plains will be
accelerated; the eagerly awaited Waiau Plains irrigation scheme will be started; and there
will be a stepping up of the work commenced last year at Maniototo, which scheme alone
had been allocated $500,000 this year for continuation of work promoted and commenced by
a National Government after years of talk and deliberation by the Labour Government,
which did absolutely nothing. These are examples of what the increased expenditure means,
an indication that this National Government means what it says when it speaks of assisting
farmers in the best use of water for production. It is tangible proof that when this
Government speaks of multi-purpose development of water resources farm needs are well to
the forefront. The people of the Clutha Valley have these benefits ahead of them in the

The National Government has courageously and comprehensively tackled the problems
of transport and roading. The two are closely linked. My firm belief is that, arising from the
Budget decisions, we will have a more efficient transportation system. At the local level and
as a Wellingtonian I welcome the assistance to urban passenger transport.
In 1970 the National Government initiated proposals in the Carter report to assist urban
passenger transport, but when Labour came in the thought of practical assistance was
forgotten. The availability of $6.8 million in the current year as part of a 5-year programme
involving $50 million will be good news to the municipalities that recently have been fighting
a losing battle against rising costs to try to maintain a viable passenger transport system. It
will mean that vehicles still in service despite having outlived their economic lives can now be
gracefully retired. Despite its having been obvious for several years that major changes were
required to goods transportation methods, it is this Government in this Budget that has
taken action. The extension of the road limit from 40 miles to 93.5 miles, or, in metric terms,
from 64 kilometres to 150 kilometres, will indeed give motor hauliers greater flexibility and
efficiency in operation.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: What will the distance levy be?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: That is a good question that I shall answer in due course, if the
honourable member will only be patient. He need not expect it tonight. When he was
Minister he could not come up with the answer. The Auckland-Hamilton and Wellington-
Palmerston North routes are now a venue for competition between rail and road. What did
the Leader of the Opposition have to say about that? He said that this Government was anti-
energy and anti-railways. He nods his head. What a short memory he has! It was a National
Government that introduced the Silver Fern and Silver Star between Auckland and Welling-
ton, the Endeavour express to Napier, and modernised the Southerner and the Northerner, as
well as introducing containers and heavy diesel locomotives. Those were National Govern-
ment railway achievements that the Labour Government never looked like matching. It is
putting on 25 cabooses. For the information of the member I should explain that they are
elaborate guards' vans.
However, to come back to road operators: at the same time as they are being given an
extension of their operations it has been decided to reassess the charges levied on heavy
vehicles to ensure that their operators pay their proper share of road charges. At present the
ratio of charges levied on lighter vehicles has been disproportionately high, and conversely
that on heavy vehicles inadequate for the demands they make on roading. It should mean
that roading will get its proper payment for heavy transport wear and tear, which could be
accentuated as a result of the road haulage limit extensions. Unquestionably in recent times
there has been too much uncertainty about roading finance. It is common knowledge that
the Labour Government would have abolished the National Roads Board. It is common
knowledge that in its green paper it spelt out its abandonment in the statement, "One might
question the appropriateness, in the light of modern development of the roads board's
organisation and method of securing finance."
The Labour Government would have liked to see the National Roads Board disbanded.
However, to give credit where it is due, the Rt. Hon. Hugh Watt stood up for the roads
board; and I think the Opposition could do with him back in its ranks. It seems he might be
staging a comeback, and he would be a worth-while acquisition. However, if the Labour
Government did not directly destroy the board, its policy did it incalculable harm. For the
year ended 1975, when Labour went out of office, inflation in the construction industry was
more than 20 percent per annum. Compounded inflation, a direct result of Labour policy,
more than doubled roading costs. A punitive increase in petrol taxation reduced sales and

the board's revenue. The Labour Government could have afforded to make some of the $75
million available to the board by way of adjustment.
Major works can take 3 years or longer, and the roads board has been in a most difficult
position in opening up major work without assured forward finance. While, as chairman of
the National Roads Board, I have appreciated Government assistance over and above basic
income, that has not meant that the board could plan with assurance. This Government gave
the board $21 million last year—its biggest ever grant-and this year provided an extra lc
per litre as of right. Although this last grant placed the board's finances on a firmer footing,
there were uncertainties about the future.
Further steps announced in the Budget will provide the board with two sources of
reliable income: petrol tax from the car users, and a new distance charge to be introduced on
1 April 1978 on heavy commercial vehicles. Under this system, roading will be operated on a
true user-pays basis, which has always been intended in the National Roads Act, but which
has fallen into disrepair over recent years. The board itself will be involved in determining
the rates for these user charges, assessed in such a manner that a programme of works that
has been agreed on by both the Government and the board can be implemented. Undoub-
tedly, the downhill slide in roading works will be arrested by this system, and many of the
improvements deferred over recent years will have better prospects of becoming reality.
Transportation costs are a vital factor in New Zealand's internal and external economy.
An improved roading system aimed at minimising transport costs can only help the situation
we all face at present. The National Roads Board has proven itself to be one of our more
successful institutions in achieving the purposes for which it was established. With the
improvements announced in the Budget we are entering a new era, in which the board will
continue to play an even stronger part in the transport economy of the country. However, we
should not forget that roading activities have been seriously depressed over recent years, and
many areas have been reduced to a policy of almost care and maintenance only. This cannot
be changed overnight, but the stage has been set for a move in the right direction.
Speaking in general terms, many Budget provisions will be looked forward to by the
community, but the Opposition has failed to see their importance. The $25 rate rebate is a
forward step, as is the adjustment in taxation for the man on a low or medium income.
Surely those measures are worth a word of praise from the Opposition. The Opposition has
not said a word about the impetus given to education, or about social welfare and health
measures, which show the Government's humanitarian attitude. No mention has been made
of the incentives given to the farming and fishing industries. I wonder if the Opposition has
read the Budget, because it has had little to say about its contents. There is much good news
in the Budget for all sectors of the community. The Opposition recognises this, not by what it
says, but in what it does not say. Its dispirited opposition is an indication of the soundness of
the Budget. Rarely have I seen a member go to sleep while his leader was speaking, yet this
was witnessed tonight as an indication of the Opposition's general disinterest in and laxness
toward the Budget. The Government has given a lead and provided incentives. It is up to the
country to follow the lead, and if it does so we will be taking a very great step, not sideways,
but forward to prosperity.

Time will show whether the proposed new roading approach mentioned in the Budget,

Roading, bridging, and maintenance have been run down to the worst levels for many years.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Unemployment-Labour Department Survey
1. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) asked the Minister of Labour: Can he confirm that the
many hundreds of women who have lost or who will soon lose jobs following the closure of
Millers' two clothing factories in Christchurch, the impending closure of the Kaiapoi
Woollen Mills, and the closure of Unilever's factory in Christchurch, will not be represented
in the official statistics of the registered unemployed, and when does he intend to carry out
the promised Department of Labour survey to establish how many people are actually
unemployed in New Zealand, in the light of the 1976 census returns, which confirmed that
the actual unemployment figure was already above 20 000 in March 1976?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Any unemployed person seeking work,
whether male or female, married or single, may register with the Department of Labour.
This has been the case under both Governments, and I can assure the member for Avon that
official unemployment statistics include any married women who have become redundant,
are seeking full-time work, and have enrolled with my department for assistance in obtaining
another job. Last year I indicated that the Government was considering the possibility of a
household labour force survey to measure employment and unemployment. I have convened
a technical working party from members of my own department and the Department of
Statistics, and this working party is at present investigating in detail the feasibility of
undertaking such a survey.
Mrs Batchelor: Would the Minister confirm that many married women, when they lose
work for whatever reason, do not register with his department, and that therefore the actual
unemployment figures would be much higher if they were taken into consideration?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Any such statement must be pure hypothesis and conjecture.
Any married woman who wants to work 30 hours a week or more can apply for a job and be
registered as unemployed. For the week ending 1 July 1977 there were 178 married women
and 248 widowed or divorced women so registered.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Imports-Raw Materials and Manufacturing Components
2. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry:
What proportion of total imports is made up of raw materials and components for
manufacturing industries operating within New Zealand?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Trade and Industry. The end use of some imported raw materials and components can be
inputs for industry or consumer items, and for this reason a precise answer cannot be given.
Table 54 of the Monthly Abstract of Statistics for April 1977 indicates that those categories
listed as raw materials or component imports for industry in the 1976 June year accounted
for 66.6 percent of all imports.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Energy Conservation Policy
3. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: Does he
support an energy policy that gives encouragement to the use of energy by way of reduced
tariffs for heating swimming pools, and, if not, what measures does he propose to take that
would more properly reflect conservation and social needs rather than the ability to pay?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Energy Resources. His answer is as follows: "I do not endorse the action of energy

Young Physically Disabled in Geriatric Wards
4. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Health: Is it true, as was stated in the
television programme "Access" on Sunday, 17 July 1977, that it is common practice to place
young physically disabled people, such as those suffering from multiple sclerosis, in geriatric
wards of public hospitals, and, if so, (a) how many of these young people are so accommo-
dated; and (b) does he have any plans to change this situation?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): In certain hospitals when other more appropriate
accommodation is not available, it may be necessary to nurse some severely disabled
younger patients in geriatric wards. The actual numbers so nursed at present are not
available, and could only be obtained by circulating all hospital boards. This would take
some time, and the final result would not be accurate as it would not include those in similar
circumstances in private hospitals. The Department of Health is well aware of the accommo-
dation needs of this group of patients, and has stressed to all hospital boards that they should
survey the needs of this group in their areas and, where necessary, make purpose-built
accommodation available.
Mr Hunt: Does the Minister feel that the comments made on the TV2 programme,
which I am sure all members would agree was a very moving and important one, indicate
that this problem of placing young people suffering from the crippling disease of multiple
sclerosis in wards along with geriatric patients could perhaps be circumvented, even if only
by putting up a curtain to divide the ward?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I did not see the programme. I understand that the "Access"
programme brings emotional and very close-to-the-heart problems to the people, but there is
no opportunity for those under criticism to reply at the time. I agree entirely that what the
honourable member says is very desirable. There are circumstances sometimes, particularly
in the smaller hospitals, where the types of staff and facilities needed for round-the-clock
care for these patients are exactly the same as those that are needed for geriatrics. Often,
although a patient might be moved 100 miles to a more suitable hospital, he would thereby
be taken away from the visiting opportunities by mothers and fathers, brothers and sisters,
friends, and relations, so that a balance has to be taken in each case. I have tried to draw to
the attention of hospital boards—not that they necessarily needed it, but I felt it incumbent
upon me to do so—the desirability of trying to arrange for purpose-built accommodation for
these particular young patients.

Mr O'Brien: As the Minister has seen the claim by the board's chief executive that the
Wellington Hospital Board forgot to say that the land purchase was not being proceeded

the need or the absence of any real plan by the Wellington Hospital Board, and will he

Hon. T. F. GILL: I cannot give the last assurance asked for, as it is the responsibility of

board required a site for its proposed limb and orthotic centre. It owned already in Mein
Street Nos. 44 and 46, but to provide the area needed it had to take either No. 42 or No. 48.
It negotiated the purchase of one property, but omitted to inform the Ministry of Works and
Development of this, so the ministry was taking action to acquire the second property

Mr T. J. Young: Does a hospital board have to seek permission from the Minister

understanding is that when a hospital board wants to do some capital development of this

cost have to be authorised, and this would involve authority for the acquisition of land. If the
local authority has zoned the land appropriately and it is required for a purpose of this kind,
then at that stage, having received the Minister's approval to the overall project and his
authority for the expenditure of the money to acquire the land, the hospital board would be
free to take such action as was necessary, either negotiate directly, or, if necessary, in the
case of hospital work, approach the Ministry of Works and Development for authority to
acquire the land under that Act.

for him reading the newspaper or making a comment, the property would have been
acquired. As financial authority had not been issued for the purchase of two properties, they
would not have been acquired. The Department of Health, with, I might add, some
assistance from Treasury and the Auditor-General, closely supervises such expenditures to
make sure they conform with the policy approved by the Government, and also with the
financial powers issued by the Government. At no time was there any danger of two
properties being acquired when only one was needed, because the board would not have had
the money to pay for them.

Petroleum Exploration Licences, Taranaki
10. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines: When were the on-
shore petroleum exploration licences for the Taranaki areas first advertised; in what
countries were they advertised; how many tenders for each licence were received; and have
any licences actually been issued?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Mines. Areas of on-shore Taranaki were advertised in November and December 1975 as
being available for application for petroleum prospecting licences. Advertisements were
placed in five recognised petroleum publications, all having international circulation: the
World Oil Publication in the United States; the Oil and Gas Journal in the United States; and
three U.K. magazines-Petroleum Times, Off-shore, and Petroleum International. No
applications were received in response to this advertising, and consequently no licences were
issued.
Hon. F. M. Colman: In view of the wide interest that was displayed, and the pressure
that was applied to release the licence area in Taranaki, can the Minister say why no such
licences were taken out?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No, I cannot. That is entirely over to the major petroleum
companies the people who apply. Since the early 1970s there has been a restructuring of
the New Zealand legislation, and of the whole approach to licensing, as the member well
knows. There have been difficulties in securing action because of the terms and conditions
on which successive New Zealand Governments have sought to maintain the interests of this
country in prospective petroleum reserves.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Was the reason that no licences were taken up the Government's
uncertainty about the taxing of any possible discoveries?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I cannot say that that is the reason. The whole question of
working out a petroleum regime is under discussion, as it was under the previous Administ-
ration. We are concerned with energy resource development, and we will work with the
overseas companies. At the same time, we are determined to explore our own resources, and
the Budget has made this clear.

11. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Postmaster-General: To what extent was

borrowing additional funds, the losses were covered by subsidies from the vote Stabilisation.
Mr Wellington: Apart from an extra burden on the taxpayer, can propping up Post
Office finances with massive subsidy payments have an adverse effect on its administration?
Mr Hunt: A point of order, Mr Speaker. That question clearly asks for a hypothetical
answer about something that has no relevance to or is in elucidation of the answer to the
original question. I have always believed that questions can bring in political points, but they
must in some way be relevant to the original question, and must seek elucidation.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: Speaking to the point of order, the question relates to the
extent of subsidy assistance during the years concerned, and I suggest that a question about
the effects of the subsidisation is extremely relevant.
Mr SPEAKER: Like so many questions that honourable members love to ask, this
question is, I believe, out of order. The point is properly taken. The question states, if
finances are propped up in a certain way, would this have an adverse effect on morale. That
is a matter of opinion. The question is also hypothetical: it makes a postulation and asks
what effect would this have on the morale of officials, or something to that effect. The point
having been raised, I must rule it properly raised. The question is out of order.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: A point of order, Mr Speaker. I respectfully point out to you
that this situation is not a hypothetical one, as was revealed by my answer to the initial
question.
Mr SPEAKER: I have already ruled that the question stating "If finances are propped
up" in a certain way is a hypothetical question. There the matter must rest.

services.

questions.

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: That is correct. During the period of the massive subsidies, the
demand for telephone services went up, and it was actually cheaper for an Australian

publication of Hansard, how has this time altered in the last 5 years, and is there any
possibility that the Hansard record can be published more quickly?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister in Charge of the Government Printing Office): The
present time gap between proceedings in the House and the publication of Hansard is 6 to 7
weeks. This is 1 to 2 weeks longer than the average time for the years 1972 to 1975. In 1976
Hansard was produced for the first time by computerised typesetting equipment and,
because of problems with the new system, the publication of Hansard became progressively
delayed until, by the end of the session, it was 3 months late. This year Hansard has been
redesigned to facilitate a quicker turnround, and the Government Printer is aiming at a 3-
week to 4-week time gap.
Mr Hunt: In view of the fact that in the Australian House of Representatives a printed
edition of Hansard comes out on the day after a debate, would the Minister not think that an
increase in the delay of 2 weeks over 2 years, whether or not a computer is involved, is a
cause of concern, when, in fact, we should be reducing the delay of 6 to 7 weeks down to
about 6 to 7 days?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: The computerised system was ordered by the previous Labour
Government. It has caused quite considerable upset, and is now being overhauled by
engineers from the United Kingdom. It is now expected that the 3-week to 4-week
production target will be met, once the backlog is overtaken. A more expeditious printing of
the Journals of the House would be a matter for some further representation to the
Government.
Mr Latter: If experience shows that the computer, instead of speeding up the printing,
in fact slows it down, makes it more difficult for the Hansard staff, and does away with the
well proven methods of colour coding, and so on, will the Minister consider selling the thing
at a profit and returning to the use of proven methods?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: That will certainly be considered if it is proven to be
inefficient.
Mr Kirk: Can the Minister confirm that the delays have been caused because the work

contracted out under the National Government, and also by a restriction placed on overtime
by Government Printer staff?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: That has no foundation in fact whatsoever. A considerable
amount of work is still contracted out to private firms.

programmes for pupils at risk for truancy and of the procedures used to check attendances
and follow unexplained absences; and a review of liaison with parents and with other
agencies that have responsibilities in this matter.

Coal Imports from Australia
14. Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast) asked the Minister of Electricity: In view of the
statement in the National Party's full election policy that it recognises New Zealand's
increasing dependence on coal and its promise to encourage the coal industry, why does he
permit his department to consider the possibility of coal imports from Australia to fuel New
Zealand power stations when they could be fuelled from New Zealand's already proven coal
reserves?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Electricity, and hope I can put the mind of the member for West Coast at rest. Because of
the importance of energy to a modern economy and the alarming forecasts for future
supplies, the New Zealand Electricity Department has been investigating the possibility of
electricity generation using imported Australian coal as one of a number of options open to
this country in the longer term—that is, 15 years away. Australian coal has not been seen as
an alternative to any local coal which could be made available. Indeed, as the Budget
indicated, the Government is accelerating investigation of local coal resources, but the use of
Australian coal is seen as a possible means of deferring a nuclear power programme should
local supplies run short in future. In short, the study being undertaken has arisen out of
questions asked before the Royal Commission on Nuclear Power, and is designed very much
for the longer term.
Mr Blanchfield: Can the Minister give an assurance that one of the reasons the
Government is so desirous of getting more coal into New Zealand is the fact that coal is the
cheapest of the three fuels at 34c per therm, compared with 62c for oil and 64c for electricity?
Does the department want more coal brought in to even out the cost of electricity?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I should make it clear to the House that the investigation has
not arisen from any wish of the department but out of questions raised before the Royal
Commission on Nuclear Power, where it has been suggested that in the longer term supplies
of fuels necessary for power stations may not be available in this country. I hope that the
investigations into New Zealand's coal reserves will cover that point adequately in the
future.

WANGANUI COMPUTER CENTRE ACT COMMENCEMENT ORDER
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Wanganui Computer Centre Act Commencement
Order being a regulation within the meaning of and passed pursuant to the Regulations
Act 1936. The committee recommends that there is no matter on which the special attention
of the House should be drawn to the regulation. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
The committee's report is lengthy and complex. It is not my intention to read it to the
House, but I shall table it in written form for perusal by those who might be interested—
particularly in any precedent it might establish. Instead, I intend to give a brief summary of
the committee's findings, and to make some comments of my own. I emphasise that,
contrary to my normal practice in delivering committee reports, the remarks I shall make on
this occasion will be very largely my own summary of the overall situation that has occurred
since this matter first came before the select committee on 20 April this year.
The Wanganui Computer Centre Act was passed by the House on 1 September 1976,
and was assented to on 9 September. Section 1(2) of the Act provided that it should come
into force on a date set by Order in Council. Such an order, the Wanganui Computer Centre
Commencement Order 1977, was promulgated on 10 February 1977, bringing the Act into
force on 17 February. Acting under Standing Order 379, five members of the Labour
Opposition referred the commencement order to the Statutes Revision Committee for
consideration pursuant to Standing Order 378. The complaints made by the Labour


## p. 1626 (#82) ############################################

1626
27 July
Wanganui Computer Centre Act Commencement Order
members could be summarised in this way and in the alternative: first, that the Act was
brought into force too early, or, second, that the Act was brought into force too late.
In considering the written report it will be useful for the House to know something of
the history of the Wanganui Computer Centre. On 23 April 1974 the Labour Government
Cabinet committee on State Services approved a tender for the design, development, and
implementation of the Wanganui computer system, to be developed over 38 months. On 7
November 1974 the then Minister of State Services, the member for Otahuhu, gave an
undertaking in this House that no contract would be let for the Wanganui Computer Centre
until such time as appropriate privacy protection legislation had been introduced to the
House. That undertaking is to be found in Hansard, Volume 395, at page 5692. The Bill was
introduced in July 1975, but 9 months earlier-in fact on 15 November 1974, only 8 days
after giving his undertaking in the House-the member for Otahuhu authorised the signing
of a "Heads of Agreement", as it was called, by the State Services Commission on the one
hand and the contractors on the other. This document recognised the intention of the two
parties to enter into a binding contract, the form of which was actually attached to the signed
Heads of Agreement.
The Heads of Agreement provided that a contract be signed no later than 31 August
1975, prescribing penalties if this did not eventuate. In the meantime, acting pursuant to the
signed Heads of Agreement, the development of the Wanganui Computer Centre system
proceeded. The actual contract was signed on 27 August 1975. The important point to note is
that there is absolutely no difference, in legal effect, between the Heads of Agreement that
was signed 9 months before the Bill was introduced into the House and the actual contract,
which the member had told the House would not be signed until the Bill was introduced. The
contract itself laid down a programme which had to be followed by the State Services
Commission and the contractors for the establishment of the Wanganui Computer Centre.
The essential dates were: 31 August 1975, by which date the central equipment had to be
installed; 15 July 1976, by which date some information had to be fed into the computer; 15
November 1976, by which date certain further information had to be fed into the computer;
and 15 March 1977, by which date all the remaining information had to be fed into the
computer.
So it will be seen that the programme for establishing the Wanganui Computer Centre
was laid down almost entirely by the previous Labour Government. It was originally
intended that the Act would be brought into force on 1 April 1977. During the debate on the
second reading of the Wanganui Computer Centre Bill the present Minister of State Services
stated that the system would not be operated—that is, information would not be drawn off
the computer-until the Bill had been passed. I emphasise that he said nothing about the
Act being brought into force. That is important, because the date on which it would be
appropriate to bring the Act into force would depend on a number of things, particularly
whether it was possible for the various privacy safeguards contained in the Act to be brought
into operation.
For instance, under the Act the Wanganui Computer Centre Privacy Commissioner is
obliged to supply to any person who asks for it a print-out of the information on that
individual held in the computer system. As members will know, the procedure to be
followed in such circumstances is very complicated. Among other things it is very important
that the commissioner gives information only to the person who is entitled to it. In the report
which was tabled in the House today, the commissioner records that these procedures are
still being worked out in consultation with the Post Office and the departments using the
computer system that is still, now, in July 1977, in trial form. No information has yet been
sent to any applicant.
What we have is a programme laid down by the previous Labour Government that
called for a substantial amount of information to be stored in the computer and capable of
being drawn off from the computer by November of last year, approximately 4 months
before it was intended that the Act should be brought into force, and at the same time we
had the situation where the privacy safeguards could not be brought into force until some
later date. Faced with that situation the Government advanced the date for the commence-
ment of the Act from 1 April to 17 February. For that it is to be commended. At all times it
was necessary for those responsible for selecting the commencement date to weigh several
factors: the fact that information was capable of being drawn off the computer on the one
hand, and the fact that the privacy safeguards had to be fully operational on the other. In the
end, even those who argued at the committee that the Act was brought into force on the
wrong date were unable to suggest any other date, either earlier or later, that might have


## p. 1627 (#83) ############################################

27 July
1627
Wanganui Computer Centre Act Commencement Order
been more appropriate. The Wanganui Computer Centre Commencement Order does
nothing more than bring the Act into force, and, therefore, that was the sole issue with which
the committee had to content itself.
I turn now to Standing Order 378 and to the three possible grounds on which the
committee could have made an adverse report on the regulation. I emphasise that the
committee was quite satisfied that this was a regulation within the meaning of the Regula-
tions Act 1936. The first possibility was that the order might have trespassed unduly on
personal rights and liberties. We concluded that the order did not trespass on personal rights
and liberties. What it does is to bring the Act into force earlier and thereby furnish the
privacy safeguards which were not previously in existence. Not one member of the Statutes
Revision Committee was able to suggest a better date for bringing the Act into force-and
that includes the member for New Lynn, who is trying to interject.
The second possibility was that the making of the order might have been an unusual or
unexpected use of the powers conferred by the Act; but the Act states that it will be brought
into force by a commencement order and so one could hardly argue that the passing of a
commencement order was an unusual or unexpected use of the powers contained in the
statute. The third possible ground for review of the regulation was that its form or purport
called for elucidation. The order is simplicity itself and certainly does not require any
elucidation. So the committee has concluded that there are no grounds on which it needs to
look at the order and no recommendation to the House is needed. Even if there had been
some irregularity we were not in a position to deal with the matter retrospectively, and it is
almost certain that we would have exercised the discretion contained in Standing Order 378
and made a not unfavourable report to the House.
Finally, I shall comment generally on the circumstances in which this matter came
before the House. I said on a previous occasion that the power contained in Standing Order
378 should be used sparingly. I do not think this was an appropriate regulation to have
before the select committee in the first place. I am certain that Labour members regretted
having brought it before the committee because we discovered in the process that the
Government had advanced the date of the commencement of the Act and that, of course,
meant that the statutory protections contained in the Act were available earlier. We also
discovered that the member for Otahuhu, having given an undertaking that the contract
would not be signed until the Bill had been introduced, in fact authorised this somewhat
amazing Heads of Agreement that was a document legally binding on all parties. In all the
circumstances I think this must have been a considerable embarrassment to the Labour
members of the select committee. I am sure this experience alone will discourage them from
bringing matters such as this before the select committee in future.

an Act being brought into effect, but there is no difference between an agreement and a

Wanganui Computer Centre Act Commencement Order
Act was passed, and the computer was not operated until the Act was passed.
Section 12 of the Acts Interpretation Act 1924 reads: "Where an Act that is not to come
into operation immediately on the passing thereof confers power to make any appointment,
to make or issue any instrument . . . to give notices, to prescribe forms, or do anything for
the purposes of the Act, that power may, unless the contrary intention appears, be exercised
at any time after the passing of the Act, so far as may be necessary or expedient for the
purpose of bringing the Act into operation at the date of the commencement thereof." The
date that the Act was passed is a significant date. It allowed the Minister to proceed with the
appointment of the Privacy Commissioner and the policy committee. It allowed the Minister
to pass regulations to approve proclamations and orders. It allowed him to do everything
necessary for the Act to come into force. That is precisely why the Minister of Labour said he
would not use the computer until the Act was passed.

and unless the Act is brought into force it has no effect whatever. The Minister gave an
undertaking that he would not allow the computer to be used until the Act was passed, and

Interpretation Act. He carried out that undertaking to the letter. It has not been suggested
by the member for Auckland Central that the Minister did not observe that undertaking to

The history of the computer centre project is interesting. It was initiated in 1967 when
National was the Government. A long and detailed study was made, and in February 1972,
under the National Government, a report was made to the Cabinet committee on State
services. In March of the same year, under the same Minister, the committee gave approval
to the State Services Commission to invite computer companies to submit proposals for the
development, design, and implementation of an integrated system for law enforcement
agencies. We were not opposed to it. A working party was set up, it drew up specifications,
and issued them to interested parties in July 1972. A constraint was placed on the issue of
specification documents; and then the Government changed in November of that year. In
December 1972 the new Government approved the continuation of the construction of the
building at Wanganui, which was being built under an agreement, or contract—I shall not
argue about those two words; I could not care less-entered into by the National Govern-
ment. However, we asked for a further study of the proposed system; the Government was
concerned to ensure that before the centre became operational there would be adequate
safeguards against the violation of personal freedom and privacy.
To allow time for an adequate study of the privacy question, the development of the
system and the acquisition of equipment was split into two stages. This is where we get to the
business about the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, who was then Minister of State
Services, signing the Heads of Agreement. There is nothing wrong with that. We were
introducing the Bill, it had been approved in principle by both sides of the House, and in the
normal course of events the then Minister of State Services went ahead with getting the
equipment ready. I gave the same undertaking as did the Minister of Labour, and I think
the undertaking is fair enough. In January 1973 the Cabinet approved the commission's
negotiating and entering into a contract for a systems design study as a first step. The Deputy
Leader of the Opposition, who was then Minister of State Services, carried out a Cabinet
decision that he quite justifiably believed enjoyed the support of both sides of the House.
During 1973 a Government caucus committee, chaired by the member for St. Albans,
investigated the privacy issue as affected by the computer, and prepared a report that,
incidentally, has received a great deal of support all over the place. In October 1973 the main
computer companies were invited to submit new proposals, and so it went on. Preliminary
work for a draft Bill relating specifically to the Wanganui Computer Centre was completed
in 1974, and at the end of the year the Minister of State Services-it was I at that
time-announced that a special Government committee had been set up to consider
submissions and prepare a final draft for the legislation. That is exactly what we did. We
introduced the Bill into the House, as other members have reported. There was another
change of Government, and the Bill went on-substantially unchanged except for one item
in the schedule that we argued about at the time-to the select committee during the period
between the 1975 and 1976 sessions of Parliament.
There really was no great disagreement between us, except for one item in the schedule
that I still have some reservations about. We argued the toss, and heard the evidence. I am
very proud of the way in which that Bill was drawn up. We brought in all interested parties.
Anyone could come-17 groups came to that caucus committee, and we sat down and
drafted a Bill that we thought not only helped the law enforcement agencies, but also
protected the right of the individual to have information about him made available only to
those entitled to have it. That is what was drawn up and signed, and both parties endorsed it
in their 1975 manifestoes. The idea that everything bad is done by one side or the other is
just nonsense. There was substantial agreement. Nobody is particularly blamed for the
legislation. The Labour Party's attitude was clear; the present Minister's attitude was clear.
The computers were not to roll until the legislation was in operation. That did not happen,
and it is a serious matter worthy of debate in the House. It confirms and endorses the need
for a committee to have surveillance over the regulations. Such a committee would be useful,
although I know it is a difficult area and there could be serious delays.
It is not correct, however, for anyone to suggest that all the problems of the Wanganui
computer originated with the Labour Party. I have heard that claimed in the House, and
outside it as well. Both Governments were deeply involved, and both agreed that the
computer was needed. We agreed that it should operate only after the law was in operation.
Well, it was read as being in operation when the House passed it, and we now find that
unfortunately that was not so. We did not do the work on the commencement date that we

The Wanganui Computer Centre Act has two basic purposes, which are important to
this discussion. First, the Act sets up the Wanganui Computer Centre, and, secondly,
provides legislative safeguards designed to ensure that the privacy of the individual is not
adversely affected. I emphasise those words "adversely affected", because, as the member
for Hastings rightly said, what is stored or processed in, or is capable of being retrieved from,
the Wanganui Computer Centre is information which is already held in various offices

1635

throughout New Zealand.
The computer centre gives the user departments-Police, Justice, and Transport-a
better means of law enforcement. Of course, when one talks of law enforcement, obviously
one is concerned about infringements of the rights of the individual. The Act provides
several safeguards. It limits what can go on to the system, and restricts access to the system.
There are express provisions that the Wanganui Computer Centre should stand alone, and
should not be linked to any other computer centre. The Act provides a dual system of
control-a policy committee to look after the privacy and the rights of the individual, and a
management committee. It also appoints à Privacy Commissioner, and provides penalties for
infringements. There is no correct date at which the Act should have come into force. Initial
consideration was given to introducing various parts of the legislation in steps, but that was
discarded as being impracticable. I ask the member for New Lynn to say on what date. he
thinks the Act should have been brought into force, and, of course, if he does speak, he will
say that there is no correct date.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I should like to round off some of the
suggestions that have been made as a result of the report of the Statutes Revision
Committee. This inquiry was set in motion by a letter signed by five Opposition
members-the principal mover being the member for Auckland Central-requesting a study
by the Statutes Revision Committee under Standing Order 379 of the regulations bringing
into force the Wanganui Computer Centre Act, which was passed, after considerable
debate, on 9 September last year with the support of both sides of the House. Indeed, during
the debate on the report the former Labour Government's Minister of Labour—and I think
in 1975 Minister of State Services-the member for Roskill, reminded the House of the
praise he had given the Act and of the way both parties had worked together to formulate
the best possible legislation to provide for the security and proper control of the computer
filing system at Wanganui.
We all thought at the time the Bill was passed-and, indeed, the present Minister of
State Services specifically told the House-that no action would be taken on loading the
computer system at Wanganui until the Bill had been passed. What he said has been quoted
by the member for Auckland Central and others, and certainly it was set out in the member's
letter to the Statutes Revision Committee. The Minister of Labour stated: "Both the Labour
Government, and the National Party in its manifesto, gave an implicit undertaking that this
Bill would be passed before the centre came into operation. I want to make that crystal
clear." It was crystal clear, and the centre did not come into operation until February of this
year, some months after the Bill had been passed.
The request by five Opposition members was made in April of this year, some 2 months
after the commencement order had been made by the Governor-General in Executive
Council, so that it was a post factum request. It has now been suggested that there is so much
virtue in the use of Standing Order 379, and its concomitant 378, that a full-time select
committee of the House should be established to examine every regulation made by the
Executive. That is taking things to the point of absurdity in a House of 87 members. All
members know that we have obligations to sit on, usually, several select committees. To add
another standing committee to look at every regulation would make our work in the House
even less effective than at present when already we have several committees to attend.
It is a good Standing Order when there is serious reason for using it, as there was
recently when the Statutes Revision Committee, working under Standing Order 378, looked
at regulations made about diving for crayfish. That was triggered off by the request of a
group of interested citizens and, in particular, a member of the faculty of one of our law
schools. We were able to make remedies. I point out the difference between that instance,
where the procedure was properly used, and this instance, in which I do not believe that it
was properly used. On the crayfish regulations, the group and the member of the law faculty
concerned had approached the ministry for information and for a hearing, and had tried to
get the ministry to change its attitude. Only when that had not been successful did they ask
for Parliament's authority to be used and for the Statutes Revision Committee to engage in
the study.
Had the member for Auckland Central followed that common-sense and practicable
course, he would not have this report today, which indicates there is nothing in the bogies he
has aroused. He did not go to the Minister of State Services and say, "I think there is
something wrong in this commencement date for the Wanganui Computer Centre." He just
flew straight in and demanded action by the Statutes Revision Committee under Standing
Order 379. As a result of that it has been demonstrated that he cannot even now suggest to

I have been shocked and astounded at some of the claims made by Opposition members
during this debate. Those claims were of the most irresponsible kind because they were not
based on any facts placed before the select committee or on any fact contained in either of
the two reports which have been tabled today. They were based on idle, dangerous, and
irresponsible chatter and nothing more, and can serve only to reduce the confidence of the
public in the computer system, which members opposite support as much as do members on
this side. What members opposite failed to tell the House-and this applies to the member
for New Lynn, who said that information was being drawn off in December 1976-was that
that date was in accordance with the programme laid down by the previous Labour
Government.
When he mentioned that the safeguards were not in operation in December 1976 he also
failed to tell the House that that too was in accordance with the programme laid down by the
Labour Government. Inevitably, under the programme laid down by the previous Adminis-
tration, there would be a hiatus between the date on which information could be drawn off
the computer and the date on which safeguards would be available. The member for
Mangere asserted that it would be possible for the Government to prime the system to
prevent information from being drawn off but to enable message switching to be used, but
there was no evidence before the select committee, and there is no evidence before this
House, that that would be technically possible. In fact, the moment information was fed into
the computer it was at risk of being taken off, and the earlier the commencement date
chosen by the Government the better, consistent with the safeguards within the Act.
I was surprised to hear the member for New Lynn claim today that he and other
members of the Opposition had had great difficulty in having regulations referred to the
Statutes Revision Committee. That is just not correct. Only three attempts have been made
this year to have regulations considered by the Statutes Revision Committee. First, there
were the rock lobster regulations, which were dealt with by the committee in a manner which
even the member for New Lynn complimented. The second was the Wanganui Computer
Centre Act Commencement Order which we are discussing today, after having been dealt
with by the Statutes Revision Committee. The third attempt was when the member for New
Lynn wrote to me and to the Clerk of the House asking that the regulations relating to
School Certificate assessment be reviewed by the committee, but we discovered that there
were no such regulations. So we have had three attempts by members opposite to have
matters referred to the Statutes Revision Committee. The first two were acceded to because
there were regulations in force. In the third instance we could not consider the regulations
because they did not exist.
The most irresponsible statement I heard this afternoon was that the Cabinet had
authorised the placement of false information in the computer system. That statement was so
highly irresponsible that I should have expected the member for New Lynn, who made it, to
withdraw it immediately. There was absolutely no suggestion in the material tabled today in
the House, that Cabinet had authorised the placement of false information. Finally, I remind
the House that Opposition members who had this matter before the committee tried, as the
Minister has suggested, to have ten bob each way. They wanted to assert on one hand that
the Act had been brought into force too early, and in the same letter-in almost the same
paragraph-they suggested it had been brought into force too late. They cannot have it both
ways. The select committee decided that the Act was brought into force on the best date
possible.
Motion agreed to.

Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): The Minister of Works did not use all the
time available to him last night, because he obviously found it impossible to defend this
Budget. I do not propose to deal much further with his speech except to say that, next to the
Minister of Finance, he is the Minister with the most disastrous record. He presided over the
cutback in the Government works programme that sent builders and construction companies
into bankruptcy, liquidation, and idleness, forcing skilled workers into voluntary unemploy-
ment. He also cut roading and bridge programmes, and deferred vital export-boosting
irrigation and development works at a time when they were urgently needed. That policy is
in direct conflict with the Budget's call for greater export earnings. The Labour Government
would not have deferred the Wairau, Maniototo, or Clutha schemes.
The Minister of Works spoke about the level of Government expenditure that was
necessary under the Labour Government to offset the fall in private spending and to
maintain momentum in our economy when export prices fell. I remember what the Prime
Minister said during the Budget debate last year on that subject, and I quote from Hansard,
Volume 405, at page 1908: "In 3 years under the Labour Government the proportion of the
New Zealand economy in the public sector increased from 30 to 42 percent-12 percent of
the economy was taken by the Labour Government and moved from the private sector into
the public sector. That is socialism by stealth, because the people did not know it was
happening." In this year's Budget he has this to say: "Last year we succeeded in bringing
expenditure down to approximately 36 percent of GNP. This year, the indications are that
Government expenditure will amount to about 38 percent of GNP." The Minister of Finance
is now increasing Government expenditure as a percentage of the gross national
product—and, to use his own words, is this socialism by stealth? The Budget gives ample
reasons for believing it is, because the Government is nationalising oil exploration in this
country. The Government is in fact practising socialism by stealth. In a recent editorial
headed "Private Enterprise RIP 1980", the New Zealand Contractors Federation said that
the National Government was replacing private enterprise contractors with Ministry of
Works and other Government operators. I could say that this is socialism by stealth, but I
will not.
The truth is that, because of his inexperience in economic management, the Prime
Minister cut Government expenditure too heavily last year, which brought the economy and
many businesses to the verge of collapse. It is essential that he correct his mistake and
increase Government expenditure as a percentage of national product. Nevertheless, I want
to suggest that his judgment is still faulty. He has not increased Government spending
enough, and has not allocated sufficient funds to critical areas. Savage cuts have been made
to housing when people are crying out for houses and the building industry is on the brink of
collapse. The Prime Minister has backed away from the critical challenge that New Zealand
faces if growth and stability are to be restored. The Budget has failed to restore business
confidence and confidence to invest, and hence fails to make that vital contribution to
increased output and productivity that is so essential to overcome our basic economic
problems. It fails to lift productivity, profits, wages, and salaries, and yield the Government
the extra revenues that are necessary to enable it to offer realistic incentives to encourage
investors and exporters to have a go, and it fails to encourage businesses and those who work
for them to face the future with confidence, knowing there is something in it for them after
tax when they have helped increase production and build a more prosperous New Zealand.
Without business confidence and investment one cannot build a strong economic base, and
without a strong economic base and an expanding economy it is not possible for the
Government to provide the range of services expected in hospitals, for the handicapped, for
child care, and for the needs of the elderly members of the community. Without a sound
economic base there can be no realistic tax concessions, incentives, grants, or subsidies, and
there can be no incentives to aid industry and regional development. There can be no
additional money for law and order, for our police and defence services, and for aid to
developing countries, either. The Budget strikes a disastrous blow at the building industry,
on which the propsperity of so many other industries depends. Knocking the building
industry means knocking manufacturers of building supplies, electrical fittings, plumbing
and roofing supplies, furniture, bedding, glassware, furnishings, stoves, refrigerators, and
washing machines, as well as plumbers, drainlayers, roading contractors, and many other

27 July
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement.
associated tradesmen.
In announcing reduced house building contracts the Minister of Finance said: "The
Government is concerned to ensure that the building industry's adjustment to a lower level
of activity proceeds gradually. A limited amount of support is considered desirable now to
prevent too abrupt a contraction." Those two sentences mean the end of the road and
certain bankrupty or liquidation for many people in the housing construction industry.
The housing vote and housing finance have been cumulatively cut in the Govern-
ment's two Budgets by $230 million-less any second mortgage money that the Government
will make available this year-compared with the levels of expenditure under the Labour
Government. As another deterrent to home ownership, the Government has increased the
prime lending rate of the Housing Corporation. I suggest that it does not make sense to
knock industries supplying the domestic market. It does not make sense to have people
unemployed, plant and machinery idle, and unutilised resources when the country wants
increased employment opportunities, jobs for the people, increased productivity, and
greater cost and price stability. The Government has an obligation to find the money to put
idle manpower and resources together instead of plunging them into further unemployment
and idleness.
At this time when we face a battle with inflation we need rising output to overcome it. If
the Government does not know how to proceed, because of a shortage of overseas funds, it
should encourage activities that use a minimum of products and services requiring expendi-
ture of overseas funds. The Government should promote, as the Labour Government has
done in the past, efficient import substitute industries, and this is now being done in the
Budget. Price controls and other administrative measures have their place in dealing with
inflation, but in the long run if the Government is to beat inflation it must do it through
efficiency in production, by raising productivity, by improving the cost structure of our
industries, and through increased output. It is essential and highly desirable to have
increased output so that overheads can be spread over more units, thus reducing the
overhead per unit.
Where is the declaration to tackle inflation in the Budget? Page 43 of the Budget states,
"After 20 months in office the Government can claim that substantial results have been
achieved." Is that seen in the balance of payments? In March 1976 the deficit was $1,017
million. By March 1977 the deficit was $861 million. It is forecast that next year the balance
of payments deficit will increase by more than $100 million to $965 million, and that will be
after the Government has had the benefit, in this March year, of an increase in export
earnings of $1,300 million more than was available to the Labour Government. I ask the
Goverment if that is an achievement.
In 1975, before the election, the Prime Minister said in the House, "I tell him now
across the House that either before or immediately after the election either his Government
or another Government will put direct restraints on importing." Did he do that? Is the
employment record of the Government an achievement? Is a 7.4 percent increase in the cost
of living in the first 6 months of this year an achievement? More than 3400 people left New
Zealand during May of this year. That is a record loss in any month since World War II, and
hardly the achievement that the country wants.
The Government has other achievements to its record. Total taxation, tax per head of
population, and tax as a percentage of national income are at all-time record levels. The total
tax for this year is $4,750 million, and the tax per head of population-man, woman, and
child-is $1.530. That is a startling figure. The tax as a percentage of national income is 38.79
percent-nearly 39 percent. The growing burden of tax has increased by $893 million, but no
significant tax relief has been granted to people on middle incomes and to many on lower
incomes. This group includes beneficiaries who were compulsorily transferred to national
superannuation, which is taxed. Before national superannuation they received a pension that
was non-taxable. In the Budget, tax is increased by about $300 per head of population, an
all-time record.
That brings me to the Budget provisions for the young-family rebate and for the one-
income families. The Leader of the Opposition and Opposition members have urged the
Government to take action for these families. Last year the Government's Council of Social
Service pointed out the deteriorating family income situation and made urgent recommenda-
tions to the Government to act. The Government failed to do anything until the Budget, and
then only in a limited way. On the face of it, the provisions for young-family rebates and for
the one-income family look generous, until it is remembered that the family benefit has not
been increased to offset inflation since it was last increased. One must remember that


## p. 1643 (#99) ############################################

27 July
1643
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
executives and wage and salary earners have received wage increases to compensate for the
increased cost of living, but the Government has not given them a compensatory personal
tax exemption so that they can retain the benefit of that increase. The wage increase was
given to compensate for the cost of living, but it was subject to Government stabilisation
policies, and hence the people did not receive the full cost increase due to them.
The Government had an obligation to ensure that what the wage and salary earners
received was conserved by increasing the personal tax exemptions. In adjustments to salary
levels since this Government took office-with the amount necessary to compensate for the
rise in the cost of living and the increased tax imposed-the man on $100 a week should have
had a personal tax exemption equivalent to $7 a week. That would be necessary to conserve
the cost of living increase. Tax is at an all-time record because the Government taxed the
man instead of giving him that money. A man earning $120 a week should have received $10
a week reduction in taxation equivalent, a man earning $150 a week should have received
$14 a week tax reduction, and a man earning $200 a week should have received $19 a week.
Further, the Government failed to implement the recommendations of the Council of
Social Service to increase the family benefit. In an answer to a question in the House some
time ago, it was shown that the family benefit should have been increased by $2.25 to equate
with the purchasing power when it was last increased. The $2.25 should now be $2.50. That
means that, for every child, parents have been receiving $2.50 a week less than they should
have received. Take a man with three children. He should have got $2.50 a week extra for
each child, which would be $7.50 a week. If he had an income of $100 a week he should have
received a $7 tax rebate to offset the effect of tax on the cost of living increase. He should
have got $14.50 a week, but under this Budget he gets $13. On the face of it the provision
looks generous but, when one looks at the facts, the one-income family and the family with
dependent children are losing out.
Take the man on $150 a week. If he had three children he should have got $7.50 a week
in additional family benefit. He should have had $14 in additional tax rebate, making $21.50,
but the Government has given him $13. He has been short changed by $8 a week. A man on
$200 a week with three dependent children should have received $7.50 in additional family
benefit and tax relief of $19, a total of $26.50, but all he got was $8 a week. When one looks
at the one-income family provision and the provision for dependants, one finds it is not
generous. The Government is cunningly short changing those people. While we welcome
any tax relief that can be properly given at any time, equitable tax relief for all families is
essential now.
That tax relief has been limited to families with children up to 9 years of age. It is a pity
it was not extended to all families with dependent children 10 years of age or more.
Everyone knows how high are the costs of children at secondary school-shoes, clothes, and
food. It has been suggested that women with children over 10 years of age should go out to
work. What about the Cabinet committee on family affairs? It is driving the mothers out to
work instead of protecting the family. If mothers stay home to look after their children they
should receive tax incentives and rebates the same as those who go to work. Indeed, with
unemployment as it is at present, how many women can get jobs when they need them?
The National Party's conference condemned the Government and the Budget and
demanded that there be further tax relief and exemptions for the family man. The
Government has an obligation to honour that. The President of the New Zealand Society of
Accountants, Mr Mann, speaking yesterday in Tauranga, said that New Zealand must make
up its mind whether it supported the family concept of the mother's prime responsibility
being to her home and the upbringing of her children, if that was what she chose, or,
alternatively, whether all women should go to work. The chairman of the Cabinet committee
on family affairs should have a talk with the Prime Minister about that, and about the way
the Prime Minister is treating mothers with dependent children, particularly those with
dependent children 10 years of age and over.
I make my final point to the Minister of Social Welfare. In statements to newspapers I

$50.18, or $3.16 a week less. Secondly, a married couple with one partner under 60 and other

industry as a whole. As the new system is phased in, the other taxes on heavy vehicles will be
either abolished or phased down, including sales tax, petrol tax, mileage tax, and heavy
traffic fees. On 1 April next year the sales tax on all vehicles other than motorcars and motor

Members opposite have now become very silent. The heavy traffic fee will be taken over
by the new distance charge. Petrol tax will be rebated against the distance charge, which will
be calculated on the basis of the vehicle's weight, axle configuration, and metered run. The
major objective is to ensure that each type of vehicle is taxed according to the costs it
imposes on the roading system. This system is designed to come as close as is possible in the
New Zealand context to an ideal road taxation system.

I wish to devote the major part of my address this evening to what I see to be the
objectives in a health service for New Zealand in the 1980s. The Labour Party believes that
the aim of New Zealand's health service should be to ensure that all New Zealanders are
able to pursue their individual goals and live socially and economically productive lives
without unnecessary restrictions arising from disease, illness, and physical or mental
handicap. In pursuing this aim. New Zealand's health service in the 1980s should operatate,


## p. 1651 (#107) ###########################################

27 July
1651
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
as I see it, under eight specific principles.
First, it should be recognised that the provision of professional health services is only
one of many factors relative to this aim. Today, life is significantly influenced by such things
as our use of air, water, and land, the conditions of housing and transport systems, work
places, the quality of food, and the proper use of leisure time. Hence our health services
should work to ensure that all relevant attitudes and actions in areas such as these are fully
consistent with the maintenance of good health. Secondly, since the decisions and actions of
individuals are of overwhelming importance in determining their health status, the
consumer-the person who most frequently uses the services provided for him—should be
involved in key aspects of planning and delivery of health services.
Thirdly, our health services should provide, within the resources available, and as
efficiently and effectively as possible, appropriate treatment and attention and care and
support to those people who are not in good health. Equal priority and opportunity should
be given to people with disabilities, handicaps, and restricting illnesses, who need care,
support, and rehabilitation, as opposed to those people for whom an effective cure is now
available. Fourthly, all New Zealanders in need of these services should not be denied equal
access to or use of them because of their race, religious or political beliefs, sex, wealth,
knowledge, or geographical location.
Fifthly, I am very strongly of the opinion that there should always be scope for the
operation of private and voluntary institutions and agencies-such organisations as our
Plunket Society, which does a magnificent job in the community. Sixthly, where possible,
our health services should ensure co-ordinated, consistent, comprehensive, continuous, and
effective services without unnecessary fragmentation, duplication, and imbalance.
Seventhly, where the community pays, supports, or subsidises any health service, it should
be in a position to assess these services by receiving regular reports of objectives, policies,
and performance. Eighthly, our health services should be increasingly oriented towards
preventive medicine. We need to give top priority to overcoming the avoidable accidents,
diseases, and ill health that result from modern life styles—and I include both physical and
mental ill health.
A number of problems are currently impeding the effective functioning of New
Zealand's health system in 1977. First, we have a fragmentation of delivery resulting from
lack of clear aims and priorities, no overall co-ordinated planning, and an absence of a
rational means of establishing priorities that all can accept. This leads to ineffective and
inefficient use of resources, and the provision of substandard health services in the
community. Lack of accountability of those concerned with the delivery of health services
leads to ineffective and inefficient use of resources, and probably is a factor in the escalating
cost of our health services. Health expenditure is rising considerably, with insufficient visible
benefits. The answer is not just more money by itself. The present Government is proving
that the problems of fragmentation, lack of accountability, and recognition of changing
patterns of disease and illness are not being taken into account at present, but a realistic
growth in our health services is essential, and must be accepted. We are not achieving this
today under the present Government.
Let us compare the figures in real economic growth terms. We must take account of
inflation first, before we talk of increases in expenditure. What were the percentages under
the Labour Government? In 1973-74 there was an 8.3 percent increase; in 1974-75, a 9.8
percent increase; and in 1975-76 a 6.2 percent increase. Now we come to the years of the
National Government: in 1976-77 there was a decrease in real expenditure of 1.9
percent-and I challenge any Government member to prove that statistic incorrect. In 1977-
78 that 1.9 percent decrease has been replaced with a 2.1 percent increase; in other words,
after 2 years of a National Government, the realistic growth it has determined is an increase
