the equivalent of 16.6 percent.
However, if the investor has a taxable income of $12,000 per annum, the return he will
receive under this measure would equal an interest rate of 20 percent per annum-lent at 10
percent it would be equal to an interest rate of 20 percent. What other opportunities do small
savers have to earn rates of 16.5 percent to 20 percent? Certainly, there is no similar
opportunity on an investment that is totally gilt-edged. These loans are safer than Govern-
ment stock. They have the guarantee of the New Zealand Government, and there is a
mortgage of real estate thrown in. I am satisfied that every solicitor, accountant, and other
adviser, once he is aware of these terms, will advise clients that no better investment exists.
What better way is there to create a massive influx into private housing loans?
Mr Prebble: It won't produce houses.
Mr BRILL: And that, in answer to the member for Auckland Central, is how it will help
the house mortgage market. It will also be noticed that the best return is available for the
small parcels. This package is ideal for second mortgages. The beauty of the scheme is that
second mortgages are also gilt-edged, as the Housing Corporation will guarantee anything
up to 90 percent of valuation. The home owner pays 10 percent interest on the second
mortgage, but the lender receives the equivalent of a 20 percent return on his investment.
The Government takes up the balance by way of tax forgone. It is a high interest return with
negligible risk-the best investment available.
Fourthly, I refer to the vendor mortgage scheme, which is directed at existing dwellings
that are under utilised. The measure provided in the Budget will lead to a much more
economic use of existing housing stocks. The incentives are similar to the direct lending
scheme I have just mentioned, but are aimed at first mortgages; the equivalent interest
returns, tax paid, range from 13.3 percent for lenders with an income of $6,000 to 15 percent
for lenders with an income of $12,000. Again, absolute security is assured by a Government
guarantee through the Housing Corporation.
This eight-point package constitutes the greatest single stimulant ever offered to the
New Zealand building industry. All that is required now is that its ramifications be fully
publicised and understood. The industry itself is obsessed with the terms of loans from the
Housing Corporation. It should look beyond this to the larger field of building, to the less
restricted area financed by the private sector. I know that builders have been hard hit by the
recession of the past 3 years, which has struck particularly heavily in growth areas like
Auckland, and in boom areas in my own electorate such as Whitby, Paraparaumu, and
Waikanae. I address myself to those people in particular when I say that the Budget marks
the end of the dark ages. Some little time will pass before full realisation dawns that the
Government has now made housing the most attractive investment available. This realisa-
tion must ensure a steadily increasing flow of funds into the vitally important housing area.

I want to speak about inflation-proof bonds. On page 37 of the Budget it is stated: “In
recognition of the difficulties small savers face in protecting their savings against inflation,
the Government is to introduce an inflation adjusted savings bond which will preserve the
purchasing power of a basic savings nest egg." People will be able to open an account with a
deposit of $100, with future deposits of $50 for each bond, limited to $1,000 in any one year
and $5,000 in any one account. At the present rate of inflation, I believe there is no better
investment for any person.
At the time of the 1972 election, a Methodist minister told me how difficult it was to
save for a future home. He felt there should be some method to help those people who have
homes provided with their jobs to obtain homes for themselves in the future. Workers on
hydro-electric construction sites, who move from one site to another, were also concerned
that they could not provide homes for themselves. It was on that score that I felt some
research should be undertaken. In 1974 and 1975 I introduced the Investment Bonds Bill,
but the member for Manukau, who was then Postmaster-General, gave seven reasons why
the scheme should not be ventured into. In 1972, with an inflation rate of 5.5 percent, the
return from the savings bonds would have been 7.5 percent. Of course, 5.5 percent would
not be a tax commitment. In the following year, the return would have been 10 percent and
the interest 2 percent, giving a total return of 12 percent. The return would be very high
today, although that has not always been so.
I quote from my speech in reply on the introduction of the Investment Bonds Bill, as
reported in Hansard, Volume 390, at page 1451: "I have worked out a table covering the 20
years from 1952 to 1972, and I find that if this Bill had been operative over that period there
would have been a return of 5.88 percent on the investment. It would have required 3.58
percent to restore the purchasing power over that period, and it would have had an effective
rate of 2.3 percent over the 20 years. I realise that we had a National Government for 17 of
those 20 years, but if a Government acts responsibly it is conscious that it has a duty to see
that the purchasing power of the people's savings is restored. Over that period of 20 years, in
7 years it would have been necessary to support an investment to bring the interest rate up to
a full 5 percent. So looking at the historical angle it would be possible to operate such a
scheme." The Government is confident that it will get on top of inflation. In projecting this
scheme, the Government is confident that its attractiveness will be such that people will
subscribe.

Mr LUXTON: It is limited to $5,000. Last night the Leader of the Opposition said that
this was another savings scheme for the rich. The fact is that a person need contribute only
$100 to start the account. The scheme is not for the rich; it is for the small savers. That is the
whole idea behind it. There was much comment when I introduced that Bill before. An
economist wrote to me and said that he felt the scheme should be tied to first-home
ownership or first-farm ownership rather than going as far as was expected. Another
economist felt that it was a good scheme that should be continued. Another point discussed
was that, as the bond would be negotiable, there was no reason it should not be listed in the

investment when the rate of inflation was going up, and give some stability to the economy.
Many people are looking for a safe investment, and I know this measure will be
welcomed. Many people who have small savings invest in Post Office savings accounts and

country that in 1972 our total petroleum imports cost less than $73 million. By 1976 the
increase in that cost was six-fold, to $442 million. If you relate it another way, 22 000 dairy
farmers required 20.9 percent of their total export receipts in 1972 to pay for our petroleum
imports. By 1976, although there were fewer dairy farmers their total production was
greater, but the total production of the dairy industry did not pay for our petroleum imports.
There has been a disastrous down turn in our terms of trade. Some of our standard of
living now belongs to the petroleum-producing countries, and we have great difficulties. Our
petroleum requirements have not greatly increased, however; we have been able to keep
them stable. The same applies to our requirements for other products. But when it comes to
phosphate, we need three times the percentage of our dairy products to pay for it than was
required in 1972.
This has been a good Budget for the farmers, and for everyone else. In the present
economic circumstances, it was a very wise Budget. It has covered many facets of our way of
life. The reduction in the number of livestock units required means that more farmers will
qualify. Many dairy farmers in may electorate were not able to participate in the old stock
incentive scheme, but they will be able to participate in this one. To 1 June, we had 2485
applications covering 2 400 000 stock units, in an area where there had been no growth in
stock numbers for some years. It is in the interests of all New Zealanders that we should have
a strong agriculture, because we will have to farm our way out of our economic problems.
There is other assistance for farmers. Additional money is to be spent on noxious
weeds. The vendor finance scheme will be welcomed by many farmers who wish to retire;
they will be willing to leave money in the land at lower interest rates than those offered
elsewhere. It is true that farmers have been reluctant to leave money in farming, because of
the poorer return. So often farmers want to get as much money out as possible, so that they
can invest it at the market rates. This concession will assist retiring farmers to leave a greater
portion of their money in land. This is a good move.
The Minister of Housing has a good rural housing policy, and a great deal of activity has
taken place in the last 18 months. The overall activity in my electorate has been good since
the change of Government, even in the small service towns. In Morrinsville, in the first half
of 1976, 24 buildings were being erected; in the first half of 1977, 37 buildings were in the
course of erection. In 1976, the average price was $15,000; in 1977, it was $22,000. That is
not an increased price; better homes are being built. In the Morrinsville area and the country
areas in my electorate, there is undoubtedly strong activity in the housing field now; farmers
have a certain amount of confidence, and they are moving forward.
I should like to compliment the Minister of Labour on the announcement made in the
Budget about profit sharing. I believe it will take out of the arena some of the negotiations
we have had in the past for higher and higher wage levels. Employees who are keen to see
that their firms are productive will receive greater benefits as a result.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10.31 p.m.

Mr MALCOLM (Eden): I give notice that next sitting day I shall move, That this House

ises with his audiences, but is astonished—
Mr SPEAKER: Order! This is a notice of motion that I am almost certain I have
disallowed, unless there is some modification. [Interruption.] Order! I had hoped that
members would be a little more gracious in accepting the fact I am protecting some members
of the House from some of the more frivolous or offensive notices of motion. The reason for
this mistake is that the notice of motion came in from one person, the copies were put back
on his table by the Clerk marked "Disallowed in the present form", but other members had
apparently been given copies in order to give notice of the motion. That is how the mistake
has occurred. The notice of motion must be held over.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I am
disturbed about the procedure that has been followed today about the notices of motion. It
appears that, at the moment, notices of motion have been ruled out by you, but the members
involved have not been given the reasons why they have been ruled out. It has been
suggested that the notices of motion have been left on someone's desk. Surely that is not our
procedure.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): I share the Prime Minister's
concern. You commented that the notice of motion was submitted in the name of one
member, and when it was ruled out that member, or his office, was advised, but now another
member has given notice of the motion. It is clear that the breakdown has occurred
somewhere in the National Party caucus.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I do not need assistance on that point. The position is simply that
I receive an unfortunately large number of notices of motion that either contain assertions of
fact that are not authenticated, or are on the verge of being frivolous or of doubtful
appropriateness for moving or putting in as ostensible notices of motion. Today we have had
several. Normally the Clerk gets in touch with the person who intends to give the notice to
move. In this case the person who signed the notices of motion was not in his room, but the
Clerk left the notices in the member's room on the assumption that he would receive them in
due course. Apparently, as he is not able to be present in the House, he arranged for
someone else to read them. He did not receive the message, not being back in his room, and
the members to whom he had handed the notices for reading in the House were unaware that
the appropriateness of the notice of motion as proposed was in question.
However, I shall take further steps to improve the communications in future. It would
be desirable, when members are giving notice of motions on behalf of other members, that
they should make a late check as to whether the notices of motion have been approved by
the Clerk or, when referred to me, by the Speaker.

State House Tenancy Scheme
3. Mr BELL (Gisborne) asked the Minister of Housing: Does the new 6-year, State
house tenancy scheme apply to existing tenants who voluntarily exchanged their now
oversize house for a smaller one more suited to their present needs?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): No, providing the existing tenant had
signed the old form of tenancy agreement, which is not limited to a term of 6 years.
Mr Bell: How many transfers of this nature have taken place over the last 12 months, or
perhaps for the year ended 31 March 1977?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I cannot give the member the number of transfers that have
taken place, but I can tell him that during the 1976-77 March year the Housing Corporation
considered that it had gained 638 bedrooms in its own rental housing by transferring tenants
from larger homes to smaller ones. Translated into terms of houses, this is estimated to be
the equivalent of about 210 rental houses, or a saving in monetary value of more than $5
million by the transfers.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Do I take it that in the circumstances outlined in the question,
where the tenant of a State house transfers to another State house, the original tenancy
agreement continues? It is my understanding that that is not so, and if I am right, do I take it
from the Minister's reply that a safeguarding clause will have to be inserted in the new
agreements?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: A tenant who transfers from one State house to another
would be granted only a 6-year tenancy. This has been made quite plain all along. A person
who transfers under circumstances that will allow for better use of the State house-for
example, a widow transferring from a three-bedroom State house to a single-bedroom State
house would be on a limitless tenancy and would not be required to sign a 6-year tenancy
agreement. That was the answer I gave to the honourable member.
Mr Bell: In view of the obvious advantage of encouraging people to make these
exchanges, does the Housing Corporation engage in an active programme to encourage
people with large houses to move into smaller ones?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: The Housing Corporation does undertake such a prog-

ramme, and to the extent that its manpower allows it, it brings to the notice of tenants the

part, has estimated that, assuming "present policies"-the estimates were prepared in
1976-for supply expansion and conservation continue, OECD countries would be import-

resources and increased emphasis on conservation this figure could, the secretariat consid-

EIB-Training of Intelligence Officers
6. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson), on behalf of Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt.
Albert), asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Is the report in the Christchurch Star of 9 July
correct in stating that the resources of overseas posts of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and
the Department of Trade and Industry are being used to train intelligence officers attached
to the EIB, and, if so, how many and which overseas postings within the Ministry of Foreign
Affairs and the Department of Trade and Industry are being held by intelligence officers of
the EIB?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of
the Minister of Foreign Affairs. The resources of the overseas posts of the Ministry of
Foreign Affairs and the Department of Trade and Industry are not being used to give
intelligence training to officers of the External Intelligence Bureau. It is not uncommon for
departments to arrange inter-departmental exchanges to broaden the professional experi-
ence of their staff. One EIB officer has been seconded on this basis to the Ministry of
Foreign Affairs. He is serving overseas, and is undertaking duties assigned by his adoptive
service—that is, the normal range of tasks of a junior foreign service officer. The host
Government was given this background to avoid any possible misunderstandings.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Are EIB trainees being seconded to departments other than the
two mentioned?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have no such information. I am informed that the
course being followed was agreed to in principle by the late Rt. Hon. N. E. Kirk, and
supported by the present Leader of the Opposition during the term of the last Labour
Government. This procedure is simply an implementation of the principle then agreed to.

Indigenous Timber Price Increase
9. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) asked the Minister of Forests: To what extent has the
increase in the price of indigenous timber been reflected by a reduced demand for native
timber and an increase in the use of exotic woods?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): There have been two recent increases in sawn
timber prices. On 14 March 1977 increases in exotic and indigenous prices were granted on
the basis of economic submissions by sawmillers, and on 1 June 1977 further increases were
granted in prices for the decorative grades of indigenous timber, the objects of the latter
increase being to encourage maximum recovery of the higher grades, and greater discrimina-
tion in the end use of indigenous timber. Apart from the effect of any price movements, the
volume of indigenous sawn timber has declined. In the year ended 31 March 1976 round-
wood removals from State forests amounted to 4 360 000 cubic metres, with 530 000 cubic
metres, or 12 percent, coming from the indigenous forests, and 3 830 000 cubic metres, or 88
percent, from exotic. Provisional figures for 1976-77 show a marked drop from indigenous
forests to 433 000 cubic metres, or 9 percent of the total, and a substantial increase in exotic
wood removals, which reached 4 352 000 cubic metres, or 91 percent. At present it is too
early to be able to judge what effect the latest increase in the price of indigenous timber will


## p. 1672 (#128) ###########################################

1672
28 July
Oral Answers to Questions
have on the future demand for native timber and the use of exotic woods.
Mr Blanchfield: Is there any difficulty in selling inferior quality native timber, such as
sap-cuts or shaky heart, at higher prices, and is there any buyer resistance from home
builders for this second-quality timber?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: As the member knows, there is a large variation of quality of
timber in a native log. My information indicates that in Christchurch, which is the best area
in which to get a comparison, building A grade rimu is selling at $109 a cubic metre sawn,
radiata framing at $107, and treated radiata at $139. I have no indication at present of any
effect of different prices on the demands for timber.
Mr Schultz: Does the Minister's statement mean that we are now getting a greater
recovery of exotic timber, and will the policy be operated so that we get a greater lifetime out
of the remaining indigenous forests?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The policy of successive Governments has been to obtain a better
extraction rate from indigenous sawn timber, and to encourage its use for higher value
purposes. The effect will be a decrease in the amount of native timber extracted over the
years, but it is part of the Government's policy to phase down the rate of extraction from
native forests, not to phase it out.
Mr Rogers: Would the reason for the drop in the use of native timber last year be that
the National Government announced an increase in the price, and that sawmillers stopped
cutting native timber until the price was raised?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The member's assumption is quite incorrect. The figures I gave
were for the extraction of roundwood from forests last year, and that was in no way affected
by any price alteration this year.
Mr Prebble: Does the Government consider that the amount of indigenous timber being
milled at the moment is too large, or not enough; and what is the Government's policy if the
amount is not in accordance with its present hopes?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: As the member knows, the Government held a seminar in the area
of New Zealand most critically affected by any diminution of our indigenous logs—the West
Coast. Two hundred people of all shades of opinion attended the seminar on the future of
our native forests. They included West Coast people-who are naturally concerned about
the social implications of the reduction of logging there-the timber industry, the timber
processing industry, conservationists, and scientists. At present, in accordance with Govern-
ment policy, the future of the logging of our native forests is being evaluated on the West
Coast, and subsequently it will be evaluated elsewhere.

AGRICULTURAL WORKERS BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That the Agricultural Workers Bill
be introduced. This Bill replaces the Agricultural Workers Act 1962, which has two main
functions: it makes certain requirements for the accommodation and employment of
agricultural workers; and it provides for the making of Orders in Council to prescribe the
wages and conditions of employment of such workers. The accommodation requirements are
retained in the Bill, but a new system is instituted for the fixing of wages and conditions of
employment. Also incorporated are provisions to better ensure the safety and health of
agricultural workers.
The method of settling wages and conditions of employment in the agricultural sector
will undergo a fundamental change. Under the present Act the Governor-General issues
Orders in Council fixing these matters. The orders normally incorporate provisions either
agreed to by the main parties involved or recommended by the Industrial Commission. The
Government is of the view that the parties should be able to negotiate without direct
Government involvement. The Bill initiates a new system, replacing the Orders in Council
with instruments that will be either voluntary agreements or conciliated agreements, or
awards of a specialised agricultural tribunal.
The emphasis is on voluntary and conciliated agreements. To this end, a system of
registration is introduced providing for exclusive recognition of organisations of employers
and workers in any particular class of work. Each defined class of work becomes a
recognised category, and for each recognised category there will be one employers' organisa-
tion and one workers' organisation. The organisations concerned will be those most
representative of the respective parties. The schedule to the Bill defines the recognised
categories of work that will prevail when the Bill becomes law.
Certain organisations of employers and workers are listed as being given initial exclusive
recognition for the recognised categories. Machinery is provided for amending the defini-
tions of the recognised categories and for adding further categories if necessary. Also,
although exclusive rights of representation are initially given to the listed organisations,
where certain conditions are fulfilled another organisation may obtain exclusive recognition
in place of the existing one. Under this new arrangement every agricultural worker will be
given the right to join any workers' organisation of his choice, or to decline to join any or all
of the organisations. The organisation having the most members of the class concerned will
be given the exclusive right to represent that class.
As I mentioned previously, the accent is on voluntary or conciliated settlements of
disputes. The role of the Agricultural Tribunal in the disputes procedure is limited to
deciding unresolved disputes when agreement cannot be reached, even after conciliation.
The decision of the tribunal becomes an award. Agreements between the parties are deemed
to be awards once they are lodged with the tribunal. A breach of an award is an offence.


## p. 1675 (#131) ###########################################

28 July
1675
Agricultural Workers Bill
Procedures for the settlement of personal grievances and for the interpretation of awards are
set out in the Bill. The opportunity has also been taken to include safety and health
provisions in the Bill, which will provide some basic and general requirements for the
protection of agricultural workers. I therefore commend the Bill to the House as a measure
that will improve industrial relations in the agricultural sector and one that will lead to better
conditions for agricultural workers.

UNIVERSITY ACTS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I move, That the University Acts
Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill is similar in structure to the Statutes Amendment
Bill, with amendments to the Universities Act and the Acts of the various universities
introduced as one Bill that, in its final stages, is separated into eight amendment Acts: the
Universities Act 1961; the University of Auckland Act 1961; the University of Waikato Act
1963; the Massey University Act 1963; the Victoria University of Wellington Act 1961; the
Lincoln College Act 1961; the University of Canterbury Act 1961; and one that I am sure
would be of interest to members-the University of Otago Ordinance 1869.
The Bill results from several requests over the past 3 years by the University Grants
Committee and the universities for minor legislative changes, mostly of a machinery nature.
All the amendments have been discussed with the University Grants Committee, and have
the committee's support. The amendments to the Universities Act recognise that Massey
University is no longer an agricultural college, and has not been for some years; and add the
chairman of the Lincoln College Council to the list of persons to be consulted about all
appointments to the University Grants Committee. It first came to my attention at the time
of the appointment of the chairman of the University Grants Committee that the existing
Act rather curiously omitted the chairman of the Lincoln College Council from the list of
persons the Minister of Education must consult before making that appointment.
The amendments also provide for deputies for the professors on the curriculum
committee, and increase the number of university teachers on the research committee of the
University Grants Committee. Since the independence of the various universities was
established in 1961, each institution has developed its own view of how its governing body
should be constituted. These views are reflected by amendments expanding the membership
of councils through the addition of representatives of staff, student associations, other
tertiary institutions, and, where appropriate, local bodies. The addition of student and staff
representatives recognises the contribution those groups can make in determining the
policies of the institutions in which they work. Where other tertiary institutions have close
links with the local university, in Dunedin and Hamilton, representatives from the technical
institute or teachers college, as the case may be, have been included.
The growth of the wider urban area of Christchurch has led the Canterbury University
Council to include the chairman of the Waimairi County Council, while the heavier duties of
the Mayor of Auckland are recognised by allowing him to appoint another councillor as his
deputy. One change of special interest to members is that Lincoln College is to reduce the
number of members of Parliament on the council from two to one. Although the college has
greatly valued the contribution made by members of Parliament, the nature of their duties
often makes it increasingly difficult for them to play a full part in the work of the council,
especially committee work. For example, recently two council members so elected were
appointed Ministers of the Crown. One member of Parliament to be retained on the council
will be elected by all members of Parliament, instead of South Island members only,
following each general election.
A further example of the attitude towards the contributions of staff and student
representatives in university administration is demonstrated in the clauses adding represen-
tatives of these groups to the constitution of professorial boards, senates, and academic
boards, where appropriate. Several changes are made to the administrative structure of the
University of Waikato-professorial boards become academic boards, and schools of studies
and boards of studies are instituted. Other machinery clauses deal with the appointment and
functions of some university officers, and minor internal administrative matters. One
5.


## p. 1684 (#140) ###########################################

1684
28 July
University Acts Amendment Bill
amendment common to all the University Acts, except that of the University of Waikato
where consideration of it has not yet been completed, makes provision for the various
universities to enter into contracts of employment with staff; previously there was some
doubt about this. The amendments to the Universities Act 1961, and those to the Acts of the
individual universities and Lincoln College, represent the development of ideas about the
administration of the university system since devolution in 1961.

MONEYLENDERS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Moneylenders
Amendment Bill be introduced. This short Bill implements the Budget decision to amend the
Moneylenders Act 1908 to increase from 10 percent to 15 percent the interest rate that may
be charged by a person lending money in the course of his business, without his being
required to register as a moneylender under the Act. The Bill is essentially an interim
measure to recognise prevailing interest rates while a new Credit Contracts Bill is drafted
along the lines recommended by the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee.
The Government hopes to introduce a Credits Contract Bill into Parliament this year for
recess study.
The existing legislation causes problems, because non-compliance with the provisions of
the Act by a moneylender has fairly serious results. For example, the loan may not be
enforceable by the lender. It therefore becomes of paramount importance for a lender to
know whether or not he is a moneylender for the purposes of the Act. Unfortunately, it is
difficult to determine whether any particular organisation is in fact a moneylender. Organ-
isations such as stock and station agents therefore adopt a cautious attitude and lend at a rate
lower than 10 percent, while current interest rates have risen above that figure.
The present 10 percent limit in the Moneylenders Act is causing distortions in the
money market. The new Credit Contracts Bill will not contain any similar provision, and this


## p. 1686 (#142) ###########################################

1686
28 July
Moneylenders Amendment Bill
amending Bill is not therefore incompatible in any way with the recommendations of the
Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee. Because this is an interim measure
requiring enactment as soon as possible, and is a Budget policy measure, I do not propose to
refer it to a select committee.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I was particularly interested in
the Minister's comment that the Bill is an interim measure. I point out that some time ago,
during the period of the former Labour Government, representations were made seeking an
amendment to the 10 percent limit because it was difficult to enforce; of course, it has
become much more difficult. The Minister said it is an interim measure, but, as I read it, the
Bill does not set any limit to the period during which 15 percent is to replace 10 percent as
the deciding factor. I should like the Minister to indicate whether the Bill is to have any
definite period of effectiveness in case the other measure he referred to the one that has
still to be studied by a select committee-does not come through the parliamentary
machinery in the time he expects. You see, that was given to me 2½ years ago as a reason
why we should not simply amend the Moneylenders Act by varying the percentage, and
certainly not by raising it by 5 percent. It is obvious that that Bill has taken some time to
prepare, but I think the general public would like to know whether the Government is in fact
taking only a temporary step or making a permanent surrender to inflation, because that is
the only fair inference that can be drawn from the bald fact that, in the Bill, the definition of
a moneylender is to be a person who takes interest at a rate higher than 15 percent, whereas
for many years past he has been defined as one who took more than 10 percent.
I wonder whether Government members would like to reconsider what took place at
their party conference in this connection. I feel that the Bill sets the seal on the National
Party's decision to run away from the claim that there has been a Muldoon economic

Budget measure that was made absolutely unavoidable by Budget decisions, which involved

few figures to illustrate the change that has come about, and ask members opposite whether
they really consider that this is an interim measure. I stress that in the view of Opposition
members it is an abject confession of failure of the National Government's monetary policy,
and the best that can be said for it is that the Government is co-operating with the inevitable
situation of its own creation, and asking the public to acquiesce in it.
While the Government pursues its policies, people who lend for long-term housing

Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: I feel the point was very validly raised. In 1974 the Standing
Orders Committee said: "The committee considered various proposals to amend the
procedure relating to the introduction of Government Bills. It was agreed finally that the
present procedure should be retained, but that a time limit of 2 hours should be allocated to
the debate." The present procedure was that laid down and accepted by the House in 1972.
No change has been made by the House since. "The committee considered the introduction
of Government Bills at considerable length in 1972. There was general agreement that the
introduction of a Bill, except in exceptional cases, need not be a lengthy process and that in
general all that is necessary is a brief explanation from the Minister"—and we have had that
2 minutes' worth-"followed by a limited period of questions. It is unnecessary for the
Minister at this stage to give a detailed analysis of the Bill as this material is contained in the
printed explanatory note attached to the Bill, and it is also not the appropriate time for
members to make impromptu speeches that would be more suitable on a second reading
after they had had an opportunity to study the legislation."
So, in terms of the Standing Orders, we are not permitted to give a second reading type
of debate on the introduction of a Bill. At that stage we are permitted to ask questions of the
Minister for a brief period. The maximum time allowed for the introduction of a Bill-not
the total time allowed, and not inevitably the time allowed, but the maximum time
allowed as agreed in 1974, is 2 hours divided equally between the Government and the
Opposition, so that the Opposition is allowed 1 hour and the Government is allowed 1 hour
in which to make points as to whether or not the Bill shall be introduced. The Deputy Leader
of the Opposition was referring to rates of interest, to the Budget, and to matters in it, and
he was trying to develop an argument on whether the Bill should go further than it does. I do
not consider those matters were entirely pertinent, because the Bill cannot be discussed in
great detail until it has been introduced and is in the hands of the House. At that stage
members have an opportunity to go into the full details and to discuss the principles involved
in the Bill. The question before the House is simply to decide whether it will accept or reject
the introduction of the Bill.

Mr LANGE (Mangere): I question the purpose of the introduction of this Bill, because
it seems from the speech the Minister gave that there is a misconception about the functions
of moneylenders under the Moneylenders Act. The history of the Act is that it was to protect
those people who because of their need to procure money, perhaps in somewhat desperate
circumstances, could have been taken to the cleaners by those prepared to lend money to
them. The purpose of that Act was to provide them with a clear expression of their
obligations and also to give them relief if those who lent them money went beyond the odds.
Banks and insurance companies are not obliged to comply with the terms of the Moneylen-
ders Act because Parliament recognised years ago that some people can be trusted to be
reasonable in their dealings with those who wish to borrow, and with other people. The
people that the Minister and the Prime Minister have been talking about-those who would
make money available for house mortgages-are not bound by the provisions of the
Moneylenders Act now, nor are those who lend under solicitors' nominee companies,
because they are not in the business of lending money.
This Bill proposes to protect those who gather in money from other sources and lend it
out at high rates of interest, while gaining something on the way. Those are the people who
are properly called moneylenders and they are the people who will not now have to complete
their documentation if their rate is up to 15 percent. I believe the Moneylenders Act has a
greater role than that which the Minister has revealed to the House. There are terms and
contracts under which the Moneylenders Act can give relief to people, but, by this proposal
merely to allow 15 percent instead of 10 percent, we are taking away a protection that people
have enjoyed for years. I would be the first to agree that the Moneylenders Act has created
difficulties, probably because we always have to marry the money interest of those who
would be avaricious against the needs of those who are desperate. We will always have that
problem.
The Government is doing the House a disservice by introducing a Bill that does not
tackle the major issue but simply provides for a 50 percent increase in the interest rate that
can be charged before people have to go to the bother of a small amount of documentation.
Where is the benefit in that? It is a perfectly simple procedure to document a transaction in
accordance with the Moneylenders Act, and no honest person needs to fear it. It is a
safeguard that everyone would look for in every other form of consumer protection, and it
sets out exactly the obligations of the borrower. I believe this should be looked at as an
incentive to people to say that the sky is not the limit, because this is only an interim
measure. But wait until the Minister of Justice delivers the goods and completely removes
the moneylenders' protection and obligations.

The professed objective of the Budget-at any rate in all the before and after rhetoric,

The truth is that this is a Budget of defeat, accommodation, and resignation. The
Leader of the Opposition made this point vividly and strongly in his opening address, and I
want to try to elaborate on that theme. While ostentatiously and noisily proclaiming to shape
up for battle, the Government has quietly sold the pass. The most abject and faint-hearted

Moneylenders Act was out of date. But in recent months the pressure for reform has become
irresistible. To think that to make this simplistic substitution of one figure for another is any

body borrowing rates. The proportion of rates and other local body income leaking away

to use, and I turn it back on him on this occasion-about the state of the share market? With

today are already nudging their permissible borrowing limits but still finding themselves

see it? I ask that question in all seriousness, because despite the panoply, despite the
forecasts, despite what may be something more than forecasts of what was in the Budget,

"Inflation accounting" is the heading of a paragraph to be found in the Budget. It is dealt

There is no doubt that many company accounts are misleading today and should be treated

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): It was indeed a little saddening that
in one of the swan-song addresses from our old friend the member for Henderson, who is
about to depart from the ways of Parliament, he was so dispirited about the argument he was
advancing that he saw fit to sit down a little past half his time. It was a brave effort. He began
with a great rush of verbosity-his verbal dexterity was indeed worth noting. He talked
about bureaucratic bombast, oratorical smokescreens, political preferment, and the corridor
for corruption. There was a lot of interesting verbiage, but not a great deal of substance in
his criticism. I can appreciate his predicament, because, although the Budget has been the
subject of a little criticism by those who have not seen fit to study it carefully, the honourable
member for Henderson was presented with a very real problem. He was asked to criticise a
Budget which is eminently sensible and realistic in the circumstances of 1977. That is the
strength of this year's Budget, and the weakness of the Opposition's attack upon it. Many of
the Government's achievements survive even the most strident criticism, if that is what it can
be called, from the Leader of the Opposition.
I shall remind the honourable member for Henderson of some of the achievements and
records this Government has chalked up. First, it has succeeded in reducing the Government
deficit before borrowing. The member for Henderson departed from the Treasury benches
with his discredited Labour Government leaving in prospect a deficit before borrowing of
$1,200 million to March 1976, and $1,400 million to March 1977. By grasping the real
responsibilities, including politically and economically difficult tasks, the National Govern-
ment turned this terrible record of the previous Labour Government into a dramatic
recovery; today, the deficit before borrowing is just a little over $500 million, while this
year-and I refer the member for Hutt, who is trying to interject, to page 43 of the
Budget-it will be about $382 million, a vast improvement on the $1,400 million his
Government left behind.
Tonight I shall concern myself more particularly with a very important and positive
feature of this year's Budget; I refer to pages 6 to 11 inclusive, the section devoted to energy
matters. The National Government is aware of the very real problem confronting New
Zealand and many other countries today, and it has resolved to tackle it resolutely, quickly,
and effectively. The problem centres on the fact that the demand for energy has been
growing faster than the world's ability to meet it. Nowhere is this problem more critically
evident than in liquid fuels, especially oil. The demand for oil will overtake supply some time
within the next decade, possibly. We may argue whether it will be 1981 or 1985. Very serious
studies have prophesied both dates, but, no matter what the date, it is within the foreseeable
future and within the time span that is clearly the responsibility of Governments in office
today, which must address themselves to this problem and act accordingly.
In 1972, when the second National Government left office, New Zealand spent $94.5
million in overseas exchange to import sufficient oil for its needs. This year, about $500
million will be required to meet the same objectives. Since 1972, inflation has increased by


## p. 1701 (#157) ###########################################

28 July
1701
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
90 percent, but the cost of imported fuel has increased by 470 percent. Needless to say, a
comparatively small country, which finds it difficult to earn and to save and to accumulate
overseas reserves, will be poorly placed indeed to bid against the economic and financial
resources of countries like West Germany and Japan when demand overtakes supply. At
that point, prices can be expected to skyrocket even further, and so it becomes very
important that we should act now and do all we can to best prepare ourselves to meet this
situation.
Obviously, we must encourage the Government and the country to learn to live within
their income. This message has been presented very strongly and, in political terms, very
courageously by this Government, not only in office, but also on the hustings before the 1975
election. As the first major step in our energy policy, my predecessor, now the Minister of
Housing, introduced the energy pricing policy late last year, which set out to lay the
foundation by establishing the cost of one fuel in relation to another. By using such a price
mechanism, we can discourage the use of certain fuels and encourage a diversion to other
fuels. The policy was established to maintain a clear cost margin in favour of coal and natural
gas as indigenous fuels, and to direct and husband the supplies we would need of imported
oil and of electricity, which, although in many respects it is based on indigenous resources, at
the marginal end does require imported oil as its original energy source.
We have set out in the Budget this year to reinforce in many important ways the
momentum begun with the energy pricing policy. For households in most areas where
natural gas is available, this fuel will be very competitive with electricity, and we want to
keep this margin of advantage. A number of items in this year's Budget are designed to
encourage people to act in this way. Later this year, as I announced at the Wellington energy
conference some weeks ago, the Government will be producing a booklet of goals and
guidelines. That document will be the first important step in presenting a comprehensive
range of proposals within a broad energy policy. It will be entitled Goals and Guidelines for a
New Zealand Energy Policy-first public draft. Indeed, from the very nature of the matter it
will have to be tentative in some respects, because there is still much we need to know about
some of the resources that we must either establish as being available or find alternatives for
before we can develop a firm long-term policy. I shall give more about that in a moment.
We have also recently introduced a Ministry of Energy Bill, which, as I am sure
members appreciate, will do much to give new strength and co-ordination to the Govern-
ment's administrative responsibility for handling energy matters and in guiding our energy
future. The Ministry of Energy will be responsible, among other things, for mineral
development, but its really urgent tasks will be to do all it can to encourage conservation, to
encourage full understanding of the nature of our resources, and to propose the best course
for the future so that we can make the most efficient use of the energy supplies available to
us. The Bill also enables the Government to form and to participate in companies
undertaking activities relating to energy or mineral development, to transfer the responsibil-
ity for pricing petroleum and coal from the Department of Trade and Industry to the
Ministry of Energy, to transfer geothermal licensing and related matters from the Ministry of
Works and Development to the Ministry of Energy, and to make provision for the transfer of
the assets, liabilities, rights, and responsibilities of the Natural Gas Corporation and
Off-shore Mining Ltd to a company wholly owned by the Government.
How clearly these recent moves stand in contrast to the inactivity of the third Labour
Government in energy matters!, I remind the Labour Opposition of the following quotation
from its 1972 policy: "Labour will expand and strengthen the Ministry of Energy Resources
to become wholly responsible for the co-ordination and development of the country's energy
resources." In fact, all that Government did in 3 years was appoint 10 additional staff
members to the Ministry of Energy Resources. It further said, "The Ministry of Energy
Resources will administer and operate the State coal mines, administer and operate the New
Zealand Electricity Department, and prepare estimates of the long-term needs of New
Zealand fuel and energy requirements." The third Labour Government did none of those
things.
It also said, "Approved industries in special areas will be offered an assured supply of
electric power at low cost." It made no such move at all. All it succeeded in doing in
electricity in its 3 years was freezing electricity charges, despite the rise in costs, to the point
that the Electricity Account had to be rescued by the Stabilisation vote in 2 out of the 3 years
Labour was the Government. For the information of the member who is trying to interject,
the consumer paid part of the bill and the taxpayer was expected to pay the other part. Not
only did the Labour Government not amalgamate the three departments as it said it would,

but it had three separate Ministers, one for each department, and in the case of electricity it

The Budget steps forward confidently and resolutely and with considerable political
bravery into the task of tackling the energy problems before the country. We have begun
with the basics in research. We have more than doubled the provision for research in this
year's Budget, and that research, to be undertaken partly by the Maiden committee and
partly by several Government departments that are most directly concerned, will be moving
into exciting new areas where it is most important that New Zealand learns much more about
its true potential. For instance, the money available to the Maiden committee will amount to
about $470,000, and for the research sections of the various departments the figure is
$630,000, making a total of $1.1 million.
The research programme will include such projects as new research contracts on heat
pumps, wind energy measurements, energy use in the commercial and transport sectors,
small hydro possibilities, private energy generation, and a study of alternative methods of
undertaking energy farming. Among the projects that the Government departments will
directly concern themselves with, using their own resources funds, will be, in the case of the
DSIR, investigation of geothermal, coal, hydro, and petroleum resources. A Forestry
Research Institute pilot plant will be established for the conversion of wood into a useful
fuel. Ministry of Energy Resources studies are continuing, and will be developed in industry
in price elasticity for energy demand and distribution costs. There will be a new survey of
household energy consumption; the last such survey was in 1971. There will be the New
Zealand Electricity Department studies on electricity generation, distribution, and supply so
that this work may be done more efficiently and effectively. The New Zealand Electricity
Department will also investigate the potential use of wind energy for electricity generation.
Another exciting and important new development in this year's energy budget is the
provision for resource proving in three main areas, the first of which is geothermal. There is
no doubt there is considerable geothermal potential in parts of the North Island, but much
more work must be done to prove its true extent and the degree to which we can confidently
rely upon it as a source of future electrical power. The drilling capacity of the Government's
exploration team will be doubled by the end of the year. We will recruit and train a second
drilling crew so that two rigs can be brought into full operation in the 1978-79 financial year.
An aspect that will please my friend the member for Hobson is that drilling in Ngawha in
Northland this year will be exploring the possibility of what is believed to be dry steam,
which lends itself very readily to harnessing for electricity. My colleague the member for
Rotorua, who is the Minister of Tourism, will be interested in the drilling we shall be doing
in Tikitere early in the new year.
We will be making interesting investigations in Broadlands; and when I was speaking
today to our colleague the member for Taupo-who will be back in the House shortly-he
was very anxious to learn of the work being done at Broadlands. Those concerned are pretty
confident we shall have a 150 MW station operating by 1982. Interesting work is also being
done at Kawerau, where geothermal studies will link very appropriately with the develop-
ment of the timber industry. We shall be getting two new rigs in the 1978-79 financial year,
each with a nominal depth rating of 1750 metres. This will allow the replacement of the
existing rigs, which are about 25 years old and have only a 1000-metre nominal capacity. We
are stepping up the work of the DSIR into research that will support this programme. In a
full year, the cost of geothermal drilling will be about $7.5 million.
We are greatly accelerating the coal exploration programme. Members would have
heard me speak on this subject earlier this year. I am most anxious that we develop our coal
resources much more effectively than we have done. Before we can speak confidently about
the future of coal, we must know the true nature of the extent and the type of coal resources
we have. It has been shown that coal reserves in the "Indicated" category amount to 258
million tonnes, and that there are a further 180 million tonnes in the "Inferred" category in
the Rangiriri West, Ohinewai, and Waikere fields. Many of the seams are very thick and
very deep, and a lot of study will have to be undertaken before the technical problems of
developing these fields can be solved. Provision has been made in the Budget to build up
more strongly a programme to explore and to prove the nature of our coal reserves; this
programme will be developed to cover the whole of the North Island.
Perhaps the most exciting drilling and proving programme relates to on-shore gas and
oil. It is most important that the true nature of our on-shore petroleum resources be
established as quickly as possible, because it is not possible confidently to develop a long-
term energy programme without a much clearer picture of the nature of these resources. A


## p. 1703 (#159) ###########################################

28 July
1703
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
new company, totally Government owned, will be set up; it will absorb the Natural Gas
Corporation and the Off-shore Mining Co., which are both Government instruments at
present. The company will employ its own specialist staff, but meantime the work is under
the supervision of and is being supported by experts in the DSIR, the Ministry of Works and
Development, and the Ministry of Energy Resources. The first practical steps should be
obvious about the end of September, when there will be a spudding in at Mason Ridge in
Hawke's Bay. As a result of previous drilling operations, extensive seismic work has been
carried out here, and there is reason to believe that the well that was drilled and abandoned
in 1971 was not drilled in the right place. However, traces of gas were discovered, and it
would certainly be an interesting prospect to prove this field. The Government will be
purchasing a deep drill in the next few months that will be used in Taranaki and possibly
elsewhere. Other drilling programmes, all within the next 3 years and starting within the next
few months, will take place on the West Coast of the South Island, in the Manawatu, on the
East Coast, and in Canterbury, north of Christchurch. The cost of this programme will be
$10 million a year.
Another important feature of the energy section of the Budget relates to the new moves
in local hydro schemes. It is estimated that of the total remaining hydro potential of between
45 000 GWh and 55 000 GWh a year, about 4000 GWh a year could come from the small or
local hydro schemes-schemes of 50 MW or less. The Government will assist local supply
authorities to do what a Government department would do perhaps not as well, because it
concerns local areas, local projects, and comparatively small schemes. Collectively, these
local schemes could make a very important contribution to our total sources of energy. The
local supply authority will be expected to carry out the initial feasibility study, but the
Government will provide the money for the detailed investigation and design work, and will
carry the cost unless the project proceeds, in which case it will be added to the cost of the
scheme.
The Government will find 90 percent of the cost by way of loan to the supply authority,
which will find the other 10 percent. The loan will be on the basis of 10 percent per annum,
and the interest rate will be reviewed every 3 years. If the scheme operates at a loss in its
early years, the deficit will be met by further loans from the NZED, at whatever interest rate
the NZED pays to the Government for the money it borrows. Any indebtedness, either on
original capital or on loans from the NZED to meet earlier losses, will have first claim on any
profit the scheme returns. After original capital advances plus interest plus any loans to meet
operating losses over the years have been repaid, any further net revenue will go to the local
supply authority. This will provide the incentive for the local supply authorities to develop
schemes they have proposed; I know of about 19 prospective schemes of this nature.
Very important taxation incentives for industrial and commercial energy conservation
were announced in the Budget. Provision is made for an immediate 100 percent tax writeoff
in the first year for approved capital expenditure. The previous deduction applied only to
equipment for evaluation of energy used; expenditure on industrial insulation, with the
exception of buildings; and expenditure on energy control equipment. The scheme will now
cover equipment for recycling or re-using waste material; heat exchange equipment;
equipment for the recovery of waste heat; insulation of industrial and commercial buildings;
the sealing of energy leaks; new plant using indigenous energy resources; the conversion of
existing plant to use indigenous energy resources; and plant and ancillary equipment that, in
association with approved energy-using plant and equipment, mitigates pollution effects.
That is a major development, and I do not believe the Opposition appreciates the size and
the importance of that step. The 10 percent sales tax on any new machinery that is eligible
for the tax concession will be refunded by the Customs Department. Approvals will now be
given by the Commissioner of Inland Revenue instead of the Commissioner of Energy
Resources, and further details of this change are available from both departments.
Domestic use of natural gas is also being encouraged. The Government has set a
minimum target of two gas appliances for each consumer in 50 percent of the homes in a
reticulated area. To encourage this, a grant of $200 will be made by the Ministry of Energy
Resources to natural gas undertakings for each new household connection made where the
householder has opted for two of the three major uses of cooking, water heating, and space
heating. Duty on gas stoves imported from Australia will be waived temporarily, and the
rate on gas stoves imported from other countries will be reduced to 5 percent from the
present 45 percent, to help bridge the gap between the cost of gas and electric stoves. The
Government undertakes to provide interest-free loans on a 4-year term of $100 for gas
stoves, $100 for water heaters, excluding swimming pools, and $200 for space heating where

more than one room is involved. The loans will be available to creditworthy builders, and

In new homes where the home owner takes up both the home insulation loan and the gas

I mentioned that certain matters of political courage were involved in the energy
policies announced in the Budget. An example is the compulsory requirement that, as from 1
January 1978, building permits for new residential buildings will be granted only if they
comply with the minimum insulation requirements. There is no doubt that this requirement
is a very important conservation move. The element of compulsion is not something that any
Government introduces lightly, but the Government believes that it is necessary in the
national good. The standards will in general conform to the standard already required under
the existing home insulation scheme. Incidentally, the interest-free loan period is to be
extended from 2 years to 4 years, and the maximum loan available is to be increased from
$300 to $400. Again, these are examples of the Government's doing something positive and
constructive about meeting the energy problem.
The member for Henderson was at pains to discount the value of the car-pooling
proposal outlined in the Budget. He seemed to think that, because it was initiated on the
North Shore by some very enterprising local bodies, including the Auckland Harbour Bridge
Authority, that meant it was wrong or that it favoured one area of the country. That is not
so. The North Shore is a particularly good area for a car-pooling experiment, because many
people there travel at peak hours across the same narrow traffic avenue from a common
point of origin to a common destination. The Auckland Harbour Bridge Authority
approached me and some of my colleagues on the North Shore to seek our co-operation. The
authority thought that $42,000 would be sufficient to carry out the pilot scheme. The
Government took the matter very seriously and studied its implications. It realised that
$42,000 would not be enough to fund the scheme adequately, so $70,000 is being provided. If
the average capacity at peak hours could be increased from the present 1.2 passengers per
car to the national average of 1.5 passengers per car, this one act could save $2 million in
imported oil.
The Government has introduced a range of sales taxes on certain petroleum products
and energy-intensive appliances-estimated to provide $10 million this year and $20 million
in a full year-in order to finance some of the savings programmes and also to discourage the
use of oil where other indigenous products are to be preferred. In this way, and in many
others, the National Government is proving that it can face facts and problems in a
responsible manner, and does so in such a way that it is prepared to act.

The increased price of oil was the real factor that set off the worldwide inflation in 1973.
It could be argued that the OPEC countries did the world a good turn, because the increase
in the price of oil at the wellhead from $1 a barrel to more than $10 a barrel drew attention to
the non-renewable nature of oil as an energy source. The world had pretended not to know
that one day its oil resources must finally be depleted if people continued to depend on liquid
fuels to such a large degree for their life style. In New Zealand, for example, because oil was
cheap before 1973, it had largely replaced coal as a fuel. Our motorcars ran on oil, it was
used also for international transport, our new railway engines were diesel driven, and we
were using oil for home heating. Nobody gave much thought to the fact that one day the
supplies would no longer be available. In 1972, our bill for imported oil was $94 million. This
year, as the Budget stated, it will be approximately $550 million, or $1.5 million a day for 365
days of the year. Not only has the price of oil escalated, but in a CIA report a short time ago
President Carter was advised that by 1985 the demand would exceed the supply. Members
should dwell for a moment on the significance of that. In this country, researchers have told
us that if we continue to use our coal and gas at the present rate we will exhaust New
Zealand's large reserves of fossil fuels by 2030.
Several factors point to the reason why urgent changes must be made to our pattern of
energy use. First, there is the escalating cost of imported fuels and its effect on inflation;
secondly, we must reduce our dependence on the non-renewable energy source of fossil
fuels; thirdly, by 1990 a 1500 MW thermal power station will be needed every 3 years if we
continue our present fast rate of growth in energy requirements; and, fourthly, we must
change our policies to avoid the imminent use of nuclear power.
A recent study carried out by the New Zealand Energy Research and Development
Committee, chaired by Dr Colin Maiden, Vice-Chancellor of Auckland University, suggests
three possible scenarios for energy use in New Zealand. The first is called continuation, and
involves an extension of the trends, policies, and attitudes we have had for the past 50 years.
The second involves a lower New Zealand pollution strategy. The minimisation of pollution
is a primary objective in governmental, business, and personal decisions; a small amount of
economic growth must be sacrificed to achieve this. The final scenario is limited growth, and
represents a strategy by which New Zealand can reduce its dependence on the rest of the
world for energy and other resources by slower population growth, slower economic growth,
and switching to indigenous renewable resources.
These models predict that New Zealand's population will move from its present figure
of approximately 3 100 000 to 5 000 000 in 2025 under the continuation scenario, and to 3 700
000 in 2025 under the limited growth scenario. In the interests of maintaining our slow
growth figures we would gladly sacrifice the two members opposite who are trying to
interject. A good example of the different results is that, in 2025, we would use eight times
the present amount of imported energy under the continuation scenario, whereas we would
not need to import energy at all under the limited growth scenario. Those are the extremes
between which our energy policies must develop. Agriculture will grow faster under the
limited growth scenario, and would suffer the most under the low population scenario, and
so on.

We worked out an expenditure pattern for them, so that each week their total

$1.98 a week for fuel and light, but spend it all on electricity. Even then, they have to cut
back their consumption by about 30 percent. No money is left for coal, gas, or oil. The same
applies to furniture, and to floor coverings. As telephone rental fees cost $1.66, they have

TRUSTEE SAVINGS BANKS AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That the Trustee Savings
Bank Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill contains the amendments necessary for the
implementation of the measures announced in the Budget to give trustee savings banks the
freedom to set the structure of, and the interest rates on, investment and other term deposit
accounts. The changes in the Bill are complementary to those already implemented by
amendments to the Trustee Savings Banks Interest Order and Regulations. Clause 2
removes the interest-bearing deposit limits on all accounts except the farm ownership
account. The limit of $60,000 in respect of this account is retained, but provision has been
made for this limit to be increased by Order in Council. The provisions limiting to one the
number of accounts a depositor may have in any one class of account, and the requirement of
a trustee savings bank to give 3 months' notice of a reduction in an interest rate payable, are
also repealed. Clause 3 gives the trustee savings banks freedom to accept deposits, for a term
not less than 30 days, in such investment accounts or term deposits as each bank may wish to
offer. The Trustee Savings Banks Interest Order 1977 provides for the concurrence of the
Reserve Bank to changes in the interest rates payable and the conditions applying to such
deposits. The previous conditions relating to the breaking of investment account deposits
have been repealed.
The Bill is a straightforward one, giving effect to the Budget measures that are a further
step in the Government's policy of encouraging increased competition among financial
institutions in order to facilitate the development of an efficient and flexible financial system.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I have two questions and one
comment. The comment is that this is a recognition of continuing inflation. The size of the
various deposits upon which interest can be paid reflects those facts. Why is section 5 of the
Trustee Savings Banks Amendment Act 1975 to be repealed? In the past the banks were
required to have in effect 3 months' notice of an intention to reduce interest rates, and that is
no longer applicable. Is this a reflection of the fact that other competing institutions have not


## p. 1717 (#173) ###########################################

29 July
1717
Trustee Savings Banks Amendment Bill
had to do that on their term deposits? I am thinking more specifically of the call deposits, the
largest volume of savings, the form of savings that the ordinary small saver considers. Does
this mean that the banks are now free to reduce those at any time they want?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The Bill is in line with the
Government's election policy of giving more flexibility in this field, and bringing the
controlled and uncontrolled interest rates closer together, and this has been carried out.
There is not the slightest doubt that the institutions with controlled interest rates were very
much at a disadvantage as against those with uncontrolled rates, with results that were not
good for the economy. Indeed, some of the collapses in the financial sector were of
institutions with uncontrolled interest rates. By giving the trustee banks greater flexibility,
they have a greater ability to compete, which is in the long-term interest of the financial
sector. The honourable member is correct in his assumption that the reason for this change is
to put them on the same basis as other financial institutions.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): What is the logic behind the
argument that because there have been financial collapses among institutions where interest
rates are not controlled the solution to the problem is to make all institutions uncontrolled?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The logic should have been apparent
to a former Minister of Finance. This institution has a total Government guarantee.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
PRIVATE SAVINGS BANKS AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That the Private Savings
Banks Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill contains amendments necessary for the
implementation of the measures announced in the Budget to give private savings banks the
freedom to set the structure of, and the interest rates on, investment and other term deposit
accounts. The changes in the Bill complement those already implemented by changes in the
Private Savings Banks Regulations and Interest Order. Subclauses (1) and (4) of clause 2
remove the interest-bearing deposit limits on all accounts. Subclause (2) excludes term
deposits from interest payment conditions applicable to demand deposits only. Subclause (3)
repeals the section limiting to one the number of accounts a depositor may have in any
prescribed class of account. This is a straightforward Bill. It gives effect to the Budget
measures that are a further step in the Government's policy of encouraging competition
among financial institutions in order to facilitate the development of an efficient and flexible
financial system.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I recognise that the Bill
parallels the Trustee Savings Banks Amendment Bill, which has just been introduced. In
view of the comment made by the Minister of Finance that a reason for removing the control
on the trustee savings banks was because they had a complete guarantee by the Government,
does the Government intend to give the same guarantee to private savings banks?
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Hoist with his own petard!
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The member for Timaru has this
remarkable ability to lead with his chin. Again I would have thought that a former Minister
of Finance would realise that private banks associated with the five trading banks would be
able to provide an absolute guarantee, as against the various institutions that have collapsed
during the period of successive Governments.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: You're just being a bit too smart for your own good.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I know who is being a bit too smart for his own good; it is
the Deputy Leader of the Opposition. Surely he, at least, can understand that the savings
banks have a much lesser degree of risk than organisations such as Securitibank, the Cornish
Group, and Circuit Developments, to name just three that come to mind immediately, and
that it is desirable that they have more flexibility and a greater ability to compete for the
deposits of the small investors. Surely the Deputy Leader of the Opposition does not contest
that; and, if he does not, why does he feign ignorance?
Bill introduced and read a first time.

Mr Marshall: In view of the fact that the department is now losing social workers at the

Electricity and Gas Users-Payment of Accounts
4. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Electricity: Has he read an article in the
Otago Daily Times of 12 July 1977 that "many electricity and gas users in the Dunedin area
are having to be pressured into paying their latest power bills by the Dunedin City
Corporation", and, if so, has he any information to indicate that this disturbing trend is
being reflected in other parts of New Zealand?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Electricity): I have read the article referred to. Following
up overdue accounts is a normal part of a supply authority's operations, and disconnection
warning notices are necessary for late payers. If firm credit control is not maintained, a
consumer's indebtedness would continue to increase to such an extent that the account could
never be paid, and disconnection would be inevitable. The policy of a quick follow-up does
result in fewer disconnections. The point is that although the number of warnings has
increased, the article does indicate that the number of disconnections has remained steady at
six or seven.a week. I would expect the position to be much the same throughout the
country.
Mr Hunt: In view of the fact that the last part of my question referred to "being
reflected in other parts of New Zealand", could the Minister indicate whether he has any
information with him about the state of affairs in the Waitemata Electric Power Board,
where there has been a particularly large increase in electricity accounts in the last few
months?

Rarotongan Hotel
5. Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury) asked the Minister of Tourism: Can he give any
indication of the success or otherwise of the Tourist Hotel Corporation's participation in the

Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): The Rarotongan is owned by a private
company, Cook Islands Hotels Ltd, whose three equal shareholders are the Cook Islands
Government, Air New Zealand, and the Tourist Hotel Corporation. Tourist Hotel Corpora-

for the first stage of this year.

spent there will be of the order of $300,000 a year, and considerable purchases of fruit and
vegetables are being contracted for within the Islands. A number of private entrepreneurs
from the Cook Islands are supplying vehicles and boats for tourists.

Waiheke County Council Rates
6. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Local Government: Has he
seen the two Waiheke County Council rates notices in the New Zealand Herald of 20 July in
which the rate in cents per dollar varies inversely with the land value of the property, and can
he state whether such rating is in accordance with the differential rating provisions of the
Counties Act 1956?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I have seen the public notice
referred to. In relation to differential rating, the Counties Act 1956 provides that a council
may divide the county into differential rating areas. Any one differential rating area may be
a combination of several individual properties not necessarily contiguous with one another.
A county council is empowered to make and levy rates of varying amounts in the dollar as
between differential rating areas. Subject to the maximum total rates prescribed in the Act, a
council in its own discretion may determine the rate to be levied in each such differential
rating area. If it comes to a contest as to whether or not the Waiheke County Council has
complied with the letter of the law, this must, of course, be left to the courts to resolve.
Mr Prebble: Is the concept of the Waiheke County Council, which I think could be
paraphrased as "those who have least shall pay most", in accordance with the Government's
rating policy?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: If there is any doubt as to whether the law is being complied with,
it is a matter for the courts to resolve.

vessels. This request was considered as part of a programme of New Zealand assistance to

equipment were naturally drawn to the attention of the Fiji authorities. However, Fiji
already employs the same Australian equipment, and the Fiji authorities were concerned
about standardisation of equipment and uniform training of maintenance officers. The issue
of standardisation and maintenance is a particularly difficult problem in all our Pacific aid
programmes, and the New Zealand Government has agreed to play its part in trying to
reduce the complications of too many different sorts of equipment. The Australian marine
transceivers were accordingly purchased for Fiji. In general, however, it remains the
Government's policy to provide New Zealand-made equipment under the aid programme to
the maximum extent possible.
