BASTION POINT (VESTING AND EMPOWERING) BILL
Mr HARRISON (Hawke's Bay): I am directed by the Committee on Bills to present the
report of the committee on the Bastion Point (Vesting and Empowering) Bill. In the opinion
of the committee the Bill is a public Bill, and, being a public Bill, it is a local Bill. I move,
That the report do lie upon the table and be adopted and agreed to.
As instructed by Standing Order 218, the committee has inquired into the character of
the Bill and expresses its opinion on whether the Bill is a public or private Bill, and whether,
if a public Bill, it is a local Bill. Standing Order 279 defines a private Bill as one, not being a
local Bill, designed for the particular interest or benefit of a person or body of persons.
However, Speaker's rulings such as 14/2 and 14/3 provide that matters superficially falling
within this definition may nevertheless constitute a public and not a private Bill. The
involvement of public policy appears to be the guide. For example, in one Speaker's ruling,
the State guarantee to the Bank of New Zealand was taken as a measure of public policy and
therefore the Bill was ruled to be a public and not a private Bill.
However, Bills dealing in some way with Crown land do not, because of that, require to
be public Bills. Standing Order 294 allows for a procedure whereby a private Bill can affect
the property rights or prerogatives of the Crown. The Palmerston North Showgrounds Act
1974 is an example of Crown land being affected by a private Bill for the benefit of a body of
persons. Bills which amend public Acts have been ruled to be measures of public policy
which cannot be passed as private Bills. The committee then had to ask itself whether the
Bill amends a public Act, since its intention, as with many private Bills, is to create an
exception to the general law for the benefit of a particular group.
Standing Order 218 requires the committee to inquire into the character and intention
of the Bill. From that inquiry it is clear that no matter what the Bill's intention, or the
intention of its promoter, it does not in its terms alter any of the provisions of a public Act,
although it does seek to limit some Acts, either explicitly or by implication. On the occasion
of Speaker's ruling 14/2 being given, the Bill in question amended the text of a public Act
and, therefore, proposed to amend its application generally, and not just a particular set of
circumstances. Therefore, the committee resolved unanimously that the Bill was not a
private Bill. Obviously, then, it must be a public Bill, and the question was then whether it
was a private member's public Bill or a local Bill.
Standing Order 257 defines local Bills as those which, not being private Bills, affect a
particular locality only. Speaker's ruling 9/3 appears to contradict that Standing Order by
stating that a Bill to amend a public Act is a public, not a local, Bill, even if it relates to a
district only, or a particular locality. In all of the examples given, the proposed Bills sought
to amend the text of a public Act, but this is not the case here. As the committee found when
deciding the Bill was not a private Bill-no matter what the intention of the Bill or its
promoter-it is clear that in its terms it does not alter any of the provisions of a public Act,
although it does seek explicitly to limit the Maori Trust Board Act 1955 and the Lands Act
1948, and perhaps by implication the Public Works Act, and possibly some others.
Crown land clearly may be the subject of a local Bill, although Speaker's ruling 10/3
indicates the opposite, because Mr Speaker Steward ruled in 1893 that although the
Gimmerburn Forest Bill dealt with a particular locality, it did not propose to divest the
Crown of that land and was therefore not a local Bill, but a private member's public Bill.
However, the Gimmerburn Forest Reserve Bill of 1890 was ruled to be a local Bill, because,
although it was promoted by the Government and provided for the alienation of Crown land,


## p. 1728 (#184) ###########################################

1728
29 July
Bastion Point (Vesting and Empowering) Bill
its vesting was in the Maniototo County Council, which was the local authority. Local Bills
thus affect a locality rather than the jurisdiction, although in most cases this will be involved
as well. This, of course, is in accordance with Standing Order 257. The Bastion Point
(Vesting and Empowering) Bill is similar in that it vests Crown land in a group of people
other than the Crown, and, therefore, cannot be a private Bill. Also, as it is restricted to a
particular locality—the land in the Orakei block in the North Auckland Land District-it
must be a local Bill, rather than a private member's public Bill. That is what the committee
found.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): As a member of the Committee on Bills, which
considered the status of the Bastion Point (Vesting and Empowering) Bill, I believe that the
Bill could have been considered a private Bill, a public Bill, or a local Bill. While a technical
argument can be raised in favour of the committee's conclusion that it is a local Bill, I believe
it is a borderline case. I was disappointed that the committee did not deal with it as a public
Bill, which was clearly the intention of the Bill, and I believe that the decision of the
committee will strangle the Bill with technicalities.
The Bill could have been dealt with as a public Bill. Standing Order 279(1) defines a
private Bill as a Bill which, not being a local Bill, is designed for the particular interest or
benefit of a person or body of persons, whether incorporated or not. Although the Bill was
designed to help the Ngati Whatua it was clearly not just a private Bill. It must be then either
a local Bill or a public Bill. A public Bill is not defined in the Standing Orders, but Standing
Order 257 defines local Bills as those which, not being private Bills, affect a particular
locality only. Presumably, if it does more than that it must be a public Bill.
The Bill, while containing elements of a local Bill and a private Bill, also contains
something more. Under clause 4, the Maori Trust Board can enter into what arrangements it
sees fit with the Auckland Regional Authority, the Auckland City Council, and other
municipal authorities, with a view to providing for the management, development, protec-
tion and care of all parts of the Bastion Point land reserved for recreational purposes. That
means that the people of Auckland will benefit, and I submit that it is wrong to determine
that it is a local Bill just because only one piece of land is involved. The ramifications of the
Bill spread beyond Bastion Point itself, because the Ngati Whatua, who are the primary
beneficiaries of the Bill, are now scattered throughout New Zealand. The Maori Trust Board
is empowered to enter into arrangements with a local body, and the Bill makes it clear that
the municipal authorities with which the trust board may deal must be in different localities.
Speaker's ruling 10/2 states that a Bill which affects a whole provincial district and not a
particular locality is not a local Bill, and it seems to me that the empowering clause contained
in the Bill to negotiate with different local bodies means that most of the Auckland Province
could be affected by the Bill. Under Speaker's ruling 11/1, a Bill which enabled a local body,
in this case the Wellington City Council, to transfer land to the Victoria University College
Council as a site for the university college, and to receive land in exchange from the
Wellington College Board of Governors, and enabled the Wellington Hospital Trustees also
to transfer land to the Victoria University College Council-the trustees to be paid out of the
Consolidated Revenue Account-was deemed to be a public, not a local, Bill. The
explanatory note to that ruling says that the university college was designed to serve the
middle districts of New Zealand. Presumably that is why the Bill was ruled to be a public, not
a local Bill.
I believe there is a direct parallel between that ruling and the Bill before us. A number
of local authorities in Auckland will be affected, as will Crown revenue, because it is Crown
land that will be transferred. On that basis, the committee, if it wanted to, could have ruled
that it is a public Bill, because it is obviously more than just a local Bill.
A third reason for ruling it a public Bill is the fact that the Bill modifies a number of
Acts. Clause 5 states that notwithstanding anything contained in any other Act, such and
such shall be the case. Clause 8 states that the Bill shall bind the Crown, and clause 7 states
that the land will be inalienable, which would seem to have an effect on the Public Works
Act. If a Bill seeks to amend a public Act, it must be a public Bill, even if it deals with only
one piece of land. I have no doubt that the Bill would have been deemed to be a public Bill,
had it been framed slightly differently and had it named the sections in the public Act it was
seeking to amend. The effect of the Bill as it is worded is exactly the same, which is quite
proper. I believe the Bill does seek to modify a number of public Acts-and one could argue
whether "modify" means "amend". I believe it does-and clearly the Bill should be dealt
with as a public Bill. Unfortunately the committee decided to lean to the technicality, and
the Government used its majority to determine otherwise.


## p. 1729 (#185) ###########################################

1729
Bastion Point (Vesting and Empowering) Bill
The House should be aware that alternative drafting, while making no difference to the
effect of the Bill, would have made the Bill a public Bill. The method used for drafting will
affect public Bills. The matter is a borderline one. The committee should have looked at the
overall purpose of the Bill, and whether it was intended to be a local Bill. It is clear, when
one looks at the Bill as a whole, that it was intended to be a public Bill, and the House should
take notice of that intention. The land involved has emotional and historical significance not
only to the people of the Ngati Whatua, who are spread throughout New Zealand, but to all
New Zealanders. It must be remembered that Michael Joseph Savage, the first Labour
Prime Minister, is buried at Bastion Point, and even today people visiting Auckland go there
to pay their respects to his memory. For that reason it can be claimed that the land is more
than just local land.
The Bill was put forward by the member for Northern Maori as a solution to an
extraordinarily difficult problem which goes far beyond Auckland. The ruling of the
committee that the Bill is a local Bill will strangle it with legal technicalities. The Bill should
have been given a second reading. It is a borderline case, and a member of the House has a
historical right to bring forward a private member's Bill. The Committee on Bills should
have leant over backwards to allow the member to bring forward what he considers to be the
proper solution to a problem within his electorate. The Bill should have been dealt with as a
public Bill and given a second reading. Many members believe that the Bill is a good one,
and the proper solution to the difficulties of Bastion Point. By giving the Bill a second
reading it was hoped that the Government would be persuaded that the Bill should be
adopted. I oppose the committee majority decision, and the House should oppose the
decision of the committee on Bills as being an extraordinarily unfortunate precedent.

TERRITORIAL SEA AND EXCLUSIVE ECONOMIC ZONE BILL
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I am directed by the Foreign Affairs Committee to
present the report of the committee on the Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone
Bill. The committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move,
That the report do lie upon the table. The Foreign Affairs Committee heard submissions from
members of the public on this very significant legislation. In all, 17 submissions were made,
and the committee was grateful for the effort that went into their preparation. Several
amendments have been proposed by the committee. In general they are of a minor nature.
Almost without exception the submissions endorsed the overall scheme of the Bill. Many
focused on the way in which the zone should be managed when the Bill comes into force
rather than on the Bill itself. The committee has also adopted a number of drafting
amendments which have shortened and simplified the text. We have also taken the
opportunity to close a number of possible loopholes which may have existed in the Bill.
I shall highlight some of the amendments. The first is to clause 2(1), where the
definition of "fish" has been tightened to clearly include crustacea. We have also clarified
the definition of "fishing" by inserting a new paragraph (c) to emphasise that the powers
contained in the Bill will apply not only to vessels actually fishing in the zone, but also to
mother ships and support vessels providing supplies and assistance for foreign fishing vessels.
It is conceivable that fishing operations could be conducted from submarines or craft
without propulsion, and to close up any possible loophole these have been included in the
definition of "fishing craft". The "nautical mile" is internationally recognised to be 1852
metres, and it seemed desirable to add that to the definition for the sake of clarity. The
definition of "New Zealand fishing craft" has obviously created some difficulties. It was
clear from many of the submissions that the complex legal formulae used in the Bill have led
people to suppose that joint venture craft are classified as foreign craft. Although it is not
technically necessary, an amendment to simplify the present definition seemed desirable,
and the amendment clearly establishes the position of joint venture boats, which are all
registered under the Fisheries Act.
In clause 15(3)(h) it seemed desirable to include the words "pipelines and cables".
There is a clearly established right under international law for a coastal State to claim
compensation for damage caused to submarine cables and pipelines, and we decided to
insert this provision specifically for licences issued for foreign fishing vessels. At the same
time the committee also considered measures to protect pipelines, particularly the Maui
pipeline, from damage. The Bill will have the effect of conferring jurisdiction over foreign
vessels in that regard within the 12-mile limit of the new territorial zone. Beyond that the
Submarine Cables and Pipelines Act 1954 establishes control over New Zealand fishing
boats. Those are the limits of New Zealand's jurisdiction. It seems that the Law of the Sea
Conference will not give coastal States jurisdiction for this purpose over foreign ships on the
high seas. Accordingly the committee and officials have looked at alternative means of
protecting New Zealand's pipelines and cables.
This Bill gives the Government wide powers over foreign fishing vessels. There are
heavy penalties, and it is proposed that the powers should be used to effectively prohibit


## p. 1740 (#196) ###########################################

1740
29 July
Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill
activities which might present a danger to pipelines. That proposal is acceptable to Maui
Development Ltd. Similarly, administrative action will be taken to guard against the much
more remote possibility of damage by foreign merchant vessels. The committee received
written confirmation from Maui Development Ltd about its original concern. Its chairman,
Sir Arnold Nordmeyer, said, "These proposals are acceptable to my company and will, I
believe, give the basic protection we need." It is very important that Maui Development Ltd
is quite satisfied with the Bill as it is now being reported back.
Subclauses 19(2) and 19(5) referred to owners. They have been deleted, because under
clause 15(1) licences may be issued only to owners of vessels. It is also proposed to establish
a new offence in respect of a vessel which conceals or falsely displays a licence or
identification. Subclause (7) has also been amended to ensure that a New Zealand observer
or fisherman on board a vessel for training purposes under clause 15(3)(k) is not guilty of an
offence under this section. In a submission on clause 23 dealing with the review of the
Minister's powers by the courts it was felt that the provision was inadequate, and a new
clause 20A was drafted on the basis that foreign fishing vessels should not have the right to
challenge the Minister's decisions in the courts.
Members will note a major amendment to clause 23. Several submissions referred to the
desirability of ensuring that security is lodged to cover the value of the fish caught by an
arrested vessel. The proposed amendment ensures that the Crown has the power to hold fish
on either a detained vessel or elsewhere. If it is held elsewhere, the Crown may recover the
costs and will not be liable for any deterioration. In addition, if the vessel is released on
bond, security must be lodged for the value of the fish as well. Clause 27 is of major
importance. Many submissions stressed the need for interim measures to protect fish
resources before the Bill as a whole came into force. The new subclause (2) strengthens and
tightens this provision by specifically providing that such regulations may establish offences
and impose penalties.
The amendment to clause 29 is a technical one, because recent nautical charts have not
been using the mean low water spring tides as a basic point for the low water mark.
Accordingly, the previous wording is not accurate in all cases, and the problem has been
solved by referring to specific charts held by the Navy hydrographic office in Auckland which
are used as a master set for establishing these lines. The proposed amendment makes the
clause considerably shorter and simpler, and means that the definition of low water mark
contained in clause 2 can be deleted. The proposed new subclause in clause 31 deals with the
problem presented in a number of Acts that specifically refer to the 12-mile fishing zone,
which will be abolished when this Bill becomes law. It was therefore necessary to provide
that these references shall be construed as references to the territorial sea, which will now
extend to 12 miles in its place. The Bill is very important for New Zealand's future
development, and I am pleased to report that, without exception, the submissions supported
an early implementation of its provisions.
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson): I am proud to have been a member of the committee that
considered the submissions from people in the fishing industry, and particularly those in the
off-shore fishing industry, which this Bill will help to protect. The Opposition supports the
Bill, because it is a measure giving control over the exploitation of, and seeking to conserve
and manage, one of our natural resources. The message that came through to the committee
was that the Bill should be passed as quickly as possible. Most of the submissions pointed out
that the protection of our resources was a matter of urgency. Some people said that we
should not overemphasise the size of the resource, which is unknown at the present time; but
we all hope it will be significant. Our present fishing stock and the future of the off-shore
industry must be protected. I am sure it will mean a lot in the future.
The Bill follows closely the revised single negotiating text that formed the basis of the
Law of the Sea Conference held in New York. The chairman of the committee drew
attention to the amendments. I suggest that the Minister of Fisheries should note carefully
the comments made about clause 27. A request was made to act immediately to retain the
status quo. There was not much criticism of the Bill, but the New Zealand University
Students Association did not want us to share the resources with anyone, and a gentleman
with interests in the Chatham Islands suggested that all fish caught around the islands should
be landed there, or that a tax should be imposed, which would go to the Chatham Islands.
Many of the submissions made constructive comments on the regulations that will cover the
issuing of licences. Clause 15(3) states that the Minister may attach to the licence conditions
relating to all or any of 18 categories. The general feeling from the submissions was that this
gave the Minister wide-ranging powers, and the Opposition also feels some concern. The


## p. 1741 (#197) ###########################################

29 July
1741
Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill
industry has asked to be kept informed on the issue of licences, and the conditions that have
been attached. The industry also wanted to be kept fully informed of the terms and
conditions that will apply to each country involved in joint ventures.
On the question of licence fees, some of the submissions suggested they should be set at
a low level so as not to work against our tuna fishermen who might have to enter the waters
of foreign countries. Others felt that the fees should be set at a very high level to put
something back into the industry for future development. Some interesting opinions came
forward on fish-meal plants, and most people felt that foreign fishing vessels should not be
allowed into our zone with fish-meal plants on board. Although some members felt they
should be allowed, I am apprehensive about that. Another good point put forward by the
Federation of Commercial Fishermen and the Fishing Industry Board was that the maximum
sustainable yield from our 200-mile economic zone and our catching capabilities should be
recognised, and that in establishing the catching capabilities a certain amount of room should
be allowed for expansion and development of the industry. We must be mindful of the
future, and if we rapidly expand our off-shore fishing interests within the 200-mile economic
zone we should leave a margin to accommodate the expansion that will no doubt follow. It
will develop despite the Government, not because of it.
The Opposition supports the legislation. There was concern about maintaining competi-
tiveness between our fishermen and foreign fishermen, and about the responsibilities placed
on the Minister. Concern was expressed about the need for an interim transitional measure
to be applied to clause 27, and the need to continue discussions about the implementation of
the Bill. The Minister should keep the industry fully informed about the conditions for
licensing and joint ventures. The Opposition is pleased to see the legislation come back from
the committee, and will support it by assisting the House to move the Bill through all its
stages with urgency.
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I am very pleased that the Opposition is giving its full
support to this most significant and important legislation. It is important that the Opposition
and the Government go forward together to pass the Bill, because of the impact it will have
on our short-, medium-, and long-term development. I am very pleased with the support
expressed by the member for Nelson, and I ignore the few political asides that he made. New
Zealand has the fourth largest economic zone in the world. The reporting back and the
passing of the Bill will present a great challenge that will be accepted by the Government and
those responsible for the development of our fisheries and other resources within the
economic zone.
Motion agreed to.
RESERVES BILL
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture Commit-
tee to present the report of the committee on the Reserves Bill. The committee recommends
that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
The committee received 53 submissions on the Reserves Bill, and 22 people appeared before
the committee. Submissions came from local bodies, conservation organisations, concerned
individuals, Maori groups, and other groups that will make use of the Bill's provisions, such
as the Historic Places Trust and the Play Centres Association.
A very pleasing aspect of most of the submissions was the large measure of acceptance
the Bill received. This confirms that the time is right for the consolidation and updating of
the existing legislation, the Reserves and Domains Act 1953. Most of the criticism, and this
appeared in 14 submissions, was about the lack of greater opportunities for the public to
have its say before decisions are made affecting reserves. The validity of this criticism was
accepted by the committee, and amendments to overcome the deficiency have been
recommended.
Clause 25 deals with a change of classification or purpose and the revocation of reserves,
and includes provision for advertising and objection procedures. It is intended that similar
procedures be introduced into other clauses where some disposition of the reserve, or some
loss of general principle of freedom of access to a reserve, is involved. The clauses are clause
48, grant of easement; clause 54, leasing of recreation reserves; clause 56, leasing of scenic
reserves; clause 73, leasing of recreation reserves for farming, grazing, or afforestation; and
clause 74, grant of temporary leases to occupy. The same procedure will apply to clause
16-Minister to classify reserves-as the initial classification of a reserve is fundamental to
its future management.


## p. 1742 (#198) ###########################################

1742
29 July
Reserves Bill
A slightly different procedure is proposed for clause 41, management plans; and the
committee has recommended an amendment that, first, requires an administering body to
publicly notify its intention to prepare a management plan and invite public comment and
suggestion; secondly, requires the body, when the draft plan is prepared, to publicly notify
its availability for inspection and invite comment in writing, with the right to appear before
the administering body in support of that comment; and, thirdly, requires the administering
body, when submitting the plan to the Minister for his approval, to attach a summary of
objections with comment on the extent to which these have been accepted or rejected. The
adoption of these amendments will place the Reserves Bill in the forefront of legislation,
making provision for extensive public involvement.
Some of the submissions raised the question of the relationship of the Bill to the Town
and Country Planning Act, and asked which Act takes precedence. The present position is
dictated by the designation of the district scheme. This is expressly provided in the Town and
Country Planning Act, under section 33A, which states that land designated for a public
work defined to include reserves does not come under the zoning of the operative district
scheme as far as construction, execution, or operation of the public work is concerned. In
effect this puts a reserve designated as such beyond the zoning of the operative district
scheme as long as use or development is in terms of that designation, and is authorised in
terms of the Reserves and Domains Act. Nevertheless, as a result of submissions, the
committee has accepted two cases where district scheme provisions could be accepted in lieu
of the public notification of the Reserves Bill. These are clause 14, headed "Local authority
may declare land vested in it to be a reserve," and clause 15-"Exchange of reserves for
other land". Amendments to both clauses are accordingly recommended by the committee.
Submissions were made by the New Zealand Maori Council, the Terawhiti District
Maori Council, and the Maori Graduates Association. The three submissions covered
similar ground, and were based on a concern for the retention and promotion of, and respect
for, Maori culture and tradition. As a result of the submissions the committee proposes
amendments as follows: the inclusion in clause 2 of an additional subclause that provides that
Maori reservations created under the Maori Affairs Act are not subject to the Bill; in clause
25(a)-effect of revocation of reserve or change of classification for purpose-the inclusion
of a subclause to provide that where the land was gifted by Maoris the Minister shall, unless
he considers it would not be in the public interest, offer the land back to the former owner or
his descendants; a provision in clause 35 that a Maori trust board may be appointed to
control and manage a reserve; the widening of the provisions of clause 38 to include a Maori
trust board and Maori incorporation among those that may be appointed to control and
manage land that is not a reserve.
Concern was expressed that where Maori land not on a land transfer register was to be
taken under the Public Works Act for reserve purposes there was no procedure for the
owners' interest to be protected. To meet this, subclause 12 has been amended to provide for
notice to be served on the Registrar of the Maori Land Court so that the owners can be
advised and a trustee appointed to look after their interests. General concern was expressed
in the three submissions about the dwindling area of land retained in Maori ownerships, and
its vulnerability to alienation, particularly as so much of the land remaining is still in its
natural state, or is so located that it is admirably suited for reserve purposes. The concern is
appreciated, and it is for these very reasons that provision exists in the Bill for alternatives to
outright purchase.
Following the introduction of the Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill,
and the increasing level of fishing activity in the general area of New Zealand's outlying
reserves, it has been agreed that a new clause be inserted in the offences provisions of the
Bill concerning the stopping and searching of boats, and also that the existing penalty and
breach of bylaw clauses, Nos. 102 and 103, be omitted and replaced with clauses providing
for a variable penalty depending on the importance of the reserve. The outlying islands are
of international importance, as they include some of the world's last remaining areas of
vegetation unmodified by man or his introduced animals. Landing rights to the reserves are
strictly controlled, and generally granted only for genuine scientific reasons. Uncontrolled
visits could lead to the introduction of foreign plants, fires, the release of cats or rodents, or
interference with nesting birds or nursing mammals. The very isolation of the islands makes
them difficult to police, and the New Zealand Navy is really the only means. The new clause
99A provides that a vessel can be boarded if it is suspected that an offence has been
committed. Without this kind of authority the islands would be unprotected from man or his
introduced fauna or flora.

I have dealt only with some of the major points that arose from the submissions received
by the committee, which gave such detailed consideration to this piece of legislation. Many

CONTRACTUAL MISTAKES BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Contractual Mistakes Bill. The committee recommends
that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
This is a complex Bill based on a report of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform
Committee. It is appropriate that, before summarising the changes recommended by the
Statutes Revision Committee, I should outline briefly the original intent and purpose of the
Bill, which remain intact even with the changes recommended by the committee. I do this
because all those who made submissions to the committee, except one, appeared to us not to
understand fully the intent and purposes of the Bill.
In the contractual situation several different types of mistakes can arise. The first
possible mistake is as to the nature of the document. The second is as to the terms on which
an agreement has been reached. The third is as to the identity of one of the contracting
parties. The fourth is as to the subject-matter of the contract itself. Until now, the whole
field of contractual mistakes has been dealt with by case law, which has categorised various
types of mistake and developed different lines of authority in each. However, the common
principle that can be gleaned is that in all cases the law must strike a balance between
avoiding the inference of holding a party to an inappropriate transaction, on the one hand,
and protecting parties to a contract and those who claim through or under it, on the other.
There have been a number of criticisms of the present law. First, the tests for mistakes
have been described as inherently meaningless, and have resulted in conflicting decisions. In
order to reach a just result, the courts have created illusory distinctions; that this has
occurred in such an important field has caused considerable criticism. Secondly, the law had
considerable difficulty in coping with the concept of negligence in this area. Again, there
have been conflicting decisions, which have failed to distinguish between carelessness on the
one hand and negligence on the other. Thirdly, the theoretical foundations of the law in this
field have always been regarded as suspect. There has been confusion between common law
and the equitable doctrines of mistake, which are directly contradictory in many respects. By
comparison, the United States of America has a uniform approach to this field of law, and
the view of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee was that the problems
involved in contractual mistakes are not so complex as to require more than one legal
doctrine to unravel them. Fourthly, the legal remedies available as the result of a mistake are
drastic and inflexible, resulting basically in no contract. As a result, the courts have been
reluctant to commit themselves to a clear policy in defining mistake, thereby avoiding a
substantial injustice to one party.
The Bill as introduced, although it did not interfere with a number of equitable
doctrines and did not interfere with the court's discretion to decline to order a decree of
specific performance, did provide that relief should be granted where a mistake by one party


## p. 1744 (#200) ###########################################

1744
29 July
Contractual Mistakes Bill
to a contract is known to the opposing party, or is a common or a mutual mistake. The Bill
then prescribed various types of relief that would be available in those circumstances.
The committee received seven submissions on the Bill. Five were from parties
connected either with the building industry or with property development, and suggested
that the Bill should not apply to contracts for the sale of land or contracts for construction,
and to other certain types of contractual arrangements. None of these submissions, however,
appeared to understand that the Bill applies only to mutual or common mistakes, or where a
mistake is known to the other party. Drafting changes have been suggested, particularly to
clause 5, that should make this point very much clearer.
The New Zealand Institution of Engineers made submissions on the question of
arbitration, and this is dealt with in the new proposed clause 8B.
The final submission, which caused the committee the most concern, was from Mr
Hughes of Metropolitan Real Estate, very ably supported by his solicitor, Mr V. M. Gray. In
essence, this submission suggested that the Bill, which both Mr Hughes and his solicitor
clearly understood, would open up a whole new area of litigation and a new line of legal
authority, which would of itself create uncertainty in contractual arrangements-and these
contractual arrangements might very well involve very large sums of money. The committee
gave that submission the most anxious consideration, and has proposed a number of changes
that are designed, basically, to make the Bill's intention clearer. First, we recommend that
the definition of mistake in clause 2 should be limited to mistakes of law and fact only.
Secondly, in order to make the intention of the Bill clearer, we propose to add clause 3A,
which sets out the purpose of the Bill in greater detail. In its original form, although it
correctly expressed the purposes of the Bill, clause 5 was not easily understood-particularly
by the majority of lay persons who came before the committee. The clause has therefore
been substantially redrafted by the committee, although its intention remains unchanged,
with some minor exceptions.
The remaining changes to the Bill are very largely procedural, giving jurisdiction to a
small claims tribunal for claims under $500, and to an arbitrator when a matter is referred
under the Arbitration Act 1908.
As I have emphasised in this report, the Bill is complex; in the initial stages particularly,
it caused the committee some concern. This concern was to a very large degree alleviated by
the detailed discussion we had with Mr Colin Patterson, who is the chairman of the Contracts
and Commercial Law Reform Committee; the Chief Parliamentary Counsel, Mr Iles, who is
also a member of that law reform committee; and with Mr Wright of the Department of
Justice, who is the secretary of that committee. We are indebted to these gentlemen for their
help. The committee is now confident that the Bill in its amended form will not only give
effect to the intentions of the original report by the law reform committee, but is also now
very much clearer and very much more easily understood; and thus, we hope, it will very
largely allay the apprehensions expressed by those who made submissions on the Bill.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I can agree with the member for Birkenhead in at
least one respect: the law of contractual mistake is complex and the situations envisaged by it
are by no means easy to comprehend; but for the rest I feel obliged to say at the outset that I
intend to move that the Bill be referred back for further consideration. The real trouble is, of
course, that the word "mistake" means one thing to a lawyer-at any rate in relation to a
contract—and a very different thing to the man in the street. This confusion was encouraged,
as was obvious from the way some witnesses approached their task of giving evidence, by the
terms of the original Bill, which defines "mistake" as including an erroneous opinion and an
erroneous calculation. To the layman, that could readily include the wrong addition of a
column of figures; that is a mistake in ordinary layman's language, but it is not a mistake in
law. What a lawyer means by a contractual mistake is a very different thing.
The original Bill was based on the report of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform
Committee, which put forward what seemed to me at the outset to be an attractively simple
manner of reforming the law. When I first saw the Bill that was based on that report, I must
confess I leant in its direction. However, my faith in it was considerably shaken by, amongst
other things, the evidence given to the committee by Mr V. R. W. Gray-not Mr V. M.
Gray-a lawyer for whom I have a mounting respect every time he appears before a
parliamentary committee. His criticism was blunt indeed. He said, "If the Bill is enacted in
its present form, it will be (a) a godsend to lawyers now underemployed after the demise of
matrimonial property litigation; (b) a haven for the ruthless, the desperate, and the
unscrupulous; and (c) a curse to the honest, fair-dealing, and innocent." To be quite honest,
I think that that criticism is a little extravagant, but at least it shows clearly where he stood on


## p. 1745 (#201) ###########################################

29 July
1745
Contractual Mistakes Bill
the subject.
While we have made some changes that I believe he would approve of, I still have little
doubt that he would adhere to his original proposition, which was that, although the existing
law is complex, it is comparatively well settled, and to change it either as originally
intended or even now with the Bill as amended-will set in motion a whole new round of
litigation in order to determine just what the apparently simplified provisions of the law
really do mean, and how they apply to the situations that face the courts.
Just to give the House an indication of the kind of complexity involved, I shall
summarise six different conceptual situations that the law has to wrestle with; these were put
before the committee by Mr Gray. I make the basic assumption that a factual situation, that I
can describe as X, is fundamental to the parties entering into a contract. It is imagined that A
and B are the two would-be contracting parties. A tells B that he believes X to be true. This
may have a number of consequential results: (1) B has no idea whether X is true or not; (2) B
doubts it, but says nothing; (3) B doubts it, and tells A of his doubts; (4) B knows X is not the
case, but says nothing; (5) B knows X is not the case, and raises the doubt-for example,
tells A to check-but does not categorically disabuse A; and (6) B knows X is not the case,
and tells A so, but A disbelieves it. That may sound rather confusing; it certainly presents a
confusing set of circumstances, all of which may, as the law now stands, produce different
results. So what seems on the face of it to be a simple failing of minds to come together can
result in a number of very different legal consequences, and that is the kind of situation the
law has to grapple with. It is by no means to be concluded that those exhaust all the
possibilities that must be contemplated.
On two or three occasions the committee found it prudent just to say, "Well, we have
debated this for several hours. Let us stop, go away, and come back again." We did that—I
think with some improvement to the Bill-but I am still very much in doubt as to whether we
have achieved perfection yet. I have very grave doubts that we will not be calling upon the
courts to fill up the gaps that we leave, and to apply new interpretations. What troubles
me-and this view was put to the committee very strongly-is that this will have to be done
at the expense of the private litigants. Our job is to make the law as complete, as perfect, and
as fine as we possibly can. Inevitably, some statutes have to be the subject of judicial
interpretation, but we should minimise that to the greatest possible degree. I have a fear
that, if we enact the Bill in even its amended form, we shall be submitting to the courts, and
to those who will have to take their problems to the courts, the task of interpreting the law we
have set out to make. I do not believe that we should repose the expense and trouble of
doing that on the private citizen. If we had another go at it, we could come up with a still
better Bill than the admittedly improved one that has been reported back. Accordingly, I
move, as an amendment, That all the words after "That" be deleted, and the following words
substituted, "the Bill be referred back to the Statutes Revision Committee for further con-
sideration.
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) seconded the amendment.

some element of disagreement on this point in the select committee. We were unanimous
that they should take the oath. We were also unanimous that we could not write it into the
Bill and that we should ask the Minister to see what he could do from an administrative point
of view.
The member for Auckland Central has moved that the Bill should be referred back to
the select committee for further consideration as to the status of aliens. I challenge that, and
suggest that the member for Auckland Central, in the course of his remarks to the House,
has not established how any further consideration of the status of aliens will assist the
committee on this matter. The Minister, both in the committee and in the House today,
indicated the possibility that all reference to aliens would be removed from the Bill, but none
the less we proceeded in the select committee on the basis that aliens were included in the
Bill, and dealt with that section accordingly. Can the member for Auckland Central state
what matters were raised in evidence or in discussion in the committee, before I received the
Minister's letter, to indicate some apprehension about the status of aliens? I believe there is
no good reason that the matter should be referred back to the select committee.
I was disturbed at the suggestion of the member for Auckland Central-to some extent
cleared up by the comments of the member for Henderson-that there had been some
discourtesy to the committee in the matter of the Minister's letter. I emphasise that the
relevant portions of the Minister's letter, which he read again to the House, were read to the
members of the select committee. In other words, it became a matter of record at the select
committee that the Minister possibly intended to remove that portion of the Act which
relates to aliens. I suggest that the committee was in absolutely no doubt about the Minister's
possible intention and of the possible course open to us in the select committee. Any
inference that there might have been discourtesy-and I realise that that suggestion was not
made by the member for Henderson, but that was certainly the word used by the member for
Auckland Central-or any suggestion of discourtesy are totally incorrect.
The House divided on the question, That the amendment be agreed to.

TUESDAY, 2 AUGUST 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Motor Cycle Gangs and Overstayers
1. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Prime Minister: Will he provide
specific examples of the manner in which the Ministers concerned had "not shirked their
tasks" (New Zealand Herald of 25 July), as he claimed to the National Party conference, in
dealing with motor cycle gangs and overstayers?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): As to overstayers, the Minister of
Immigration as early as February 1976 said, "No Government can afford to let a situation
develop in which its immigration requirements are being disregarded." This was clearly the
position at the time of the change of Government, and it was necessary for the National
Government to deal with a situation that had been allowed to develop for some considerable
time, in which those who flouted the law were placed at an advantage over their fellows who
obeyed the law and returned home at the expiry of visitor permits. As to motor cycle gangs,
contrary to the practice of the Labour Government the National Government has given full
support to the police, and has amended the Criminal Justice Act, the Police Offences Act,
and the Arms Act, to enable the police to search gang members suspected of carrying
weapons, to enter gang houses in certain conditions, and the courts to confiscate motor
vehicles, a course of action that was promised by the Labour Party in the 1972 election but
never carried out. At the same time financial support has been provided for social workers
working with gangs, and other assistance has been given to assist in bringing them back into
the mainstream of society.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Is the Prime Minister not on record as saying that the
overstayers' affair was an unholy mess; and in what way are the courts being given greater
powers to deal with motor cycles?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I have said something similar, and, indeed, it is correct. We
inherited that unholy mess from the Labour Government, which did nothing about over-
stayers or gangs, although it was a major plank in the policy of the Labour Party during the
1972 election campaign. The change of law for motor vehicles has been used by the courts
this year to confiscate the vehicles of gangs.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

of the area.

Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: Talks between the ARA and the Railways are continuing
about the report on this area.

Estate and Gift Duty Receipts
4. Mr BELL (Gisborne) asked the Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Depart-
ment: Could he advise the receipts from estate and gift duty separately, for the years ended
31 March 1974, 31 March 1975, 31 March 1976, and 31 March 1977, (a) in dollar terms, and
(b) as a percentage variation on the previous year?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department):
The amount of estate and gift duty received for the respective years was as follows: for estate
duty, for the March year 1974, $31 million, or a percentage increase of 16.1 percent; for the
March year 1975, $38.4 million, or an increase of 23.8 percent; for the March year 1976,
$50.5 million, or an increase of 31.5 percent; and for the March year 1977, $51.7 million, or
an increase of 2.8 percent. For gift duty, the figures are as follows: for the March year 1974,
$2.8 million, or a percentage increase of 51.3 percent; for the March year 1975, $2.75
million, or a decrease of 1.89 percent; for the March year 1976, $3.64 million, or an increase
of 32.47 percent; and for the March year 1977, $2.99 million, or a decrease of 17.58 percent.
Mr Bell: Can it be assumed that more property has been transferred because of the
greater exemptions provided in the 1976 Budget?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: The 1976 Budget increased the basic exemption from $4,000
to $8,000, which would explain the relatively small intake of gift duty of just under $3
million, which was a small decrease from the previous year. There must have been a
considerable increase in transactions as a result of that change.

Woollen Mills at Mosgiel and Ashburton
5. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Can he confirm that
the remarks of the managing director of Kaiapoi Textiles Ltd, in the Christchurch Press of 10
June, in which he is reported as saying that Mosgiel's decision to close the woollen mill and
the reduction in the mill's viability were partly attributable to the costs of fuel and transport
under this Government are correct, and can he also confirm that the difficulties being
experienced by the Ashburton woollen mill, now employing more than 300 people, are also
due to the doubling of transport charges under this Government?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I have seen the
newspaper report, and have noted the remarks attributed to the managing director of
Mosgiel Ltd. They certainly do not suggest that fuel and transport cost increases contributed
to the company's decision to phase out operations at the Kaiapoi mill. I can find no
justification for the conclusions drawn by the honourable member. The age of the boilers
and the relatively small scale of present operations may have made fuel costs more
burdensome at Kaiapoi than at the company's other mills. Transport costs borne by the
Kaiapoi mill undoubtedly reflect the distance of that plant both from the Dunedin mills and
the major markets. Mosgiel Ltd had actually stated that even a direct freight subsidy would
not significantly assist Kaiapoi. Lane, Walker, Rudkin Ltd, the owner of the Ashburton mill,
has, to my knowledge, not cited transport costs as a factor in its decision to withdraw from
woollen milling. In fact, the Ashburton mill made a good profit in its most recent trading
year.
Mr Kirk: How helpful was it to the industry to double its transport charges?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: It is quite evident from the press statement made by
the managing director, a copy of which I have here, that that factor was not a major one in
the firm's decision to go ahead with phasing out the mill. As the honourable member knows,
that trend started as far back as 1972, when the staff was gradually reduced during Labour's 3
years in office.
Mr Lambert: Could the Minister confirm that some increases in transport charges are
largely attributable to the previous Administration artificially holding down those costs?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Unequivocally, yes.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Have the departmental officers who went to Kaiapoi and Ashburton
to investigate the proposed closures of those undertakings presented their report to the
Minister; and, if so, is he or the Government in a position to take any positive action to
ensure that the mills do not close?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have received reports on approximately a weekly
basis of the discussions held by the officers of my department with the officials and
management of both mills. I have also had at least weekly discussions-perhaps more often
that that—with the members of Parliament for Rangiora and South Canterbury, who have
kept closely in touch with me on these matters.
Mr Talbot: In relation to the reply the Minister gave to the question about transport
costs from the member for Sydenham, would it be more correct to say that the main reason
for the planned withdrawal of Lane, Walker, Rudkin from the Ashburton mill is a desire by
that firm to rationalise its production?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Yes, and that is to some extent at the back of the
decision by Mosgiel in respect of Kaiapoi.
Hon. W. W. Freer: I ask the Minister to go back to my earlier supplementary question.
Can he or the Government take any action which is likely to ensure that either or both of
those mills do not have to close?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have made it clear in press statements and in
answering questions in the House that the Government is taking every initiative it possibly
can. We have several proposals before us in respect of both mills. Indeed, the member for
Rangiora has placed before my department, and before me, several alternatives if the mill
does close. He has interested other people in using the facility, to provide avenues for the
people now in employment to be re-employed in that building. One proposition would
include possibly five different companies operating in the very large mill area of 225 000 sq

Irrigation Schemes
6. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) asked the Minister of Works and Development: How
many major irrigation schemes are in existence in New Zealand, how many schemes have
been completed since the election of the present Government, and how many schemes have
been planned and remain in the pipeline awaiting approval?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): There are 24 major
irrigation schemes completed and in operation over an area of 103 740 hectares, and these
are all in Otago and Canterbury. They were established from the 1930s through to the late
1960s. With the approval by the present Government of the large Waiau Plains and
Maniototo irrigation projects, there will be 10 new irrigation schemes under construction this
year, and these have a total estimated cost of $27.7 million. They will irrigate a further 59 790
hectares. Maniototo and Waiau Plains represent 45 percent of this total area. Although not
yet completed, many of the schemes under construction are supplying water to some of their
area. A further 11 irrigation scheme proposals covering an area of 18 760 hectares are at
various stages of the design and approval process. A further 21 potential irrigation schemes
are at early stages of investigation.
Mr Cooper: Can the Minister confirm that the 11 schemes being planned and the 21
under investigation are in the Otago and Canterbury areas?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: I can confirm that half the 11 irrigation scheme proposals are in
the Otago and Canterbury areas, and that the bulk of the 21 potential irrigation schemes are
in the Otago and Canterbury areas.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that 8 of the 11 schemes that the Minister states
are under way or commencing this year were approved or approved in principle by the
outgoing Labour Government, and that the remainder were subject to feasibility studies
under the Labour Government?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: The fact is that the schemes I have mentioned are under action by
this Government. We know that the Labour Government had many pipe dreams, but we are
establishing those schemes and they are getting under way this year.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Is the Rakaia scheme one of those that the Minister considers is
urgently necessary and is proceeding rapidly?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: The Rakaia scheme is one of several which are being looked at at
present.

Foreign Fishing Vessel Entry Tax
8. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Customs: On how many
occasions since its inception has the foreign fishing vessel tax been imposed?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): The foreign fishing vessel entry tax was
introduced on 1 September 1976. During the period 1 September 1976 to 30 June 1977 there
were 656 foreign fishing vessel arrivals in New Zealand ports, 41 of which were exempted
from the tax because the arrivals were due solely to reasons of emergency. Thus, the tax has
been collected on 615 occasions.
Mr Courtney: Does the figure given by the Minister indicate that there has been a drop
in the number of foreign fishing vessels visiting New Zealand ports since the introduction of
the tax?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: I regret I cannot give the member figures for earlier periods,
because no aggregate nation-wide figures were kept by the Customs Department before the
tax was imposed. We could get a comparison only by checking through individual arrival
records at each separate port, but from now on, of course, a close watch will be kept on the
position so that we are able to assess the trend.
Mr Allen: Can the Minister tell us the countries of origin of the foreign fishing vessels
visiting New Zealand during the period for which records have been kept?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: Of the 656 arrivals, 598 were from Japan, 13 from Taiwan, 25
from Russia, 8 from the United States, and 12 from other countries.

Car Pooling Schemes
9. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Finance: Will the support
of $70,000 to be made available for a car pooling scheme to operate across the Auckland
Harbour Bridge also be available for similar schemes developed by other local bodies
elsewhere?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The question of financial support for
car pooling schemes must be seen in the context of the budgeted level of Government
assistance for urban transport. It is anticipated that in the future the urban transport
authorities that are to be set up will initiate and co-ordinate car pooling schemes as part of
their overall responsibility for urban transport. Government assistance for the urban
transport authority is to be channelled through the Urban Transport Council, and will be
disbursed on the basis of approved comprehensive transport plans. Centres without urban
transport authorities will be eligible for project aid from the Urban Transport Council. Until
the new arrangements for urban transport have been established, the approach adopted by
the Government towards schemes developed by other local bodies will depend on the
progress of the North Shore to Auckland scheme and on the merit of the individual
proposals put forward.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: As the Auckland Regional Authority seems likely to become the
Urban Transport Council for the Auckland area—
Mr Birch: The urban transport authority.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: I stand corrected. As the Auckland Regional Authority appears
likely to become the urban transport authority for the Auckland area and, on the available
evidence, seems to have had nothing at all to do with the proposed car pool scheme across
the harbour bridge, why is it that the North Shore has been singled out for this preference
above all other areas?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Principally, I think, because it is the one that has been put
forward. I know of no others at the moment.
Mr McLay: Does the fact that the Auckland Harbour Bridge Act says that the bridge is
the major practical road link between the North Shore and the Auckland isthmus mean that
the Auckland Harbour Bridge particularly lends itself to a pilot car pooling scheme, in the
course of which the value of car pooling as a conservation measure can easily be evaluated?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I should think that if that question was put into a simple
proposition, the answer would be yes.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: I take up the Prime Minister's simpler proposition that a car pool
scheme between the North Shore and Auckland has been put forward, and ask whether that

been no later publicity to correct the implications made in the article of a July publication. I

Miller's Ltd, Christchurch-Sackings
11. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Has he seen the
report in the Christchurch Star of 29 June 1977 in which Miller's Ltd blamed the mass
sackings of clothing workers in its Christchurch factory on clothing export quotas negotiated
with the Australians by this Government; and, if so, can he clarify what he meant by the
claim that Miller's had nobody to blame but itself for having to sack 100 workers?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I have seen the
report of Miller's Ltd in the Christchurch Star of 29 June 1977, and I have also seen the report
of 29 June, in which I was misquoted in the way the honourable member has suggested. I put
out a press statement at that time to make my position clear. The NAFTA arrangement on
apparel has assured New Zealand manufacturers of the opportunity to send at least 4 000 000
garments to the Australian market this quota year. It has minimised the disruptive effect of
the restrictions Australia found itself obliged to impose. Obviously the ceiling that was set on
New Zealand exports will, however, have affected different companies in different ways,
depending on how they had geared up in the expectation of further expansion in their sales
to Australia.
Hon. W. W. Freer: How can the Minister reconcile his statement to the garment
manufacturers at their conference in Queenstown that they should go ahead and expand
their sales to Australia with his press statement to the effect that a number of companies
brought this problem upon themselves?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The statement was made late last year, before the
impetus developed by the New Zealand industry was known to the Government-or to
anyone for that matter, because many factories are involved. At Queenstown, I said I was
seeking to encourage manufacturers to export to Australia and elsewhere, but, at the same
time, I made it quite clear that, as the Australians were moving towards some restriction on
apparel exports, the New Zealand industry should be warned and take that fact on board in
its consideration of further development. At the conference it became clear that the rate at
which New Zealand had been exporting—that is, about $14 million worth a year—would be
increased quite spectacularly. At that, point I told the garment manufacturers that they
would have a problem if they went ahead at that rate.
Mr Downie: What would have been the alternative for the New Zealand clothing
manufacturers had the Government not negotiated with Australia for an export quota?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The Minister of Overseas Trade and I were
informed in September 1976, when we undertook initial negotiations during the period this
Government has been in office, that the Australians had questions about their access to our
market and about the acceleration of our exports to Australia. On my return to New
Zealand I informed the New Zealand industry of the tenor of the discussions. It became
obvious that, if we accepted the Australian recommendation of making the cut-off point the
March or even the June 1976 year, we would have a much smaller quantity of exports to
Australia rather than the 4 000 000 garments that have been established.
Mr SPEAKER: Question 12.
Hon. W. W. Freer: A point of order, Mr Speaker. With due respect, we have had only
two supplementary questions on this important question, and I am wondering whether it is
not possible to address one or two more supplementary questions to the Minister.
Mr SPEAKER: In the ordinary course, I would not mind, but the relative Standing
Order says, "At the discretion of Mr Speaker supplementary questions to elucidate an
answer may be asked by any member." The honourable member has already asked one. It
was not seeking elucidation, but was generally germane to the particular subject. We have
already used seven-eighths of our time with just over half the questions asked, and the
proper procedure for me is to try to nudge the House on a little. That is my sole motive.

Drugs-Illegal Importation
DRUGS ILLEGAL IMPORTATION
Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga): I am directed by the Social Services Committee to present
the report of the committee on the petition of Canon I. A. Clarke and 258 others, praying for
a full and public inquiry into the financing and importation of illicit drugs. The committee
heard evidence from Mr Paul Phillips, acting for the petitioners, and from Superintendent
Churches of the Police Department, on two occasions. By reason of the nature of the
evidence tendered, Mr Phillips was placed on oath. Evidence from the petitioners was
submitted in written, oral, and taped form. Many of the tapes had already been supplied to
the Police, and the committee is of the opinion that the House should require the petitioners
to supply the balance to the Police in order to provide a complete series of information.
The committee is not persuaded that a public inquiry into the importation and financing
of illicit drugs would be an effective vehicle for combating a problem of increasing
dimension, nor does it believe that an inquiry, at this stage, and bearing in mind the recent
commencement date of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, would achieve anything beyond that
attainable by current enforcement measures-if only because information which might be
provided could, in all likelihood, fall short of the standards required to secure a conviction.
On the other hand, an inquiry would put on guard those who deal in illicit drugs. In fact,
such an inquiry may well be counter-productive if law enforcement agencies were
constrained to divulge their methods of operation. Moreover, the committee is well aware of
the danger of suggesting that a situation be created wherein it would be possible, under the
cloak of immunity from legal action, to accuse a person of illegal dealing in drugs without a
shred of sustainable evidence. The law makes ample provision for the citizen to pass on
information about criminal activity. The committee does not intend to recommend another
avenue of a purely transient nature.
While in no way denigrating the worth of the petitioners' evidence, the committee
cannot escape the impression that it simply disclosed, albeit in a dramatic form, situations of
a type well known to the Police. It did not lend weight to the actual prayer of the petition-it
illustrated the known problem. However, the committee considers that there are certain
matters upon which the House should recommend to the Government that action be taken.
First, any difficulty or doubt experienced by a public servant arising from the Public Service
Regulations 1964 in communicating information to the Police about international or domes-
tic dealing in drugs should be removed. Evidence was tendered which suggested that public
servants have some difficulty in reconciling an interpretation of regulation 42(2) and (3) of
the 1964 regulations with their inclination to supply information to the Police. The position
of officers and employees of the Inland Revenue Department is a separate matter and the
committee makes no recommendation in that regard. Second, the committee submits that
the House recommend to the Government that it examine ways and means of increasing
manpower and resources within those departments charged with the administration or the
enforcement of the provisions of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, so as to enable those
departments to perform their functions and duties on a wider basis.
The committee recommends that the House order that all evidence, but not including
tapes already surrendered or about to be surrendered to the Police, be held by the Clerk of
the House and that no person be granted access to that evidence without express authorisa-
tion from the Speaker. The committee also recommends that its report be adopted and
agreed to. I move, That this report be adopted and agreed to, and that it be referred to the
Government for serious consideration.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I raise the matter
of the procedure adopted by the chairman of the committee. As you know, the effect of his
last few words is to present the House with a non-debatable motion. In effect, the committee
has recommended that some portion of the petition be referred to the Government for
consideration, which permits only a short thank-you speech by the member who presented
the petition. However, before those words were spoken the chairman made quite a lengthy
speech containing material that some members might want to debate. This puts everybody in
an awkward position in that the procedure being followed-after a most interesting oration
by the chairman-deprives other members of the opportunity they ought to have to
comment, if they wish to, on what has been said. We should not be stifling debate by a non-
debatable motion. I wonder if you could consider the propriety of a procedure of this nature.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I gathered that the member was reporting
to the House a resolution of his committee, on which, doubtless, members on both sides
were represented. There is no doubt whatever that we have given ourselves Standing Orders
with a certain purpose in mind. I do not know whether the committee's resolution was
unanimous or not, but even that is immaterial. The motion is in front of the House, and our

Standing Orders are so framed that we do not debate these matters unnecessarily. I am sure

Hon. T. F. Gill: Read on: "or any other purpose".
Mr HUNT: If we use the words "or any other purpose", we must consider what comes

obtained from a motion directing the committee to do so.

from the Opposition, but nevertheless there are 80 other members of Parliament who have
rights, just as the 7 members who served on the committee have rights.

the circumstances. The matter should end there. The member for Henderson probably

as it was being read. There is no provision for debate.

APPROPRIATION BILL-FINANCIAL STATEMENT
Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata): The 1977 Budget looks to the future in its dramatic
emphasis on priority for New Zealand's energy needs and transport requirements; yet it still
emphasises the present in its protection of family life. That protection is evident in the
introduction of rebates for families with children under the age of 10, and the extension of
the rebate for families with children under the age of 5 which was introduced in last year's

youngsters will be much better off than their parents could have envisaged in November
1975. The Government made no promises about family rebates at that election, but its
record in this area is unequalled. The Opposition has offered carping criticism at the
introduction of the rebates, but its period of administration was noted only for the revision of
the tax scales with no comparable benefit for family life.

under the age of 5, and $4 a week for single-income families with children under the age of
10, are provided for. No earnings limit for rebate qualification by families with children
between the ages of 5 and 9 has been set. The limit for families with children under the age of
5 is $240 a week, the rebate being reduced when earnings exceed $150 a week. The third tax
reduction in the Budget is the increase in the wife's rebate from $375 to $520 per annum.

benefits are passed on to them from 1 October this year. I imagine that very few Opposition

I now wish to turn to the other aspect of the introduction to my speech, namely, energy,
and what the Government has done in the energy sphere through the Budget. As a young
member of Parliament, I am concerned as I look at the future prospects for energy in New
Zealand. It should be apparent to all that our cities have grown and sprawled because of the
availability of cheap petrol and the inexpensive nature of motors. The position is changing
already, and it will reach its final breaking point, in my view, by about 1985. In the
meantime, it is obvious that the New Zealander will not accept an immediate stop to urban
sprawl because, regrettably, the need to change our way of life is not readily accepted. I
should mention in passing that there has been a fairly effective stop to urban sprawl in west
Auckland. Members may recall that the Government promised in its election manifesto to
fence off our cities. Well, thanks to the policies of the Auckland Regional Authority in
refusing to allow further sewerage development in the west Auckland area, the Auckland
Regional Authority has sewered off west Auckland.
While the present position continues in Auckland, one can envisage the growth of
Manukau City and the south Auckland area at a rate of about 7000 people a year, Waitemata
City in west Auckland at the rate of about 5000 people a year, and Takapuna City in the
northern part of Auckland at the rate of about 4000 to 5000 people a year. This growth is
taking place on the periphery of Auckland at a distance of about 10 to 15 miles from Queen
Street, the one-time heart of Auckland City.
This growth must be viewed against our future supply of energy. The recent report by
the New Zealand Energy Resources and Development Committee indicates that in the long
term the availability of oil is probably the dominant factor in determining current and future
energy prices. The report states that there is little doubt that world oil production will peak
before the turn of the century, and possibly by 1990. That is only 13 years away. If we
imagine the position in 1985, when the world's resources of oil are starting to be depleted
and the countries with oil are selling to the highest bidder, and when we know that some of
the richest countries have the greatest need for oil, we realise that New Zealand will hardly
be in the race. Some members will have been to North America, where people are heavily
dependent upon oil for the comforts of life.
Mr Hunt: Too dependent.
Mr D. M. J. JONES: I agree with the member for New Lynn that they are too
dependent-wastefully dependent. Although North America has oil resources at present, by
1985 it will be experiencing difficulties. If we try to imagine New Zealand competing in this
area, we will realise that it will have difficulty being in the race at all. It is beholden upon us
all to conserve energy, to install insulation in our homes, to install solar water heaters, to
ensure that when that time comes at the end of the century we will be in a good position to
protect ourselves. We may think that coal will protect us in the future, but we have only
sufficient reserves of coal for 10 or 12 base-load coal-fired power stations each of 1000 MW
output—that is, each the size of Huntly—and each with a lifetime of 30 years. This highlights
the urgency of the energy problem, and the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy
Resources should be congratulated for the emphasis placed in the Budget on the spending of
funds to ascertain our reserves with certainty. One of the likely sociological changes in the
future is a return to an extended family relationship, when we realise that we can no longer
live too far away from our relatives because we will never see them. We will start living in
smaller houses that are well insulated, and we will return to the extended family which will
be a much better way of life than the present nuclear family.

been to cut the fertiliser subsidy far more ruthlessly than was ever contemplated by the
National Government.
In the sporting arena there is no question in my mind but that visas and passports would
have been withheld. A Labour Government would have taken great notice of statements
made by the interest groups that it normally listens to, and I am sure would have withheld
visas and passports. However, from the comfort of the Opposition benches, where they do
not have to suffer the consequences of what they say, Opposition members now apparently
claim that they would not have done that.
The comments made on the superannuation scheme have been really interesting. The
member for Hutt repeated warnings that we have heard frequently in the last few weeks that
the Labour Party plans to cut back the superannuation scheme if it becomes the Government
again. All people who have reordered their lives on the assumption that their superannua-
tion income will continue-and I am talking now about those who are above the poverty line
but who for many years have felt the very sharp, grinding effect of inflation—should be
warned that they will have to make yet further plans to reorder their commitments, their
assets, and their lives in the event of Labour's being returned to office. There is no doubt in
my mind that a future Labour Government would reduce the national superannuation
scheme, perhaps by way of imposing a means test. It might do so in a number of ways, and
we cannot say which method would be adopted. However, let us see what that would mean.
If a means test was reintroduced, it could be assumed: first, that the majority of
beneficiaries formerly receiving universal superannuation—that is, almost 112 000 New
Zealanders-would no longer be eligible for national superannuation, or would have a
reduced entitlement; secondly, that the majority of the 64 000 new applicants—and we are
not talking peanuts, but in tens of thousands-would no longer be eligible for national
superannuation, or would have a reduced entitlement; thirdly, that the majority of the 21
000 people who received age benefits paid at a reduced rate as at 31 March 1976 would have
a reduced entitlement. The reintroduction of a means test could result in 197 000
beneficiaries being affected in some way. The figures I have given are just estimates, but
they show that nearly a quarter of a million New Zealanders would have to change their life
styles and the plans they have made if a means test were imposed and their superannuation
income reduced.

We would have to assume that this spokesman on Post Office affairs has a very limited future
