I come to the equation on which were based the increased Post Office charges. We
started the 1977-78 year with a profit of approximately $20 million. The extra revenue from
the new charges is estimated to bring in during the balance of the year approximately $60
million, making a total of $80 million. We deduct from that the $50 million estimated
increase in costs to date, plus a further notional cost increase allowance for the rest of the
year of, say, $10 million, making a profit for 1977-78 of about $20 million. The all-important
assumption here is that this is boosted by the $60 million we will receive in revenue from the
extra charges. Had we not done this, we most certainly would have been in the red again
because of cost increases-a problem that I think every member in the House is familiar
with, and which this Government is working hard to deal with.
The increased charges from early 1976 restored the finances of the Post Office to a
proper basis, but the additional $104 million in revenue was largely taken up in recovering
from the previous year's $38.7 million loss—in the last year of the Labour Government's
administration—and in meeting additional costs of $44.4 million. In addition, borrowing
from the National Development Loans Account was $32.5 million less, thereby saving a
substantial amount in interest charges. I have been asked what effect these price increases
will have on the consumer price index. The calculation is based on the assumption that the
cost will be spread over two consumer price indexes, one of 0.44 percent for the quarter
ended 31 December 1977, and another of 0.20 percent for the quarter ended 31 March
1978-not astronomical increases.
During the last 2 weeks I have been disturbed by suggestions of inefficiency in the Post
Office, and this is an occasion to place before the public some facts and figures that will give
an indication of its achievements. Much has been achieved in running an organisation of its
size and in maintaining services of the size and scale of those that the Post Office runs. First,
the postal service handles about 2 000 000 articles each day; about 90 percent of all letters are
delivered within a day, and about 40 percent of all rural people receive at least a five-days-a-
week mail delivery service. Only a tiny fraction of 1 percent of mail fails to arrive at its
destination. There is a vast service for overseas mail; for example, a letter posted in
Auckland this afternoon will be delivered in many places in England or Europe by Thursday
morning. I challenge anyone to produce a postal system that supports a record of that sort
over the distance to which this particular service operates. Subscriber toll dialling already
serves more than 39 000 subscribers. More than 93 percent of all subscribers have automatic
service. The density of telephones in New Zealand compares very favourably with that of the
rest of the world.

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: Members can see how easy it is to get under the skin of the

something of the role of the largest trading department in the country. It employs about

weathered particularly well the challenges placed upon it, including the catastrophic
management of its finances between 1972 and 1975 by the Labour Government. This

future financing of this great trading department. We have already absorbed the social as

of the service under the Labour Government. We have faced many problems with our
capital programme.

I turn now to the livestock incentive scheme, and the fertiliser subsidy. In my opinion
the present taxation system fails to distinguish between the efficient and the inefficient
farmer. It rewards capital, particularly capital gain, rather than production. Taxation can be
a positive step towards achieving the Government's economic and social goals, but it must be
used to stimulate farmers, not to force them to retrench. The Government has said it will
remove some of the incentive to spread fertiliser, so a farmer will be able to grow less grass,
yet the Government is providing an incentive to put more stock on less grass. It certainly is
an accountant's Budget. How silly to pretend that by growing less grass, and encouraging
more stock, a good deed is being done for the farming community.
During the second world war British farmers were told how to operate their land. One
farmer received an instruction to carry on ploughing. He sent back a brief message, “Sorry,
busy lambing". He received another message from the bureaucrats, "Postpone the lambing,
get on with the ploughing." That story reminds me of the present Government. In two
successive Budgets the Government has reduced the subsidy on fertiliser. When a farmer has
feed and grass available he knows best whether to put more stock units on to the grass, or to
grow them bigger, put more weight on them, or produce more wool. He should be left to
make the decision. But the Government is making it for him, because this is a bureaucratic
Government run by an accountant.
The Budget mentioned a second modification to the livestock incentive scheme, aimed
at easing the entry requirement for smaller farmers. It is proposed that the stock unit
increase be reduced from 100 to 50. The Government has not reduced the requirement,
because it is still necessary to have 65 cows or 1000 stock units. What is written in the Budget
is just humbug. The Minister of Finance has no understanding or maybe it was the
Associate Minister of Finance who wrote that portion. The Ministers should consider the
farming people, who know something about these matters.
I turn now to a more important consideration—the balance of payments. The deficit for
the March 1977 year was $861 million, as shown in the July Abstract of Statistics. The
Government has failed to grasp the opportunity to use the extra $1,000 million. It had the
income and blew the lot. On page 2 of the Budget it is stated that our job is to expand
production. No one else can do that for New Zealand-I go along with that. It is the
Government's job to help the farmer increase his production. Page 2 of the Budget states,
"world demand and market access, are largely beyond our power to influence". If we cannot
increase production to meet our overseas balance of payments we will be broke—that is what
the Government is saying.

is in trouble on other scores anyway, and I do not think I will have to withdraw on this one. I
understand, from viewing television tonight-and perhaps that was what was worrying the
Leader of the Opposition when he was speaking-that Labour members are going to win 12
seats in Auckland, and that they have 16 sitting or former members of Parliament wanting to
stand for those 12 seats. There are some very interesting possibilities. We are probably going

vying for the same position.
The Opposition has failed to grasp the true significance of this Budget. I want to go
through it carefully with members opposite, because I am sure they would appreciate being
shown its real value. I turn to the first sentence in the Budget: "The international economic
outlook is one of continuing uncertainty. In the short term there are no grounds for
optimism. There is no sign that international conditions will assist New Zealand's adjustment
to the difficult circumstances of recent years." A little further over, on page 2, we see: “Our
balance of payments outlook, which is a major determinant of economic policy, will depend
on three things: the growth in export production, world demand for our exports, and access
to markets. It is our job to expand export production. No one else can do that for us. The
other two factors, world demand and market access, are largely beyond our power to
influence." I have already dealt with the claim made by the member for Christchurch
Central about the results of the multilateral GATT agreements, and pointed out to him that
the Prime Minister made one of the biggest breakthroughs in this field that we can have.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Ha, ha!
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The member can laugh, but there was no chance of the previous
Government's achieving that. This is a matter upon which we should compliment the Prime
Minister, and not take the attitude that the member for Christchurch Central has taken. I am
trying to set these matters out so that members opposite can understand the statements in
the Budget. Table 2 of the Budget shows that the internal deficit, which in 1976 was more
than $1 billion, was reduced last year to $506 million. That is a substantial reduction in our
internal borrowing commitments.
This year, in spite of an increase in Government expenditure, we have still been able to
forecast a borrowing requirement of $382 million, which is too high, but a great improve-
ment on what we had before. Substantial reductions have been made in the internal deficit.
The Budget states on page 4 that there has been a very good recovery from a situation where
New Zealand was living far beyond its income-which is exactly what it was doing. It states
further: "We are still living beyond our income, but the gap is narrowing, and we have a
clear idea of what is ahead. . . . Economic growth is not an end in itself. It is, however, a
necessary prerequisite to the attainment of our society's individual and collective objectives,
whether they be expressed as the spending power of personal incomes, the quality of family
life, the quality and quantity of our social services, or the economic, social, and physical
environment in which we and succeeding generations will live."
That is the background against which the Budget should be considered. It has three
basic objectives, one of which is to increase the proportion of exports. How does the Budget
go about this? It emphasises, first and foremost, forestry, farming, and manufacturing. If
members opposite cared to look, they would see that under the section on farming there are
11 methods by which this objective could be attained. There are two most important
modifications in the livestock incentive scheme. The Budget also emphasises land settle-
ment, recommends deer farming as an export potential, makes changes in the concessional
internal rates of interest, provides for rural housing for farm workers and assistance to young
farmers buying their first homes, gives stamp duty exemption, and proposes a noxious plants
control scheme. The Opposition has been looking for some great cure-all-one sweep of the
brush and it will all be painted clean. That is impossible, so the Budget approaches the
matter on a broad basis.
Other matters that failed to draw the attention of members opposite were those
pertaining to my portfolio of education. The member for Christchurch Central spoke about
rural labour. One of the most important ways of retaining such labour is by providing
bursaries for rural school children. The National Government has a proud record in this. In
the past 2 years, boarding bursaries have been increased from $300 to $400, and in this
Budget by another $100, making $500 in all-an increase of 62 percent. In addition, and
related to agricultural production, is the increase in the allowable income for taxation
purposes for the payment of school fees. That is extremely important and is having a
beneficial effect upon people living in rural areas. There has been a continual upgrading of
rural opportunities with the opening of schools catering for children from Forms 1 to 7,


## p. 1779 (#235) ###########################################

2 August
1779
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
which means that the children of farm and other rural workers can remain at home instead of
going away to school. Another small but very significant item in the Budget provides that
people in remote areas need pay only the first $10 of fares for sending their children away to
school. I should highlight that the maximum rebate of $350 on school fees-and donations
for charitable purposes would be included-will total $3 million, taking into account the
rural sector involved.
The Budget includes seven separate policy proposals for increasing fishing, which has
very important export potential. I do not intend to go through all those proposals, but
members opposite would do well to look at them. I am sure that members on both sides of
the House wish the Prime Minister well in his coming talks with the Prime Minister of Japan
about an increase in that country's meat imports in return for fishing rights. Those talks are
vitally important to our country.
The Budget also emphasises the development of the efficient import replacement
industries, the most important of which deal with energy. Members opposite should examine
this in detail, as they would then see that the Government is making a substantial effort to
obtain the equivalent of an import replacement industry—that is, the equivalent in energy of
the vast sums we are paying for imported oil. Science has a very important role to play, and
my department is involved in a geological and geophysical assessment of geothermal and
coal exploration and investigation, and in the geophysical and geological exploration for oil,
and natural gas. It is also involved in solar heating research and thermal insulation. All these
come together to form a packet, and, although there may be many pieces, it is a very
comprehensive policy aimed, among other things, at reducing the cost of our imports. It
would be true to say that no other Budget has attempted so much.
The Budget contains a great number of very important and significant proposals for
implementing education policies and filling in gaps in education. I have a list of the policies
as they were set out, and the order in which they were placed. Had I been able to, I would
have given the reinstatement of the day relief scheme a lower priority. However, last year I
asked the teacher organisations where they placed it, and as it was their first priority put it in
that order. The restoration of the $2.2 million cost of the day relief scheme limited me in
what else I could do for primary and secondary education.
Next in the order of priority were the grants for the maintenance of schools, which were
increased from $23.9 million to $28.2 million-an overall increase of some 18 percent. That
was very important. Although some people are critical and say that the fabric of education is
being imperilled, they do not realise the amount of money that has been made available both
for grants of this sort and also for building programmes.
In addition, because we think it is important, there will be increased activity with the
National Council of Adult Education. The package includes early childhood education, and
we have been able to take a big step forward towards the possibility of all children, where
feasible, being able by 1980 to participate in pre-school education. We have approached the
problem from the point of view of using the manpower and physical resources available to
us. In the ensuing year, about 8000 more children will be able to have some form of pre-
school education.
One of the first steps has been to move from a reliance on purpose-designed buildings
towards greater use and adaptation of existing community facilities, resources, and person-
nel. To encourage people to understand the great value of early childhood education, a
further 15 pre-school community workers will be placed in selected rural areas in the
northern half of the North Island, and in selected urban areas, to advise and encourage
people to use the pre-school services in their localities. We are looking at the possibility of
using primary classroom accommodation, and of making more economic provision for pre-
school education buildings at selected new schools, and in some cases at existing schools
where there is continuing growth. This is an expansion of pre-school services at less cost than
that required for specific purpose-designed accommodation. Groups of very dedicated
people are working around New Zealand in small, non-profit-making, pre-school activities.
They have been ineligible for Government grants because, in general, their facilities are too
small or otherwise cannot meet the requirements necessary to become free kindergartens or
play centres. They will now be given grants towards the supervisors' salaries or for operating
expenses, or, in some cases, subsidies on equipment.
We will give increased assistance for alterations to buildings used as playcentres. Under
the present policy, playcentres get a subsidy of $4 for $1, with a maximum of $4,000, which
may be spent on renovating existing buildings. One of the problems has been that the
playcentre had to own the building, or have it for its sole use. We will waive the restriction

that the playcentre must have sole use of the premises, and we will increase the maximum
expenditure on which a subsidy is payable to $7,000. In addition, we will give grants of up to
$500 for the training of officers on-the-spot and of supervisors in playcentres. We will also
increase our activity in the mobile pre-school area. All these things form a package. None of
them are big in themselves, but taken together they make it possible for about 8000 more
children to get pre-school education.
We have a group of policies that deal with technical institutions and community
education. Now that we know the way in which to establish community colleges, the criteria
are clear. The first three community colleges will be established next year, at Whangarei,
Rotorua, and Southland. We have had problems for some time because students in senior
technical divisions in some secondary schools have been doing tertiary courses, but have not
been able to receive tertiary bursaries, and in other respects their position has been a little
uncertain. We have expanded the training in certain senior technical divisions of secondary
schools to provide for their qualification for a subsidy. We have set up a whole new
programme of courses of considerable interest that are very important in relation to the
export drive in primary industries, with which most of them are associated. The courses
cover industrial implementation, auto electricity, auto mechanics, and motorcycle
mechanics-which are important for the maintenance of chainsaws, farm motorbikes, and so
on. Other courses include printing and photo-engraving, and timber machine and saw
doctoring, which are very important to the forestry industry. We have also established two
new paramedical courses. There has been criticism of the amount by which tertiary bursaries
have been increased. We inherited from the previous Government a standard tertiary
bursary.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: What did you promise?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It was hastily put together, and full of anomalies. We made some
promises for immediate implementation-for example, the A and B bursary. That has been
implemented. We promised that we would have a reformed bursary, and that it would be
devised in close consultation with all the interested parties. Last year, the conference
identified a whole group of further anomalies, almost all of which have been rectified in the
Budget.
In addition, although there was no real compulsion according to our policy, we agreed
to increase the standard tertiary bursary. If the Deputy Leader of the Opposition looks at the
policy carefully, he will see that we agreed to increase the reformed bursary. Because of the
circumstances, I believed that it was necessary to increase the present bursary. The standard
tertiary bursary was worth $24, with an abatement of $11, so that people who did not qualify
for the boarding component received only $13. It was instituted by the previous Govern-
ment, and the first payments were made last year. It is interesting that the increase from 1975
until the presentation of this Budget is from $14.6 million to $27.2 million. Even taking into
account that extra people are obtaining the standard tertiary bursary, the Government
money spent on bursaries represents an increase of 86 percent in 2 years.
Members might like to know that that amount represents about three times the
expenditure on pre-school education, about six times the expenditure on the National
Library Service, and about 18 percent of all the expenditure on university education—that is,
teachers' salaries, maintenance of university buildings, research work inside the buildings,
and lectures. It can honestly be said that to the majority of students who received the abated
bursary, the increase is about 15 percent this year, which can be justified as reasonable. I
have already dealt with what is involved within the package for rural education. The Budget
also implements other policies relating to special education. One of particular value is the
payment that will be made to parents who have to relocate their families in order that
handicapped children may attend special schools. Those parents will be given an allowance.
Probably one of the most interesting matters in the Budget, to which I shall refer only
briefly, shows clearly that the Government is aware of the need for conservation. I suppose I
have had as much satisfaction from the decision to continue microfilming our precious
newspaper records as I have had from anything else. I regard that decision, at a time when
we have financial restrictions, as praiseworthy, and emphasise that it is essential for
conservation. The Budget consists of a great number of small items, which in the aggregate
will help to form the basis for our great movement forward in the next few years. If
Opposition members look carefully at the way in which the Budget has been drafted they will
see that it is an exercise in sensible government; a basis for our final move away from the
dreadful economic conditions we inherited from the Labour Government.

Corporation as from 1 November 1977, and this is particularly important to Whangarei. The
scheme will not only encourage the construction of larger vessels in our shipyards, but will
also help to develop new fisheries. Whangarei has greeted this with enthusiasm.

am extremely sceptical of the designation and zoning, which are based on need rather than
on what is wanted. There are still a few sections left in some of these areas. As they are not

daughter, or decide later what you will do with it. If you do not use it now, you do not need
it."
I consider this principle extremely dangerous, as in some areas it has reached the stage
where private landowners have no say in the use of their land. In some cases, it is said that
the land is not being taken directly by the Crown-although in some cases it is, and
inadequate compensation is being paid. It is argued that the use of the land is being restricted
in the public interest. We are playing right into the hands of extremists and left-wingers who

sucked in by socialists posing as environmentalists. On page 118, Professor Morton states:
"Different attitudes will be required of us as individuals.'

Auckland. He has been the member for that region for many years,so he should know all

they took the area for granted. Their approach to the needs of the area bore no relation to its
requirements or reasonable demands.
I shall illustrate this. By December 1975 there was chaos in the health services. There
was no real plan, although a plan was needed in the light of two particular developments.
The first was the population explosion; the second the influx of our neighbours from the
Pacific Islands. The region demanded a review of the health services provided, but no
serious consideration was given. I pay tribute to the Auckland Hospital Board and Dr Frank
Rutter, its Chairman, for the way in which the board is now-backed, supported, assisted,
and encouraged by the Minister of Health-facing up to the challenge the region offers.
Much credit must go to the Minister of Health for the series of visits he has paid to south
Auckland to discuss with Dr Rutter and Dr John Jeffrey, the District Medical Officer of
Health, ways in which the Government can best assist, and to bring the two together in some
sensible arrangement. The result has been two-fold. First, there has been a realistic
assessment of the health needs of one-fifth of a million people—that is the number we are
talking about in south Auckland. As a result of that assessment, some action has already
been taken. For example, in the last few months approval has been given for the acquisition
of land for the construction of general hospitals in east Tamaki and Papakura. Each hospital
will contain 300 acute general beds, a 120-bed geriatric unit, and a 20 to 40-bed obstetric
unit, plus accident and emergency departments, and the usual supporting clinical depart-
ments. In addition, the Auckland Hospital Board has opened a base at Middlemore Hospital
for extramural services, which it intends to expand into the south Auckland area. The aim of
the National Government, in co-operation with the Auckland Hospital Board, is to
decentralise services so that health is taken to the community. There is no better vehicle for
doing that than an extension of Auckland's extramural services.
Approval has been given to acquire land in the Manukau City centre to build a health
centre. Indeed, the purchase of land adjacent to the city centre shopping mall is being
negotiated, and planning is proceeding. That centre will be built by the Department of
Health, and the people of south Auckland are deeply indebted to the firm guidance,
leadership, and assistance provided by the Government and the Minister. The centre will be
manned by doctors and allied health professionals, and will specialise in community care. In
addition to the initial health centre, there will be further decentralised health centres in the
southern parts of the region.
In December 1975, the south Auckland district office of the Department of Health was
run down, and staff morale was poor. It was a neglected area. The present Minister has
increased the nursing establishment by 10, 6 of whom have already been recruited and are
operational, and some of them are working in schools in the area. There has been major
restructuring. Health services in the region have had a shot in the arm and are at the take-off
point. What did the Labour Government do in the area; why were such radical measures
required so urgently; and why were there three or four visits by the Minister of Health in
such a short time? Because of the neglect of the region by the local Labour members of
Parliament-the members for Otahuhu, Mangere, Manukau, and Manurewa. It ill behoves
the member for Henderson to enter the House, wailing and gnashing his teeth about neglect.
The people of south Auckland have known for years all about neglect, and they know where
the responsibility lies.

areas of education. That is a system whereby people are given a mass of information and
diverse opinion to sort out, so that they can form their own judgment on it. That is quite
appropriate in an institution of higher learning; it is a proper function there, and the
discretion of what to accept or reject is left to the pupils, who by that time have reached a
degree of maturity and can benefit from such an approach. That approach has moved
increasingly down into the lower educational institutions, and is the basis of considerable
differences in educational philosophy. It is inappropriate that the eclectic approach should
move from the universities down in to secondary schools and now, increasingly, into primary
schools.
A pupil is given a variety of approaches and is left to choose what he will. We see this
most destructively in social education and in moral or ethical training, because the schools
are no longer prepared to give a firm, definite, and consistent line of guidance. A variety of
opinions are handed out for the students to take. Most members have been invited to speak
to liberal studies classes, and when we inquire what sort of people come to speak to them we
find that that approach is given in all sorts of fields. That applies even for quite young ages.
Students are given a variety of approaches on a variety of disputed social matters, and they
are quite unable to make discriminatory judgments. The only thing they really learn from
that approach is that the way they approach the subject does not matter, because no one will
say which of the various approaches is good or bad. They know they can have any approach
to social matters, to violence, to sex, and to promiscuity, because these are being handed out
by a multiplicity of lecturers who go to liberal studies classes. We are seeing this confusion
reflected in the young people emerging from our schools.
I am particularly concerned at the lack of appreciation of the difference between
education and training. This has had a destructive effect on the students in training colleges,
and increasingly it is presumed that, once a person is told about something and is taught its
basic skills, he knows how to do the job. I believe that a training programme that is repetitive
and teaches the rules appropriate for discipline is essential. It is not appreciated that training
has as important a part to play in education as has the imparting of information, but young
people are leaving school untrained in the social virtues, and unable to make moral and
socially valuable judgments.
Mr Elliott: What about the place of the home?
Dr WALL: The policies implemented by National Governments over the past 15 years
have made it increasingly impossible for this training to be given exclusively in the home,
because it is now necessary for both parents to work.
Miss Dewe: Teaching them morals is a home job.
Dr WALL: At last we have heard the story. The member for Lyttelton says that
teaching morals is the home's job. That philosophy is causing the trouble. The school is given
no part to play, and that is why violence in our streets is increasing, as is the number of
children the education system has failed.
Provision has been made for community colleges in three areas. When the Minister took
up his portfolio, another two community colleges were planned. They were scrapped last
year, and I am pleased this decision has been reconsidered. I believe that to a considerable
extent community colleges will be seen as "second chance" schools. Most people consider
them to be a second chance for the pupils, but I believe that they should be more correctly
regarded as a second chance for the teachers. The children for whom our education system
has proved inadequate will be able to attend these colleges, and the teachers will be able to
give them a second go. I am thinking particularly of people in the lower-income groups, and
it is unfortunate that this group includes so many people of Polynesian ancestry-whether
from the Maori community, or from the Pacific islands.
Great steps were made under the Labour Government, and some have been kept up
under the National Government, to cope with the disorientation these children feel by
introducing into our educational system a sense of the value of their cultural background.


## p. 1798 (#254) ###########################################

1798
2 August
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
That was a forward and imaginative step, and more should be done with it. If, by doing this,
anyone imagines they have coped with the cultural differences of the people brought up in
the marae system, whether in New Zealand or overseas, as against the cultural requirements
of the European community, they are sadly astray.
This matter was summed up by a deputation of Islanders, led by a remarkably intelligent
Cook Islander from my electorate, who visited the former Minister during the last few weeks
of the Labour Government. They said that one of the reasons they had come to New
Zealand was to promote the education of their children. The schools in the islands were
good, but the standard was not high enough. They were tremendously disappointed to find
that, after being used to an educational system in which children were made to learn, in New
Zealand the children were merely taught. One has only to think of the cultural background
of the marae to realise that such an approach to children promoted the feeling that they were
deserted, disappointed, and let down by our education system. In the marae tradition, every
adult caring for or associated with the children was seen in some way to be in loco parentis,
through the community of interest and the concern of the whole community. When the
Islanders sent their children to school, they expected the school to do exactly what the
parents would have done if they had had the opportunity and the expertise-to see that their
children learned. The education system has failed those children, and children from lower-
income groups, because it no longer sees that the children learn. It merely sees that the
children are taught.
Over the last 30 or 40 years, there has been a great move to remove all aspects of
compulsion from the learning process, and a tendency to promote discipline by attraction
rather than compulsion. Whilst this may be of benefit to those of an intellectual capacity,
who welcome and enjoy the whole education process, it fails those who do not view school
with such enthusiasm, and particularly children from homes where there has been no
continuing tradition of academic achievement and respect. That is the case for practically all
children from lower-income groups. These groups need the extra pressure of compulsion and
discipline imposed in the learning process, but they are being failed by our schools at
present. For this reason, schools are no longer compatible with the cultural background and
traditions of people involved in the marae culture. The schools are not fulfilling the
requirements of the Polynesian groups and the lower-income groups, where the children do
not have pressure put on them.
If pressure were applied to the children of poorer families they would achieve academic
success, whether they intended to achieve it or not. Peter Fraser introduced that characteris-
tic into the education system, and he has been lavishly praised tonight. We saw a tremendous
development of people from the lower-income groups, and their advance into the higher
academic echelons. That is no longer happening, because the development of the education
system has increasingly catered for the needs of the affluent, of those with a strong academic
tradition, and of those who have the means to provide the necessary support for their
children while they are at school. Until our educationalists face the fact that, under
changing, modern conditions, what is needed to make progress is to go back to the system
that supplied what is no longer available, we will achieve nothing. They must ensure that
children are not allowed to make judgments that may be destructive of themselves. The
schools must insist by discipline-imposed, if necessary, by force--that the children attain
some degree of academic excellence. Under that system the children of the poor did well;
under the present system they do not.

early stages of borrowing. I shall present the true and factual picture. The interest rate has

He said that the Government had not lowered the basic stock units in the stock incentive
scheme. I find that very difficult to understand—perhaps he cannot read the Budget. It is
very easy to quote a minimum. The member could have said that anyone with 10 stock units
would not gain anything from this reduction. I invite him to think about what constitutes an
economic sheep and cattle farm. I am sure he knows enough about agriculture to agree with
me that 1000 stock units—the figure he mentioned-do not constitute an economic unit in
this day and age. If a farm carries about 2500 stock units, the reduction of the qualifying
increase to 50 stock units equates with the initial minimum 2 percent increase requirement,
which is the other wing of the stock incentive scheme. That 2 percent requirement, which
previously covered 5000 stock units, has now been reduced by the minimum qualifying
increase to 2500 stock units.
The livestock incentive scheme introduced in the 1976 Budget has been very successful.
To the end of June this year, over 3300 applications had been received, resulting in a stock-
unit increase of 3 500 000. As New Zealand is carrying about 109 000 000 stock units, that
represents a 3.2 percent increase. I should like to compare that to the increase in the stock
unit numbers in the previous year, most of which was during the socialist Labour Govern-
ment's term in office. The increase in 1975 was only 0.066 percent. The stock incentive
scheme has given vital and effective encouragement to sheep farmers-and I remind
members opposite that the Labour Government encouraged farmers to kill their stock. I
would put that increase of 3.5 million stock units directly to the credit of the stock incentive
scheme. The Budget has adjusted the required increases in stock unit numbers, in terms of
developing carrying capacity, from the previous 2 percent a year for a 3-year programme to 2
percent in the first year-no change-to 1 percent in the second year, making a cumulative
total of 3 percent, and a further 1 percent for the third year, making a cumulative total of 4
percent, as against the required cumulative total of 6 percent when the scheme was
introduced. If a farmer with 3000 stock units opts for the cash option of $12 per stock unit,
that will net him a further 60 stock units over the 3-year period, or an extra grant of $720.
The farmers in the Gisborne electorate-and I am sure I am speaking for farmers
throughout New Zealand—were battered and bleeding from the complete lack of under-
standing and support shown by the Labour Government. One of the first policy undertakings
the National Government put into effect on taking office was the extension of the fertiliser
bounty. Straight away, the farming community responded to the attitude of the National
Government, and this is the result today—and do not forget that we have been in office only
a little over 18 months. The adjustments in stock-unit increases and qualifying stock units
have answered, in the main, the complaint of the smaller farmer, to whom the minimum of
100 stock units represented an increase of over 2 percent, and also of those farmers-and
fortunately New Zealand is well endowed with them-who had in the past achieved a high
level of production, but had found the 2 percent increase per annum for the 3-year period
difficult to achieve, without the further increase necessary to obtain a taxation or cash
benefit. The Government promised to review the scheme in the 1976 Budget. After a year's
experience, the review has been carried out; these two areas of mild criticism have been
answered.

legislation for those contemplating farm purchase. The 1977 Budget has extended that initial

immediately, on Budget night. The National Party's 1975 manifesto, which has been freely

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Drug Law Enforcement Courses
1. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Customs: How many drug law
enforcement courses were conducted by his department during the year ended 31 March
1977?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): My department's training curriculum
does not include courses devoted solely to drug law enforcement. However, all formal
training courses conducted by the customs central training school—that is, some 53 in the
year ended 31 March 1977—include sessions on narcotic identification, detection, and
current trends in importation and use. This system of education has been found to be the
most effective in teaching and updating the knowledge of the many officers likely to
encounter narcotics in the normal course of their work. The needs of the smaller number of
officers requiring more in-depth knowledge of narcotics legislation and investigation tech-
niques are catered for on courses organised and run by the Police Department. Co-operation
between Police and Customs in these courses is excellent, and Customs staff play a full role
in providing both course members and instructors.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Electors-Proof of Identity
2. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Justice: Is he aware
that President Carter has stated his intention of legislating for electors to be able to vote on
election day on reasonable proof of identity, even though not enrolled, and that several
states in the United States already have such a system which works successfully, and, if so,
will he draw this to the attention of the Chief Electoral Officer and ask for a report on
measures to facilitate the exercise by New Zealanders of the democratic right and duty to
vote on election day?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Every state in the United States has its
own electoral law, and there is no one law for the United States of America. I have no details
of the proposal the honourable member referred to. New Zealanders already have the
democratic right and responsibility to enrol as registered electors, and it is on this basis that
they are eligible to vote. However, I shall watch with interest any development in the United
States.
Hon. Michael Connelly: If I supply the Minister with information on the report, will he
arrange for such an investigation to be undertaken?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I will be happy to refer to the Chief Electoral Officer any
such information the member gives me.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: In the light of the last part of the original question, referring to the
exercise by New Zealanders of the democratic right and duty to vote on election day, will the
Minister take into account the need to amend existing legislation which allows non-New
Zealanders to vote in national elections in New Zealand?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I am conducting a study into the electoral law at present.
Mr Prebble: In view of the large number of people who are entitled to vote in New
Zealand but who have their votes disallowed every year because for one reason or another
they are not properly enrolled, will the Minister consider introducing the American system,
assuming that New Zealanders are at least as honest as Americans?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I have already told the House that a study of the electoral
law is taking place now, and in that study, of course, we will be considering whether any
amendment needs to be made to facilitate registration and voting.

Custody Orders-Fathers' Rights
3. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the
Department of Justice statistics 1976 for domestic proceedings, which indicate that a total of
2397 custody orders were made, including custody orders to the mother in 2150 cases, and


## p. 1808 (#264) ###########################################

1808
3 August
Oral Answers to Questions
does the Government propose any steps to overcome the inequality of fathers in such
situations?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I have seen the figures referred to. The
honourable member will know that the existing law, as set out in the Guardianship Act 1968,
focuses on the welfare of the child and does not discriminate against fathers. In many cases,
custody will be sought by the mother and not seriously opposed by the father. In other cases
the father will be unable to convince the court that he can make satisfactory arrangements
for the day-to-day care of the child while he goes out to work. The courts must retain a
discretion to act in what they see as the child's best interests, but it may be possible to
improve the practical application of the law in relation to fathers. This is currently being
studied in connection with the review of the law on matrimonial proceedings.
Mr Lange: Do the 2150 cases where custody awards were made in favour of the mother
include those cases where custody was awarded by consent of the father, and do they also
include those cases where some of the children in the family were awarded into the custody
of the mother and some children into the custody of the father?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Presumably, that is so.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is it not correct that many fathers consent to custody being given to
the mother because they know it is a waste of money to try to get the courts to accept the
principle that families also need fathers?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I have no way of answering that question.
Mrs Batchelor: Does the Minister know in how many cases the father actually applies
for custody of the children?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No, I do not keep the answer to that question in my mind,
but it may be possible to obtain that information if the honourable member would give
notice of the question.

Department of Labour is regarded by my department as the official adviser on employment

matters and these things have occurred frequently under successive Governments—the
department refers companies to its appropriate division or to agencies such as the Develop-

Coastal Trader-Freight Charges
6. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Transport: Can he give the dates and
details of the increases made in the Coastal Trader's freight charges since December 1975,
and can he also indicate how the new transport pricing policy announced in the Budget will
affect the Coastal Trader's freight charges?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): The following freight rate
increases have been applied to the Coastal Trader service by the Shipping Corporation: on 12
February 1976, 30 percent on southbound cargo, and 26 percent on northbound cargo; on 14
July 1976, 35 percent on southbound cargo, and 29 percent on northbound cargo. On 1 July
1977, following a complete restructuring of the existing tariff, based on historical cargo
movements, the calculated increase in scheduled freight rates was a weighted average of
approximately 11 percent. On the question of the differential freight rates referred to in the
Budget, the Shipping Corporation began operating such a system for the Coastal Trader in
February 1976. The extent of any change in the present differential will be governed to a
large degree by any future movement in rail freight rates with which the corporation
maintains a relative competitive position.
Mr Kirk: As the Minister has said that any future movements in the freight rates for the
Coastal Trader will be tied to any increase in railway freight rates, can he indicate whether
during the next 6 months there will be another increase in railway freight rates?

Freight Rates
8. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Transport: Can he
elaborate on the recently announced changes in transport pricing policy to allow freight rates
to reflect actual costs to a greater extent, and can he state clearly how and over what period
this new policy will be implemented?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): The proposed restructuring of
inter-island freight rates has been designed not only to assist South Island manufacturers but
also to apportion the costs of freight services more equitably. As the predominant flow of
goods is at present from north to south, greater capacity and hence greater capital
expenditure must be provided to cope with this southbound traffic. The net result would be a
differential between northbound and southbound rates. Discussions have been initiated with
the Railways Department and the Shipping Corporation, who have agreed to implement
such a differential in their next review of freight rates.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: In view of the Minister's claim that the transport pricing policy
announced in the Budget would assist regional development, can he indicate the form any
differential would take, and which modes of transport will be affected?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I believe the new policy will affect all modes of transport.

It will introduce more competition into the transport sector, which should have the effect of
looking after the person who pays.

State House Tenancies-Rent Outstanding
9. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Housing: What is the
outstanding amount of rental due to the Housing Corporation from State house tenancies as
at 31 March 1977, and are any steps being taken to improve the arrears situation?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): Outstanding rental due to the Housing
Corporation from State house tenancies as at 31 March 1977 was $691,441. This amount was
owed by 3735 tenants, and represents 6.57 percent of the 56 000 tenancies administered by
the corporation. This favourably compares with the position as at 31 March 1976, when 4476
tenants out of a total of 55 005 owed $731,198, representing a percentage of 8.14. The
corporation is adopting a firmer line with defaulting tenants, which is reflected in the
improved arrears position. The corporation's housing officers, who are in direct contact with
tenants, have played an active part in arrears collections. Where co-operation cannot be
obtained from the tenants, legal action is being taken through the courts, and in some serious
arrears cases possession of the properties has been obtained.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Can the Minister give the comparison between the arrears, which
were more than $600,000, and the annual revenue received from the 50 000 State tenants?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I do not have that figure immediately available, but my
memory is that it is about $30 million. If the honourable member would like to write the
figures down, he will see that $691,441 is about 6.5 percent.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Of the houses, not of the rent?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: No, of the rents, so he can work that out by simple
arithmetic.
Mr Lange: Could the Minister not come to an arrangement with the Minister of Social
Welfare so that persons entitled to benefits might have their rental paid by direct credit from
the Social Welfare vote?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: The suggestion made by the member overlooks the fact that a
deduction from a social welfare benefit cannot be made without the recipient's authority. I
do not believe it would be practicable to automatically deduct the rental. The problem can
be resolved only with a great deal of manpower and by people discussing the payment of
arrears with the tenants. I have asked the Housing Corporation to introduce a pilot scheme
to investigate the methods that might be necessary to improve the position, and I am hoping
to have its report within the next few weeks.
Mr Lange: Does the Minister agree that when tenants do seek to have the Department
of Social Welfare discharge their rental obligations, insuperable difficulties are placed in
their way?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I am not aware of that happening, but if the member can
bring specific instances to my attention I will undertake to have them investigated.

Education-Student Bursaries
15. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Education: What has been
the increased payment in bursaries to students since 1 February 1976?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): School boarding bursaries were
increased from $300 to $400 per annum from the beginning of term three 1976 and will be
further increased to $500 per annum from the beginning of term three this year. The total
payments for this form of assistance in recent financial years were: 1975-76, $840,000; 1976-
77, $899,000; and in 1977-78, $1.36 million. Tertiary bursaries were increased substantially
with the introduction of the standard tertiary bursary at the beginning of 1976, and set at an


## p. 1814 (#270) ###########################################

1814
3 August
Oral Answers to Questions
unabated rate of $24 a week. The Government has approved an increase of $2 a week in all
rates from the beginning of the 1978 academic year. Total tertiary bursary payments per
annum over this period are as follows: 1975-76, $13.7 million; 1976-77, $24.6 million;
1977-78, $25.9 million. In effect, therefore, this represents an increase of 88 percent in total
Government expenditure on bursaries in the last 2 years.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is this 88 percent increase in the payment of bursaries to students in
accordance with the Government's policy?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The 88 percent comes about largely from the substantial increase
last year, following the introduction of the standard tertiary bursary in the 1975-76 year.

will meet the students' needs?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I am certain that nobody is ever satisfied with what he gets by

perspective, however. In the last 2 years Government expenditure on bursaries has increased
by 88 percent. The university component of the standard tertiary bursary represents nearly
20 percent of the total expenditure on universities.

means of boarding bursaries is a most important component.

WRITTEN QUESTIONS
Tongan Earthquake-Radio New Zealand Communication Service
1. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: Following the recent severe
earthquake in Tonga: (a) was Radio New Zealand able to use its 7.5 kW shortwave
transmitter to demonstrate our willingness to assist, and, if not, why not; (b) was any attempt
made to liaise with Radio Australia in an endeavour to keep communications going between
the local Tongan community and Tongan families in New Zealand; and (c) were the first
reports which were broadcast by Radio New Zealand sent by its own correspondent in
Tonga, a newspaper correspondent, or from what source?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: I am advised that the
answers to each of the honourable member's specific queries are as follows: (a) The present
Radio New Zealand shortwave service relays domestic services only, and does not originate
programmes. Following the earthquake, national programme news bulletins relayed to the
Pacific by the shortwave transmitters reported that the New Zealand Government would
meet any request for aid to the best of its ability. They also advised that CORSO had $3,000
on hand for immediate aid and would be making inquiries about the type of assistance
needed. (b) No. It is doubtful if liaison with Radio Australia could improve communication
between Tonga and New Zealand. The Radio New Zealand shortwave station can be readily
picked up at any time in Tonga-Radio Tonga rebroadcasts a daily news bulletin from Radio
New Zealand as well as a weekly bulletin in Tongan-while Radio Tonga can be received
through the receiving station at Quartz Hill. (c) The first report broadcast was received from
The NZPA-Reuter service, quoting the United States Geological Survey in Washington.
The first report on the effects in Tonga came from Radio Tonga, monitored through the
Quartz Hill receiving station.

Recreation and Sports Grants-Community Distribution
3. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Recreation and Sport: Has he seen the
statement by Mr W. G. T. Wiggs, Chairman of the Wellington Community Arts Council, in
the Dominion of 24 June that "local bodies were deliberately dissuading arts and culture
groups from applying for recreation and sports grants", and, if so, is the statement true; and
will he supply the breakdown of the grants provided through local authorities during the last
financial year to (a) sports groups; (b) arts and cultural groups; and (c) other community
groups?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Recreation and Sport) replied: I have seen the
statement by Mr Wiggs as reported in the Dominion. It would not be true that local
authorities in general are dissuading arts and cultural groups from applying for recreation
and sport grants. There may be one or two examples of this, but the great majority will be
guided by my advice that the needs of cultural groups must be considered together with those
of sports and other recreation organisations. Returns from 223 local authorities last year
show the following breakdown: (a) 1832 distributions involving $671,951 for 45 different
sports; (b) 312 distributions involving $108,495 for 11 different categories of arts and cultural
activities; and (c) 1467 distributions involving $664,159 for 60 other kinds of recreational
activities. Although this represents a higher proportion of funds going to arts and cultural
groups than for the previous year, I believe these groups are still getting less than their fair
share.

Maputo Declaration-Prime Minister's Speech
6. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Will he
give the full text of the speech made by the Prime Minister to the Commonwealth Heads of
Government Conference relating to the Maputo Declaration?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: The
Prime Minister's address was not made from a written text and the only record that exists is
that taken down during the conference itself, and as that is a classified document the relevant
text cannot be reproduced in a public statement. The Prime Minister has, however, given a
general indication of what he said. He indicated that he agreed that it was essential to put the
maximum psychological pressure on Mr Smith now if a peaceful solution was to be achieved.
He had concluded that New Zealand could support the Maputo Declaration as a means of
doing this. There were some minor difficulties in the text for New Zealand, but it provided a
basis from which the Heads of Government meeting could decide on an agreed line of
action.
(7/7/77)
Maputo Declaration-New Zealand Stance
7. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Will he
amplify his written answer to me, appearing as No. 11 on the Order Paper for 29 June, by
setting out in detail which provisions of the Maputo Declaration the Government supports,
which provisions it does not support, and what reservations it has to the declaration as a
whole?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: I do not
believe the document in question lends itself to the kind of clause-by-clause examination the
honourable member seems to require, but the following more detailed comment may serve
to answer his inquiry. As indicated in the reply referred to, the Government supports the
general thrust of the declaration and the objectives of the plan of action. The Government's
principal reservation is that the document reflects the belief of many nations that armed
struggle is a legitimate means of bringing about majority rule in Rhodesia and Namibia. A
number of other countries-and New Zealand is among them-remain opposed to armed
struggle and believe that the necessary changes can, and should, be brought about by
peaceful means. The attitudes and efforts of these countries are also accepted in the
document, and that is where it differs from other declarations and resolutions to which New
Zealand has not been able to give support. There are also a number of less fundamental
points which New Zealand cannot accept without some reservation. We do not, for instance,
believe that South-west Africa People's Organisation should be the only group that has a
right to take part in the independence process in Namibia. Nor has the Government yet
taken a position on the question of Walvis Bay, and it cannot, therefore, endorse the
declaration's assertion that Walvis Bay is an integral part of Namibia. In addition, there are
both technical legal obstacles and considerations of principle which prevent New Zealand
from responding positively to every extension of the sanctions against Rhodesia called for in
the text. Finally, many of us in New Zealand will have reservations about the extreme nature
of some of the terminology used. These reservations are not without substance, but in the
Government's view they in no way invalidate its support for the overall objectives reflected
in the document.
(7/7/77)

Beer and Cigarette Tax Estimates
9. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Statistics: Have any
estimates been made, and, if so, would he give them, of how much in total per annum extra
consumers would have to pay if the Government imposed a le increase in the price of a glass
of beer and a lc increase in the price of a pack of 20 cigarettes?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics) replied: No such estimate had been
made before the honourable member's question. For his information, the Government
Statistician estimated that the total extra expenditure per annum would amount to about $24
million. This assumes that a price rise equivalent to the lc per glass was also to be imposed
on beer sold by the flagon or jug, and on bottled beer, and that the level of total
consumption of beer and of tobacco was not affected by the increases in price. To the extent
that such price increases might depress the total level of consumption, the total extra would
be less than that estimated above. If the estimate of personal consumption of $7,465 million
for 1976-77, prepared by the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research, were to prove
approximately valid, the extra payment for a glass of beer and a pack of cigarettes would add
0.3 percent to expenditure on personal consumption.

Railway Engine Drivers
12. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) asked the Minister of Railways: Can he tell the
House how many locomotive and railcar engine drivers have emigrated from New Zealand
in the last 12 months, and (a) how many of these have gone to Australia, and (b) what steps
has he taken to train replacements, and does the Railways Department have a sufficient
number of engine drivers at present?


## p. 1819 (#275) ###########################################

3 August
1819
Questions and Replies
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: In the past 12 months 22
engine drivers have resigned from the service to take up employment in Australia, with the
Mt. Newman Mining Co., the Hammersley Iron Co., or the Goldsworthy Mining Co. In
October 1976 a new training scheme was introduced to provide staff with the practical
experience and theoretical tuition necessary to qualify as engine drivers in the shortest
acceptable period. One hundred and eight employees are at present in training, and it is
expected that the first will qualify as engine drivers in September this year. This training
scheme is a continuing exercise and will serve to alleviate the shortage of engine drivers in
some areas and provide replacements for future losses through retirements, resignations,
and promotions to supervisory positions. The shortage of engine drivers is mainly in
Auckland, Wellington, and Christchurch, and is due to a reluctance of members to transfer
to these localities. This attitude is, of course, not confined to locomotive running staff.

Civil Aviation-NAC and Air New Zealand Co-operation
13. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Civil Aviation and
Meteorological Services: Has he seen the Trans Tasman news sheet dated 9 June in which the
General Manager of NAC, Mr D. A. Patterson, is quoted as suggesting that if airline costs,
notably fuel, continued to rise at present rates some form of merger of the operations of

such a merger is desirable, and to what extent?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services)
replied: I have seen the text of Mr Patterson's speech and agree that fuel costs are reaching
a level where, to maintain maximum savings to the traveller, each aircraft must be fully
utilised. The management of both Air New Zealand and NAC are encouraged to explore
every avenue where combined action can achieve cost savings. A special committee chaired
by the Secretary for Transport and known as the Joint Airline Co-ordinating Committee is
also charged with this responsibility.
(7/7/77)
Railways-Tradesmen's Wage Relativity
14. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Railways: In view of the
present critical situation brought about by the loss of tradesmen in the railway workshops,
why has the department failed to retain remuneration relativity for the key trade
groups-welders, armature winders, grade I iron machinists, instrument mechanics, and
relay mechanics?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: The relativity between
tradesmen and semi-skilled groups such as welders, armature winders, grade I iron machin-
ists, instrument mechanics, and relay mechanics has not yet been established. By agreement
between the parties the wage rates of these semi-skilled employees have not been increased
by the recent ruling rate survey, and the question of the appropriate relativity has been
placed in the hands of an independent arbitrator for adjudication. The independent
arbitrator's decision is expected soon.
(7/7/77)

times as efficient as aircraft", and has he taken steps to seek further information on the
claims made?

and myself are aware that, in terms of energy used, railways are more efficient than road or
air, although perhaps not to the extent enunciated in the article referred to. I would refer the
honourable member to pages 17 and 18 of the Railways Department's annual report for the
year ended 31 March 1974, where this subject was discussed.

Gross Earnings-Ratio to Price Increases
23. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Finance: In view of the Institute of
Economic Research prediction that inflation will continue and average 15 percent for the
year to next March, what increase in gross wages will the family man with a non-working
wife and two children under 5 years need to maintain his standard of living if on 1 April 1977
he was on: (a) $120; and (b) $129.21; and what further increase will be needed in gross
earnings to compensate for the effect of inflation on the family benefit?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance) replied: The New Zealand
Institute of Economic Research's "assumption that the March year 1978 average rate of
inflation as measured by the CPI will be 15 percent" (page 9, June 1977 quarterly
predictions) does not mean that the CPI will increase by 15 percent between March 1977 and
March 1978. What it does mean is that the average CPI for the year to March 1978 is
assumed to be 15 percent higher than the average CPI for the year to March 1977. In theory,
then, if one were to use a calculation based on a 15 percent projected increase in prices
between March 1977 and March 1978, the increase would be: (a) $30.94, or 25.8 percent;
and (b) $30.46, or 23.6 percent. The further increases on the family benefit would be $1.81 in
the first case and $1.86 in the second, or 1.2 percent in both cases.
(8/7/77)

Questions and Replies
Import Barriers to Primary Products
25. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade:
Could he list all barriers to imports of foreign primary produce into New Zealand?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied: There are
three main factors which could influence imports of foreign primary produce into New
Zealand: import licensing, tariffs, and quarantine measures. Import licensing restrictions
apply mainly to primary produce which has been processed or prepared in some form, or
packaged for sale—the aim being the protection of New Zealand's processing industries.
Basic primary products generally have unrestricted access. For example, there are no
licensing restrictions on unprocessed wool, fresh or frozen meat and edible offals, fresh milk
and cream, or milk and cream preserved in solid form, butter, cheese, eggs, raw coffee, rice,
tea, raw sugar and molasses, and raw cocoa. A similar situation exists on tariffs, most duties
on unprocessed primary products being low. In the few areas where tariffs are levied, they
are moderate by international standards. Many duties on primary products were lowered
with the phasing out of the British preferential tariff. Quarantine measures taken by New
Zealand are considered essential to maintain the present disease-free environment on which
our major agricultural product exports depend.
(19/7/77)
Disabled Young Persons-Research into Needs
26. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: In view
of the concern expressed recently by many people working with younger physically disabled
persons, does he intend to take up the statutory obligations embodied in section 8 (2) (c) of
the Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act 1975, and appoint a person or persons to
carry out research into the needs of these young people in the community?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: Section 8 of the Disabled
Persons Community Welfare Act relates to the functions of the Advisory Council for the
Community Welfare of Disabled Persons. Subsection (2) (c) provides that the advisory
council may make recommendations to the Minister on any matters relating to "areas of
investigation for research into aspects relating to the welfare in the community of disabled
persons". I have yet to receive any recommendations from the advisory council in this
regard. However, I understand that the advisory council has very recently held discussions
with researchers who are interested in examining the needs of the physically disabled. If
support from my department is to be sought, I have no doubt the advisory council will be
making recommendations to me in terms of section 8 (2) (c).
(19/7/77)
Marriage Counselling for Domestic Purposes Benefit Applicants
27. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: In view
of the report in the Christchurch Press, 23 May 1977, that Cabinet approval has already been
given for more social workers to be employed to assist in the counselling of marriage
partners when an application for a domestic purposes benefit is made, can he say: (a) when
recruitment will commence; (b) how many social workers will be employed; (c) what
provisions are being made to ensure that adequate training in counselling will be given; and
(d) from where will these social workers be recruited?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: The department's social
workers will not be engaged in direct marriage guidance counselling. Discussions have
commenced with the National Marriage Guidance Council to assist in marriage counselling
work in appropriate cases. Additional positions are being established within the department
for extended interviewing procedures and to assist in liaison with the Marriage Guidance
Council. Approximately 70 staff will be required for the new interviewing procedures, and
appropriately experienced staff are now being selected within the department. The majority
of the interviewing officers will be appointed from experienced benefits staff. A smaller
number of additional social workers will be appointed to provide social work back-up. The
final numbers in each group will not be known until each new district establishment is
approved. Their positions will be filled from the recent staff approvals. Staff selected will be
given appropriate training in the particular responsibilities involved.

War Service Pensions
28. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Would he
enumerate the "several little perks" which he alleged war veterans were receiving when he
was talking on Radio i talkback on Tuesday, 28 June?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: A person receiving a war
veteran's allowance or a war service pension may elect to forgo his war pension and fringe
benefits and transfer to national superannuation if he can meet the eligibility criteria. If he
elects to remain on his war pension, the various fringe benefits he would automatically retain
include: (a) an age supplement of $1.50 a week on attaining age 65 for both the pensioner
and his wife; (b) a war veteran's gratuity paid regardless of financial circumstances, for the
widow payable for 2 years after the veteran's death (current maximum rate of the gratuity is
$3,127.80 a year) or, in the case of the widow of a war service pensioner, either a gratuity
payable for 6 months after the pensioner's death (current maximum rate $3,484 a year) or a
lump sum payment equal to one-quarter of the annual rate of war service pension payable in
respect of the pensioner and his wife at the time of the pensioner's death; (c) education
bursaries for children; (d) entitlement to the telephone and television concessions; and (e)
full entitlement to additional benefit under the existing criteria.

Broadlands Power Station-Progress
45. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Electricity: What stage has been
reached on the work of planning the Broadlands 150 MW power station?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Electricity) replied: Preparation of an environmental
impact report on the Broadlands power station proposal is now well under way. It is hoped
to publish the report in August 1977. Once the audit is received, applications will be made
for the necessary statutory clearances. The present programme proposes that Government
approval to construct the station will be sought in April 1978.
(19/7/77)
TV2-Coverage Programme
46. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: (a) Can he advise how
the programme to extend TV2 coverage to those parts of the country that are at present
unable to receive TV2 transmission is progressing; (b) can he advise how many transmitter
stations that are partly completed have been unable to go ahead because of restrictions in
expenditure imposed since December 1975, and can he indicate the location of each of these
transmitters; and (c) can he indicate in the case of each of these transmitters (i) how much
has been spent so far, and (ii) how much will need to be spent in each case before the station
can transmit?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: (a) The development
programme to extend TV2 coverage to areas without that service is generally proceeding on
schedule. At the present time permanent TV2 systems cover 73.5 percent of the population,
with pilot systems providing for a further 3.6 percent. In total just under 2 500 000 viewers
have the service available to them. In the present financial year it is planned to provide
service in the Wairarapa, Hawke's Bay, and Gisborne areas, bringing coverage up to about
83 percent of the population. (b) and (c). The only station that might possibly be placed in
the category is the transmitter on Mt. Egmont, which is to be upgraded to improve TV1
service and where the sum of $337,000 has been spent and expenditure of a further $87,000 is
required. However, within the available resources of finance and manpower this develop-
ment is not considered to have the same degree of urgency as other areas like those referred
to above which have a very inadequate or non-existent service from TV2.
(19/7/77)

Regional Development Assistance-Marlborough
49. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Regional Development: What was the
total amount spent from the Regional Development vote for the Marlborough regional
development district for the year ended 31 March 1977 and how much Development Finance
Corporation loan money was injected into that area during the same period and what are the
comparative figures for the year ended 31 March 1976?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development) replied: For the year ended 31
March 1977, regional development assistance amounting to $108,762 was approved for the
Marlborough region. Loan approvals for the region in 1976-77 by the Development Finance
Corporation (compiled on a June year basis) were $1,233,000. Comparative figures for
1975-76 are nil and $100,000*. The lower level of approvals in New Zealand in 1976-77
reflects a more cautious approach to investment by the private sector in consideration of the
overall economic situation. However, in the Marlborough area several worth-while propos-
als were put forward in contrast to the national trend, and this resulted in a considerable
increase in assistance for that region over the previous year. This illustrates the Govern-
ment's willingness to assist where projects come forward.
"DFC loan approval figures include regional development and export suspensory loans.

Wainuiomata Road Upgrading
51. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Works and Development: Would
there be any other community so inadequately served or so dependent on road access as
Wainuiomata, and when will this road be accorded a priority rating that would ensure an
early start on upgrading the present road and the construction of an alternative outlet road?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: The matter of
adequacy or otherwise of roading access is one on which strong local views are often held,

Vietnam Veterans-Rehabilitation Loans
52. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister in Charge of
Rehabilitation: How many Vietnam veterans qualified and received rehabilitation loans for
farms and homes?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister in Charge of Rehabilitation) replied: Farming loans
were not made available for ex-servicemen who served in Vietnam. The extent of the
concessions available for this purpose for Vietnam veterans is by way of preference in farm
ballots conducted by the Department of Lands and Survey. Separate statistics according to
the area of conflict are not compiled and it is not therefore possible to state the number of
Vietnam veterans who have qualified for and received housing loans. However, I can tell the
honourable member that in the year ended 31 March 1977 a total of 484 rehabilitation
housing loans were approved. These had a value of $6,045,485. Because of the time lapse
since previous conflicts, all of these loans could reasonably be assumed to have been granted
to servicemen who served in South-east Asia.

Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: At 31 December 1976 a total of
6871 children and young persons were under the care of the Director-General of Social
Welfare, and of these 3502, or 51 percent, were being cared for in foster homes, 2877 in
private foster homes, and 625 in departmental family homes. These are the latest statistics
available.

Foster Care Children-Court Appearances
54. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: What
percentage of children in foster care appeared before children's boards or children and
young persons courts in the years 1974, 1975, and 1976?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: Children's boards and the
children and young persons courts came into operation from 1 April 1975. Statistics,
therefore, can be given only for periods after that date. During the period 1 April 1975 to 31
December 1975 a total of 53 children and young persons in foster homes appeared before a
children's board or a children and young persons court. This represented about 1.5 percent
of all children in foster care in 1975. During the period 1 January 1976 to 31 December 1976
a total of 109 children or young persons in foster homes appeared before a children's board
or a children and young persons court. This represents about 3 percent of all children in
foster care in 1976.
