Huntly Coal-Government Control
60. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines: In view of his reply to my
question of 30 June 1977 that much of the coal north of Huntly is privately owned: (1) can he
state what control he or the department has over the development and/or mining of these
privately owned deposits; and (2) does he believe that these mines should or will not be
planned before the middle of the next decade?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied: (1) The Coal Act requires the owner of any
mine, be it privately owned or Crown owned, to work the mine in the manner approved by
the inspector of coal mines, and so as to avoid any unnecessary loss of coal. This requirement
is set out in section 11 of the Coal Mines Amendment Act 1950; and (2) in the interest of
energy conservation any large new underground coal mine must be planned to obtain
extraction rates well above those at present being achieved, and it will be necessary in the
case of the deep coal north of Huntly to develop new technology to do this. I do not believe it
will be possible for any coal mine operator to develop satisfactorily a new technique of
mining quickly enough to begin planning a large new underground mine in this area until
about the mid 1980s.

61. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: What steps does he

New Zealand Herald of 22 June?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: I am aware of the areas of teacher
shortage in technical and other departments of secondary schools, and as an immediate
measure to meet these shortages I have obtained the Government's approval to mount a
recruitment scheme in the United Kingdom. Full details of the scheme have been sent to the
controlling authorities of all state secondary schools inviting them to participate if they
consider it will assist them with particular staffing problems. In addition, but as a longer-
term measure, special emphasis is being given during the current campaign within New
Zealand to recruiting for the subject areas in which there has tended to be a shortfall in
previous years.

Questions and Replies
Nuclear Bomb Tests-Mururoa
63. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: How many
nuclear bomb tests by the French Government at Mururoa have been detected by the
Government, and does it know what further tests are planned by the French Government?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: I assume
the honourable member is referring to tests conducted underground by the French Govern-
ment, as all atmospheric tests were detectable from monitoring of radioactive fallout. Since
the French Government commenced underground testing New Zealand seismological
stations have detected four seismic events, with the known characteristics of underground
nuclear explosions, conducted on Mururoa atoll, and a previous two which were conducted
on Fangataufa atoll. We have no knowledge of any plans the French Government might
have for further tests.
(22/7/77)
Telephone Waiting List-Dunedin
64. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Postmaster-General: Has he seen the
report in the Otago Daily Times of 14 January 1977, in which it was stated that there were
500 applications on the waiting list to have telephones connected, and can he tell the House
how many applications for telephone connections the Dunedin Post Office has at present?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: I have read the report. The figure
quoted represented the approximate number of applicants in the Dunedin central exchange
network at 31 December 1976 who could not be provided with service because of a shortage
of cable or telephone numbers. At the same date an additional 203 applicants in the area
were awaiting installing resources or their requests were under review. At 30 June 1977 a
total of 806 applicants in the same area were waiting for service, of which 572 could not be
connected because of cable/telephone number shortages and 234 were awaiting installing
resources or were under review. In the year ended 31 March 1977, 408 new connections were
added to the Dunedin central exchange network.

Electoral Rolls
67. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Justice: In view
of his reply to the member for New Lynn on 25 May that copies of the updated electoral rolls
would be available to electorate officers after June, can he state (a) whether they are in fact
now available; (b) if copies can be purchased by the public and at what price; and (c) when
he expects the town and street index to the new electorates to be available?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: (a) Updated electoral rolls are not
available to the public. A single copy of a computer printout for each electorate has been
forwarded to each electorate officer as a basis for classification into the new electoral
districts. It was decided to proceed with this step before completely updating the rolls so that
the new rolls can be brought up to date before publication for the 1978 elections; (b) it has
never been policy, nor would it be economically justifiable to publish rolls except for the
immediate purpose of the conduct of an election; and (c) the index of places and streets is
not a public document, but is prepared administratively for the guidance of electorate
officers and polling booth staff. The index for the new electorates will be prepared in
conjunction with the classification of electors into the new electorates. The classification will
be done by reference to census meshblocks, but it will be possible to print a list of towns and
streets within each electorate.
(27.7.77)
North Canterbury Catchment Board—Akaroa and Lyttelton
68. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Works and
Development: Has he seen the Christchurch Star of 11 July, in which the mayor of Lyttelton
denies any knowledge of recent attempts to bring Lyttelton Borough under the North
Canterbury Catchment Board's authority and in which, in addition, the chairman of the
board says little if any effort has been made to bring the area and Akaroa County under its
control; and can he reconcile those reported statements with his answer to my urgent
question of 5 July, in which he said he has attempted to obtain acceptance of the full services
of the catchment board by both the Akaroa County and the Lyttelton Borough?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: In my answer of 5
July I did not state that my attempts to obtain acceptance of the full services of the catchment
board by both the Akaroa County and the Lyttelton Borough were by direct personal
contact with these two authorities, although the mayor has apparently taken this inference.
All attempts to date have been made on my behalf by the National Water and Soil
Conservation Authority and the Ministry of Works and Development. I have also, in
correspondence with the member for Lyttelton on erosion problems, referred to the need for
direct discussion between Lyttelton Borough and the North Canterbury Catchment Board.
The situation prevailing at present exists because the local people did not want to be
included in the catchment district for soil conservation and rivers control purposes. If the
people agree that it is now in their best interests to accept full catchment service, then this
can be arranged by agreement between the local territorial authorities and the North
Canterbury Catchment Board. A successful getting together of the parties can arise only
from mutual agreement, not by direction, and I am hopeful that such an agreement can be
reached.

Neutron Bomb-Objection by New Zealand
69. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Will the New Zealand
Government be conveying to the Government of the United States its possible objection to
any proposals for making a neutron bomb?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: The possible production
and deployment of a new nuclear weapon by any country is a matter of concern to the
Government, which has made it plain that it wants to see a reduction in the present levels of
nuclear weapons, a cessation of all nuclear testing, and ultimately international agreement
on effective nuclear disarmament. I am aware of the conflicting arguments surrounding the
neutron bomb. While the United States Government has approved funds for continuing
research on the development of the bomb, President Carter has indicated that a final
decision has yet to be taken on its production and deployment. The Government will, of

which have a bearing on its policy towards nuclear disarmament. At this stage, however, it
would not consider it appropriate to express any special concern to the United States
Government.

Wood-based Liquid-fuel Industry
72. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: Has the
Government any proposals to prove the process for the establishment of a wood-based
liquid-fuel industry in New Zealand outlined in DSIR report No. 575 of June 1977?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied: I have just received a copy of
the DSIR report and have asked for an evaluation of it. The process considered in the report
is one of a number which could be used for the production of liquid fuels from wood.
Another is the hydrolysis, and subsequent fermentation, of wood. Following the Budget I
announced that funds had been approved for the Forest Research Institute to build a pilot
plant based on this process. The DSIR itself has carried out research on the process
described in the report, and is continuing these investigations.

St. George and Co., Dunedin-Closure
75. Mr WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister of Regional Development: In view of
the announced closure of the Dunedin food canning company of St. George, would he
advise the House whether this company has been or is in receipt of regional development
assistance; whether the company has approached either the Otago Regional Development
Council, the Development Finance Corporation, or the Government with any specific
requests for assistance to upgrade or rebuild its Dunedin factory in the past 18 months;
whether any prior notice of the closure was made by the Sharland group to him; whether the
closure is due to anything other than a normal business decision on investment by a company
and whether he agrees with claims by the member for Dunedin Central that the closure is
due to lack of action on his part; and what assistance is being extended by any Government
department to find employment for the 70 persons facing termination of employment?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development) replied: St. George and Co.,
Dunedin, was the recipient from 1973 to 1976 of a freight subsidy of 25 percent of qualifying
freight costs. This subsidy was renewed on an annually diminishing basis of 20 percent in
1977, 15 percent in 1978, and 10 percent in 1979 to give the company a "breathing space" to
undertake the necessary upgrading which would have helped it to improve efficiency. In
addition to the freight subsidy the company was given assistance towards the transfer of key
employees from Pukekohe to Dunedin in June 1976 following the closure of the company's
Pukekohe factory as part of a move to rationalise production into its traditional field of fruits
and jams and locate nearer to its source of raw materials. It was known that the company's
premises in Dunedin required considerable investment to comply with hygiene regulations,
and the Government would have preferred to aid the company with capital assistance
towards this necessary investment. However, despite the efforts of the Otago Regional
Development Council to encourage the company to undertake a development project, no
proposal was forthcoming. I can, therefore, confirm that no specific requests for assistance


## p. 1839 (#295) ###########################################

3 August
1839
Questions and Replies
to rebuild the factory have been made either to the development council, the Development
Finance Corporation, or the Government. I received no prior notice of the closure from the
Sharland group, which, in its public announcement of this decision, indicated that a major
factor taken into consideration was the high level of investment required if the operation was
to be re-established to comply with hygiene regulations. I consider there is no basis to the
claims by the member for Dunedin Central that the closure is due to any lack of action on my
part. The Department of Labour is interviewing St. George employees with a view to placing
them with other Dunedin companies. Five employees have already been offered alternative
employment with other Sharland subsidiaries in Dunedin.

SEATO-Distribution of Assets
78. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Can he
confirm that the Thai Government will purchase SEATO property in Bangkok; state how
the remaining assets will be distributed; and indicate what New Zealand will receive, if
anything?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: The Thai Government
has already exercised its option to purchase the former SEATO headquarters building
(including air-conditioning plant and telephone equipment). New Zealand's share of the
proceeds, based on its 8 percent share of the cost of construction, came to about US$43,290.
Apart from a few items donated to the Thai and Philippine governments, most of the
chattels, comprising largely furniture and office equipment, are to be sold and the proceeds
apportioned to member governments in accordance with their agreed rates of contribution to
the last budget. In New Zealand's case this is 11.58 percent. New Zealand will not physically
receive any of the former organisation's assets.

Huntly-Development of Underground Coal Mines
83. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines: In view of the coal
shortage and the Minister's answers to several of my questions, stating that the development
of underground mines is being delayed by lack of knowledge about suitable mining
technology and the need to develop a new mining technique, preventing development of new
underground mines before the mid-1980s, will he state whether the development of these
mines is regarded as having any urgency at all, and, if they do have urgency, the steps he is
taking to speed up the obtaining of knowledge about development of such techniques?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied: There is no question but that the future
development of underground coal mining at Huntly is regarded by the Government as a
matter of urgency. We know, however, that following the further development at present of
the two new mines at Huntly, large underground mines in this area will have to be in deeper
and thicker coal. To recover the major part of this deep coal, new technology will be needed.
Investigations are now being made into the progress being made on deep mining technology
in other countries. Mr W. S. Partel, the Assistant Secretary of Mines, is overseas studying
the progress which is being made in Poland and West Germany. I should add that the
development of new technology is only one of the things that will delay the planning of new
underground coal mines at Huntly. The others are equally important: the gaining of
experience in operating large mines in New Zealand conditions, and the building up of a

skilled work force. Neither of these can be done until the new mines now being developed at
Huntly are operating at full capacity. The developing of these two mines is not being delayed
by any lack of technical knowledge; it is going ahead without delay.

National Superannuation-Cost
89. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Has he seen the
advertisement in the Wanganui Herald dated 21 May 1977 which states that "the net extra
cost of National's pension scheme is $200 million a year and that $6 a week of every family's
belt tightening is paying for the scheme", and, if so, is this correct?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: I have seen the advertisement.
It is not correct. Current income taxation rates are the same as under the last Labour
Government, with the exception that the National Government has given substantial tax
deductions to assist the low-income family. Furthermore, from 1 October 1977 the PAYE
tax table will include an expanded young family rebate for the principal income earner in
families with a child under 5 years of age. Instead of the present rebate of $6 a week on
incomes up to $100 a week, the rebate will be increased to $9 a week on incomes up to $150 a
week. A more favourable method of rebating excess income will be introduced, which will
result in those whose income is less than $240 a week being eligible for a rebate. In addition,
a new rebate is to be introduced for single-income families with a child under 10. It will also
be available to widows and other solo parents with a child under 10. This new rebate will
considerably reduce the disadvantage suffered by single-income families under the present
personal income tax structure.

Railways-Removal of Subsidies
91. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Railways: Has he read the Labour
Party advertisement in the Wanganui Herald of 21 May 1977 which states, "We are told that
removal of subsidies and increased Government charges are to help New Zealand's
economy", and, if so, will he state what subsidies have been cancelled in his department
since December 1972, for what reason, and to what value, and what is the reason for any
increased charges?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: As a result of the policy of
the previous Administration, Railway Department fares and charges which applied in
December 1972 were held at that level until 1976. The effects of higher wage costs and
inflation imposed on a "frozen" tariff caused the Railways Department to incur substantial
losses over ensuing years. These losses, save for the 1972-73 year, which was met by an
interest-free national development loan, were recovered from the Stabilisation vote which
was a charge on all taxpayers. In 1976 the present Government instituted its policy of
restoring the Railways to a commercially viable organisation by approving an increase in all
Railways Department charges, although it recognised that the process would take some time
to achieve because of the magnitude of the loss being incurred. The losses incurred since
December 1972 were 1972-73, $3,349,822 1973-74, $8,652,983; 1974-75, $45,259,655; 1975-
76, $62,953,504. Since February 1976 there have been four adjustments to Railways
Department charges, effective from 1 February 1976, 16 June 1976, 1 January 1977, and 15
May 1977. The February 1976 adjustment applied to all charges, but it had a limited effect in
the 1975-76 financial year. Over a full year the increase was estimated to increase revenue by
$46 million. The increase effective from 16 June 1976 applied to all charges except passenger
fares, and was estimated to inject $38 million into Railways Department revenue. On 2
January 1977 passenger fares were increased, with an estimated return of $1 million
additional revenue during the remaining 3 months of the 1977 financial year and $4.8 million
on a full year of operation. The most recent increase, effective from 15 May 1977, applied to
all rail and ferry freight rates. This increase, which averaged 9 percent, is expected to
provide a further $18 million this financial year and $20 million in a full year.
(22/7/77)
Regional Development Suspensory Loans
92. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Regional Development: Does he
intend to make it possible for industries receiving regional development suspensory loans to
apply for and receive more than one such loan?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development) replied: I have announced in
elaboration of the Budget that the "once only" rule applying to regional development
suspensory loans will be relaxed. The relaxation will permit companies growing and
diversifying in a priority region to undertake their development in phases, where approp-
riate, without prejudicing their case for assistance beyond the first stage. However, it is not
intended that the regional development suspensory loans scheme should provide a continu-
ing source of funds for companies undertaking normal ongoing business expansion in the
region, and each application for further suspensory loan assistance will have to be considered
on its merits.

NAC-Sale of Boeing Aircraft
106. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Transport: Are there any proposals to
sell further Boeing aircraft of NAC's fleet, and what were the reasons for the sale of ZK-
NAQ, the Boeing 737 aircraft recently disposed of by NAC?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) replied: NAC's ninth Boeing 737,
ZK-NAQ, was purchased ahead of demand to avoid a substantial price increase, and to
ensure that it was available to meet the considerable passenger growth forecasts at the time
of purchase. However, a slowing down of the economy reduced passenger growth rates, thus
making it more profitable to lease the aircraft overseas than use it in New Zealand. NAC
experienced little growth during the period of the lease, and the market overseas was such
that it was preferable to sell the aircraft rather than enter into a further lease arrangement.
At the time there was a demand for that type of aircraft, and prices were high.

Houpapa Shooting Grounds for Refusing Inquiry
123. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Police: On what grounds
did he base his decision, conveyed by him to the member for Northern Maori in his letter of 5
January 1977, that a public inquiry into the shooting of Daniel Houpapa was neither
necessary nor desirable?


## p. 1851 (#307) ###########################################

3 August
1851
Questions and Replies
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police) replied: The decision of Cabinet that a
public inquiry into the shooting of Daniel Houpapa was neither necessary nor desirable was
based on the following: First, the opinion of the Solicitor-General who conducted an
independent and extensive review of the Police file and concluded that the policeman who
fired the fatal shot was justified in terms of sections of the Crimes Act. In regard to section
41, the Solicitor-General's opinion stated that "the circumstances were such that the officer
who fired the fatal shot did so to prevent an act which he had reasonable grounds for
believing would, if done, amount to the commission of an offence which would be likely to
cause immediate and serious injury to others." The opinion also stated that the officer was
justified in using such force as was reasonably necessary to prevent Daniel Houpapa from
shooting again, and the only practicable means of force available was a firearm. Secondly,
the verdict of the coroner included the finding that Daniel Houpapa's death was caused by a
gunshot wound "which was received from a firearm fired by a member of the police engaged
in the course of measures being taken for the prevention of likelihood of serious injury to a
member of the police".

Cerebral Angiography
124. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Health: Can he tell the House
the number of occasions on which cerebral angiography was used in New Zealand in the
years 1974, 1975, and 1976?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: I hope my answer will be helpful to the
House. I should like to say, first, that angiography involves the injection of a dye into the
blood vessels in the neck and the taking of X-rays to establish the blood circulation. It
involves some risk to the patient and it is painful. It costs between $400 and $700 per patient,
depending on whether only one side of the brain is examined or both. An earlier question
was asked on pneumography. That involves the injection of air into the brain cavity and the
taking of X-rays to detect an abnormality. That too is risky and painful, and it costs about
$300 per patient. Fifty percent of angiography and 70 percent of pneumography would be
unnecessary if we had a scanner and, as opposed to the cost of $400 to $700 per patient in one
case and $300 in the other, the cost with a scanner would be $45, The figures for angiography
are as follows: In 1974, 1114; 1975, 1281; and 1976, 1385.
(8/7/77)

House Mortgage Refinancing Problems
127. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Housing: Has
he seen the New Zealand Herald of 6 April 1977, in which it is reported that "he assured
home owners facing mortgage refinancing problems that the Government would not allow a
massive forced sell-out of houses to occur", and how does he reconcile this with his
statement in the Christchurch Star of 25 June 1977 that "the Government would not
guarantee that people would not lose their homes in refinancing crisis"?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: Yes, I have seen the article in the
New Zealand Herald. In my opinion there is no conflict between that statement and my later
statement in the Christchurch Star. The Government has no intention of assuming the private
sector's role in the refinance field, and the thrust of its policies is to improve the quantity and
quality of mortgage finance. The small refinance fund, administered by the Housing
Corporation is geared to assisting families in low to medium cost houses in a last resort
situation. However, I am sure I made it clear at the time that other factors had to be taken
into account, even in those cases where the corporation might otherwise be able to assist. In
those instances where it is shown that families have been irresponsible in their raising of
excessive short-term mortgages, or have already clearly proved by their poor performance
that they are not capable of home ownership, then corporation assistance is unlikely to be
forthcoming.

## p. 1853 (#309) ###########################################

3 August
1853
Questions and Replies
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: Inflation was one of the four
major problems areas which the Government inherited when it took office, and further
reducing inflation remains one of the Government's main priorities. Quarterly movements in
the consumer price index have reflected in recent quarters price increases which were
deferred during last year's price freeze, as well as the timing of various Government charge
increases and pricing decisions deferred for up to 3 years by the Labour Government.
Quarterly movements are not currently indicative of the underlying trend of inflation.
Annual figures, which are therefore more indicative of the underlying trend, show that price
increases over the last year have clearly been slower than in the previous 2 years. The
Government is not planning to reverse this trend.

International Lending-Treble A Credit Rating
144. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Finance: In which international
lending market does New Zealand have a treble A credit rating?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: The United States domestic
capital market is the only major capital market which requires that a formal credit rating be
made before a borrower can enter that market. In this market New Zealand enjoys treble A
status. The other major international capital markets do not have such a formal rating
system, leaving it to the particular market to signal the attractiveness of a borrower by the
response to the loan terms and conditions offered. As evidence of that fact, in 1974 the
Labour Government borrowed in Germany at 9.25 percent, and this year the National
Government borrowed in the same currency at 6.25 percent.

Energy Price Rises-Flow-on Effects
155. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: What
specific actions will he take to counter the flow-on effects of the recent energy price rises as
revealed by the huge rise of 27.3 percent in the June quarter in the fuel and light subgroup of
the consumer price index?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied: The increase in the June
quarter for the fuel and light subgroup of the consumer price index reflects the increase in
energy prices that took effect from 1 April 1977. These price increases bring electricity prices
back to reality after being frozen by the previous Labour Government. We are all aware that
the true situation was hidden by asking the taxpayer to subsidise electricity charges by way of
the Stabilisation vote to the tune of $18.5 million in 1974-75, and $13.1 million in 1975-76.
Had there not been a change of Government, and the introduction of new policies to remove
the subsidy by unfreezing the charges, the Stabilisation vote for electricity, as estimated
by the Treasury, would have been as high as $52 million in 1976-77. No specific actions are
contemplated as a result of this recent price adjustment. It is an essential part of energy
policy development that energy supplies are properly priced, having regard to their true
value and their true cost.

## p. 1859 (#315) ###########################################

Meat and Wool Properties-Estimated Capital Expenditure
162. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Agriculture: What estimated capital
expenditure for future growth has there been on meat and wool properties over the past 12
months compared with the 3 previous years on an annual basis?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: Official figures for aggregate
capital expenditure on farm holdings are available only up until March 1975. A frequently
used proxy for investment on sheep farms is expenditure per stock unit. Because this figure
comprises some expenditure which is capital in nature, it can be used as an indicator of the
overall investment on sheep farms. It is generally accepted that about $4.40 per stock unit in
real terms-1965-66 input prices-is required for maintenance on sheep and beef farms. Last
year, real expenditure per stock unit is estimated to have equalled $5.07, a 9 percent lift over
the $4.67 per stock unit recorded in 1975-76. This in turn was 12 percent greater than the
depressed level of $4.19 for 1974-75. Recent estimates of livestock numbers suggest that the
investment levels achieved over the last 3 years are about to be reflected in a renewed
upward movement in total livestock units.

Consumer Price Index Increase-One Income Family
164. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Statistics: What
increase in gross wages will be required for a married earner with a non-working wife and
two children, one under 5, on $129.52 as at 1 April 1977 and whose wife receives the family
benefit for both children, to maintain the family standard of living in the face of the record
rise of 4.8 percent in the consumer price index between the March and June quarters of this
year?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics) replied: In the hypothetical case
referred to, the earner, after allowing for any tax rebates to which he is entitled, would
receive an after tax take-home pay of $100.51. A 4.8 percent increase on $100.51 if evenly
applied would make it $105.33. The pre-tax gross family income would, to arrive at $105.33,
be $141.45, an increase of $11.93. I need hardly say that this simplistic question, without
regard to the state of the economy and to productivity, entirely overlooks the inflationary
impact of such an approach to wages and fiscal policy. It also overlooks the impact of jobs
and employment.

Nuclear Bomb Testing at Mururoa
178. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What steps
has the New Zealand Government taken to indicate New Zealand's opposition to the
conducting of nuclear bomb tests in the South Pacific by the French Government at
Mururoa?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: Since the
French Government commenced underground testing in 1975, following the cessation of
atmospheric tests, the New Zealand Government has viewed the conducting of each test
with the same regret with which it has witnessed underground tests carried out by each of the
other four nuclear weapon states. There is a difference between atmospheric tests, which
pose greater environmental hazards-which a multilateral treaty, the partial test ban treaty,
was designed to prohibit-and underground tests which every nuclear weapon state has
continued to conduct in the absence of any proscriptive multilateral treaty. New Zealand
does not, therefore, single out France for condemnation, but rather condemns all nuclear
testing by all states in all environments and has urged the nuclear weapon states to conclude
a comprehensive test ban treaty as a matter of urgency. I shall arrange for the honourable
member to receive a copy of the Government's latest statement on the subject of a
comprehensive test ban treaty as soon as it is available at an early date.
(22/7/77)

Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister in Charge of the Government Printing Office) replied:
The present time gap between proceedings in the House and the publication of Hansard is 6
to 7 weeks. This is 1 to 2 weeks longer than the average time for the years 1972 to 1975. In

because of problems with the new system, the publication of Hansard became progressively
delayed until by the end of the session it was 3 months late. This year Hansard has been
redesigned to facilitate a quicker turnround, and the Government Printer is aiming at a
3-week to 4-week time gap.

Coal Imports from Australia
194. Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast) asked the Minister of Electricity: In view of the
statement in the National Party's full election policy that it recognises New Zealand's
increasing dependence on coal and its promise to encourage the coal industry, why does he
permit his department to consider the possibility of coal imports from Australia to fuel New
Zealand power stations when they could be fuelled from New Zealand's already proven coal
reserves?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Electricity: Because of the importance of energy to a modern economy and the alarming
forecasts for future supplies, the New Zealand Electricity Department has been investigating
the possibility of electricity generation using imported Australian coal as one of a number of
options open to this country in the longer term—that is, 15 years away. Australian coal has
not been seen as an alternative to any local coal which could be made available. Indeed, as
the Budget indicated, the Government is accelerating investigation of local coal resources,
but the use of Australian coal is seen as a possible means of deferring a nuclear power
programme should local supplies run short in future. In short, the study being undertaken
has arisen out of questions asked before the royal commission on nuclear power, and is
designed very much for the longer term.

urgently investigate the position with a view to any necessary action being taken without
delay? Will he also arrange for a similar investigation to be made of the Rolleston-Otira
section of the West Coast line?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: First, I shall explain that I
am able to answer this question because I have seen the report in the Christchurch Star
referred to. The district engineer personally inspected the track this morning, and, while it is
agreed that there are a number of loose fastenings, this is not in itself dangerous. There is no
evidence at all of any movement of the track. All main line track, including this section, is
inspected daily, and these fastenings had already been reported upon and scheduled for
maintenance in the normal way. I am assured that the track is safe for the existing traffic
density and authorised speeds. With regard to the Rolleston-Otira section of the West Coast
line, some allegations were recently made about its safety, but it was fully inspected at the
time, and these allegations, too, were found to be unsubstantiated.

Discussion of Questions-Adjournment
I refer to questions 35 and 62, which deal with exports and imports. Since the Labour
Government was kicked out of office the exports of dairy, meat, and wool products have
increased by some $679 million. The current account balance has improved from minus $76
million at June 1974, to minus $46 million at June 1977-not where the Government would
like to see it, but the balance is nearly twice as good as it was under the Labour Government.
The deficit is the lowest it has been in 4 years, and has been achieved despite the invisibles
the Government has had to meet because of the borrowing of the Labour Government.
Despite these invisibles, exports have improved and the deficit is down to half of what it was.
What is perhaps more important is that New Zealand is a trading nation and depends on
exporting to live. That is where the money comes from to pay people such as university
students, who want bursaries. That is where the income of the country and the Government
starts.
I wonder if the people who demonstrated outside here today really think about that.
They demand more money, but they do not think. Somebody said that it was an orderly
demonstration, but I thought it was a scruffy mob. I wonder who organised the demonstra-
tion. Some students were holding up a banner that said, "We would be better off
unemployed". They do not seem to realise that they are unemployed, and that they want the
people to pay them to be that way. They smoke, drink, and go to entertainments, and they
want us to pay for it. I do not think that is reasonable. No matter by whom they were
organised, those people should rethink the problem, and do something about it. It reminds
me a little of the demonstration at the opening of Parliament in 1976, and the very violent
demonstration in Dunedin not so long ago. There seems to be a pattern.
The Deputy Leader of the Opposition, a former Minister of Finance, says we should be
controlling imports by licensing control. Only 28 percent of our imports are under licensing
control, and the reason for that was made very clear by the Prime Minister yesterday when
he opened a trade fair and pointed out we are a trading nation and that, as such, the
Government believes that the fewer barriers to free competition the better. He pointed out
also that New Zealand needed imported goods in the shops, and needed imported raw
material and other components used in factories to keep industry going and to create jobs.
Another statement made by the Opposition in its efforts to make the Government appear to
be losing the battle against trading—which it is not—is that imports have increased. In fact,
last year the volume of imports decreased by 17 percent. That trend is continuing. True, we
have to pay a lot more for our imports than we did previously. Import costs increased by 26.9
percent in 1974, 30.6 percent in 1975, and 23.6 percent last year. The Government is getting
on top of the trading position, despite the increased costs of imports.
Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori): I shall not elaborate too much on what the member for
Tauranga said about imports and exports, but merely refer to the ability of the Hon. Joe
Walding and the Hon. Colin Moyle, the Minister of Overseas Trade and the Minister of
Agriculture and Fisheries respectively in the previous Labour Government. I am sure that
the National Government would recognise the tremendous work done by those two men.
I refer to question 50, which deals with regional development. I am glad that the
National Government has seen fit to support the Labour Government's regional develop-
ment policy even though it opposed that policy when it was introduced. I support wholeheart-
edly the efforts of both governments to assist regional development councils on the East
Coast, but point out to the Minister of Trade and Industry and the Minister of Regional
Development that they should not only look at industry, but should assist people to move
into the rural areas. No industry can succeed without the people to support it. The town of
Ruatoria is now recognised as the centre of the forest industry on the East Coast. The
Government should assist the establishment of industry there, and help people to settle in
the area. Without such help people are reluctant to move.
In replying to the question from the member for Napier, the Minister of Regional
Development said: "The lower level of approvals in New Zealand in 1976-77 reflects a more
cautious approach to investments by the private sector in consideration of the overall
economic situation." It is a pity that the Minister could not have elaborated on that caution
about industry. If it is because there are no people in the rural areas to start industry, the
onus is upon the Government to encourage people to move back to the rural areas. A lot of
people have converged on the urban areas, particularly Auckland, because industry is there;
and industry does not want to move away from those areas because the people are there.
Central government is the only body that can assist, and if it wants to support regional
development it should go into all the aspects-not only the establishment of viable industry,
but assistance to people to move into those areas.

ment should have done and about what he would have done to improve the balance of trade.

the prices and disregards the volume of imports. We know that the prices of imported goods
have risen steeply, but let us consider the volume of imports. During the year ended March
1977 the volume of imports was 1.1 percent lower than in the previous year, but the receipts
from exports for the year ended June 1977 were 34 percent higher. Opposition members

back over the years we see that our balance of payments position became steadily worse
under the former Labour Government. In 1974 the deficit was $1,126 million and in 1975 it
was $1,109 million. In 1976 the position improved considerably, and the most recent figures
show that it is improving even further. The most recent figures include invisibles, and we all
know how high they became under the Labour Government because of the amount of
interest paid on borrowed money. The invisibles grew so high that we are committed to a
large debt for many years. Nevertheless, although the trade balance in 1975 was a deficit of
$674 million, in 1977 it was a positive $42 million.

LEAKAGE OF BUDGET TAXING PROPOSALS
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): On behalf of the committee set up to
inquire into the alleged Budget leak, I report as follows: The committee was appointed to
consider and report upon the allegation of a serious leak in Budget taxing proposals, which
was made by the member for Auckland Central in a notice of motion on 22 July, the text of
which is: "That this House notes with very great concern that the Dominion newspaper on
the morning of the Budget in its front page story correctly predicted that the tax on cigarettes
and liquor would be increased in the Budget, and notes that the Dominion stated that the


## p. 1879 (#335) ###########################################

3 August
1879
Leakage of Budget Taxing Proposals
story was revealed by political sources, and that this House concludes that it appears that
there has been a serious leak of Budget taxing proposals, and the House calls upon the
Government to explain this leak from the Budget, and to hold an inquiry to discover who
leaked the Budget information and whether any persons have benefited from the premature
disclosure of Budget secrets." The committee has examined the authors of the article.
Claiming a convention of privilege under the code of ethics of professional journalists, they
refused to divulge the source of the material complained of. It is a matter for regret that the
effect of this refusal may be to leave some suspicion on wide groups of individuals. The
committee can see no prospect of eliciting further information in regard to the source of the
material, and accordingly recommends that no further action be taken. I move, That the
report do lie upon the table and be adopted and agreed to.
It may help honourable members if I quote an extract from the minutes, particularly the
answer to the first two questions asked of the authors, and a statement they made to the
committee after being advised by counsel. To the first question, Mr Neville said that while
the article in question was written jointly by himself and Mr Long, he had written the
sentence, "Political sources revealed last night that Parliament will take urgency to pass a
special Customs Bill increasing the Government's bite on tobacco and alcoholic products."
The words "political sources" were used by the news media in a wide sense to mean any
person in the political, parliamentary, and Government sphere, including departments. The
second question asked whether the information in this sentence came from a Cabinet
member, a member of Parliament, or another source, or whether it was an inspired guess.
Upon Mr Neville's indication that he was unable to answer this question because of
journalistic ethics, the witnesses were invited to withdraw to consider their reply.
The minutes then report that, after some consultation with the Clerk of the House, the
witnesses returned and Mr Neville read the following statement: "There had been wide-
spread public discussion, including public statements by members of Parliament, as to a tax
on tobacco and alcohol. There had been no denial by any Government spokesman that it
would be in the Budget. As experienced journalists, it was decided that it was in order in the
circumstances to publish the information regarding a special Customs Bill. It was not an
inspired guess, but as a matter of professional integrity I am not willing to identify the class
of political source from which the information came." That paragraph then ends with Mr
Neville thinking, on recollection, that confirmation of both the Bill and urgency had been
given to him.
The authors of the article claimed professional privilege, and it is of interest, although
not exactly analogous, that a recent report of the Torts and General Law Reform Committee
comments upon the question of journalists' statutory privilege in the courts. Parliament does
not necessarily follow that absolutely, but the report gives these reasons for believing that
journalists should not be granted special privilege. I quote from page 70 of the report: "The
enactment of a privilege could create its own problems as it would protect bad as well as
good journalism. It is not unknown for an irresponsible journalist to interview his typewri-
ter, and publish a fictitious story ascribed to a fictitious source. While the journalist has the
ability to inform the public, he also has the ability to mislead. The accuracy of the
information and the validity of comment must be open to public scrutiny, otherwise the very
purpose of supplying information to the public-to inform it and enable it to act
responsibly-may be frustrated." The report continues at page 71: "The negative effects of a
journalist's privilege on legal proceedings should also be emphasised. The most likely civil
proceedings in which disclosure of journalists' confidences would be an issue are libel suits.
The operation of a privilege in such proceedings would be totally unmeritorious. A person
defamed by untruths should have a legal remedy, and that remedy should not be frustrated
by a defendant able to plead defences such as qualified privilege and fair comment, and at
the same time plead confidentiality in respect of his sources of information."
The authors of this report have claimed that sort of privilege. The press report is an
allegation of a breach, and that only. Whether one believes it must depend on the individual
reader's judgment as to the credibility of its authors. In my own view their refusal to assist in
a proper investigation of their serious charges not only leaves a slur upon a great many loyal
public servants, members of the Executive, and officers of the House, but also undermines
completely their credibility.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I take up first the proceedings of the committee,
and report to the House that the member for New Lynn, who is currently absent, but will, I
hope, be back before the debate terminates, moved that the proceedings, short of delibera-
tion, be open to the press. That was an important motion and should have been agreed to.


## p. 1880 (#336) ###########################################

1880
3 August
Leakage of Budget Taxing Proposals
This was an important topic, and while it may be said that in this matter the press perhaps
concentrates public attention as well as expressing it the matter has aroused, and will no
doubt continue to excite, throughout this debate, a good deal of public comment. That
motion was lost on a majority vote. The member for New Lynn also moved that I take the
chair, the reason being that the real concern of the committee was not what was said by the
journalists, but what was said to them. The journalists concerned were not on trial; there was
never any suggestion of that. There was no impropriety on their part whatsoever in
publishing the revelations made to them. Any blame must lie on the person or persons
making the disclosures to them.
Hon. T. F. Gill: How about the person who made the allegation?
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: The person who made the allegations is pointing to the person
who made disclosures, and as I will show the House, disclosures were made. Those
disclosures, as I will tell the House, were shown to have come from a source that could only
be a Government or Government-controlled source. That again was decided by a majority,
both the nominees for the chairman abstaining on this occasion.
I turn now to the question of journalistic privilege, to which the Minister has been
referring. There is no such thing before a court of law, and a journalist can be compelled to
answer questions about how information published by him came into his possession when
directed to do so by the judge. Whether that applies without qualification to a person
appearing voluntarily before a parliamentary committee, I am not prepared to say. Person-
ally I think the matter is not beyond doubt. But even in a court of law it is not a requirement
to be enforced rigidly, but should be tempered with discretion. That is to be derived from the
leading case of the Attorney-General v. Mulholland and Foster, which developed out of the
Vassal Admiralty inquiry. In that case the case for journalistic privilege was summarised in
counsels' argument and cited in our own law reform committee report, which the Minister
has referred to. The report states: "1. A journalist has an obligation towards his suppliers of
information and it would be dishonourable for him to reveal them. 2. A journalist owes a
duty to his employers not to imperil their receipt of information in the future, which would
clearly appear if an informer knew that the reporter would break his confidence. 3. A
journalist has a self-interest in the matter because he would be out of business if it were
known that he revealed confidential information. 4. The law will not force a man to disclose
his trade secrets. 5. Journalists have a conscientious objection for revealing secrets of
information, which is part of the ethics of their profession. A person should not be asked to
commit a breach of professional ethics."
It should be added that the case was made that the police are not required to disclose the
sources of their information, and without protection from disclosure many sources of
information would cease to be available. The same report quotes from the judgment of Lord
Denning in that case, and it is set out in the Law Reform Committee's report. I personally
prefer what was said by Lord Donovan, and I should like to cite that. "I add a few words
only about the need for some residual discretion in the court trial in a case where a journalist
is asked in the course of the trial for the source of information. While the journalist has no
privilege entitling him as of right to refuse to disclose the source, so I think the interrogator
has no absolute right to require such disclosure. In the first place the question has to be
relevant to be admissible at all. In the second case it ought to be one, the answer to which
will serve a useful purpose in relation to the proceedings in hand. I prefer that expression to
the term necessary. Both these matters are for the consideration and if need be the decision
of the judge. And over and above these two requirements there may be other considerations
impossible to define in advance, but arising out of the infinite variety of fact and circum-
stances which a court encounters, and which may lead a judge to conclude that more harm
than good would result from compelling the disclosure or punishing a refusal to answer."
The committee in New Zealand concluded that it was desirable that this discretion be
clarified and defined.
I turn from what was in fact written by the journalists concerned to the more important
question of what may have been said to them. I have been driven to the inescapable
conclusion that something was said, or perhaps done, by a knowledgeable political
party-and I call it that-which should not have been said or done. Much of political
journalism consists of putting two and two together; sometimes the answer adds up to the
right figure, sometimes it comes out wrong. In the article with which we were concerned it is
a fact that there was more wrong than right, but one correct answer was stated with such
confidence that it aroused suspicion, and that confidence was confirmed before the commit-
tee. I want to repeat some of the matter that was given in evidence-not all, because the


## p. 1881 (#337) ###########################################

3 August
1881
Leakage of Budget Taxing Proposals
Minister has cited some of it—but I quote from the written statement given by Mr Neville
after he took legal advice. Speaking of the revelation he went on to say, "It was not an
inspired guess, but as a matter of professional integrity I am not willing to identify the class
of political source from which the information came." From recollection Mr Neville thought
the confirmation of both the Bill and urgency was given to him. Later he said, "The
possibility of urgency being taken on Budget night was the subject of a specific question put
to certain people on Wednesday morning." Later Mr Neville confirmed that he had asked
political sources the question, "Would urgency be taken on Budget night to pass a customs
measure?"
The question of urgency, of course, is crucial, because once a journalist knows that
urgency is to be taken, and particularly when there has been public speculation about
customs measures, he is aware that there will be some change in the incidence and probably
the rate of customs duty. That is the crucial question. It is hard to avoid the conclusion that
on that point someone made a direct and explicit statement to the journalist concerned. For
the rest it may have been no more than a nod or a wink; and one has the wisdom of proverbs
to know that one is as good as the other. But even that is a breach of trust and
confidentiality, which in other times and in other places has been roundly condemned and
visited with dire consequences.
I concurred in the committee's report after some alterations had been made, at my
suggestion, and while in its own terms it absolves Parliament from any further action, it
certainly does not exculpate the Government or dispose of its responsibility. In a word, the
consequence of the report is that the journalists concerned were explicit that questions had
been put to people in political circles who were knowledgeable, and they confirmed a
view-perhaps one that they had already formed from the questioning and follow-up studies
they had done. There was a direct confirmation, which enabled them to state with the
confidence that would otherwise have been untenable a matter which directly relates to a
taxing proposal of the Government, and which came from a breach of confidentiality. There
was, in terms of the motion the committee was originally invited to discuss, a leak from
Government or Government-controlled sources, for which the Government must take
responsibility.

purchase price of the land on mortgage, and this has been implemented in the 1977 Budget.
It is an effective way of encouraging more private investment in farming, to the benefit of the
industry as a whole, and certainly to the retired farmer.
The increased noxious weeds eradication subsidy will be welcomed by farmers in my
Gisborne electorate. The estimates show a reduction from the $10 million spent in 1976-77,
to $8.7 million in 1977-78. However, it should be noted that in 1975 the last Labour
Government closed off its ill-founded weed control scheme at only $2 million, making it
necessary for the National Government to find at least $4.5 million-

Government's scheme was $4.5 million, which has meant that the actual effective expendi-

Farmers within commuting distance of townships will be pleased at the provision in the

3 August
1885
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
this as an opportunity to live in an urban area with the educational and social advantages
normally found in such areas. It indicates that the imaginative National Government is
aware of the problems facing many farmers in keeping their farm employees. This housing
provision can be allied to home ownership inclusion in the Budget for all persons living in

building of new houses, should generally be in the first home-seeker category, be at least 45

housing. If such houses are available for renting, they will help satisfy the housing shortage.
Further evidence of the recognition of rural problems is highlighted in the Budget under
the heading of education. The public will be aware that the Government intends to provide
mobile pre-school units in rural areas. The people living in those areas can thank the
member for Pahiatua for including the suggestion in his maiden speech. The school boarding
bursaries are to be increased to $500 a year, and $10 a term travel assistance will be paid to
parents whose children are forced to live away from home to complete their schooling.
Farmers in the remote areas, whose transport costs are increasing, are pleased at the
fertiliser freight subsidy re-adjustment.
Mr Bruce Barclay: How much?
Mr BELL: The freight costs to many farmers in my electorate will be reduced by about
$2 a tonne.
Some weeks ago I received a letter from a young married farm employee, who is typical
of many people in this category, complaining that although his wages had increased from
$110 to $120 a week, his tax had increased by $5.48, leaving $4.52 as his share of the $10
increase. I explained to him that this sort of distortion occurs when an income limit is
imposed, but that it was possible that such anomalies could be rectified in the Budget. As my
prediction proved to be accurate, I think this man's case is worth outlining. Before the 1977
Budget, his weekly taxation on his $120 gross wage was $21.70, or 18 percent. However,
from 1 October 1977, and backdated to 1 April 1977, his taxation will be $9.23 a week, or 7.7
percent of his salary. His take home pay will increase by $12.47. In October 1972, taxation
for the average wage earner amounted to 15 percent. Members opposite talk at great length
about taxation, but in October 1975, under the Labour Government, the same average wage
earner paid 18 percent of his salary in taxation. In October 1976, under the National
Government, the young single income family wage earner was paying 16.3 percent. Today,
such wage earners-and there would be many thousands throughout the country-are
paying 7.7 percent of their gross wage in taxation.
I have already mentioned the inflation-proof savings scheme, which will be another aid
to the farm or home seeker, as well as to the retired couple. Everyone who has a modest nest
egg, and has seen its spending power dwindle because of inflation, will now have full
inflation protection, tax free, on savings, plus a small interest return. It is obvious that the
Government is looking after the modest savers in our community, who it considers are
valued persons who should be encouraged in their savings.

I turn now to transport, and say straight away that I am not totally opposed to the
extension of the 40-mile limit for road transport haulage-or perhaps I should say the
proposal to extend the limit from 64 km to 150 km. Having advocated that the Minister
should have acted sooner, I am sure he is not surprised to hear me say that I am not totally
opposed to the extension. However, I have some reservations about the proposal, and shall
tell the Minister and the Government of my reasons for them. I do not make statements
unless I have a reason for doing so, and I believe the Minister will accept that assurance.
First, the extension from 64 km to 150 km should have been phased in over a 2-or 3-year
period, for several reasons. For example—and let us go back to miles-it should have been
extended from 40 miles to 60 miles, then to 80 miles, and then to 93.5 miles; or,
alternatively, if it was found more desirable to extend it in two steps, it could have been
increased from 40 to 70 miles and then to 93.5 miles. Talking in kilometres again, it could
have been increased from 64 to 100 km, and then 12 months later to 150 km; or, if an
additional phase was thought desirable, it could have been increased from 64 km to 95 km,
then to 120 km, and later to 150 km. I am not arguing about the proposal to extend the
distance, but about the manner in which it is to be applied.
I am sure the Minister of Transport is aware that at the time the former Labour
Government left office it was on the verge of implementing a similar proposal, which would
have been phased in rather than taken in one jump. The Minister of Transport has no doubt
been informed of that proposal by the very good officials in his department. That would have
given the Railways Department a chance to adjust and compete with road transport. That is
very, very important.
Government members talk about the importance of the railways system. Recently the
Minister said that in his view there is no alternative to a railway system for long haulage, and
that it is the most economic means of internal transport. I entirely agree with him. The only
possible alternative would be coastal shipping, and for the life of me I fail to see why we have
not yet been able to institute a competitive coastal shipping system. I hope that will be done
in the not too distant future. As an island country, surely to goodness we should have the
wit, the intelligence, and the wherewithal to establish a coastal shipping system that can
compete with road and rail on a long-haul basis. It is an absolute must.
I have another reason for stating my reservations about the move from 64 km to 150 km
in one jump. Indeed, I know that some members of Cabinet had reservations about the
proposal, and wanted it phased in over a period of 2 or 3 years.
Hon. W. L. Young: Who told you that?
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: I am not going to say who told me, but I know for a fact that
there was a difference of opinion and that as a result the decision was delayed for about 6
months. The proposal was considered by a special Cabinet committee on transport, and
some members wanted the extension to be made in one move, while others wanted it phased
in over a period of 2 or 3 years, for the very reasons I am advancing. I am sure that, in the
long run, the minority members in the committee will be proved right. I do not know which
group the Minister was in, but think he was probably in the minority group and will therefore
be proved right in the long term.

inevitable competition. Given a phasing-in period, the smaller road transport operators

I ask the Minister and Government members generally to explain the new distance

support for the Government's move; they do not know how the distance charge will be

The Minister will be aware that one of the reservations the Road Transport Association
has had for several years, ever since the Wilbur Smith report was made public, has been that
if the Government of the day opted for an open slather transport system, with free
competition between road and rail, some of the smaller operators would virtually be forced
out of business and be unable to compete with the major combines operating on our roads
today. They were firmly opposed to that possibility. The extension to the 93.5 miles or 150
km limit that has been set is within the range acceptable to the Road Transport Association,
and I am glad that the Government has decided not to accept the recommendation made in
the Wilbur Smith report and allow a completely open slather system.
We must also consider the question of competition between road and rail haulage in
relation to energy, the other package deal introduced in the Budget. One can see a
contradiction here, in that there is likely to be an upsurge in the operation of road transport,
which, in turn, is likely to cause a greater demand on our energy resources. At this time we
are all very much aware of the need to conserve energy. The Wilbur Smith report, which the
Government has leaned on rather heavily, was presented to the Government of the day well
before the increase in oil prices. Many of the recommendations in that report immediately
became irrelevant with the new cost of oil. We were obliged to have another look at the total
scene and view the Wilbur Smith recommendations in light of the new situation. I question
whether the Government has done this, and that is another reason for my recommendation
to phase in all the increases over a given period of 2 to 3 years, to be certain that all these
factors have received due and proper weight.
I turn now to another point, also under transport, and attack the Government for the
treatment accorded to the Transport Advisory Council and the Road Transport Association.
Ever since this Government took office, from the Prime Minister down, it has said, "You
will have consultation before decisions are made." The New Zealand Herald of 1 August
quoted statements by Mr Norris Collins and Mr Neil Clark, members of the Transport
Advisory Council, and statements from the Federation of Labour, the road transport
industry, and others on the council, condemning the Government for its stance. The Press of
27 June carried this headline, "Abuse makes me hot". Well, when a Minister does not do the
things he says he will, what can he expect? I can perhaps understand why he got a bit hot.
The Government's treatment of the Transport Advisory Council, which was to have been
the principal adviser to the Government on transport matters, is nothing but a blatant breach
of the solemn undertaking that the Government would consult with them and the Road
Transport Association before final decisions were made regarding the extent of the 40-mile
limit for road transport haulage without a permit, and matters related thereto. The railway
organisations were treated with a similar, cavalier attitude. The much lauded Road Trans-
port Advisory Council was brushed aside until Tuesday 19 July. It had not met for 11
months. Under the Labour Government, that council met regularly every 2 months, and
sometimes more. It also had special committees for certain jobs.
The present Government and the Minister have been pacifying transport organisations
with a firm assurance that they would be consulted before a final decision was made. That
promise was broken throughout 1976 while the officials committee and the special Cabinet
committee argued behind the scenes on the transport industry. The practical transport men
have not been consulted. In February 1977, driven to the limit and having no confidence in
the Minister, the Road Transport Association wrote to the Prime Minister. The key point of

I shall spend a little time discussing the problem of New Zealand children's health. I
remind the House that statistics indicate a continuing decline in infant mortality. In the 1 to
4-year age group in 1965, there were 106.6 deaths per 1000 children, in 1972 the figure had
decreased to 95.3, and in 1974, to 83.3. People read statistics and believe them without
understanding them. The fact is that New Zealand's infant mortality is declining year by
year-there is no doubt about that. In the 1 to 4-year age group in 1972, motor vehicle
accidents accounted for 15 of the 95 deaths, drownings for 9 and other accidents for 11. The
infant mortality rate is not only related to health and health services, but to accidents and
congenital abnormalities. If one splits the figures one finds that in 1972 only 45 percent of the
infant mortality was due to illness, in 1973, 42 percent, and in 1974, 37 percent.
I hope that members on both sides of the House will take note of these figures. The
Government is doing its best to improve infant mortality, and the situation is not worsening
as has been suggested by the media. Dr David Geddes, the Director of the Plunket Society
said, "If we wish to improve our mortality rate we must first and foremost make our country
a safer place for children to live in". That applies to all aspects of living, including health. We
have to do more in the area of health, and will do more. The Government has an
understanding of the problem, knows its limitations, and is tackling them rigorously. Of the
$17 million, $1.5 million will go to family health. It is expected that a substantial part of that
allocation will go to the Plunket Society, enabling the employment of more plunket nurses.

It is important that the country be reminded again of some of the activity and inactivity

Zealand almost bereft of overseas financial reserves, and produced an uncontrolled, massive
internal deficit. This cannot be overlooked, and it is important continually to remind the
House and the country of it. Members opposite might well sit in silence and ponder on these
facts, because the seriousness of the position was unprecedented in our history. From a level
of more than $1,000 million when Labour came into office in 1972, our overseas reserves
were eroded until we had a massive balance of payments deficit of approximately $1,200
million when Labour was thrown out of office in 1975. That is an incredible figure and, what
is more, the internal deficit before borrowing was predicted to be $1,400 million. This has
been said before, and it will be said again and again until its significance is clearly and
properly understood: what was to have been a $1,400 million deficit at March this year was
reduced to $506 million by careful, intelligent management of the affairs of State. That was
achieved not by letting things drift along, nor by neglecting expenditure, but by careful
control and responsible management. People now realise that the country is being controlled
by a responsible Government, led by a man who understands the difficulties facing the
country and who is tackling those difficulties responsibly.

one of the main points in the Budget this year is its incentives, which have been well
accepted. Incentives are basic to the National Party philosophy, and have been built in to
encourage the conservation of energy. After all, we know only too well the tremendous costs
today of imported and fossil fuels. We all know what we need, and we also have reserves; we
have resources within this country that we must use to the full.
The incentives for industry are to encourage the changeover to plant that makes use of
coal, LPG, or natural gas. There are tax concessions for businesses prepared to use these,
and also 100 percent tax writeoffs in the first year for equipment designed to control the use
of energy, for industrial insulation, and for all these areas that collectively make the
difference between having adequate reserves and using them intelligently, as we must. The
heat exchange equipment and adjustment, the sealing of energy leaks, and the insulation of
industrial building are all part of the total policy to conserve energy, to use it intelligently
and not wastefully. The conversion of equipment from electricity to indigenous resources is
another very important point. The incentives have also been taken into the home, with a
$200 grant for the natural gas service connection to each new household.
Before long, Maui will go on tap; we will have considerable reserves there, but again we

The National Government wants to see young family people able to contemplate home
ownership, and it wants to see that those who are prepared to work and save are given the

scheme very generously, and that is why in recent months I have been exhorting young
people-whether married or single-to think ahead, to plan, and to save for their own first
home. That is why I have been stressing that, by putting aside not too large an amount—say,
$25 a week-in a home savings account, those individuals can achieve a home of their own.
In other words, if over a 3-year period an individual saves $4,150 of his own money, he will
have accumulated an additional $272 in savings bank interest and tax rebates of $1,610.
Therefore, after 3 years that individual will have $6,032 available in cash as a deposit towards
his first home. In other words, he will have $4,150 of his own and $1,882 in interest and tax
rebates.
Some people have suggested that this savings system is defeated by inflation, but they
have failed to realise that to turn $4,150 into $6,032 represents an effective interest rate far in
excess of the rate of inflation that we could expect, even under a Labour Government. I
want to emphasise again that two people-whether married or single-can combine their
savings and between them have $12,000 towards their own home in 3 years. They can have
about $16,800 in 4 years and, finally, after 5 years, with tax rebates and interest, they can
have over $23,000.
