A target of between 26 000 and 30 000 new house constructions has been set for this
year. The Government will continue to take steps to make sure that this target is met,
because its policy is to ensure that the building industry is strong and profitable. The targets
set over the last 2 years were determined with three principle objectives in mind: first, to
build the number of houses that reflects a reasonable demand; secondly, to have regard to
the availability of resources, of money, and of materials and labour in the context of the
demands made on these resources by other sections of the economy; and, thirdly, to sustain
the building industry at a level that avoids the peaks and troughs caused by economic and
other factors.
The building industry plays a vital part in the social welfare and commercial aspects of
our economy, it must be kept viable, but it must not expect to be spoon-fed and feather-
bedded every time a chilly economic wind blows. Sudden upswings, such as those experi-
enced in 1974 and 1975, are as disruptive to the industry as is a depression, and it is certainly
in the best interests of the industry that we quickly find the level of activity that is attainable
and sustainable in the long term. The building industry has been reasonably co-operative and
understanding during this gradual reduction in targets. Some disapproval has been voiced,
and some concern has been expressed by individual builders about their future. However, I
believe that the Government must look after the industry as a whole, and not the affairs of
individual builders who have been adversely affected.
Two other aspects of saving are related to the question of housing finance. The first is
the freedom given to the savings banks to fix the interest rate on their investment accounts,
and the second is the issue of inflation-proof bonds, both of which are aimed at providing
more savings, which in turn means more finance for houses. Institutions that are housing-
oriented will be those on which we will rely for future housing finance. Trustee savings
banks, private savings banks, and building societies will play an ever-increasing role in New
Zealand's housing. I leave this aspect of housing with one final plea: for many people, home
ownership is as possible today as it ever was; it needs some planning, some effort to save,
much self help, and some determination, but for the people who possess those qualities
home ownership is not far away.
Attention has been paid during this debate to Housing Corporation interest rates.
During the last 2 years, two concessional rates of interest have been in force, 3 percent for
people whose income was less than $85 a week, and 5.5 percent for people whose income
was between $85 and $115 a week, above that income, the prime rate of 7.5 percent applied.
These income figures were subject to an additional $5 for each dependent child. Under the
new Budget proposals, three concessional rates will be in force: 3 percent for incomes below
$85 a week, 5 percent for incomes between $85 and $120 a week, and 6.5 percent for incomes
between $120 and $160 a week, for incomes above $160 a week the prime rate of 8.5 percent
will apply. The effect of these changes is that people who qualify for concessional rates will
pay less for their mortgage than they have paid, and more families will qualify for the
concession rates.
As an example, I shall consider a married couple with two children, who borrow $17,000
as a basic amount from the Housing Corporation, including the low income supplement.
Under the old rate, they would have paid 5.5 percent interest, or $23.35 a week, for the first
3 years. Thereafter, they would have paid interest at the rate of 7.5 percent, or $28.75 a
week. Under the new scheme, for the first 3 years of their mortgage the interest rate will be 5
percent, or a weekly repayment of $22.07. For the second 3 years the interest rate will be 6.5
percent, or a weekly repayment of $25.70. Thereafter, they will pay 8.5 percent interest.
Under the proposals in the Budget, they will pay $1.28 a week less for the first 3 years of
their mortgage, and $3.05 a week less in the second 3 years of their mortgage, altogether, in
the first 6 years of their mortgage they will pay $672.90 less than they would have paid under


## p. 1903 (#359) ###########################################

3 August
1903
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
the previous arrangement. That is a worth-while reduction.
By reducing the weekly payments a mortgagee is required to pay in the early years of his
mortgage, the Government is helping the family with young children. A borrower with two
children and an income of between $130 and $170 a week will pay 6.5 percent during the first
3 years of his mortgage, as against 7.5 percent at present. The difference in weekly payments
is a saving of $2.13. We hear so much from the Opposition about increased interest rates that
it is surprising we have not heard a comment from the Opposition during this debate about
the advantageous effect of these interest rates. The spread of interest means that a person
who qualifies for a 3-percent loan will not be paying the maximum rate of interest until the
tenth year of his mortgage, instead of the seventh year as at present. It might interest
members to know—and I am sure many do know that the average time within which a
Housing Corporation mortgage is paid off is about 9 years. I believe that the adjustments to
the interest rates are worth while, and will help the family man.
A number of other aspects of the Budget refer to housing, and obviously I do not have
time to deal with them all. I shall just briefly repeat some of them. The tax exemption of
$300 on mortgage interest earned must encourage private investment back into the mortgage
market. This taxation incentive means that the return to the lender increases the desirability
of the investment, while at the same time ensuring no increase in the cost to the
borrower-effectively, both will benefit. The tax exemption of up to $500 for elderly couples
or individuals who vacate large family homes and leave at least half the Government
valuation in the property as a lender mortgage will, we hope, assist in making large family
homes available to those with young families, and it should enable better use of our existing
housing stocks.
A very important aspect of the Budget is the decision to provide finance for those who
are required to live in tied accommodation to purchase new or existing houses for their
retirement, by doing away with the provision that they must live in the accommodation on
which Housing Corporation finance has been made available. This will particularly help farm
workers who are required to live on farms in the course of their employment, but who want
to move to a town or city when they retire and wish to build or buy a house in advance of
their retirement. They will, of course, be required to manage the tenancies themselves, but
the rents will have to be approved by the Housing Corporation.
I wish to refer briefly to the announcement made last Monday. We are not concerned
by, but we are cognisant of, the fact that there are some who find it difficult to refinance their
existing mortgages. This is another legacy from the last Labour Government-short-term
mortgages that were sometimes taken out under false pretences. The position is nowhere
near as bad as the Opposition would like us to believe. Indeed, in an article in the New
Zealand Herald recently, solicitors who were interviewed on the subject said that there was
not one case that was a question of not being able to find money to refinance; it was more a
question of social reasons, broken marriages, defaults in payment, and that sort of thing. We
do not believe that it is in the best interests of New Zealand that mortgagee sales should rear
their heads, and so we have made some finance available to take care of these circumstances.
The Labour Government took a similar action in 1974, but it simply said to the borrowers,
"We will lend you some money for a year. You go out and find yourselves some new source
of finance in that time." In fact, of course, they could not. In fact, of course, most of those
mortgages are now running on, overdue.

STUDENT DEMONSTRATION
Mr SPEAKER: I should like to make a few brief interim comments on yesterday's
demonstration and associated matters. First, as I indicated before, I gave no instructions
whatever regarding yesterday's demonstration; therefore the suggestion that I said there was
to be only one speaker, the suggestion published elsewhere that I said there should be only
two speakers, and the suggestion, also published, that I put a gag on a member of the House
desiring to speak, are all equally mistaken and totally incorrect. Secondly, as I indicated, I
had no prior knowledge of the demonstration except for reading the newspaper item that
said that no permit had been obtained from the city council for a march through the streets.
Thirdly, I can fully understand the concern of the member of the House who states that he
was precluded from speaking. Fourthly, I have discussed the sequence of events with senior
members of my staff, who assure me that when approached by the police about a projected
demonstration they gave no instructions whatever about the number of speakers. Finally,
the incident does seem to me to call for further investigation, but this morning's caucus of
both parties, and tomorrow's unhappy sitting hours, will preclude me from getting very far
before next week.

Oral Answers to Questions
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Education-Standard Tertiary Bursaries
1. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: Can he explain how
he arrived at the figure of $2 per week for the increase in the standard tertiary bursary and if
any weightings were used, in view of the fact that hostel fees for 1978 in Dunedin are to rise
to $38 per week?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The member will be aware that it is the
Government's policy to reform the tertiary bursary. It had a number of options available to it
to improve bursary conditions arising from the bursary conference held in December 1976.
The decision was taken to increase the basic rate of the bursary, so that some benefit would
accrue to all students rather than to make significant improvements in more specialised
areas. No weightings were used, but I point out to the member that the $2 per week
represents an increase of 8 percent on the unabated bursary and 15.4 percent on the abated
bursary.
Mr Marshall: Is the Minister prepared to listen to further representations with a view to
raising the level of the bursary higher than an increase of $2 a week from the beginning of the
next university and polytechnic year?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The member should understand that it was stated very clearly in
our policy that we would introduce a reformed bursary, that the bursary would be increased
to take costs into account, and that it would be adjusted annually. At this point the
negotiations on the reformed bursary are not completed, but as an interim measure, which I
said might be necessary, I undertook last year to increase the standard tertiary bursary
somewhat. That we have done, in addition to removing almost every anomaly left as a result
of the former Labour Government's rather hasty and ill-judged attempts to set up the
standard tertiary bursary.
Dr Shearer: Can the Minister confirm that it has never been the Government's intention
to increase the bursary to the level of the unemployment benefit?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Yes, that has never been the Government's intention.
Mr Marshall: Is the Minister likely to consider the possibility of indexation of the
bursaries, so that the students can be sure that every year they will receive an increase
according to the increase in the cost of living?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: No, that is not the Government's intention. I hope that it is also
not the intention of the Labour Party in any future policy, because if it implemented such a
scheme it might find itself in difficulty. I envisage that the increase will be in line with our
policy. In other words, the increases, which will be made annually, will take into account
increased costs. If we are able to restrain inflation very considerably at some stage in the
future-to, say, about 1 or 2 percent-it may well be that the Government of the day will
decide to give a greater increase than the 1 or 2 percent, which would be seen by many
people to be derisory.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

600. I am sure all members will agree that the rolls of all those schools are considerably
higher than normal throughout the country and that some relief must be provided very
shortly.
Mr Hunt: Has there been any slow-down of development in the area that might lead one
to suspect that the overcrowding is not now the problem it would have been if the same level
of building construction carried out during the years 1972 to 1975 had been maintained?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I do not have any information on that point and cannot answer

National Superannuation-Hospital Patients
7. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Is any reduction
made to those on national superannuation who have been patients in hospital for 6 months
or more, and, if so, what is the reduction?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of
the Minister of Social Welfare. There is no reduction in national superannuation because of
hospitalisation unless the patient is unmarried and has no dependants. In those cases where a
reduction is applied, the provisions of section 75(2) of the Social Security Act provide for a
reduction after 13 weeks in a public hospital. The amount of national superannuation which
would be paid in these circumstances depends on the individual situation of each case, taking
into account the superannuitant's income, family responsibilities, and capacity to appreciate
the payments.
Mr Marshall: Would the Minister deny that a further reduction is negotiated on such
payments after 6 months' hospitalisation and that this, in some cases, comes down to $4.50 a
week?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have the information here, and I do not deny that.
Where one spouse is a patient in hospital, the rate of benefit is not decreased. If both parties
of a married couple are in hospital, the rate of benefit is reduced after 13 weeks following the
date of admission to hospital of the last admitted party. In the case of an unmarried person,
without dependants, the rate of benefit is reduced after 13 weeks' hospitalisation. After the
twenty-sixth week there is a review, and, at that point, the amount of benefit is decided,
having regard to the individual case. It does not go below $4.50 a week. In many cases,
having regard to dependants and commitments, it could be a great deal higher.
Mr Bell: Do these restrictions or reductions differ in any way from the provisions that
applied to age beneficiaries prior to the introduction of national superannuation?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: This is a fairly complex issue but, as far as I know,
the answer is that there is no difference. The policy of successive Governments has been to
reduce the rate of social security benefit where a person without dependants is maintained at
the expense of the State in a public hospital. It costs $100 a week to maintain a person in this
way.
Mr Marshall: Will the Minister confirm that one of the extra burdens now placed on
social workers is the requirement to visit patients who have been in hospital for 26 weeks or
more with a view to a possible further reduction in national superannuation payments?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I understand that that has been the position over the
years. Knowing social workers as I do, from the period I was Minister of Social Welfare and

Family Affairs Cabinet Committee

of Education, and, if so, what are the committee's responsibilities?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Social Welfare. The Cabinet committee does not see itself as having a watching brief on the
censorship functions or duties of such bodies as those mentioned by the honourable member.
It does, however, see itself as having a watching brief over legislation affecting the quality of
family life. It also has a responsibility, when the public expresses deep concern about a
matter, to look carefully at that matter in order to ascertain whether any measures are
required to safeguard the interests of family life. If the committee concludes that there are
deficiencies in the law, it will make proposals for change.
Mr Marshall: If the Cabinet committee considered that the decision made by one of
those bodies was contrary to the terms of reference of the Cabinet Committee on Family
Affairs, would the change be made through legislation rather than by overruling a decision?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The Cabinet Committee on Family Affairs has no power to
overrule any decision of the Supreme Court or of the Indecent Publications Tribunal.
Certainly where there is widespread public concern, as there has been recently, as the
member would know, over the distribution of a book called Down Under the Plum Trees, the
committee does take that into consideration as to the adequacy of the law and what should
be done about it.

WILLS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Wills Amendment Bill
be introduced. The main purpose of the Bill is to give effect to the recommendation of the
Property Law and Equity Reform Committee in its 1973 report entitled, "The Effect of
Divorce on Testate Succession". At present there is a legal presumption that a subsequent
divorce does not necessarily affect a testator's testamentary intentions unless he or she
expressly says so by altering or revoking his or her will. The committee has recommended
that this presumption be reversed and replaced by the presumption that a divorced spouse
would not intend his former spouse to share in his testamentary bounty. Under the present
law unintended windfalls can go to a divorced spouse because of a testator's inadvertence.
Thus a gift to a person described in a will as "my wife" or "my husband" will take effect in
the absence of revocation or alteration to the will, even though there has been a subsequent
divorce and the parties have been so divorced for many years.
The Bill applies only to final decrees of divorce, dissolution, and nullity which are in
force, and has the effect of striking out any reference to the former spouse, with exceptions,
without striking down the whole will. This is brought about by providing that the will should
be read and take effect as if the other party died immediately before the person making the
will. As mentioned, there are exceptions to the operation of the presumption, and the Bill
expressly excepts a will that is worded to give effect to its provisions notwithstanding a
subsequent divorce. Likewise, a will made after any final decree is also excepted. In
addition, the Bill contains an amendment to section 15 of the Wills Act 1937 about the
avoidance of gifts to attesting witnesses together with a consequential amendment to section


## p. 1917 (#373) ###########################################

4 August
1917
Wills Amendment Bill
7 of the Wills Amendment Act 1955 relating to the age of testamentary capacity. While the
Bill reverses what was previously a well settled presumption of English law and is therefore a
novel reform, it is one that I believe will find general approval. I propose to ask the House to
refer the Bill to the Statutes Revision Committee for study.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I do not propose to launch into a lengthy oration
at this stage. The law of wills is highly technical-perhaps over-technical—and the effect of
this seems to make it just a shade less technical than it is at present. As far as one can see at
first glance it is unobjectionable and indeed acceptable in many respects.
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: There speaks the technician.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: That is right. As the Bill is to be referred to the Statutes
Revision Committee it can be studied there and discussed later on in the reporting back.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Wills Amendment Bill
be referred to the Statutes Revision Committee, and that the proceedings of the committee
during the hearing of evidence be open to accredited representatives of the news media.
Motion agreed to.
QUEEN ELIZABETH THE SECOND NATIONAL TRUST BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That the Queen Elizabeth the Second
National Trust Bill be introduced. The Government's 1975 election manifesto policy
contained a national trust proposal to be introduced by statute. It stated that the primary
intention of such a trust would be to ensure that sufficient open space was provided for the
needs of New Zealanders. The Bill is the realisation of that promise. The proposed trust has
the added distinction of commemorating the silver jubilee of Her Majesty the Queen.
After the 1975 general election Federated Farmers made it known to the Government
that it was investigating the establishment of a heritage trust scheme. The trust was to be an
entirely voluntary scheme run by farmers for farmers. Its main object was to provide a
framework for representative landscape in private farm ownership to be preserved in
perpetuity. There would be no need to sell the land to the Crown for reserve purposes.
Obviously there was a similarity between the Government's scheme and that of the
Federated Farmers. There was no need for two bodies to be operating in similar areas, so I
discussed the matter with Federated Farmers. An agreement was reached to merge the
schemes.
Part I of the Bill establishes a board of 10 directors to manage the affairs of the trust.
Specific representation is provided for those organisations with a close and everyday interest
in land and the provision of open space. Those organisations are: the Counties Association,
the Municipal Association, Federated Farmers, and the Maori people. There is also
provision for 'members of the trust to be represented on the board. Different classes of
membership are established in clause 5, and the board will fix the membership fees.
Clause 9 deals with meetings of the board. Provision is made for six permanent heads of
Government departments to attend board meetings. The six departments listed are those
with an active and continuing interest in open space. It is considered that these departments
will be able to make a contribution to the success of the trust. It is the Government's desire
that the trust board be an independent body. Thus, the six permanent heads will have full
speaking rights but no vote. A standing executive committee is created in clause 10. The
function of the committee will be the administration of trust land, and in particular the
negotiation of open space covenants. As the land over which these covenants will be taken is
virtually all farm land, the two Federated Farmers directors on the board will be perma-
nently represented on this committee. The other clauses of Part I are of a general nature
relating to vacancies, the making of rules and bylaws, disclosure of interests, and so on.
Part II defines the functions and powers of the trust, and follows closely the National
Party's 1975 general election policy proposal. One change that has been made is to exclude
the Historic Places Trust from the direct ambit of the National Trust. The Historic Places
Trust operates nationally on a small scale, and is primarily concerned with the preservation
and restoration of buildings of historical, scientific, and architectural interest or value. The
trust has other functions in relation to archaeological sites and certain historic land sites.
However, the prime management aim of land of this type is preservation for historic
purposes, and this object takes it outside the wider scope of the National Trust. The National
Trust will be primarily concerned with landscape protection and public access to the
countryside at large. Nevertheless, there is link between the two trusts by the common


## p. 1918 (#374) ###########################################

1918
4 August
Queen Elizabeth the Second National Trust Bill
representation on both boards of the Director-General of Lands and the Secretary for
Internal Affairs.
The Queen Elizabeth the Second National Trust will have investigative and recommen-
datory rather than regulatory functions. It will provide advice and assistance to Ministers,
departments, and other persons and bodies on the provision, protection, preservation,
enhancement, and use of open spaces. It will also develop and formulate its own policies in
this area, and encourage the acceptance and introduction of such policies. Provision is made
for the trust to encourage the co-ordination of activities of Government departments and
other persons and bodies that have responsibilities in that field. The trust will also have the
power to make grants for the development and provision of open space, and to acquire open
space in its own name.
A feature of the Bill is provision for the trust board to negotiate open space covenants.
This provision is the same as the conservation covenant provisions of the Reserves Bill. The
provision is carried over into this Bill because the Government considered there may be
landowners who would prefer to deal with an independent body such as the National Trust,
rather than with a Government department, as is the case under the Reserves Bill. The
covenants provision is a means by which particular landscape features can be protected
without the necessity for the trust actually to acquire the land in question. It will be a private
arrangement between the owner and the trust, for a specific period or in perpetuity, and a
consideration to the owner is negotiable. The covenants can be registered against the title to
the land.
Part III incorporates the financial provisions, and clause 23 establishes the trust fund.
Funds will be used for a variety of purposes, but mainly for acquiring or leasing land, for the
distribution of grants, consideration for open space covenants, and payments for access
agreements and easements. The existing law relating to tax deductions and gift duty will
apply. The Government made two important announcements about the trust in the Budget.
First, donations, gifts, and bequests of cash will attract a $2 for $1 Government subsidy. I
believe that this will assist the trust considerably with finance to meet its aims. Secondly,
where the whole of the estate or interest in land of a deceased person is vested in possession
in the trust, free of all encumbrances, that estate or interest will be free of estate duty. The
Government believes that this incentive will permit the trust to receive property that it
considers should be protected and maintained in its existing state for future generations.
Part IV includes the miscellaneous provisions, and relates to access and offences. It
should be noted that the public will enjoy freedom of access to trust land subject to bylaws
and any conditions that may be agreed between the trust and the owner of any specified area
of land that is subject to an open space covenant. When the Bill is referred to the Lands and
Agriculture Committee I shall move that the proceedings of the committee during the
hearing of evidence on the Bill be open to accredited representatives of the news media.

Another Budget message relates to the conservation of energy and the wide use of our

and indicates the Government's determination to avoid wasting resources. A further Budget
message is the Government's concern for the people least able to fend for themselves in
difficult times—the elderly and the young couples on a single income providing for growing
dependent families. The Budget ensures that the difficult times do not weigh too heavily on
their shoulders. The Budget is very much one for the times.
After listening to Opposition members' criticism about the level of taxation it is
interesting to note that, except outside the House, we have heard little of what they would
do about the economy. The member for Manukau, who is the spokesman for just about
everything, has said that the Labour Party would introduce new taxation policies. Why do
Opposition members not bring the new policies into the House and debate them during the
Budget debate rather than spread them around outside where they might have a captive
audience of a few dozen Labour Party supporters?
The function of the Budget is changing in today's society. It is more than just a financial
statement, a record of transactions, and a record of planned future expenditure. The modern
Budget can influence the future and give planned emphasis to investment and production
rather than to consumption. The modern Budget must provide a plan for New Zealand's
future investment in forestry and farming. Provision must be made for these items, because
many of them are charged to the present whereas the benefits will not accrue for several
decades. The Budget must also aim at reducing inflation, holding costs, limiting Government
expenditure, and collecting taxation revenue fairly and in a way that does not undermine
initiative. In the difficult economic times we are experiencing, the Budget presents a superb
balance between today's social needs and proper economic management and conservation of
the nation's resources. It provides for the future, but it does not neglect the present.
Nowhere is this more clearly illustrated than in the energy package. The energy
programme in particular demonstrates an enlightened approach to an international problem.
This Government is grappling, where other countries are groping, with the problem of
energy, its use, development, and conservation. The Budget makes substantial provision for
energy research, for the development of indigenous energy resources, including accelerated
geothermal power exploration, coal exploration, on-shore petroleum exploration, the
expansion of local hydro schemes, incentives for conservation of energy in industry, and the
encouragement of the domestic use of natural gas, and it introduces a new policy for home
insulation and sales tax on some petroleum products in order to shift the demand for energy
from imported fuels to indigenous ones. It increases sales tax on energy-intensive appliances
to discourage the unnecessary use of energy. It makes provision for car pooling, and for
further energy-conservation publicity. It provides about $50 million to be spent over the next
5 years on transport, $44 million for suburban rail services.
In addition, the Government has recently approved special finance for research into the
production of ethynol, or liquid fuel from trees. This will enable the Forest Research
Institute to install a laboratory-scale plant for intensive research into this process. This
research is part of the Government's programme of energy research that includes the
investigation of indigenous resources as alternative supplies to imported energy. Wood is a
renewable raw material. It is produced efficiently in New Zealand. The production of
ethynol, or ethyl alcohol, is just one of the ways in which wood can be turned into energy.
Already ethynol is being used successfully as an additive to petrol. The use of 20 percent
ethynol as a petrol additive could save about $60 million annually of this country's overseas
funds. However, at present ethynol cannot be made at a cost that would match the price of
petrol. The rapid rise in the cost of petrol in recent years is expected to continue, and there
will come a time when the production of alcohol from wood will be economically competi-
tive. New Zealand must be mobilised with the knowledge required to adopt the programme I
have outlined.
In all these measures, conservation is the key word. Indeed, conservation is the only
password to take New Zealand society as we know it today into the next century. Without
the conservation of energy and other resources we make ourselves more vulnerable to the
demands of other nations with whom we cannot compete for energy in global terms. Quite
simply, we will not be able to afford to keep buying the oil required for our needs at the
present rate of consumption unless there is a dramatic reversal of trends in our terms of
trade. In 1972 our oil imports cost less than $100 million; in 1977 they cost $500 million. In
addition, the purchasing power of New Zealand's exports is sadly diminished. The same
quantity of butter, cheese, and wool will purchase overseas only 60 percent of what it would
purchase 5 years ago. Increases in the price of fuel have contributed to this adverse trade
figure, as have increases in the price of other imports.

Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
Another burden is the bill the Government has to foot for the luxury—if that is the
word-of 3 years of Labour administration. In 1973 New Zealand was a creditor nation—we
had more in overseas reserves than our indebtedness to the rest of the world. How the
picture changed during those 3 years under Labour! Those bills have to be paid by the
production of our farms, our forests, our industry, and our people. We inherited from the
previous Administration debts that we will not have repaid until the early 1980s. Our balance
of payments deficit under Labour was $1,000 million. That has been halved under the
present Government. We must aim at reducing it still further, and even at eliminating it. The
key to the problem is the huge surplus of $45 million being run by the OPEC countries, and
the $10 million surplus enjoyed by countries like Germany and Japan. Because of the
surpluses, the rest of the world's markets must live with deficits of $55 million. OPEC and
the industrialised countries have a responsibility to the rest of the world to reduce their
surpluses, because the developing and primary producing countries are carrying more than
their share of strengthening the world economy. We must do what we can to ensure that they
do not shirk their responsibility.
We need to ensure that NAFTA remains a reciprocal agreement for the benefit of New
Zealand and Australia. Our trade with Australia runs two to one in its favour. New Zealand
is Australia's biggest market for manufactured goods, and this should be recognised by the
Australian manufacturers who too often try to keep New Zealand goods out of their country.
We can enjoy the reciprocal growth of NAFTA only if the benefits are shared on both sides
of the Tasman. In this, continued sales of newsprint and pulp loom large. We must continue
to be able to supply Australia with her pulp and paper needs from our expanding production.
We have the capacity to do it, but we must rehabilitate one of New Zealand's largest
companies, Tasman Pulp and Paper Ltd. A number of factors have contributed to the
problems faced by Tasman, but let us not overlook the militant action of several unions that
helped bring that industrial giant almost to its knees. The extra construction costs and the
start-up delays caused mainly by strikes and increased capital costs meant that an extra $30
million had to be found. Other industrial stoppages caused the company to lose production
to a gross sale value of $12 million, almost all in overseas exchange. The irresponsible action
of some unions must not undermine our determination to rehabilitate Tasman so that it can
continue its pulp and paper supplies to Australia and the rest of the world.
Now I want to speak about farm woodlots. In 1970 the Government introduced the
forestry encouragement grant scheme. Its success was immediate. The area of new forests
established annually rapidly rose to 6500 hectares in 1975. Forests established and authorised
under the forestry loans and grants scheme cover in total an area half as big as the
Kaiangaroa State Forest. That gives a comparative description of the total area of forests
involved in this scheme. The annual establishment has stabilised at the 1975 figure of about
6500 hectares, mainly because inflation has reduced the maximum grant payable to well
below the 50 percent of qualifying costs that it was originally intended to meet. The most
serious effect of this decreased level of incentives has been the tendency for woodlot and
forest owners to neglect the essential tending and land preparation in their plantations. The
Budget increase in the maximum grant to $450 a hectare over the life of the crop will restore
the incentive to the level established in 1970.
Those farmers who were originally granted loans of $200 a hectare were also having
difficulty in finding the capital necessary for the proper tending of their established wood-
lots. To assist these growers it was decided to convert their original loans to grants. It was
also decided to permit these owners to receive grants under the grants scheme for any
subsequent costs required to bring their woodlots up to an acceptable standard. As well as
this, borrowing terms for local authority encouragement loans have been simplified. A single
interest rate of 4.5 percent has been introduced. It is anticipated that the restoration of the
grants scheme to its former value and the improvement in the local authority loans scheme
will encourage landowners to increase their new plantings, and in this way the target of
10 000 hectares of new plantings a year will be reached.
We must invest in the industries that are based on our own resources. New Zealand's
greatest resource is its people. We must use this, together with our soils and our climate. We
must not depend on industries that rely on imported raw materials or other components
purchased from abroad. In other words, we must continue to expand forestry and farming,
for it is in these areas that we can most readily boost our economy.
The expansion of farming and forestry, of course, depends on wise land use decisions.
Recently there has been a growing realisation that wise land use decisions are essential if we
are to maintain a sensitive balance between all man's demands on the land. It is a scarce


## p. 1931 (#387) ###########################################

4 August
1931
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
resource, and we owe it to succeeding generations to use this resource wisely. We must bear
in mind the distinction between flexible land uses and inflexible land uses; by "flexible" I
mean those that can be easily changed in the passage of time. Farming, of course, is a flexible
one. A less flexible one is that which commits land for a considerable period, even up to a
century. A commitment is made either for land for urbanisation or land for forestry. For
forestry, however, the point needs to be made that, although the land use is relatively
inflexible, there is a great deal of flexibility when it comes to the end use. Our trees can
eventually be used for building, for writing, for wearing, for liquid fuels, and as a raw
material for industry.
The distinction between land uses that are compatible and those that are incompatible
also needs to be made. For example, use as a public reserve is compatible with the use of
land as a water catchment, but land for agricultural purposes and wet land preservation is, of
course, imcompatible; and it follows from this that the compatible uses must allow, and,
indeed, encourage the multiple use of our land. All these considerations need to be taken
into account when considering wise land use.
Since assuming office, the Government has invested a large amount of skill and effort in
major land use studies. The Department of Lands and Survey and the Forest Service in
particular have been directly involved in two such studies, one in south Westland and one in
the King Country. Both these studies were undertaken because of proposals for afforestation
schemes, but, although they have that similarity, they differ markedly. In south Westland 90
percent of the land in question is Crown land, whereas in the King Country the greater
percentage of land is privately owned. In south Westland the land use study was presented at
the recent highly successful seminar on forestry held in Hokitika; and the study seminar on
forestry held in Hoitika; and the study was carried out in difficult circumstances and a
comparatively short time. Interested agencies and individuals now have the opportunity to
make submissions on that study, and, after this public input, the Government will be in a
position to make balanced decisions on the use of Crown land in south Westland.
The public participation stage, which is an integral part of these studies, has almost been
reached in the King Country land use study. Last Tuesday I received a copy of the report,
which represents an enormous amount of work, particularly by the Department of Lands
and Survey. It is a voluminous document that brings into focus the complexity of the land use
problems in the King Country. The document in itself is not a blueprint for future
development, but it clarifies those areas where policy decisions will need to be made. The
land use study adopts the scenario technique, used so successfully by the New Zealand
Energy Research and Development Committee. As with the south Westland land use study,
after a period of public evaluation and input the Government will be in a position to make
balanced decisions.
We have yet to resolve, of course, to what degree a Government should involve itself in
the land use decisions for private land. I do not believe that any Government should tell a
landowner to what purpose his land should be put. The controls and restrictions that may
apply do so under normal planning legislation. However, where it is a contribution from the
Government to a specific land use, whether it be farming, forestry, or in some cases
urbanisation, then the Government has a responsibility to influence land use decision. There
is also the question of the social and economic results of differing land use policies, many of
which are showing up on the West Coast as the new native forest policy is being
implemented. The social problems of introducing a policy that can affect an industry that is
100 years old in an area such as the West Coast, where there is little alternative employment,
provides a number of social challenges for the Government to meet, and I can give the
House the assurance that the decisions will be made fairly when it comes to the implementa-
tion of the indigenous forest policy on the West Coast and elsewhere.
The Budget indicates that the Government appreciates the need for continued emphasis
on land settlement and development. Financial support for these activities through the Rural
Banking and Finance Corporation will be increased. The level in 1977-78 will be increased to
$163 million. Last year, 1070 first farmers were settled by the Rural Bank, the Department
of Lands and Survey, and the Department of Maori Affairs, with an increase in the amount
provided for the special settlement of young farmers.
There is no doubt that land settlement and development will continue to be an
important part of the Government's activities, and in particular of the Department of Lands
and Survey. The Government is determined to settle as many young farmers as possible
through the Department of Lands and Survey and the Rural Banking and Finance Corpora-
tion. The Government is committed to the principle of the private ownership of our farm

The member for Northern Maori, who has been in the House for 15 or more years, and
who was Minister of Maori Affairs and Minister of Lands for 3 years, complained that some
of his constituents in Northland have grave housing and living condition problems. He
implied that these problems were the responsibility of this Government, even though it has
been in office for only 18 months. Why did he not do something about the problems during
his 3 years as Minister? Has he spent too much time in Auckland, and not enough time in
Hokianga and Upper Te Hapua? Has he done anything about Maori land lying idle in those
areas? Has he moved amongst his people suggesting that they should incorporate and bring
their land into either forestry or farming schemes? Recently, the Race Relations Conciliator
commented on the small number of Maori justices of the peace representing the Auckland
area. Now, the only person who can nominate a justice of the peace is a member of
Parliament, so the Race Relations Conciliator probably meant that the member for
Northern Maori and the member for Western Maori have not nominated Maori people in
Northland. I was surprised to hear what the Race Relations Conciliator had said because I
did not think he would attack those members.
All that is good in this Budget for the people of New Zealand is good for the Maori and
Polynesian peoples; but because of their special needs the Maoris and Polynesians receive
some special treatment. Most of our policy is now working, and one can compare this
Government's performance in the last 18 months with the empty promises of the previous 3
years. I should like to record one or two of our achievements. This year the Prime Minister
addressed the New Zealand Maori Council-the first Prime Minister ever to do so. With the
assistance of the member for Wairarapa and the member for Awarua, we have been making
progress in implementing our Maori policy. Good results have been achieved in Maori land
development this year, admittedly partly because of prices, but for every $1 spent $1.36 has
been returned. The figure of $9.2 million compares favourable with the $6.8 million for last
year. New grass has been sown on 1200 hectares, and buildings, fences, and roads have been
constructed. Not many people realise that the Minister of Maori Affairs is the second largest
farmer in New Zealand.
Some property that has been free of development debt has been offered back to the
owners, and in some instances they have asked the Department of Maori Affairs to carry on
running it. In regard to the sales of Crown Land and Maori Trustee interests, many owners
prefer to retain their stations rather than subdivide them among their own people, and in the
last 12 months shares worth more than $1 million have been transferred or sold to owners
paid from the profit that they have obtained from the land. We should consider the purchase
of land generally, as compared with Maori land. Much public attention has focused on the
retention of Maori land for Maori homes.
The Department of Maori Affairs has assisted in the purchase of land, and many
families have been settled on house sections. In the last 2 years more than 3200 hectares of
land other than Maori land have been bought for $3.7 million, and Maoris have been settled
on that land. That has helped the Maoris to stand on their own feet, and to farm the land. It
is a two-way traffic; some Maoris wish to sell land, while others wish to buy it. Many
hundreds of Maoris have obtained State houses in the normal way, but large numbers of
Maori people would prefer to save their money to buy their own homes, and so stand high as
house owners. On 31 March 1977, housing deposits in individual Maoris' deposit accounts
amounted to more than $2 million, an increase of $1.6 million on the previous year. This
proves that the Maoris are keen, and have the capacity to save to buy and own their homes.
The Budget contains an interest rate concession, whereby people on lower incomes can
purchase houses more easily. That applies not only to Maoris, but also to pakehas, and
mostly it applies to young families who prefer to build rather than to rent a house. Between
1970 and 1972 I arranged for some counties, two particularly, to allow Maoris to build houses
on traditional Maori land. I hope that practice will spread further, because it is of
tremendous significance, as the member for Northern Maori knows. Back in the 1920s, trust

The Budget's full impact on agriculture is not realised by many people. They look at the
Agriculture vote, but do not take into account the other provisions in the Budget that will be
of assistance to the farming community, such as the increased payments for pre-school

the 40-mile limit on road transport, but the changes announced in the Budget will be of great

The taxation changes announced will ensure a more efficient use of our resources. Sales
tax has been lifted from heavy vheicles-a call we have heard so often from the rural
community. This will mean a return of competition so that farmers will now have a choice as
to the best way of moving their produce, instead of being told by the Government that it
must be moved by rail whether or not that method is efficient. The cost of upgrading freezing
works to meet the hygiene requirements of the EEC countries is between $200 million and
$300 million, which the farmer must pay. It is therefore a welcome move by the Government
that grants have been made available so that the deadline can be met, and some of the load
can be taken away from the farmers. As an interim measure, a grant of 10 percent of
approved expenditure in the first year of use, or 7 percent in the year of expenditure, is to be
given, together with assistance of about $12 million over the next 3 years for the purchase of
plant and machinery. Freezing works will be given the option of a 30 percent depreciation
allowance in the year of first use, or a 20 percent allowance in the year of expenditure, in
addition to the 40 percent investment allowance announced in last year's Budget.
The member for Christchurch Central said the Government had done nothing to help
exports, but that is one very definite way the Government is helping. The meat authority,
which was set up last year by the Government, will survey the industry to determine the best
use of our resources and our money. The export industry has been strengthened, and this is
of great importance not only to the industry and the farmers, but also to the country as a
whole, because unless our meat is exported we will be hungry for money. The moves
announced in the Budget help everybody, a point that has not been picked up by many of the
commentators.
Another first has been achieved by the provision of farm employee accommodation. A
farmer can now buy or build a cottage in a rural village, so his farm labourer will be able to
live in the community and the children will be able to attend school without spending long
hours on the school bus. A farm worker ownership-on-retirement scheme has been
introduced, which will give to farm workers the benefits enjoyed by people living in cities
and denied to farm workers in the past.
The member for Christchurch Central grizzled about taxation. The stamp duty on the
purchase of a first farm has been waived, and under the terms of the farm vendor mortgage
scheme 50 percent of the interest earned by farmers who leave money in farms sold to
purchasers approved by the Rural Bank will be exempt from income tax if the money is left
in for 7 years. The livestock incentive scheme has been broadened, and the minimum stock
unit increase has been reduced from 100 to 50. This will be implemented retrospectively to
apply to programmes already approved. The cumulative qualifying increases have been
reduced from 2, 4, and 6 percent to 2, 3, and 4 percent. Thus, the scheme will be open to at
least 3000 more farmers who have the capacity, the land, the scope, and the will.
Last year, the Government and Federated Farmers had discussions to try to produce a

I should also like to speak out strongly tonight on a matter of even greater importance to
every man, woman, and child in New Zealand: the great international issue, which I believe
will either make or break the free world in the relatively near future. I refer to the
opportunity that must be made available for countries such as New Zealand, along with the
developing countries, to sell agricultural products at realistic prices to the rich industrial
nations. On this basic issue alone will our medium-term and long-term future and our
standard of living be decided. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Foreign Affairs are to
be congratulated on speaking out so strongly on this urgent issue in various world councils.
In recent years numerous conferences have concerned themselves with the plight of the
nations of the Third World, most of which are newly independent, and all suffering to a
lesser or greater degree from an inability to provide both productive employment and an
adequate standard of living for most, if not all, of their people. Many fine resolutions have
been passed by the United Nations and other international forums, expressing concern and
demanding action, but, regrettably, little real progress has been made. Countless millions of
words have been spoken on this issue, but there has been little result. Even considering the
period since the 1973 oil crisis, the poorer nations and the wealthier countries have
continued to move further apart in relative terms, and are still moving further apart, there
being no sign at present that the position is likely to change.
Many people in other countries, as well as in New Zealand, still think that our country is
one of the wealthiest in the world. About 20 years ago our per capita gross national product
was in fact fifth in the world, but we have now lost that high place. Today we are about
seventeenth, for the simple reason that our terms of trade are slipping against us, because
the relative value of the farm products we produce, as against the industrial products and the
raw materials we import, has deteriorated considerably during this period. Together with
this deterioration in relative value has been the extension of agricultural protectionism in
countries that today are traditional or potential markets. In some cases this results in our
products being either shut out entirely or admitted spasmodically in small and varying
quantities. Then there are other cases where the result is some kind of levy or tariff, which
causes the New Zealand producer to get only a fraction of the high price at which his product
is sold to the final consumers.
These policies are economic foolishness, in that they not only protect inefficient
domestic producers, but also encourage production while maintaining artificially high prices
to domestic consumers. In turn consumption is reduced, the final result being the accumula-
tion of subsidised surpluses. Situations such as this must put New Zealand on the side of the
Third World countries in the increasingly bitter struggle that is causing a continual and
growing sense of frustration throughout the world. Industrial countries endeavouring to be
self-sufficient in agricultural products can be considered to be bad international neighbours.
There is no way in which the relief of poverty and suffering in the nations of the Third World
can be accomplished.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Ha, ha!
Mr TALBOT: The member for Christchurch Central may think this is funny, but I do
not, and neither do the people of the Third World. These problems must concern every
thinking person in New Zealand. Industrial countries will have to lessen their present
policies of agricultural protectionism, and also jettison tariff and non-tariff barriers, which
have so often negated the apparent access to the market that they gave to the Third World
countries. It is a matter of urgent international concern that the living standards of the
wealthy should not be permitted to escalate, while the living standards of the poor remain
static.

production enters into international trade, quite apart from the subsidising of inefficient
domestic primary industries. The result is that, through climatic and other factors, the
volume of goods in world trade fluctuates violently, and prices may fluctuate as well. The

state of regional development in my electorate.
The Budget, as has been outlined by the Minister of Regional Development, directs us
towards the development of our regional resources and is a most valuable step in the right
direction, particularly as this is tied in with national spending as a whole. The Wairarapa
Regional Development Council has pressed for this since it came into existence, but the
Labour Government did nothing about it. Every regional development council is aware of
what other councils are doing to eliminate projects that seem feasible locally, but not
nationally. It is very important that local and national development be co-ordinated.
However, increased production in any sphere must be serviced by all forms of
transport-road, rail, sea, and air-and by processing plant and water resources, to name a
few restricting factors. It is essential to increase production, and the co-ordination
announced in the Budget is a definite way to do that, both regionally and nationally. Strong
regional local government is essential in any major regional development, and it is essential
that it be successful. A great deal of work in this direction has been done by Wairarapa local
bodies, and I am sure that an acceptable form of regional local government will evolve with a
continuation of the co-operative spirit that prevails in the region at present.
Another interesting provision in the Budget, also of particular interest to the
Wairarapa, is the lifting of the 64-kilometre limit on road transport. The new limit of 150
kilometres brings Wellington within the range of many of our transport firms, and will save
expensive double handling of produce from back-country farms. It will also free the railways
to concentrate on the longer haul work they do best, instead of multiple loading and
unloading of small amounts for shorter, broken distances. There will be teething troubles to
start with, but I am sure they will be overcome. New Zealand's only hope for the future lies
in greater production, and the factors I have mentioned are all parts of a continuing
programme to increase productivity and also the New Zealand content of our goods.
Our country cannot be insulated from the effects of overseas prices, so we must make
the best use of our natural resources and advantages to offset our geographical handicaps.
Our main advantages are our climate and our people. Governments, of course, are there
mainly to be shot at, especially at Budget time. Nobody-the Opposition and news media
included-mentions the things one does right, but one is soon told when one does anything
unpopular. Crimes against the voters come under several headings, such as not giving
enough money, giving too much to someone else, or, worst of all, taking $5 from someone
and not giving at least $10 back. Some people still seem to have the idea that if they yell
loudly enough the Government can always find a bit more money to keep them quiet. Any
Government, however, has at least one thing in common with a bank-before it can pay out
money someone has to pay some in. We recently had a Government that did not realise this,

4 August
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
and we are still fighting our way out of the mess it got us into. Since New Zealand's economy
is, and always has been, based primarily on agriculture we know where most of the money
must come from.
As I have said, Governments exist to be shot at. Consequently their performances tend
to be defensive, because they are usually answering complaints made by the Opposition or
by dissatisfied pressure groups. I know that the National Government has been doing a good
job under considerable difficulties. We warned the people in 1975, before they put us into
power. The Prime Minister spelt out loud and clear that things would be tough, that there
was no easy road back from the mess we were in, and that things would get worse before they
got better. A country that gets itself badly into debt is like any one of us individually. We
either have to make a lot more money, or tighten our belts, or both. Well, making more
money on today's export markets is not easy, so we have had to do a fair bit of belt
tightening. No one likes it, particularly those people who always seem to believe that belt
tightening is a job that should be done by someone else. Yet New Zealanders, or at least the
more intelligent ones, have accepted the need for this, and most of them have not
complained too much. Believe me, if there was another way to get our economy right the
Government would be only too happy to know about it and to use it if practicable. It is much
more fun being popular, like Santa Claus, than being unpopular and miserly, like Scrooge,
but economic survival is not a popularity poll; if it was, bank managers would go around all
day with happy smiles, giving away money with both hands.
I believe that the Government is doing the best it can for the country. The Budget shows
that we are making progress, and therefore I have no intention of being defensive about
what we are doing. The actions we are taking are positive, carefully thought out, and, on the
whole, successful. However, some people are obsessed by the fear that they might not be
getting their share, and the mere idea of cutting down on spending sends them into a panic.
As a country we have to live within our income, and the Budget will help us to do just that. It
makes things tougher for everyone. I would be much more impressed by some of the
complaints from people who claim they cannot afford the necessities of life if the figures for
bar takings and TAB turnover did not keep on climbing. The Budget is a skilful tool to help
us through a difficult period, and I am confident that we will succeed in clearing up the mess
left in 1975 by the sleeping beauties.
The main Opposition speakers so far-if "main" is not too strong a word for them, with
their cracked-record repetition of socialist dogma-have drearily kept on claiming they know
why New Zealand's economy is in its present state. The whole of New Zealand knows that,
which is why the present Opposition is once more back in its appointed place, on its home
benches. The electors well realise that Labour Party members are so busy trying to find a
name that will allow them to be socialists without admitting it that they have no time for
important matters like keeping New Zealand solvent. After all, if they are planning to
socialise everything by degrees the country will lose money anyway, so what is the use of
trying to stay solvent?
I come from a country electorate where life is not too complicated. Back there, when we
see an animal that looks like a sheep, smells like a sheep, grows wool, and is not too bright,
we decide it probably is a sheep. When we hear of a political party that sings the "Red Flag"
at its conferences, claims it is socialist, talks socialism, goes in for woolly thinking, and also is
not too bright, we figure it probably is a socialist party-and all the name changing in the
world will not cure that disease. Sheep also make loud bleating noises when disturbed, and I
offer that piece of information without comment.
There is a simple reason why New Zealand is in its present economic mess. Anyone can
manage an economy-whether of a home or a country-when there is more money than can
be spent, but when times are tough someone is needed who understands that if you spend
more than you earn you soon go broke. It is a tragedy that the Labour Government had no
one who could understand such advanced economic thinking. The voters put National into
power to clean up the mess, realising it would take time. Most of them still realise this,
despite the harsh steps that have been taken in the country's long-term interest. The Budget
is one of those steps, and it is designed for effect, not for show. One of the effects it was not
designed for is the weeping and wailing of the sleepy Opposition-but that is their own idea,
and one of the very few they have ever had.
New Zealanders realise that to ask the Labour Party to cope with our present economic
troubles would be like asking a tenth grade schoolboy rugby player to take over from Bevan
Wilson in the fourth test. It would mean rejecting strength, experience, skill, and achieve-
ment in favour of an unoriginal and guaranteed disaster. The selectors-the voters-took

Mr QUIGLEY: For the benefit of the member for New Lynn, who apparently cannot

exclusive economic zone.
Mr Hunt: Oh, come on!
Mr QUIGLEY: Does the member for New Lynn appreciate the importance of a
measure like that?
Mr Hunt: I do, and I support it.
Mr QUIGLEY: Then what did you say "come on" for? The fourth major achievement
in the series of provisions to help this industry is the Budget extension to 31 March 1979 of
the provision relating to the duty-free importation of larger fishing boats, giving the industry
an opportunity for long-term planning. Conditions are imposed, of course, and I shall refer
to some of them. The boats have to be more than 21 metres long. The persons who import
them have to be established operators or companies, and, in the interests of conservation
and management, there will be requirements on the fishing species that may be caught by
these boats, and the locations in which they shall fish. This is part of an approach to
encourage the New Zealand fishing industry out into the waters now being fished by foreign
fishing craft. The non-fulfilment of these conditions within a period of 5 years will render the
importer liable to repay the equivalent of the duty.
Another important part of this policy announcement relates to the possibility of building
similar vessels in New Zealand. That is part of the policy on the importation of larger fishing
boats, and has to be considered in the context of another major Budget proposal-the
provision of suspensory loans of up to 40 percent for fishing boats built in New Zealand. I see
the member for Nelson nodding his head. At long last we have found something he agrees
with. In an article, the member for Nelson said that apparently there were no financial
incentives or support to encourage new blood into the industry, and that little thought had
been given to the expansion of training, or to research. Obviously, the member did not read
the Budget.
Boats qualifying for the scheme I have mentioned must be at least 21 metres in length.
The policy is designed to encourage the building of these boats in New Zealand, but is not a
subsidy for the boatbuilding industry. Conditions will be imposed on the person having a
boat built. The availability of the loans will encourage the construction of vessels by New
Zealand shipyards, and will also give impetus to the expansion of the New Zealand fishing
industry, which, as I said earlier, is largely dominated by foreign fishing craft. To qualify, the
boat must be a new and permanent addition to the New Zealand fleet, it must be based in a
New Zealand port, and the applicant must have the necessary expertise and financial
stability to operate profitably in an export-oriented industry. The policy determines catch
targets of eligible species. The more popular varieties such as snapper or terakihi will be
excluded. The catch targets will have to be achieved before the loan is written off.
It is interesting to note what some of the prominent fishing industry leaders have had to
say about this announcement. They doubted that the measure would promote much local
construction, and mentioned the dearer prices for boats built in New Zealand, the longer
delivery time, and the fact that suspensory loans are taxable. The relevant point is that this
package forms part of the total concept, and, as I said, gives assistance to the purchaser of a
boat and widens his choice. He now has an opportunity to place an order in New Zealand, or
import a boat of a comparable size. The criticism overlooks the fact that in the past the
boatbuilding industry has had little incentive to compete, and there has been very little
demand for bigger boats until very recently. The provisions will be a substantial stimulus for
the New Zealand industry. It is interesting to see what happened to the boatbuilding industry
during the 3 years of the Labour Govrnment. In December 1975 the president of the New
Zealand Federation of Commercial Fishermen said that the fishing fleet in Timaru had
dwindled from 39 to 22 boats, and that 10 of those needed to be replaced by bigger units
capable of long-range operations.

Maori Affairs Department-Prosecutions for Theft
2. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Maori Affairs: Were any
prosecutions commenced by the Department of Maori Affairs for theft in the period 1 April
1976 to 31 March 1977, and, if so, how successful were they?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): Two prosecutions for theft were
initiated by the department in the period 1 April 1976 to 31 March 1977. Both offenders were
convicted and restitution was ordered. Full recovery has been made by the department in
one case and legal action for recovery is being taken in the other.
Hon. M. Rata: Were the thefts the responsibility of staff members or did they relate to

department or whether it was farm property on properties run by the department. I said that
I took it that the questioner was wanting to know about officers of the department. In my
answer I said that the prosecutions for theft were initiated by the department. The Minister
had nothing to do with it.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Education Shortage of Relieving Teachers
3. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: Does he have any
plans to meet the growing problem of shortage of relief teachers?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The problem of finding sufficient
relieving teachers at this time of the year is not new. It occurs each year in the winter term as
colds and influenza take their toll of the teaching force. My department is in regular
consultation with the education boards and is holding discussions with the teachers'
organisation to find ways of minimising the problem.
Mr Marshall: Is the situation this year no worse than before, and would it have nothing
to do with the cutting of day relief teachers for 12 months?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The fact that the day relief scheme has been restored has
obviously meant that we require more relieving teachers this year than last year. The
problem is not new. We have always had this type of problem in the winter term.
Mr Wellington: Is it not a fact that in some areas-for example Porirua, Otara, and
Mangere, it has traditionally been difficult to recruit relieving teachers, and are those not
the very areas on which the Minister and his departmental officers are concentrating?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: There are some areas—and the ones that are immediately
identifiable are Otara and Mangere, and Porirua and Wainuiomata- where we have
difficulty, partly because there are not in those areas large numbers of people who wish to
undertake relieving teaching work. There is also the difficulty of travelling. A third factor is
that there is some difficulty in persuading people to go into those areas. However, today we
are having discussions with officers of the New Zealand Educational Institute and the
Auckland Education Board to find out how many relieving teachers are required for those
areas. Some education boards have assured me that they do not have problems in their
districts.

Ridge Road, Paremoremo-Rubbish Tip
4. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Finance: In view of the fact
that the Town and Country Planning Appeal Board has turned down the Takapuna City
Council's plan to build a rubbish tip at Ridge Road, Paremoremo, can he assure the
residents of the area that the Local Authorities Loans Board's approval for such a scheme,
involving $1.2 million, can no longer proceed?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): As far as I can see this is not a
matter on which the Minister of Finance can give an assurance. That is more properly for the
local body concerned. The facts are that the loan for $1.2 million was approved in 1975 for
the purchase of land for general, civic, and community purposes. Although the land was
required primarily for refuse disposal, the council indicated that if it was not used for that
purpose it would still be required for recreation and reserve purposes. The key point which
the member might wish to note is that the condition attached to the loan prevented its use for
refuse disposal until the Auckland Regional Authority's plans for such purposes are
approved.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: In what respect does the primary purpose of the application for a
loan- namely, to provide a rubbish tip-equate with the alternative proposal for rest and
recreation?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am not sure. The city council may well have assumed that
there would be a conflict of interest, but it indicated that there would be another require-
ment if its primary need was not met and that it would in any case want the land for
recreational purposes before or after the creation of any tip.

Import Deposit Scheme
8. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Customs: What reduction
in imports does the Government estimate to have occurred as a direct result of the import


## p. 1964 (#420) ###########################################

1964
5 August
Oral Answers to Questions
deposit scheme in its first year in operation, and what further saving does it anticipate will
occur in the 6 months commencing 2 August 1977?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): It is impossible to estimate precisely the
extent to which imports have been reduced as a result of the scheme, as this is dependent on
the action of a considerable number of importers. It should also be borne in mind that some
goods were exempted from the scheme on 30 July 1976. However, in the first year of the
scheme's operation, imports of those goods which were still subject to the scheme as at 1
February 1977 were $117 million, representing a reduction of 2 percent over the similar 1976
year, whereas total private imports for the same period increased by 30.3 percent to $3,098.1
million for the year ended January 1977. Imports of goods covered by the scheme have
shown an upward trend in recent months, due in part to the ability of importers to turn over
deposits made on previous imports. It is expected that the scheme will continue to be a
restraining influence on ordering and stocking policies, but I am sure the House appreciates
that we cannot predict with any real accuracy what the volumes for the items concerned will
be for the next 6 months.
Mr MacDonell: In view of the definite promise made by the Government that the
amount spent on imports would be reduced below the 1975 level, can the Minister indicate
whether this has occurred?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: This question covers the whole gamut of the Government's
import policy. The undertaking given was that the Government would review the import
deposit scheme. That has been done, and now a decision has been made to extend it.
Mr Hunt: Can the Minister answer directly the member for Dunedin Central, who

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: The Government's import policy is a matter for the Minister
of Trade and Industry. This question referred only to the import deposit scheme, and I have
already stated what the Government's undertaking was in respect to that scheme.

Australian Visitors Group Tour Costs
9. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Tourism: What steps has he taken to
hold group tour costs for Australians visiting New Zealand to a level that is competitive with
the more sought after destinations by Australians which include Indonesia, Singapore, and
Hawaii?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): I do not exercise control over the pricing
of coach tours offered in Australia by the various tour operators. However, the general
manager of the Tourist and Publicity Department called a meeting of leading tour operators
on 25 May, at which factors that could be contributed to the present fall in patronage were
considered. This included pricing, competition from other destinations, trans-Tasman fare
levels and sectors, and research and promotion. These aspects are currently being explored
and developed by the department. However, while there has been a recent "softness" in the
Australian market, this is under continuing study and New Zealand is still the main holiday
destination for Australians.
Mr Kirk: Could the Minister advise whether the rate of inflation and the effect this has
on costs was discussed at the meeting on 25 May?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: The point I made at the conference was that the cost of tours
promoted to other destinations such as Hawaii was on a transport basis only, whereas the
cost of coach tours offered in New Zealand included accommodation, travel, and meals.
Mr Falloon: The question implies that the Government should subsidise internal travel.
Would the Minister agree that it would not be practicable for the taxpayer to subsidise
internal tour costs?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: I agree emphatically that it would not be in the taxpayers'
interests.
Mr Kirk: Is the Minister aware that factors like doubling the transport cost and the
implementation of a machinery tax have caused the tourist industry's costs to soar?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: Those factors go towards increasing costs. Those factors are
not only common to New Zealand; they are international factors.
