The member for Wellington Central said that the tax rates are the same as those
established by the former Labour Government. That is correct, but he failed to point out
that an adjustment should have been made to the tax rates because of the tremendous
inflation and the need for wages to keep up. The burden of income tax on the average New
Zealand family has increased by $950. In fact, the total tax paid under the Budget will rise
from $3.8 billion to $4.7 billion, or by $912 million. No wonder Government members are
finding it so hard to defend. Let us look at taxation per head of population.
Mr Hunt: They won't like this.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN: No, they won't. Following the presentation of the Budget the
New Zealand Herald, as is its custom, published a table analysing the tax paid per head of
population—that is, covering income tax and other duty taxes. In the last year of the former
Labour Government the total tax for the year ended 31 March 1976 amounted to $996 per
head of population. That may sound a lot, and it actually represented an increase that year of
$40 per head. In the first year under the present Minister of Finance the total tax per head of
population increased by $205, to $1,199. In the Budget we are now debating we find the
position is even worse, and that tax per head of population is to rise to the staggering figure
of $1,524.36 this year, making an increase of $530 per head of population under the two
Budgets presented by the National Government, or a 50 percent increase in 2 years. That is
another measure of the worth of the Budget we are debating-the Budget from which the
member for Wellington Central tried to take some cold comfort.
What incentive does the Budget give to a wage earner who has to pay 60c on the last $1
of his income? That is a further disincentive. Is it any wonder that people are leaving the
country in record numbers, and that overtime and secondary employment are no longer
attractive? Incentives should be given to increase production, and to ensure that workers
want to work more and produce more. The Budget will have the very opposite effect. Is it
any wonder that the Chief Inspector for the Inland Revenue Department, Mr McKay, was
reported recently as saying that New Zealanders trying to beat inflation are turning to tax
evasion rather than to banks in an effort to save money? He said that tax evasion was now
rated as New Zealand's biggest growth industry. Is it any wonder, when one looks at the
weight of income tax and taxation generally under the present Government? Taxation is only
part of the punishment, because consumer subsidies have been slashed, and Government
charges increased dramatically-electricity by over 100 percent; post office charges by $101
million last year, and a further $60 million this year; and rail fares and transport costs also.
Even the housing sector has been heavily hit, and the Budget is bad news for home builders
and the building industry generally.
The Budget dealt with energy at some length. The present Minister of Energy
Resources, who is well known for his public relations work, can take some credit for doing a
cosmetic job in the Budget, but, like most cosmetic public relations jobs, it reveals all the
flaws one would expect, when it is examined under a microscope. The Budget gives no real
urgency to a reduction of the tremendous import energy bill faced by New Zealand. It tells
us that energy imports will cost New Zealand $550 million, and, just when we should be
directing all our efforts to making a major impact on that tremendous cost, we find that the
weight of the Government's policy does very little to encourage use of our own indigenous
resources. Today, energy comprises one-sixth of our imports. The dramatic escalation in
price for energy imports is revealed by the fact that for the year ended March 1973 the bill
was $76.8 million, while just over 10 years ago the total bill for 12 months' imported energy
was only $39.9 million. For the one month of March this year our energy imports totalled
$45.1 million or, in other words, more than the 1966 total.
New Zealand must become less dependent on imported fuel, and the Government
should be directing its efforts to this end with great urgency. We are past the midway point of
the present Government's term of office. There have been two Ministers of Energy
Resources, both failures. The present Minister of Energy Resources was the Minister of
Housing, and there is no need for me to tell the House and the country what a shambles
housing was under his direction. The present Minister of Housing was the former Minister of
Energy Resources. What does the Prime Minister do when he has two failures? He switches
one for the other, puts a new label on them, and then presents them as saviours of the
housing and energy sectors. The present Government does not have a comprehensive energy
policy, and the public is to be asked to supply it. Ever since it took office, the Government
has threatened to produce a total energy policy, but we are still waiting in vain.
It has been quick to produce a pricing policy. The cost of electricity has increased by 100

percent, of natural gas by 80 percent, and of coal by almost 100 percent. The Government
says that its pricing policy is a conservation policy, but we see contradictions in the Budget's
encouragement of the carriage of goods by road transport, which is a heavy consumer of
imported fuel and takes business away from the railways. To illustrate another contradiction,
I can point to the heating of a swimming pool in Wellington, which consumed 80.420 units in
the 7 months from December 1976 to July 1977. At the concession rate, this cost $816.10.
The Budget sorts out the housewives and puts an added tax on the purchase of clothes
dryers, which are not overlarge consumers of electricity. Recently, the Evening Post
published a table showing the energy consumption of a whole range of household appliances.
The cost of running a clothes dryer under the Hutt Valley Electric Power Board is 21c a
week. If we balance that against the cost of heating a swimming pool at a reduced tariff, we
see the folly of the Government's pricing policy.
One would have expected it to be designed to take the pressure off the importation of
energy, but figures supplied by the Minister of Energy Resources, in response to a question
put to him on the pricing policy of the present Government, show that, instead of
encouraging the use of our own indigenous energy resources, the present pricing policy is
having exactly the opposite effect. Let us take industrial fuel oil at the time of the change of
Government in December 1975 as a base of 100 units for comparison with other fuels.
Industrial fuel oil costs $1 a gigajoule of energy output. With industrial fuel oil at 100 units,
electricity was 95, coal 38, and natural gas 45. All these indigenous energy resources had an
advantage over imported fuel oil, but in May 1977, after the present Government's pricing
policy had been put into effect, and with industrial fuel oil still being taken at 100 units, coal
had increased from 38 to 68, natural gas from 45 to 74, and electricity from 95 to 182. That is
the magnificent and wonderful pricing policy of the present Government.
If I were an industrialist using imported industrial fuel oil, and thinking about being
patriotic and doing something to save overseas funds, I would think twice about whether it
was worth my while to convert, because all the incentives and pressures are the other way if
one relates use to the actual price of the product. In December 1975, $1 per gigajoule of fuel
oil energy output cost $3.39. In May of this year the cost increased by 8c to $3.47. However,
the price of coal has gone up, not by 8c but by $1.07, natural gas by $1.05, and of electricity
by $3.10. That is the Government's pricing policy on energy. Its energy policy, and certainly
its pricing policy, are disastrous for this country. Is it any wonder that our bill for imported
energy continues to increase? The Minister and the Government made great play about
some of the incentives given industry last year to use alternative fuels. The Government gave
certain tax incentives for capital expenditure on energy conservation measures, including
evaluation equipment and industrial installation of approved process control equipment,
which could receive a 100 percent tax concession.
That all sounded very impressive as a package deal to conserve energy. Recently I asked
the Minister about the effect of that policy on industry, and he gave me the following reply,
"So far there have been no applications for evaluation equipment; one for industrial
installation, valued at $2,000; and six for improved control equipment, totalling $108,000."
That provision by the Government had an almost negligible effect on the conservation of
energy in industry last year. No wonder we are suspicious of the Government's intention to
extend the range in this year's Budget.
New Zealand does not have a good record in energy conservation generally. An OECD
industrial energy survey published in The Need for Action in the OECD Observer in October
1976 shows that, of the member countries listed, New Zealand is one of the least efficient
users of energy in automobiles, in transport, and in the production of petroleum products
and aluminium. It is the second least efficient producer of crude steel, cement, and pulp and
paper, and is the heaviest user per tonne of those products. That shows the magnitude of the
task ahead of the Government, but there is the problem of its ability to grapple with this—

public generally to do just that. I turn now to the Government's proposal to prospect for oil

On-shore licences have been advertised extensively both in New Zealand and overseas
for the past 2 years, but, because of the Government's clumsiness in negotiation and its
policy of applying levies and taxes on oil prospecting companies, no prospectors would take
up licences; nor will they until the Government clarifies what the industry can expect if a
successful discovery is made.
The National Business Review recently had some very scathing comments on the
National Government's handling of the situation: "But there is no immediate proposal to
end the deadlock that has brought oil exploration to a near halt. While the protagonists
haggle"—that is, the Government and the prospectors-"some of our best prospects are
leaving the country in disgust. The major American oil companies, once firmly committed to
obtaining exploration licences here, have withdrawn their applications, according to
informed sources. One had an off-shore drill on standby in Singapore destined for New
Zealand. Now that this rig is no longer available it could cost millions of dollars more for
mobilisation of transport to bring another rig to this country."
The oilmen said they were waiting for the Government to make an unequivocal
statement of principle before they would take up any new exploration licences. Their main
complaint is that they cannot be expected to continue investing money in a very high-risk
industry without having a clear understanding from the Government of just where they
stand. Uncertainty is the reason given by the industry for its refusal to take up new licences.
Fourteen oil prospecting licences in Taranaki have been advertised over the past 2
years. When the Labour Government went out of office in November 1975 these licences
were being advertised, and it was expected that a great deal of interest would be shown.
However, the National Government came into power and proposed a $3 a barrel levy on any
oil discovered, which was unacceptable to the companies concerned. The Government has
now proposed a different taxing measure and discussions have been taking place without any
degree of finality being reached. In the National Business Review the oil industry said of the
present Government: "Since the announcement of the energy policy, present and potential
overseas investors have likened the political climate for investment here to that of Uganda,
Bangladesh, and Indonesia." That is an indictment of the present Government. Is it any
wonder that the oil industry had this to say about the Labour Government: "Several oil men
have expressed nostalgia for the so-called socialistic Labour Government, when word of
mouth gentlemen's arrangements were honoured, and sanctity of contract preserved."?

I turn now to the Budget, and want to talk about the transport policy and the way it will

mean a considerable cost saving. Wellington and Palmerston North manufacturers will be

little slow.
The previous speaker discussed the energy plans, but he knew very little about them.
The energy provision in the Budget will make a significant impression on Palmerston North.
Many companies there have established their operations around the ability to use natural gas
effectively. The Palmerston North gas department is a very forward-thinking organisation
and has extended gas pipelines in the city. In new subdivisions, such as Westbrook, natural
gas pipes are automatically laid, and as a consequence new Housing Corporation homes will
use natural gas for space heating, stoves, and water heating. Last year 458 new domestic
services were connected by the Palmerston North gas department, subsidised to the tune of
$98,000. That gives an idea of the forward thinking of the Palmerston North gas department.
The $100 4-year tax-free loan for water heating and cooking connections, and the $200
interest-free loan for space heating are further incentives for more homes to switch over to
gas. I shall support the Palmerston North gas department if it considers loading or
restructuring gas charges for homes with single gas connections. The overall price of gas
should not be increased, but restructuring the price to homes with only one gas connection
would encourage people to switch over to using more gas appliances.
The Government's Budget policies will accelerate the use of gas in Palmerston North.
Commercial and industrial gas users have been given positive tax incentives, and I have
received inquiries from firms considering changing over to gas instead of using other forms of
energy. I shall now take a quick look at some of the reasons why this is being done. A 10
percent tax refund will be given for new machinery using indigenous resurces. The scheme
provides for a 100 percent write-off in the first year for approved capital expenditure. The
provision lists equipment for the recovery of waste heat and the insulation of commercial
buildings. Dozens of commercial buildings could be upgraded by insulation, and that goes
for Government departments too. Many Government offices should be looked at, and I
hope the Ministers are listening. How often does one go into a Government office and see
energy wasted by heaters going flat stick? Some offices are heated with stacks of heaters, but
the doors are open and draughts are coming in, thereby wasting the energy. That problem
could be overcome by insulating and draught-proofing. The third factor in the provision is
equipment used for recycling and for the re-use of waste material. The whole of the Labour
Party would probably fit into that category. Those factors will save energy.
The attitude of the Minister towards on-shore petroleum exploration is commendable,

in the Manawatu area, and I hope that a significant discovery can be made. I remind new
home builders that interest-free loans for home insulation have been increased from $300 to
$400, and the term of the loans has been extended from 2 years to 4 years. It makes good
sense to start off with a fully insulated home, thereby reducing energy loss from the word go.

Export incentives are important to many Palmerston North manufacturers. One

Another Palmerston North-based company is leading the world in the production of ear

there is also an outlet for ear tags at the South Pole, where the seals are being ear
tagged- another outlet for a Palmerston North product.
I turn now to shift work and depreciation allowances. For years some New Zealand
manufacturers have developed highly capital-intensive plants that work only an 8-hour to 10-
hour day. Statistics show that New Zealand production per man-hour is dropping, at a time
when we should be competitive on international markets. The 3 percent incentive for
machinery operating at least 6000 hours a year, or an 80-hour week, will necessitate shift
work, and is an excellent provision. This type of incentive justifies the installation of
expensive equipment which, in many cases, is now being used at only one-third of its
capacity. Why is it working to only one-third of its capacity? It is because the machinery is
being worked only an 8-hour day, and because plants are shutting down for 3 or 4 weeks at
Christmas. Added up through the year, this means that the plant-very expensive plant-is
not being used to its fullest extent. I implore New Zealand businessmen to look closely at
this incentive, and to make use of it.

I now want to talk about law and order. Since I spoke in the Address in Reply debate
there has been an increase in the intensity of violence in my electorate. I make a plea that the
Police estimates for the coming year should include provision for a police station in my
electorate. That is a fairly modest request, and I am sure it is not one that will overwhelm
those in Treasury who have the duty of assessing priorities. The presence of police in an area
deters crime more than anything else, and at this stage the efficiency of police operations is
necessary for social security. Notwithstanding the best endeavours of those from regional
headquarters who work in the area, the impact of a firm, positive police presence, obvious
within the electorate, is not felt. I make that request, and I do so in the name of the people
who have expressed that wish of late. As recently as today I saw a letter in the New Zealand
Herald referring to the climate of violence and the deterioration in the feeling of security that
people in the Mangere electorate might enjoy.
I also make a plea for departments to communicate with people, and to bring decision-
making more into the arena. I refer particularly to the information I have received that a
post-primary school is to be built in Bader Drive in Mangere. The proposed school will be a
short distance from the existing Mangere College, and on the same road; and it will be a
short distance from Ngatapuwae College, and on the same road. It will have an intermediate
section that will be about 300 yards from the existing Arahunga intermediate school-and
there are no houses between the proposed school and Arahunga. A motorway will be to the
east of the school, a four-lane highway to the south, an extensive reserve to the north, and a
fire station to the west. What consultations were held that led to the proposal to establish the
school there? What type of course will be offered? Will it provide an academic course, or will
it provide a background to industry or technology? Or will it be yet another community
college? The answers to those questions are not known, but the intention to build the school
there has been flagged by laying the drains. It is clear that there is not enough communica-
tion. What consultations does the Government have with people who ought to be involved in
making such decisions? That type of action is fundamental to the feeling that pervades this
country.
I do not hold with those of my brethren who say that the emigration from New Zealand
is purely the result of economic stress. I do not hold with those who think in terms of money
as the factor that deters or advances, but point out that we have a Government elected on
the firm promise of economic and social assurance, at a time when the people were feeling
the shock of the first waves of inflation from a new world economic order. They are still
experiencing the ripples of that shock, but we do not have a Government capable of
motivating people or of bringing out the best in them. Where is there in Government policy a
determination to tax excessive consumption or penalise it? Where is there in the Budget any
evidence of the Government's determination to give incentives to increase productivity?
Where is there in Government statements any mention of the environment? I welcome the
Manukau Harbour study, but where is there in the Budget just presented anything leading
New Zealand to the horizon of being able to adapt to what is undoubtedly a new economic
order?
The tragedy is that the Government has inevitably assumed that the pursuit of affluence
and consumerism is a political opiate that will stir people to seek refuge behind superficially
strong men who are incapable of bringing out the best in people, and are certainly productive
of division and distress. Some Government members have that strong conviction themselves.
Now is the time, in the interests of the country, for their presence as men and women of
integrity to be felt in the Government, which, at least for the next few months, will be
responsible for guiding the lives of more than 3 000 000 people. The Budget contains

Government members know that. How will the country be enhanced by the Government's

single-income supplements?

relief is given to the wife who works part time, through the wife's rebate in her husband's tax
return. That will mean that the rebate will not be affected at all if she earns up to $520 a year.
On page 44 of the Budget is a weekly table showing the totals that are allowable for

small children who need the care of a mother at home, and endeavouring to save or meet the

the cost of the building would have been so exorbitant that the tenants would not have been
able to afford the rental. Because of the proposals I have put before the Minister, and his
receptiveness, I hope that before long the health centre will be a reality.
The Opposition has also totally ignored the provision of inflation-adjusted savings
bonds. The Opposition has not mentioned them, because it is annoyed that it did not dream
up this scheme. The inflation-adjusted bonds will have great appeal to the small saver, and
they are a credit to the member for Piako, who introduced a private member's Bill that was
turned down by the Labour Government on the ground that the bonds would not be
successful. Well, it is going to work, and it is now going to be a reality. What is its basis? The
maximum investment by any individual will be $1,000 in any 1 year, and the bonds must be
held for a minimum of 5 years. Their great advantage is that they are fully protected against
inflation, and that will benefit people on lower incomes, people who are saving for their
retirement or for a motor car or a trip overseas or something like that—and I am thankful to
say there are still some such people left in our community. The basis of the inflation-proofing
of the bonds will be that their redemption value will be increased to coincide with the
increase in the consumer price index over the period of the bond. That adjustment will be
exempt from income tax.
Mr Malcolm: As well as keeping pace with inflation?
Miss DEWE: That is what the adjustment does. In addition, interest at a minimum rate
of 2 percent-small, but interest nevertheless-will be paid on the bonds, but will be taxable.
Only private individuals will be entitled to hold the bonds, and the maximum holding for any
one person will be $5,000. I hope that lots of people will have a bond. It is a revolutionary
policy. It is extremely important that small savers should realise its worth and realise that this
facility for saving is available to them. Opposition member have not said that they dislike the
bonds, but they have not said they like them. I should like a member opposite to commend
the Government for having the foresight to introduce them.
I have not dealt with many other matters for which provision is made in the
Budget-farming, energy, export incentives to the manufacturing industry, social welfare,
education, housing, or even fishing, which I intended to mention. As was said in Trans
Tasman, the Budget is a document that is an incentive for success. I point out to the
Opposition that although certain criticisms of the Budget have been made by the public there
has been less criticism of it than of many others in previous years, and certainly less criticism
than there was of any Budget introduced by the Labour Government in its 3 years in office.
The member for Petone said it was a pepper-pot budget, a bits-and-pieces Budget, and
commented that criticism along those lines had been made. Those criticisms came from
Opposition members, not from the farming sector, the industrial sector, or the manufactur-
ers or road transport operators. They were the criticisms of Opposition members, who have
been very hard-pressed indeed to find subjects to introduce into this debate rather than
discussing the Budget itself. They have studiously ignored the Budget and its proposals.
New Zealand has been going through a desperate economic crisis. The country can go in
either one of two ways. It can plunge further into economic depression, with rampaging
inflation, soaring costs, lower profitability, less capital investment, and greater unemploy-
ment. That would lead to a very dark future. The alternative is to go forward to a better and
more secure future, with the ability for New Zealand to control its own destiny and not be
subject to the booms and depressions which have upset it so often in the past. That future
must be ours, and it must be based on a thriving internal economy with productive, hard-
working, and industrious people. The attainment of that goal requires control by a
Government with a strong economic policy. The National Government has that policy and
has the ability to carry it out. I am grateful to be a member of that Government, and proud
to be part of it.

I am not in any way critical of successful people, but I should like to see more New

practises this philosophy, and I am proud to belong to a party that seeks to share the

The main justification of this Budget, as well as last year's, is to maintain an incredibly
expensive national superannuation scheme at a time when we are in an economic recession.
This is an indictment of the Government, and distinguishes between the two parties in

when we are asked to tighten our belts and when so many families are unable to do so any

New Zealand families are being ruthlessly transplanted from their home territory

De Facto Relationships—Domestic Purposes Benefit
5. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Is it correct, as stated in
chapter 5.3 of the Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee's report, that guidelines
have been laid down by the Social Security Commission for those district officers with the
delegated authority to determine whether or not a de facto relationship exists, and, if so,
how does he equate this finding with his answer to a written question from the member for
Raglan, given on 6 October 1976, that "It is not possible to set down such criteria. It is
necessary for the particular circumstances of each individual case and of each relationship to
be taken into account."?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The guidelines referred to in the
report of the Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee are general procedural instruc-
tions for the guidance of district officers. While they contain reference to particular points
concerning a relationship which should be known before a decision is reached, they do not
represent the specific criteria to be used in forming a judgment as to whether a de facto
relationship exists. As I said in reply to the earlier question asked of me by the member for
Raglan, it is not possible to set down specific criteria to cover all cases. The particular
circumstances of each individual case and of each relationship must be taken into account.
Mr Lange: Has the department delegated to district officers the power to determine
whether a de facto relationship is in existence, and have those district officers been given
guidelines by the department to determine that point?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The answer to both questions is yes. However, in all cases a
person who unsuccessfully applies for a benefit has a right of appeal to the Social Security
Commission. If that is unsuccessful the person has the right to appeal again to the Social
Security Appeal Authority, and if that fails the matter can be taken to the Supreme Court.
Mr McLay: Can the Minister confirm that in the view of the department, and probably
in the view of all those who use the English language in a normal way, there is a considerable
difference between general guidelines on the one hand and specific criteria on the other?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, I certainly do see a great difference between the two.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: In what way does the establishment of these guidelines differ
from the action the commission took some years ago in imposing restrictions on its freedom
to exercise a statutory discretion, an act which was then strongly criticised by the
Ombudsman?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I must confess that I am not sure of those previous guidelines. I
confirm that the ones currently in use give a discretion to the local officer, and experience
has shown that those guidelines and the authority given to the district officers have been used
with discretion and in a responsible manner.
Mrs Batchelor: Can the Minister clarify the situation further by telling the House exactly
what the guidelines are under which district officers act?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I think the best way to answer that question is to quote a few
sentences from the Act. Section 63(b) gives the Social Security Commission discretionary
authority to regard as husband and wife any man and woman who, not being legally married,
are in the opinion of the commission living together on a domestic basis as husband and wife.
The principle behind the legislation is that a couple who live on a domestic basis as husband
and wife should not be placed in a better situation in regard to the social security benefit than
a legally married couple. In a legal marriage the wife cannot in any circumstances draw a
domestic purposes benefit as a solo parent while living with her husband. Where a man and
woman so merge their lives that it would be reasonable to treat them no better and no worse
than a legally married couple, then for social security benefit purposes they would be


## p. 1993 (#449) ###########################################

9 August
1993
Oral Answers to Questions
regarded as husband and wife, but it would be quite wrong to place a couple living in a de
facto relationship in a better financial situation than a legally married couple by paying a
domestic purposes benefit to one party as a solo parent.
Mr SPEAKER: I hesitate to allow any more supplementary questions, because we have
had more than enough already. It is curious that whenever the term "social welfare" is
mentioned, we have a splurge of questions and we make no progress. I will allow one more.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Would the Minister be prepared to refer the propriety of this

Hon. H. J. WALKER: Perhaps the member could clarify what he wants referred. The

Nursing Graduates
6. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Health: Can he tell the House how
the number of graduate nurses recruited and trained in the technical colleges compares, as a
percentage, with those who are trained in the hospitals?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): In 1975, of the total number of 1169 nurses
granted registration, 46, or 3.94 percent, trained in technical institutes. In 1976, 1513 were
granted registration with 85, or 5.62 percent, from technical institutes. At 31 March 1977,
6252 student nurses were in training, and 465, or 7.44 percent, were in technical institutes.
Mr Downie: Can the Minister confirm that the extension of this scheme to Southland
and Waikato, which was announced in the Budget, is a result of the findings of the Carpenter
report set up by the previous National Government?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The Carpenter report recommended that as a gradual process nursing
education should be transferred from the Department of Health and the hospitals to the
Department of Education. The Government accepted this recommendation, which the
report stated would take a minimum of 10 or 11 years. By January next year this type of
training will be carried out in six districts. It is not proposed to proceed any further with this
scheme until there are sufficient nurses out of training and in employment to allow a proper
evaluation of the relative merits of the two methods of training to be carried out.
Mr Elliott: Is there any proposal to implement a combined technical institute and
hospital training programme, and, if so, would the Minister agree that the new Northland
Community College, which is sited close to the Northland base hospital, would be an ideal
place for such a pilot scheme?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I am sure that any establishment in Whangarei would be an ideal
place for any such experimentation. When the evaluation of the relative merits of the two
training schemes has been carried out, we will be able to establish whether there are any
other suitable methods. I should point out that the curriculum for technical institute training
in Auckland is quite different from the curriculum in Christchurch. Both schemes arrive at
the same results. Different methods achieve these results, and the proposal mentioned by
the member for Whangarei could well be a very acceptable one.
Mr Downie: Is the dropout rate in the technical institutes less than in the hospitals?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I do not have those figures, but I suggest they would be misleading,
because on the one hand we are dealing with about 7000 students and on the other hand we
are dealing with a small number of 5 or 6 percent. Whatever result you get over the short
term the scheme has been running could be misleading.

## p. 2000 (#456) ###########################################

2000
9 August
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
Although members opposite have said that national superannuation would cost too
much, that the Government could not afford it, and that beneficiaries would be worse off,
not one has yet given me an example of a person who is worse off as the result of the
introduction of the scheme. The beneficiaries are better off. A substantial increase in the
weekly allowance will be made on 18 August; another increase will be made on 9 February
next; and in August 1978 the benefit will be increased to 80 percent of the average ordinary-
time weekly wage. Does anyone remember how much the Labour Government thought the
beneficiaries were worth? A miserable 53 percent of the average wage. The National
Government has undertaken to correct any deficiencies that might be found. If members
opposite know of instances where beneficiaries are worse off under national superannuation
they should advise me and the deficiency will be rectified. However, they will probably use
such alleged deficiencies for political purposes. The member for Wigram said that national
superannuation would cost an extra $300 million to $400 million a year, and that because of
the number of people leaving New Zealand and the falling birth rate a greater tax burden
would be placed on a smaller work force. What a lot of nonsense!
The Deputy Leader of the Opposition pointed out that national superannuation would
cost $930 million and said that the scheme was allowing those who did not need the money to
go overseas or to buy a second motorcar. We would not expect the Deputy Leader of the
Opposition to understand the estimates of expenditure. I acknowledge that he was the
Labour Government's Minister of Finance, but we all know what happened to the country's
finances when he held that office. The $930 million referred to in the estimates of
expenditure represents the gross cost of national superannuation, including $600 million
which would have been paid had the age benefit for 60-year-olds and universal superannua-
tion for 65-year-olds still been in existence. Of the remaining $330 million, which is the
additional gross cost of national superannuation, at least $165 million will be recouped in
additional tax from people in receipt of substantial income over and above national
superannuation. Therefore, the net cost of national superannuation, including the provision
for the increases this month and next year-and for all the former age beneficiaries and
universal superannuitants-is $165 million, not $400 million as claimed by members oppo-
site.
I remind members again that in August 1978 national superannuation will be increased
to 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage without increasing the rate of
taxation. The explanation does not end there. I should like the member for Wigram to listen
closely. What better than to compare this increased cost with that of the Labour Govern-
ment's superannuation scheme, had it still been in vogue. To survive, the Labour Govern-
ment's scheme required a payroll tax over and above the existing taxation, so today, under
that scheme and with a 2.5 percent payroll tax, every worker would have had a socialist
Minister of Finance taking at least $3.24 a week extra out of his pay packet. In addition,
employers would have been paying a dollar-for-dollar subsidy that could only have added to
the cost of goods. The total additional cost of national superannuation this financial
year-which the Government is able to meet without increasing the rate of taxation-is $167
million; whereas had Labour's scheme continued the cost this year would have been $168
million-which would have been raised by extra taxation.
How can anybody say that people are worse off under national superannuation?
Labour's scheme deliberately discriminated against mothers who wanted to stay home to
look after their children, against women generally, against the sick and the disabled. What is
more it discriminated against the work force, because every worker would have paid extra
tax. In 1973, under Labour, a male breadwinner earning the average weekly wage, including
overtime, paid 19.8 percent of his wages in tax. But after 3 years under Labour that wage
earner paid 21.2 percent in tax. The figures for April this year-the latest available-show
that the taxation rate is down to 16.4 percent. Clearly, people are better off under national
superannuation. If national superannuation had not been introduced a married couple
eligible for the age benefit would have received, as at 18 August 1977, $68.84 a week. Under
national superannuation they will receive $72.24. A married couple with a non-qualified
spouse on the age benefit would have received $68.84, but under national superannuation
will receive $69.75. A single person would have received $41.30, as compared with $42.58. I
cannot emphasise it enough to make the Labour Opposition understand that that is 70
percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage compared with 53 percent paid under
Labour; and it will go up to 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage on 31
August next year.
Labour speakers claim that people over 60 who have other income should not be

2001

entitled to national superannuation. When the age benefit was in force the average bloke
who was 60 years of age would compare what he was getting in wages with what he would get
from the benefit, and he would take the age benefit. But if he went out and earned any more
the Labour Government knocked it off the benefit. Look at what happens today to those

The member for Wigram claimed that any beneficiary with $10 a week extra income
would be worse off. That is absolute nonsense. No one can be worse off on a cash-in-hand
basis where primary tax is deducted from each income separately. The deduction of
secondary tax is purely a matter of choice for each superannuitant. It is only when Labour
members start to assess terminal tax liability, not due for another 12 months, that distortions
result. Whether or not a beneficiary is worse off cannot be determined until the tax
assessments are issued for the year ended 31 March 1978—that is, after the first financial
year of the scheme's operation. By that time an individual's income position could well have
changed. There could be a different liability because of 101 different
circumstances because of different exemptions and different rebates; because of exemp-
tions for insurance premiums and donations to charitable institutions, and so on. If a
superannuitant is faced with a terminal tax bill the account does not have to be settled until
the February following the end of the financial year. By that time the superannuation will
have increased to 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage, and three additional
increases will have been made in line with wage adjustments. Where is the validity in the
claims made by the Leader of the Opposition and the Labour spokesman on social welfare
about people being worse off? Today, people receive 70 percent of the average ordinary-
time weekly wage, compared with only 53 percent under Labour. In August of next year
they will receive 80 percent. There is absolutely no validity in the claim of Labour Party
members that anyone is worse off.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke in emotive terms of extraordinarily high tax yields
and the extra tax burden laid on wage earners. Why did the Leader of the Opposition not
confirm that the tax burden was higher under the former Labour Government than it is
today under National? I quote one or two figures to demonstrate the position, and I invite
'any Opposition member who thinks he can to show that the figures I shall give are wrong.
The proportion of central government expenditure financed from taxation receipts is the
same today as it was under the previous National Government, but it took a great leap
upwards during the term of the former Labour Government. The figures have been taken
from the No. 1 report of the Controller and Auditor-General. In 1973 the proportion of
Government expenditure to taxation was 77 percent. In 1974, under Labour, it increased to
82 percent. In 1975 it was 80 percent but today it is down to 77 percent. Those figures do not
take into account the single-income family and young family rebates. Taxwise, workers are
clearly better off today than they were under the Labour Government.
The member for Avon talked of deliberate cuts in the domestic purposes benefit, and
claimed that children would suffer as a result. That statement is just another blatant example
of Labour's deliberate policy of promoting fear. The policy of Opposition members is
"Don't worry about the kids or the genuine solo mothers who are doing their best to bring up
their children in difficult circumstances, but use the kids for political purposes." That is the
Labour Party's policy. My advice to the member for Avon is to read the report of the
Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee. I would not accuse the member for Avon of
deliberately distorting the facts, but if she read the report of the Domestic Purposes Benefit
Review Committee only once I am sure she would not continue to make such outrageous,

referring to de facto relationships. Where a man and a woman have so merged their lives that
it is reasonable to treat them no better and no worse than a legally married couple then, for
social security benefit purposes, they are regarded as husband and wife, but it would be
wrong to place a couple living in a de facto relationship in a better financial situation than a

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: This Budget debate affords me the opportunity of
telling the House about the present position of NAFTA. During the debate, Opposition
members have criticised the state of trade between New Zealand and Australia, and the
relationship between the New Zealand and Australian Ministers. I can say immediately that
Ministers in the two countries have never had a better relationship than that which exists
between Doug Anthony, Bob Cotton, our own Minister of Overseas Trade, and myself, the
four Ministers involved in NAFTA. Total trade between the two countries, too, has never
been greater, and at no stage since the formation of NAFTA has the imbalance against New
Zealand been less.
I shall compare the trade statistics for the June years since 1967, the first year of
NAFTA. In that year, the trade imbalance against New Zealand was 4.06:1. I remind the
House and the country that the Labour Opposition was very critical of the National
Government's entering NAFTA. I shall not dwell on that at length, and I simply make the
point that the member for Roskill was one who spoke against the proposition. He is in the
House now, and is still in Opposition, which is rather significant. In 1972, the trade
imbalance had moved from more than 4:1 against New Zealand to 2.31:1, better than 2.5:1.
These were the early years of NAFTA, under the National Government. History shows that,
as a result of negotiations with their Australian counterparts entered into by successive
Ministers of the National Government, NAFTA was a success story.
Then we moved into the 3 years of the Labour Government. The trade imbalance
fluctuated somewhat during 1973 to 1975, but for the June 1975 year it had moved against
New Zealand again, from 2.31:1 to just over 3:1 against New Zealand. Despite present
problems with NAFTA—and I do not deny that we have had difficulties-the imbalance for
the year ended June 1976 was 1.95:1, or better than 2:1 against New Zealand. The imbalance
in trade for the 9 months to March 1977 improved to 1.92:1 against New Zealand. Despite
the problems, the total story is good. The member for Roskill may laugh, but when he was in
Opposition and NAFTA was started the ratio was 4:1 against New Zealand, and, when he
went out of office in 1975, it was more than 3:1 against New Zealand. However, today the
ratio is 1.92:1 against this country-a real success story. I repeat that the relationship
between Ministers, the actual trade imbalance, and total trade have never been better. Let
us have that in the context of the discussions on NAFTA in general.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: Is that why factories are closing down?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: For the benefit of the Leader of the Opposition,
there is nothing new in the announcement made in Canberra yesterday about the way New
Zealand goods are to be treated when Australia imposes global import licensing or quota
tariff measures. That decision was announced by Ministers on both sides of the Tasman in
April this year. The Australian Government is now merely stating it formally. Since that
announcement, both countries have been working under the arrangement entered into then,
which, in essence, provides that when Australia introduces global restrictions for protective
reasons New Zealand goods will be subject to these controls unless the goods are covered by
NAFTA arrangements. That is the first tranche. However, if there are no NAFTA
arrangements, there will continue to be opportunities to negotiate either schedule A or
article 3(7) arrangements to provide satisfactory reciprocal access. The April agreement,
safeguarding New Zealand's clothing exports to Australia, is an example of this.
I remind the House that a couple of years before that agreement, our total exports of
apparel to Australia were worth $2.6 million. Within the next 2 years-first under the
Labour Government and subsequently under the National Government, with greater
impetus our exports of apparel to Australia had increased in value from $2.6 million to $20
million for the year ended December 1976; a spectacular result that caused great concern to
the Australian industry and the Australian Government. In the April 1977 meetings, held in
New Zealand, we were able to negotiate arrangements for the calendar year that enable us
to export at least 4 000 000 garments to Australia. Remember, 2 years ago only 400 000
garments were exported to Australia, but that figure has now reached 4 000 000.
New Zealand exports a total of $24 million worth of apparel to 33 countries, of which
$20 million worth goes to Australia and less than $4 million worth to the 32 other countries,
thus showing the importance of the agreement negotiated by the Minister of Overseas Trade
and myself, working with our opposite numbers in Australia. We should have liked to obtain
more, but we have preserved exports into Australia worth $20 million. That proves that

NAFTA is working and is being honoured. I emphasise that these arrangements are well

areas in 1974-75 amounted to $30.3 million; in 1975-76, $50.3 million; and in 1976-77—the

the media and to the Opposition which have been speaking critically, that the value of our
exports is increasing. We have been making progress, and that progress has concerned the

Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: What about the factory in Palmerston North? Is that progress?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Yes, it is progress, compared with what the
honourable gentleman did. The Leader of the Opposition would not join NAFTA. The
Opposition would not join it, but it is a success story.
I shall now give some of the factors that have created the difficulties that have kept me,
as Minister of Trade and Industry, my department, and the Manufacturers Federation, with
which we work so closely, so occupied in the past year. The first problem is that unemploy-
ment in Australia is approaching 400 000 and is increasing. The second problem is the
imposition of emergency protection tariffs and quotas by the Australian Government,
particularly in labour-intensive areas such as the apparel, footwear, carpet, and household
appliance industries. Thirdly, the Australian Government decided that it would not continue
New Zealand's exemptions from global or any quotas in these problem areas.
Now we have to consider the role of NAFTA in the negotiations. First, where a product
had a NAFTA cover-for example, domestic appliances, which come under article 3(7), or
carpets, which come within schedule A even though they are on a quota-the trade was
allowed to continue despite the restrictions. We have had an assurance from the Australian
Ministers that the agreement will be honoured. Secondly, for articles such as apparel,
footwear, brassieres, and terry towelling, which come outside the NAFTA arrangements, we
have an opportunity to negotiate a special deal for New Zealand that will benefit this
country. In addition, we will be able to negotiate special arrangements for certain fabrics and
yarns; talks are going on at the moment. On the other hand, we have not concluded a deal
for brassieres or footwear although footwear negotiations are still continuing. Although we
offered reciprocal access for a number of Australian products, we could not strike a mutually
acceptable balance.
Thirdly, we will negotiate with New Zealand industries to offer reasonable access to the
New Zealand market for products of Australian industries, but we will conclude deals only if
there is a balance of advantage to New Zealand. That is fundamental. In my discussions with
the Australian Ministers I made it clear that, having regard to the size of the population of
the two countries and to their economies, there had to be a balance of advantage to New
Zealand. In the recent instances on which we have not been able to agree, the New Zealand
offers have been fair and certainly much more forthcoming than those in the past. I pay
tribute to the New Zealand industries involved for the reasonable attitude they have adopted
in agreeing to allow access to our markets. New Zealand industries have been prepared to
approve some access that was not available to Australia before. I argued that it was fair
enough for Australia, which could not get certain products into New Zealand, to have some
access. I regret that in some instances the Australian officials have asked for too much, but
happily none of the decisions has threatened the viability of NAFTA.
The Budget put New Zealand's case most succinctly when it stated: "The Government

Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: You're not going to say it hasn't?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The fact is that the cost of living in the consumer
price index is moving downwards, on an annual basis. [Interruption.] Members opposite can
laugh as much as they like, but that is what the Government Statistician says. Despite the
high single June quarter, the figure for the 1977 June year is lower than for the previous two
June years. At 14 percent, it was lower than the Labour Government's last full year, that to
December 1975, when it was 15.7 percent and rising. It had in-built factors that meant it
would increase to 17.7 percent to June 1976.
The National Government has achieved three successes in holding the cost of living.
First, it has reversed the increasing trend under the Labour Government. Under that
Government the cost of living went up from 5.5 percent, when Labour promised its way into
office in 1972, to 15.7 percent after 3 years. The impetus was there, and it would have
increased further. We have reversed that trend and brought the figure down to 14 percent on
an annual basis, and it will gradually and steadily come down. Secondly, we have absorbed
into the consumer price index the cost to the taxpayers of the very high subsidies the Labour
Government had to provide after it had promised not to increase rail, postal, and electricity
charges to consumers. Thirdly, despite the problems caused by the cost of imported inflation
and increased wage rates, which amounts to a major part of the consumer price index-as we
have demonstrated recently-we have encouraged competition in business to the extent that
several consumer items are actually lower in price than they were under the Labour
Government in 1975.
I should like to give some illustration of that. Here is a packet of Persil-persilated
soda-which in 1975 had a list price of 81c in any grocery in the electorate of the Leader of
the Opposition. On 21 July, in three shops competing for business in Karori-not in the big
smoke, where there is too much worry about parking difficulties-the price was 79c, or 2c
lower. After wage increases of about 16 percent, and after increases in pensions, consumers
and pensioners can buy Persil for 2c less than the price under the Labour Government. In
August 1975 a tin of spaghetti cost 38c, but on 21 July 1977 the consumer could buy in Karori
three tins of spaghetti for $1, which is nearly 5c a can less than the price paid under the
Labour Government. A packet of cornflakes, which cost 57c in August 1975 under the
Labour Government, cost 54c on 21 July 1977. In August 1975 Janola cost 44c, but on 21
July 1977 it cost 39c. The Opposition says that it is a difference of only 5c, but it is 5c less,
and that means something to the pensioner and the consumer. Finally, for the parents, a roll
of school lunch-wrap has been reduced in price from 26c in August 1975 to 19c in July 1977.
In October 1975 the average wage was $95.66, and by April 1977 it had risen to $118.16.
In 1975 the person on the average wage would have had to work for 1 hour 15 minutes to buy
the goods I have mentioned tonight, but that has been reduced to 55 minutes under the
National Government. The difference represents a saving of 20 minutes in time, or 27
percent in effort, and that 27 percent effort can be put into savings. The wage earner is better
off in respect to the cost of living as measured by the consumer price index as a whole than he

increase the limit on heavy road transport from 40 miles to 93.5 miles, or 150 kilometres, will

For the benefit of members opposite, who do not appear to understand that trains are
more effective and more efficient than trucks, I shall quote some statistics. A modern diesel
electric locomotive, using 10 litres of disel fuel, can move a train weighing more than 14000
tonnes 1 kilometre; that gives the locomotive an efficiency of 140 kilometres per litre of fuel.
It takes seven and a half times as much force to move a heavy, rubber-tyred vehicle along a
paved highway as it does to move a similarly loaded, steel-wheeled rail vehicle along a steel
rail. In America, it has been estimated that trains produce 238 tonne-miles of transport for
every gallon of fuel, which is four times more efficient than road transport and 125 times
more efficient than air transport. Let me make it easier for those members opposite who do
not seem able to grasp these simple concepts. It takes 50 motor trucks with a 10-tonne
capacity and 50 drivers to move the same load as a goods train with a crew of 3.
From an environmental point of view, rail has other advantages. Higher burning
temperatures in the engine mean it is cleaner burning. As trains are less frequent, they
produce less noise; they use less land for the same volume of traffic and take up less urban
and rural space; they therefore result in less disturbance of the landscape. Trains are more
efficient and keep down inflation by providing the most economic form of freight transport.

Also, incomes cannot be allowed to increase as rapidly as prices. That is a fact of
economic life, but until the people, including labour leaders and union leaders, wake up to

Tauranga has benefited by this year's Budget as well as last year's. In my electorate we
have local hydro schemes going ahead, old people's flats, industrial development, housing,
school buildings, and hospital buildings; and, of course, road transport has been helped by
moves proposed in the Budget. Perhaps more importantly, our community college is going
ahead on schedule despite the remarks made by the member for Eastern Maori. A site has
been acquired and site works have been scheduled to begin late in 1977. Sewage treatment is
going ahead. Everybody in Tauranga in the low-income bracket has benefited from the

more housing, better services for pensioners, and, perhaps more important, port develop-
ment, but I shall deal further with that later.
There is a subject which is just as serious as the economy, and that is transport. I
commend the efforts of the Minister of Transport in this Budget to solve the problems of one
of the major servicing industries in New Zealand. It probably startles some people when I
say that, but it should not if one looks at the geography of the country. With overseas trade
and internal marketing, it is obvious that the road, rail, air and ports systems should tie our
industries together, whether they be related to exports or imports, or the farm or factory.
Transport is essential to New Zealand and is one of its greatest problems and probably one
of its greatest challenges, because at the moment it is creating one of the country's greatest
costs. We must analyse what is happening in transport and what has happened over the past
decades. Obviously we have been running an adversary system among the railways, the
roadways, the airways, and the seaways. Each is fighting the other. I advocate competition,
but legislative protectionism must be very limited; and I sometimes even wonder about that.
However, this Budget provides the first step for many years towards resolving the situation.
Looking at transport as a whole, I have come to the conclusion that New Zealand
cannot afford to continue financing opposing capital and business development in transport
without using some common sense to find out where we are going. In other words, we must
rationalise and give the country the guidance it needs in this vital industry. First, we should
have one planned transport system which co-ordinates the modes and makes them
complementary as well as competitive. There has to be controlled planning, not interference
in management—I repeat, not interference in management. Someone has said, give it a
name. Well, we can call it a commission if you wish, or anything like that, but it has to be
responsible to the Minister and have the ability and the power to plan transport. The name is
not important, but positive control of transport is.
We need a body which recognises the needs of New Zealand and the needs of the users
of its transport, and consisting of people who can decide positively where the benefits lie for
the country as a whole. There would have to be a national transport plan, which it would be
charged to produce. This co-ordinating authority would need to be supported by advisory
committees from all sectors. Its aim should be to produce a flexible transport operation, and
not the patchwork political and parochial thing that we have at present. The railways, which
are required to operate efficiently, should be boosted. They need a clean up, literally and
administratively. Road operations can be made economic by eliminating empty running and
co-ordinating area services. I am pleased to see that this Budget commences to do some of
those things for both of those services.
Such a proposal would eliminate the New Zealand Ports Authority, in its present form,
and that would be one major advance. The principal task of that statutory body was to
formulate a ports plan for New Zealand. It has failed to fulfil that task, and now spends its
time interfering with the day-to-day operations of individual ports. There is no ports plan.
There has been a series of unconnected decisions made over the last 10 years which have cost

New Zealand dearly. That body's competence has long been questioned. It allows port
development in ports where there is little cargo, yet it stops development where there is

expensive development. When questioned, it hides behind socio-economic reports which are
full of opinion but lacking in fact. They are pure baloney, and costly baloney which New
Zealand cannot afford.
In my own area of the Bay of Plenty, Mt. Maunganui, and particularly Tauranga, we
have suffered continual setbacks created by this body, which has given us little co-operation
and virtually no explanation. It has prevented necessary machinery going on to the wharves
in the fastest developing export area in the country, yet in Auckland it is pushing the
development of a badly congested, inefficient terminal, where the cost is probably the
highest in the world because efficiency is at its lowest. Yet right alongside that very terminal
in Auckland is an underutilised private terminal which no one appears to know about. What
sort of planning is that? Who is really in control of the Ports Authority? That is a question
that should be put to the House tonight.
To justify all this a special subsidiary terminal is being built 21 miles away from the port
at a cost of about $15 million, but that terminal can handle only full container loads, while
Auckland, where congestion is causing problems, deals with less than full container loads,
which have to be unloaded on the wharf by labour from the wharf unions. Yet, as I have
said, the development at Wiri is to handle only full container loads, and will do little if
anything to stop the congestion in Auckland. There is another danger about Wiri, because
when wharf labour moves on to the development the cost of cargo handling will soar, and,
because of that, costs will soar in every factory, store, and works in the country. That is
something that the people just cannot afford.
Congestion in Auckland is so bad that 2 years ago a surcharge was put on on cargo going
through the port, and in 1 year the shippers had to pay an additional $35 million. That is
being repeated now. I should like to read from a report: "The Auckland container terminal
will enter a severe stage of congestion as from July of this year for at least 1 year, and
possibly 5, due to (1) the increased number of ships; (2) inadequate berthing facilities; (3)
the provision of a third crane has not been implemented fast enough; and (4) the number of
container handlings is disturbingly high for less than container loads." That is something I
mentioned before, and is what it is all about.
So, in complete sincerity, and thinking of the broad implications and of the cost to the
country, I make my plea for reconsideration of the port of Tauranga as New Zealand's No.1
export port, and approval of its full potential by proper development so that, in time,
congestion in Auckland can be relieved. Tauranga can take containers as soon as a crane is
put on the wharf; it has all the other facilities. It can handle containers and rail them to
Auckland more cheaply than they can be delivered over the wharf there. It is disgraceful that
the port of Tauranga is not able to work in that way. That happened only because the
transport industry works in an adversary situation, and with bad advice. There is a need for
co-ordination and complementary planning. So let us get some sanity back, and do
something about this. Finally, I have no personal knowledge of any port in the world that has
developed its container terminals in an old down-town area like Auckland's. Sydney,
London, New York, San Francisco, New Orleans, and all the rest, have got rid of those areas
and are running efficient ports. We could save money by learning from their experience.
I turn now to another section of the Budget-housing. We hear a lot of criticism from the

The Budget provides that, from 1 October 1977, single people can get loans from the

The Budget has provided a reduction in tax. In October 1972, the average weekly wage
was $65. The tax on that amount was $10.09, or 15.5 percent. In October 1975, when the
Labour Government was dribbled out of office, the average weekly wage was $97.33, with

$5 less than in the previous year and $4 less in money terms than under Labour. As a
percentage of the weekly wage-and that is the critical factor-it was down from 18.2 under
Labour, to 11.4.

Members opposite said that the economy is stagnating, but the Department of Statistics,

the volume of exports increased in the manufacturing sector by 34 percent"-the volume,
not just the price. It is the volume that matters. The Opposition fell into a trap of talking
about the great boom of 1972, quite forgetting that the export volume was increasing only
marginally. That is why the Labour Government pushed the panic button the next year, and
tried to keep the farmers exporting by buying up their lambs for export. Forestry exports
have increased by 38 percent in volume, and agricultural exports by 15 percent in volume.
Stock numbers have again reached a total of 100 000 000. If stock numbers had been kept at
the same level, and the lambs kept on the farms for breeding, the volume increase in
agricultural products would have been much greater. The Third World's $42 billion deficit
with industrial nations will be a great problem in the future if the position is not rectified. It is
notable that since the OPEC cartel began, Third World debts have increased to $180 billion,
a matter of deep concern to all world leaders.
What is the Budget doing for the young man who wants to become a farmer? He can go
into a cadet scheme sponsored by the Government and administered by Federated Farmers.
He can go to Massey or Lincoln Universities, and take an agricultural course that will help
him to cope with modern management problems in the farming industry. He can take part in
a savings scheme, instituted by the Government last year, that gives him tax-free savings. He
can build up a $5,000 nest egg from inflation-proof bonds. The Labour Opposition must wish
very much that it had instituted the scheme proposed by the member for Piako in a private
member's Bill during the term of the Labour Government. The young farmer can lease a
property under the new criteria instituted by the Government for the Rural Bank. He can
buy an uneconomic property, and it will not count as his first farm. He can take a tax-free
suspensory loan when, as a sharemilker, he sells his dairy herd, thus enabling him to use the
capital from the extra stock he sells to go into a smaller property and build up an asset, and
not pay tax on the profit from selling the stock. Under the last Budget, he received a 1
percent stamp duty exemption; and this represents a considerable amount. He can buy a
farm with 15 percent equity, something he could not do under the Labour Government.
Even more important, we have increased the supply of money to the farming industry by
enabling older farmers to give vendor mortgages to young farmers and claim half the interest
free of tax in their hands.

Mr HARRISON (Hawke's Bay): New Zealand is faced with four problems-inflation,
balance of payments, excessive Government spending, and unemployment. The Govern-
ment, in approaching this Budget, had the difficult task of maintaining a balance. It would
have been easy to have cured any one of the four problems, but the effect on the others could
have been catastrophic. It would have been possible to have corrected the balance of
payments in a dramatic way by cutting back on imports, but that would inevitably have
stopped the flow of raw materials and components, which would have led to the closing of
factories, the slowing down of production lines, and a massive increase in unemployment. To
a Government that eschews unemployment as a weapon of economic recovery, the social
and human results of such moves would have been even more unacceptable than the
economic results. A sudden cure for inflation could be found if the Government was
prepared to stop people spending by greatly increasing the rates of taxation, direct or
indirect. That would have destroyed initiative and incentive, which are necessary if New
Zealand is to come out of its economic difficulties strong enough to face the future with some
measure of confidence.
The Budget aims to achieve a limited number of important objectives. The first of these
is that New Zealand must produce more of the goods that the rest of the world is prepared to
buy, and prepared to buy at prices that will allow us to import what we need to sustain our
present way of life. We not only must farm our way out of our difficulties, but also work our
way out. Although the fertiliser subsidy has been reduced by $2.50 a tonne, which means a
reduction in income of $250 for a farmer applying 100 tonnes, the spreading bounty is
maintained, and the transport subsidy is improved for farmers living further from the works.
This shift in emphasis will probably mean no less fertiliser is spread in total, but more will be
spread on the hills, whence I believe comes our hope of greatest increase in production. The
livestock incentive scheme is estimated already to have resulted in an increase of 2 400 000
more stock units, and this has been improved in the Budget. I feel confident about even
greater increases in livestock in the years ahead. That will mean more meat and wool for
export, but as well as more beef and lamb it will mean more venison, with the extension of
the nil-value scheme to cover the valuation of farmed deer. I applaud this, although I am not
in the business of deer farming myself.
I am very pleased that the Government has shown its confidence in the future of farming
by putting more emphasis on the settlement of young farmers. The Department of Lands
and Survey will settle 55 young farmers this current year, and I believe we will see even more
young farmers settled this year than the 85 settled last year under the special settlement
scheme funded by the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation. This will be possible because
increased finance, that will allow more young men to settle on first farms of their own choice
and of their own finding, has been made available in the Budget.
One more weed will qualify under the noxious plants control scheme in each region.
The farmers in Wairoa will applaud that, because they have a problem with blackberry in the
surrounding hills, and have asked me to make representations about it. Hawke's Bay
farmers might find it profitable to have barley grass included in the list, because, as members
will know, barley grass has a detrimental effect on the carcasses and pelts of lambs.
The assistance given to the meat freezing industry by way of depreciation allowances on
new and altered buildings, and the estimated $12 million in grants for new plant and
machinery, will help not only the companies, but also the farmers. The assistance will enable
the companies to upgrade their works to comply with the meat hygiene regulations if New
Zealand is to continue to sell its meat in Europe and the United Kingdom. The assistance
will also mean that the farmers will not have to find the money through increased killing
charges.
I applaud the housing schemes for farm workers and farm employees. Farm workers
have made representations to me, and I have made representations to the present and the
former Minister of Housing.
We can expect increased production from our fisheries. What a brilliant stroke of
regional development it was to allow the 40 percent suspensory loans for ships built in New
Zealand shipyards. Manufacturing will continue to contribute to our export drive through
such new proposals as the shift-work depreciation allowance, profit sharing, and industry
development loans. Forestry encouragement loans will also help.
Debate interrupted.

NOTICE OF MOTION-ADMISSIBILITY
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I give notice that next sitting day I shall move, That
this House notes with concern the statement made by the Minister of State Services in this
morning's New Zealand Herald that the 3.5 percent wage offer made by the Government to
the CSSO has been leaked to the press, and, as in my view this leak has taken the sting out of
the PSA conference now meeting and to my knowledge neither the CSSO nor the State
services have ever leaked wage negotiations, the House informs the Minister that he should
begin his inquiries into the leak by looking at the Prime Minister's Department.
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I
respectfully ask you to look at the notice of motion on two grounds-first, at the allusion that
the information was leaked to the press and at the manner in which it was implied that this
was a quotation. I suggest that is incorrect. Secondly, would you care to look at the reference
to the possible involvement of the Prime Minister's Department, because I can tell the
House that there was none?
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): The Standing Orders require notices of motion to be verified
in some way. While the member has sought to verify certain aspects of the earlier part of his
notice of motion—and I have no means of disputing that-the essence of his notice is, first,
that information was leaked, and, secondly, an allegation that it was leaked from a certain
Government department. The member should be required to verify that part or withdraw it.
I draw to your attention the fact that this is not the first time in the last couple of days that
this member has made in the House an allegation of this nature which has been completely
unsubstantiated.
Mr SPEAKER: I strongly object to conversations across the floor of the House when I
am about to rule on a point of order, and when I am on my feet. Although I do not enthuse
over this jab and gibe type of notice of motion which makes a travesty of the whole notice of
motion procedure-and it happens from both sides continually-the latter part is admissible
in that it does not contravene the requirement that statements of fact shall be able to be
authenticated. The notice states "and as in my view this leak has taken the sting out of the
PSA conference”. The member is entitled to his view whether it is right or not. It continues:
"and to my knowledge"-I interpret that as meaning "to the best of my knowledge” or “as
far as I know"-"neither the CSSO nor the State services have ever leaked wage negotia-
tions". The member is entitled to say to the best of his knowledge.
However, the opening words state, "this House notes with concern the statement made
by the Minister of State Services in this morning's New Zealand Herald that the 3.5 percent
wage offer made by the Government to the CSSO has been leaked to the press". I did not
seek authentication of that statement because I imagined it would not have been made unless
there was some ground for it. As the point has been raised I will look further at this notice of
motion. The suggestion has been made that the source of the leak, if there was a leak, has
been indicated in the notice of motion. That is not so. The notice of motion alleges that there
was a leak in the press expressing certain views, and asks that the alleged leak be
investigated, with a start being made with the Prime Minister's Department. I will have a
further look at the notice of motion in view of the question raised as to the correctness of the
first portion of it.

Oral Answers to Questions
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): When the scheme was initiated in
January 1976 the Minister of Finance stated that the scheme "will be kept under review in
the light of the need for import restraint". Subsequently, the scheme has been reviewed on
three occasions, one of which resulted in the reduction of a number of goods subject to the
payment of deposit effective from 30 July 1976. There has never been any advance
commitment that the scheme will necessarily be terminated on any specified date. There are
obvious advantages in deferring reviews to permit maximum information to be available on
import trends.
Mr MacDonell: As the scheme has been ineffective in controlling the flow of imports,

effectiveness of the import deposit scheme, and I would suggest that he should consider the
consequences of releasing a sizeable amount of purchasing power as a result of lifting the
deposit from a category of goods that it was considered appropriate should come within the
import deposit scheme.
Mr MacDonell: How much money has the scheme saved the country in the last 6
months?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: If I had been asked that question today I would have had that
information.

Car Pools-Insurance Contracts
3. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Transport: In view of his

Insurance Office and the various motor insurance offices about clauses in insurance contracts
which inhibit or prevent such arrangements?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): As long as any car pooling
scheme is based on the following three principles it is not envisaged that clauses in insurance


## p. 2042 (#498) ###########################################

2042
10 August
Oral Answers to Questions
contracts for private automobiles would inhibit or prevent any car pooling arrangements: (1)
that the scheme be run on a cost-sharing basis; (2) that those involved do not make a profit;
and (3) that only commuters are involved. I am informed that these principles were set out in
the Transport Amendment (Motor Spirits Conservation) Regulations 1973 specifically for
the purpose of ensuring that those people wanting to establish a car pooling arrangement
were not prevented from doing so by clauses in the insurance contracts of their cars. These
regulations also exempted drivers and vehicles involved in a car pooling scheme from various
legislative constraints applying to passenger service licensing, including regulation 4 of the
Motor Vehicle Indemnity Surcharge Regulations 1974. This ensures that the status of the
vehicle would not be impaired by its involvement in a car pooling scheme, as long as the
scheme is run on the three principles mentioned earlier. I am also informed that no further
legislation is needed to ensure that clauses in the insurance contracts do not prevent or
inhibit any car pooling scheme.
