Post Office-Effect of Subsidy Payments
6. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Postmaster-General: What was the effect
on the Post Office administration of financing its operations by subsidy payments during the
period of the last Labour Government?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): During the period charges were frozen
the Post Office incurred losses totalling $65.7 million for the 3 years. These losses were met
by the payment of subsidies at the taxpayer's expense. The massive subsidy payments had
the effect of distorting the demand for Post Office services, because charges were held at
unrealistically low levels. The unexpectedly high demand for services not only placed a
greater burden on available resources but also disrupted the Post Office's planning proces-
ses. Furthermore, I am assured by my department that management staff morale suffers
when personnel know they are working for an organisation that is not genuinely paying its
way.
Mr Wellington: Has that procedure impeded the capital works programme, especially in
view of the increasingly high costs of imported material?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: There is no question that that period of subsidy payments was
harmful to the Post Office administration in virtually every respect.

Heroin-Disposal of Confiscated Drugs
8. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Police: As the Minister of
Health has indicated that the Department of Health does not receive confiscated heroin
from the Police Department, can he indicate how confiscated heroin is disposed of and what
supervision there is to ensure that all confiscated heroin is disposed of?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police): When heroin is seized by the Police, it
is immediately delivered to the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research for
analysis. It is then held in strict security until the court hearings and appeals, if any, in
respect of the particular case are completed. It is finally disposed of by being incinerated in
the presence of the public health pharmacist. On occasions some small quantities are
retained by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research for reference purposes,
and other small quantities are used for training narcotic detector dogs. Strict controls and
supervision exist to ensure that all the narcotic is safely disposed of, and, where it is
necessary to retain small quantities for the described purposes, maximum security is
ensured.
Dr Shearer: Can the Minister say what percentage of the total is regarded as pure
heroin?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY: I am afraid that I cannot answer that question off the cuff.

Divorce Statistics
15. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: How does he

of Waikato University sociology department as reported in Zealandia, the Catholic news-
paper, of 24 July 1977, that "the divorce rate in this country has scarcely varied in the last 30
years"?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): At no stage have I claimed that the
divorce rate is now one in three. On a number of occasions I have referred to the alarming
increase in the number of people receiving domestic purposes benefits, and in this context I
have quoted the report of the recent Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee, which
states: "Consistent with this trend are increases in separation and divorce rates (in the latter
case 1 divorce per 12 marriages in 1965, 1 per 5 in 1975, and an expected 1 for 3 in 1976), a
drop in the marriage rate, and a probably related increase in unmarried motherhood."
Mr Marshall: Is the Minister aware of the findings of Mr Swain and Mr James O'Neill,
of Waikato University, which establish that the calculations by the review committee are
inaccurate, and if so would he make a statement indicating the inaccuracy of the report?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, I am aware of the statement by these gentlemen. What
matters is what one wants to find out from statistics. They claim that there were 24 534
marriages in 1975, and that about 1 in 10 broke down. The hard, cold facts are that last year
more than 19 000 women applied for the domestic purposes benefit because of breakdown of
marriages. Do those people who criticise that report say that 14 000 women with their
children should starve? They will be cared for under a National Government, irrespective of
the unrelated claims made by a sociologist at Waikato University.
Mr Marshall: Can I take it that the Minister does not accept the criticism made of that
report, that the report is inaccurate?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I do not accept that criticism; and I regret that I was not given
equal time on television to refute the charges made by those people.
Mr Bell: Was it likely that the Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee knew
about Mr Swain's work at Waikato University, and, if so, did it have reference to his work?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee had access
to all long-term research of the Department of Social Welfare, the Department of Statistics,
all other Government departments, and the university. Submissions were also received from
46 organisations and about 100 people.
Mr Lange: Would the Minister clarify whether more than 19 000 or more than 14 000
married women applied for a domestic purposes benefit last year?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Last year more than 19 000 married women applied. The figure
of 14 000 was the difference between what the sociologist claimed for the number of
marriage breakdowns and the number who actually applied.

lot of the equipment during the winter, and the contractors, in their wisdom, will not do so.

DISCUSSION OF MOTIONS
Violent Demonstrations
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): I move, That this House is appalled at the violent and objection-
able behaviour of a section of the group outside of the National Party conference on Friday, 22
July at Dunedin and notes with no surprise that Labour Party officials were prominent in the
organisation leading up to the demonstration and calls on the Labour Party through its
president, who is a front-bench member of the Labour caucus, to publicly name and require the
resignation of those members of his party who participated in this disgraceful affair so
uncharacteristic of New Zealand society.
This is the first opportunity I have had since that conference to raise some of the issues
involved. The motion was moved to give the president of the Labour Party an opportunity to
take some positive action to remove from his party the elements that caused the violent
demonstration. I want to make it quite clear that demonstrations have, and will continue to
have, an acceptable place in New Zealand. Frequently in New Zealand's history, people
have been prepared to have their say in a peaceful yet demonstrative way. My objection to
the demonstration at Dunedin is because of the premeditated nature of the violence and that
the fact that there was to be violence was known to the organisations taking part. Group
violence is uncharacteristic of New Zealand society.
In last night's Evening Post a local magistrate, Mr M. F. Hobbs, S.M., said that the
ordinary public was entitled to go about its business without fear of violence or antagonism.
The persons to whom those remarks were directed were members of a Wellington gang,
some of whom were imprisoned as a result of their physical harassment of the public.
Although the demonstration in Dunedin might not have been as bad, in principle it involved
the same sort of action-premeditated gang violence-which was known to the Labour Party
leaders. There is evidence, which I will table, that the demonstration was pre-planned not
only as a demonstration but also as a violent one, and that the Labour Party knew that its

I now want to talk about some aspects of social welfare in Napier. I believe that about
120 social service organisations operate in Napier, and they are run by the State, the city
council, and by voluntary groups. They deal with all sorts of problems, from the elderly to
the young, from the healthy to the infirm, and from the strong to the frail. Some of these
organisations provide what can be described as ambulance care for those who cannot be
cured, and some support those in need. However, there is already a growing realisation in
Napier of the possibilities inherent in preventive services, and a realisation that many of the
social problems in the city arise from difficulties within the family, rather than simply from
those of the individual citizen. While it is recognised that there is a need to deal with
recurring problems that arise within the family from financial need, mental illness, and child
delinquency, it is also hoped that appropriate action might break the chain of events
whereby difficulties and problem situations carry their effects from one generation to
another. The sins of the father will be visited on the children up to the fourth or fifth
generation. We hope we can break that cycle.
In 1971 it was found in Napier that there had been a dramatic increase in the number of
children referred to the Department of Social Welfare. Research showed that the children
who appeared in the children's court came from homes of which only 1 in 14 could be
regarded as satisfactory. That classification was accorded those homes, not in the main on
account of low material standards-there were only three of those-nor because of financial
difficulties there were only six with those-but predominantly because of poor standards of
parenthood. In 13 homes, the children suffered from the attention of multiple parents, 29
children had separated parents, 7 had de facto parents, in 15 homes there was parental
disharmony, and drink was the basic problem in 11 homes. Truancy and repeated appear-
ances in the children's court were prevalent; indeed, 99 children came into this category.
The Department of Social Welfare concluded that, if a more definite and continuing
counselling service could be made available to the families of these children, they could be
provided with a better basis for the adjustment of their social problems. Such a move would,
of course, require a good deal more time and attention from the department's own workers,
and it was decided that the only way this could be found was by enlisting more voluntary
social workers to undertake the preventive side of the job. Consequently, a scheme was
initiated to recruit voluntary social workers, who would be trained by the professionals in the
department and guided by them in their preventive work. Volunteers were accordingly
recruited from business people, housewives, nurses, and many others.
The guiding light in these momentous changes in Napier was Mr Ivan Wilson, who is in
charge of the social workers of the Department of Social Welfare. He has been ably assisted
by Mrs Dorothy Chambers, an honorary social worker of considerable competence who has
assumed the role of guiding the volunteers in their training and their work. Professional
social workers gave these volunteers their initial theoretical, personal, and practical training.
This occurred each week until the volunteers were capable and confident enough to go out to
their allotted families. It was found that two or three families was the maximum that could be
handled by any one voluntary social worker; otherwise their own families were affected. The
youth aid section of the Police Department and the children's and young persons' court for
the most part referred these families to the Department of Social Welfare for help.
Each week a briefing session with further teaching is held, involving the voluntary social
workers as well as their supervising honorary social worker and the professionals from the
17.


## p. 2068 (#524) ###########################################

2068
10 August

department. They discuss the problems they have encountered in their attempts to help the
families, and, of course, they preserve confidentiality. Cases are written up so that there is a
record on file for follow-up or further study.
As a result of this scheme, a task that would otherwise have been impossible and soul
destroying for the department has been brought within reach of achievement simply by
mobilising the talents, good will, and energy of people in the community who are willing and
able to help in this work. In this way, they themselves are provided with an outlet for their
desire to perform good works, many families and individuals are helped to overcome their
personal or financial problems, and officers of the Department of Social Welfare are helped
to maintain a balance through contact and work with a variety of people—not just those with
apparently insuperable difficulties—and thus they have more time to devote to State wards
and other children under their legal protection. I believe there are at the moment more than
600 children under preventive supervision in the district.
It has been considered by departmental officers, and Mr Wilson in particular, that it is
fruitless to work with only the families. There is a need for the children to be given some
formal training at all levels of education to help guide them to be wise parents in the future. I
said earlier that the problem underlying these social difficulties was found to be inadequate
parenthood. The aim is to try to encourage the children to become adequate parents when
their turn comes. As a result, Mr Ivan Wilson has developed a scheme using the depart-
ment's professional social workers to train and organise specially selected voluntary social
workers to lead discussions with small groups of children in the schools on subjects related to
life and living. The aim is to develop character, conscientiousness, personality, sociability,
and communication. The instructors seek to develop sensitivity, integrity, and reliability as
well as drive, enthusiasm, and confidence, and also to inculcate a proper attitude to work,
sport, and play, and to show the importance of maintaining good health and appearance.
They also seek to teach the children self-respect and how to achieve a good relationship with
other people, be they family, friends, or strangers.
A pilot scheme was started by the Department of Social Welfare in an attempt to help
the Taradale High School with its truancy problems. Representatives of the youth aid section
of the Police Department, officers of the Department of Maori Affairs, visiting teachers, and
social workers started talking with classes on a regular basis. This attempt to come to terms
with some of the problems of young people and to discuss them openly was seen as an
essential part of school activity, because it helped to create a better balance between the
purely academic approach and the social awareness aspect of their education. Attempts were
then made to set up a regular full-time programme using volunteers as group discussion
leaders, and eventually the programme became known as "Discussion in Schools". At
present it is operating in Napier Girls High School as well as Taradale High School, and
deals with fourth form classes.
There are 16 regular discussion group leaders and 5 emergency volunteers, who take
over whenever there is any sort of breakdown in the availability of volunteer teachers. The
volunteers come from various backgrounds, and include housewives, former school
teachers, former social workers, former nurses, an engineer, and other suitably qualified and
interested people. Each spends a total of about 15 hours every week leading discussion
groups. It has been found that half an hour is too short for a discussion period, and that 45
minutes is about right. Before and after the group sessions, the volunteers get together for
about a quarter of an hour to discuss their problems or the approach they will adopt, and to
present material they are currently using in their group discussions. The sessions after the
discussions are usually the most fruitful for the group leaders, because by sharing their
experiences they are able to learn a great deal from each other. Those who are finding the
going difficult get valuable advice from others who have already experienced similar
problems. Obviously, too, discussion leaders have an opportunity to discuss new subject-
matter and to evaluate its worth in the programme.
Precis sheets are produced of specific topics for each week's discussion, but these are
now used only as a general guide. It has been found desirable to maintain flexibility so that
the discussion can develop along the lines apparently desired by the children in the group.
The aim of the discussion is to develop an understanding of relationships with other people
and the nature of the communication involved, to develop an understanding of individual
growth through self-awareness, and to develop an understanding of the relationship between
feelings, attitudes, values, and behaviour. The subject-matter produced for discussion,
therefore, attempts to present to the children real situations which influenced the lives of
group members.

Often the precis sheets that have been prepared by the workers beforehand are
discarded after the first 5 minutes or so, or perhaps not even used at all, simply because the
group has some particular matter it wishes to discuss, or moves off into another area
altogether that interests it at the time. No effort is made to draw a group back to the original
topic, because it is considered that if a group wants to discuss something else the children will
benefit more from that than if they are forced to discuss what the leader wants them to
discuss. This freedom, of course, is controlled to the extent that the leader does not allow the
group to waste time discussing unfruitful topics, and can guide the lines on which the
discussion will develop. A great deal depends on the skill of the discussion leaders in
maintaining a controlled informality on the one hand, but still fulfilling the role of facilitator
or leader of the discussion on the other.
These discussions give an opportunity to young people to develop, in a controlled but
informal atmosphere, the ability to evaluate themselves, to think about themselves in
relation to others, and to try to form a clear understanding of why and how they function as a
part of society. So far, these discussion groups in schools have been taking place mainly in
fourth form classes, but it is felt that such a programme should exist, suitably adjusted to fit
in with class and age level, in all schools from primary and intermediate to secondary.
One other aspect of social welfare I want to consider is a matter that has been dealt with
in Taradale. Following up an idea put to them by Dr Woodhouse, Mr and Mrs Dawson of
that suburb proposed to a public meeting on 12 August 1975, just on 2 years ago, that the
Taradale Senior Citizens Association should be established not merely to cater for elderly
people in need, but more particularly to provide companionship for people over the age of
60, who all too often were living in isolation, cut off from other people in their community,
and often feeling they were no longer wanted by society. Within a month of that meeting, the
Dawsons had arranged for the first hot dinner to be served to the first members of the
Taradale Senior Citizens Association, in the gymnasium of the Taradale Football Club. The
association stayed in those premises until the beginning of the 1976 football season, when the
club wanted the gymnasium. The association then arranged to rent the St. John hall in
Taradale.
Now the association has 320 members, all aged 60 years or over, and up to 50 hot
dinners are served each day-with an average of 35. Volunteers come in every day to
prepare and cook the dinner, local suppliers help with the provisions, and association
members pay 60c and sit down to a good substantial meal. At the centre there is a library,
provision for indoor bowls, a snooker table, card tables, and a spinning wheel and a loom for
weaving in addition to materials for making mats. Once a week, two children from Taradale
High School come along to the centre to help serve dinner to the elderly people, and there is
great competition in the high school to take up this task. The hospital board sends four new
nursing students from each intake for a day at a time to work with and help the elderly
people and to see what they are really like, before they start working in the geriatric wards of
the hospital. They find elderly people in a friendly and happy environment.
At present the centre is open from about 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., 5 days a week, but I have
been given the honour, on Friday of this week-2 years to the day from the original
meeting of deputising for the Minister of Health at the opening of the new Taradale
Friendship Centre, which will be the permanent home of the Taradale Senior Citizens
Association. Mr and Mrs Dawson and their committee of 16 other people have been very
busily engaged in fund raising for this project. The $16,000 they have raised has been
matched by a 3:1 subsidy of $48,000 provided by the Social Service Council from Golden
Kiwi lottery funds. The Napier City Council gave the association the use of a section in
Taradale, and the council's architect drew up plans for the new building. The association has
purchased crockery, cutlery, and furniture from funds raised locally.
The most important part of the scheme is not the provision of a hall, not the provision of
meals-a hot meal each day—but the hand of friendship that is extended. Although at first
many people are shy, or reluctant to become involved, Mr and Mrs Dawson and their
helpers soon see to it that all are made to feel welcome and wanted, and a very happy,
friendly atmosphere greets all comers. I am led to believe that one friendship has blossomed
not only into romance but into marriage, and I have heard rumours that more than one may
be on the way. I hope so.
There is no doubt in my mind that the Taradale Senior Citizens Association has not only
helped to keep many elderly people out of hospital, but has encouraged them to become
actively involved in their community. I feel certain that the example set in Taradale could
well be followed in other places to the mutual benefit of the elderly and those who care for

Party at a demonstration at the Dunedin Town Hall on Friday 22 July, in response to a

Community Colleges
1. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: When does he expect
to be able to make an announcement concerning further development of community
colleges?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I announced immediately after the
Budget that the Government had given approval for the establishment of the Northland and
Rotorua Community Colleges from 1 April 1978, and for the translation of Southland
Polytechnic, whose council had sought this move, to community college status from the same
date. Further announcements about the establishment of community colleges will depend on
the development of the work load in the senior technical divisions the Government has now
agreed will be formally established in Wanganui, Timaru, Tauranga, and Gisborne. It will
also depend upon the assessment of all priorities in educational development.

form the order of further development of community colleges?

community colleges.

Industrial Stoppages-Statistics
2. Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) asked the Minister of Labour: Can he indicate whether,
on the latest figures to hand, the marked trend of reduction in industrial stoppages shown in
the first quarter of the year has continued?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The latest provisional figures relating to
industrial stoppages cover the 5 month period that ended in May 1977. These show a marked
reduction in the number of workers involved in industrial stoppages. For the period January
to May 1977 inclusive, 57 960 workers were affected, compared with 80 563 workers during
the same period in 1976.
Mr Elliott: In which industries are the worst stoppages still occurring; and do these
include freezing works and heavy engineering industries?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I have no figures with me, and will have to rely on my memory of
figures given to me. Certainly the freezing works would be among the leaders in industrial
stoppages in the period referred to by the member-for the 5 months up until May. I would
be happier if a further question was put to me about the heavy industries.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: How many man-days were lost by the 57 000 people involved in
industrial stoppages during the first 5 months of this year, and what was the loss in wages
compared with wages lost in the previous year when he first took office?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The number of days lost-and I presume they are man-
days-from January to March 1976 were 94 809, and for the same period in 1977, 70 313.
The total wages lost during January to May 1976 amounted to $3.1 million, and for the same
period in 1977, $3.2 million.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Although the reduction is to be welcomed-
Mr SPEAKER: Order! We want a question, not a statement.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: I was coming to the question-can the Minister confirm that the
reduction is still running at a rate above the average for the past 25 years?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The number of man-days lost, number of stoppages, and so on, is
cyclic. If one goes back over 25 years, 1951 was a bad year. Generally, the year after an
election is a bad year on a cyclic rotation. I do not have the specific statistics for every year
during the last 25 years with me.

Manual Telephones
4. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Postmaster-General: What percentage of telephone
users are still using manual telephones?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the
Postmaster-General. As at 31 March 1977, out of a total of more than 1 000 000 connections
and over 670 exchanges, the percentage of telephone users still using manual telephones was
6.8.
Mr Luxton: What progress has been made in the last 10 years, and are the manual
telephones in rural or urban areas?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: There has been steady progress over the last 10 years in
limiting the number of manual connections, and in removing them. In 1966, the percentage
of manual connections was 21.8 and, as I have said, it is now 6.8. There is a steady
programme for conversion, but it depends on resources and priorities. I hope that this will
continue at a reasonable rate. It is, of course, directed now to the rural areas and the last of
the smaller exchanges.

7. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Transport: Can he indicate

as from 1 April 1978. Details on the timing of the introduction of the components within the

individual vehicle concerned, and will be determined by the gross laden weight, axle
configuration, and size of the vehicle. All operators will therefore be treated equally,
regardless of their vehicle fleet numbers.

months, but I remind the member that the first legislation will involve the abolition of what
we call the 40-mile restriction. I discussed that with the Transport Advisory Council last
Tuesday, and it is meeting again in a fortnight. Discussion on the matter the member raised
will follow that.

territories?

moves towards decolonisation in the Pacific, but also believes that any initiatives towards
self-determination lie essentially with the Island nations themselves.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Has this been the subject of discussions at the South Pacific Forum,
or is it likely to be the subject of discussion at that forum?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: I am not sure of the point of that question. The fact is, of
course, that no territory that is not self-governed and independent could become a member
of the forum. I believe that is the key point. It is recognised by members of the forum that
each one of them is an independent country, and there is certainly no prospect of either an
Island nation-a Pacific nation that is not independent-or a metropolitan power being
admitted to the forum.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Is it not a fact that a United Nations committee regularly reviews

obtain it for the honourable member, or if he wishes to submit another question I shall
obtain it for him then.

Eviction by Police of Families at Upper Hutt
15. Hon. Mrs. T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) asked the

which, according to news reports, they did?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police): Those evicted from the Upper Hutt
property comprised in excess of 30 persons, none of whom had any authority from the owner
to be there. The police acted at the specific written request of the owner of the premises,
who had made a complaint that those on the property had broken the front door, had
smashed windows, and had pulled down a shed on the property and used it to start a bonfire.
The owner was genuinely concerned for his property, and for that reason requested the
police to remove them. This is not a case of a normal citizen in lawful occupation of a
dwelling. Those concerned were in part members of the Upper Hutt "black power" gang
then on remand for the criminal offence of unlawful assembly, and were apparently intent on
wrecking the property. Surely the member for Southern Maori will agree that property
owners also have some rights in these matters when their property is in danger. The actions
of the police were entirely within the law at all times, and were carried out in a humane
manner. It is to be regretted that these people acted in the manner in which they did, but the
responsibility for the events was entirely theirs. It is a pity that the adults conducted
themselves in such an irresponsible manner, thus involving small children in such a situation
Hon. M. Rata: In view of the involvement of young children in the situation referred to,
has the Minister of Police taken the opportunity of conferring with his colleague, the
Minister of Social Welfare, to ascertain whether something can be done to ensure that the
situation of the families concerned is not allowed to reach a stage where the police will again
be required to act in the way they did recently?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY: I was asked to supply a report on the reasons why the police
acted in such a manner. I do not consider that the supplementary question has anything to do
with that matter.

more employees, had started up in various areas throughout New Zealand, and I should

Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): Yes, I have seen the report in the Eten ing Post.
The Plunket Society is the recipient of four subsidies in respect of the operations of its
Karitane hospitals: a subsidy of $2.25 for each $2 raised by the society as voluntary
contributions; a subsidy on the salaries of medical staff; since 1972, an annually approved
grant towards the annual operating deficit of the hospitals; and private hospital benefit of $9
per day per patient. All of these subsidies, except the annual operating deficit, are paid up to
date, and for this financial year so far are over $200,000. Because it is a grant to meet a
forecast annual operating deficit, time is required to fully investigate the amount of the
subsidy sought. This is particularly so when one considers that for the year ended 31 March
1973 the actual deficit was $28,797, while in 1976-77 $363,000 was paid out. I am, however,
looking at ways in which the hospitals liquidity problems can be overcome, perhaps by an
interim advance on the grant, while the necessary investigations are being completed.
A condition of the grant is that adjustments, both up and down, are made in the
following year when the final accounts are available, and although these were sought by my
department early in May this year, the society was unable to provide this information in
respect of the 1975-76 financial year until mid-July, and final accounts for the 1976-77
financial year are still not to hand. Although the grant has been approved earlier than this in
some years, in 1975 when the Labour Government was in power it was not approved until 28

MARLBOROUGH COUNTY COUNCIL RESERVES FUND EMPOWERING BILL
Mr LATTER (Marlborough): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Marlborough
County Coun il Reserves Fund Empowering Bill. This is a very short Bill of three clauses.
The long title gives a background to the restriction on the size of sections on which a levy can
be made to build up reserve fund contributions. At present the maximum area is 8000 square
metres. The Marlborough County Council has in the area of the Marlborough Sounds a
particular problem with the contour of the country and the fact that more than 50 percent of
all sections sold are over the maximum.
It is a county that is moving in a well planned way towards a recreational use of open
spaces and reserves. It is a county that has to contribute to the Marlborough Sounds Marine
Park Board and to the Department of Lands and Survey. Over the years it has been found
that these moneys must be provided from other areas within the county, because under this
maximum a levy cannot be imposed as a reserve contribution. The Bill seeks to empower the
Marlborough County Council to set aside the provisions of section 28 of the principal Act as
if the words "of less than 8000 square metres" did not appear in subsection (2) of section 28.
A remit to this effect was taken to the New Zealand Counties Association conference in
1972, and was endorsed.
Motion agreed to.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

let slip during this debate. The Budget is progressive, because the Government, like all good
things in New Zealand, is a progressive Government, which moves steadily and sensibly
toward the common national goals of a finer and fairer nation.
It is ironic to hear socialist members constantly referring to the report of the Holmes
task force. We heard hysteria from the Opposition benches when the task force was set up in
1976. It was set up as part of the Prime Minister's Department, which the member for
Auckland Central is now trying to tear apart. The socialist members have constantly referred
to that progressive thinking of the Prime Minister, who recruited people from industry and
the public service to do the research that produced the report. In a sense every word of the
report, commissioned and published under the National Government, is a reflection of the
Government's concern for the future of New Zealand. Now the socialists use the report to
criticise the Budget. Just 12 months ago they were screaming "tory think-tank”, “mini-
Watergate", and "all the President's men." Today the socialists pretend to espouse that
report as their own philosophy. Nobody in the House or the country is wearing that line.
In 1975 the National Government was elected to tidy up a monumental mess. Income
tax soared under the Labour Government, the overseas debt was at record levels, and the
Government had intentionally committed itself to spending more than $1,000 million a year
that it did not have. More than 140 000 permanent and long-term migrants were allowed into
the country, unemployment was high, house prices trebled, and thousands of people were
sitting on short-term mortgages that any economist or banker could see could not be readily
refinanced. The country was poised on the brink of disaster. What were the socialists doing
about it? Nero fiddled while Rome burned, but the member for Manukau, the dreaming,
fiddling accountant, was playing with extravagant broadcasting schemes, insatiably money-
hungry superannuation schemes, and a pathetically transparent baby bonus.
In 1976 the National Government rolled up its sleeves and started cleaning up the mess.
The Cabinet economic committee commenced a short-term emergency rescue operation.
The task force, criticised at that time, commenced a review of the direction that New
Zealand should be taking, various Ministers climbed on top of messy portfolios, and the
immigration shambles was sorted out. The Government put lost pride and confidence back
into the police force and agriculture, and rescued a bankrupt broadcasting system, while the
Prime Minister worked on the 1976 Budget. In retrospect that Budget was a spectacular
document, because it was drawn up by the Minister of Finance, who was in the position of
being a receiver rather than a manager. Nevertheless, progress was made in the fields of
energy, agriculture, and housing. The 1976 Budget introduced the most important social
programme of several decades-national superannuation.
The hard work of 1976 has been shown in the 1977 Budget. While we are not out of the
economic woods, we have turned a number of corners and now have a little room in which to
manoeuvre. Inflation is down, the balance of payments has improved, the deficit before
borrowing is down, the internal deficit is halved, and, in view of the small amount of room
available for manoeuvring, the Prime Minister has played the game like an All Black
halfback, picking up the ball that has been fed to him by his economic task force and
spinning it down the back line to get the game moving again.
There are stirring moves in the Budget that will be responsible for changing New
Zealand's future in the fields of fishing, energy, and transport. The transport moves are a
brave step, and will free up a troublesome clot that has been blocking the heart of the New
Zealand industry. The problems, false costs, and inefficiencies that have grown in New
Zealand's transport system do not impress themselves on the average New Zealander; he
feels the effect of them in his pocket and in his standard of living, but he does not directly see
how they happen. I do not expect the families in the Eden electorate to become excited
about the Government's transport policy, but over a period of years the living standards of
those families will improve because of the effects of the transport policy.
The energy policy is more likely to gain the attention of the average Eden resident,
because energy has become a matter which concerns us all. The layman easily recognises the
earlier parts of the energy policy, such as the highly successful conservation programme,

running at up to 200 percent better than target; the energy pricing policy announced last

the development of local mini-hydro schemes; and right through to compulsory home

nuclear power. As a result of this policy we may well find ways of avoiding nuclear power in

The 1976 Budget set the stage for fishing, which comes into this Budget blazing like a
sparkling firework. There has been an extension of duty-free concessions on fishing boat
imports, suspensory loans of up to 40 percent for New Zealand built fishing vessels, 80
percent loans for fishermen to buy boats, equipment, and gear, loans of two-thirds of the
cost of vessels and gear, improvement loans for fishermen in licensed fisheries, special
fishing boat ownership savings schemes, training incentives for the fishing industry, and
special grants for fisheries development. The grant to the Fishing Industry Board has been
almost doubled. This will all be supervised by a brilliant young Minister of Fisheries, who is
New Zealand's first Minister of Fisheries. The socialist Government, whose members are
silent now, was silent on fishing. It failed to provide incentives or support for fishing, and it
even failed to appoint a Minister of Fisheries.
While I am on the topic of fishing, I should like to refer to the mystery of the
plesiosaurus, which has been the subject of much speculation recently. I have some
information that may be of interest. It has been suggested that the creature is some sort of
primeval monster whose origins lie in antiquity. There have been eye-witness reports stating
that the creature was seen briefly off the New Zealand coast in the 1930s and 1950s, and we
know that a rotting carcass was recently found drifting off the east coast of the South Island.
When the stench became too much it was thrown overboard again. A creature from the past
seen briefly in the 1930s and 1950s whose rotting carcass has been recently rejected-surely
the plesiosaurus is the Labour Party.
The Budget is not just a Budget of the future-it provides real incentives to ordinary
New Zealanders right now. The people of my electorate will feel the effect of the Budget in
their daily lives in a number of ways. First, I wish to demonstrate what will happen to a
person earning an average income. Average income can be defined in all sorts of statistical
ways. I shall take first a person who, in October 1977, will earn about $141 gross weekly.
Under the Labour Government in 1973 he would have paid 19.8 percent of his income in tax.
In October 1975, still under the Labour Government, he would have paid 21.2 percent of his
income in tax. In October 1977, under the National Government, he will pay 16.4 percent of
his total income in tax. His total take-home pay will have increased by 65 percent, and in that
period the consumer price index will have gone up by 62 percent, which means that by
October he will be about 3 percent better off in purchasing power. Let us take the example
of a person with two children whose gross income is $129. His tax take increased from 18.2
percent to 19.6 percent under Labour, but by October 1977 it will have been reduced to 13.1
percent. That person will find that, while the consumer price index will have gone up by
approximately 62 percent, his take-home pay will have increased by more than 70 percent,
and he will be 8.2 percent better off. A person who, in October, has a gross income of $118 a
week would have had 16.7 percent in tax taken from him in 1973 and 18 percent in 1975, but
by October 1977, 10.9 percent will be taken from him in tax. His take-home pay will have
increased by 75.9 percent during a period when the consumer price index has increased by 62
percent. He will be 13.9 percent better off.
Nobody can tell me that by October 1977, when the tax tables have been adjusted, there
will be a substantial number of low-income people who are worse off than they were 3 years
ago. I admit that it is not as nice to be a member of a low-income group as it is to be a
member of a high-income group. That is patently obvious, and I am sure we would all like to
see low-income earners paid more, but the argument that they are worse off under the
National Government simply cannot be sustained. I turn to another group of people in my
electorate, the pensioners. By 18 August they will be receiving $82.72 if they are married,
and $49.64 if they are single. It is welcome news that national superannuitants with no other
income will no longer need to file annual returns of income.

mentioned in the Budget we are now discussing to subsidise private enterprise further for
using junior employees, are probably the most radical and dramatic steps taken in an active
employment policy. They have helped keep unemployment figures low, and at the same time
increased New Zealand's productivity. Australia has 10 times the New Zealand unemploy-
ment rate, and in May of this year the rate of unemployment in Canada was 7.9 percent,
compared with our rate of 0.53 percent at that time. West Germany, which is often held up
as a good example by many Auckland businessmen, has an unemployment rate of 4.6
percent. I also mention that in Italy the unemployment rate is 6.8 percent. Even Japan has
an unemployment level of 1.8 percent. I could quote many more figures, but shall refer only
to Britain, which has an unemployment rate of 5.9 percent-also more than 10 times the
New Zealand rate.
Not long ago, during the Nelson by-election campaign, we were told that more than
20 000 people would be unemployed during last winter. At one stage someone became really
enthusiastic and inflated the figure to 50 000. However, that rate of inflation has not been
achieved anywhere in the world overnight, in a week, or even in 18 months, the length of
time the National Government has been in office. The register of unemployed, the most
reliable indicator, gives the latest number of unemployed as 7000. This is too high by New
Zealand standards; it is manageable, but only just. It has never looked like, nor does it now
look like, touching the 20 000 claimed by the Leader of the Opposition in a by-election
speech. We will leave the figure of 50 000 to those extravagant back-benchers who like a
little literary licence. The Government has also found over 7000 productive jobs for those
who have registered and have been in need of assistance in the last 18 months.
For the benefit of the member for Avon, who questioned me on this, if married women
want assistance, are seeking a job, and are prepared to work a minimum of 30 hours a week,
they can approach the employment service of the Department of Labour. Then, if a job is
not found for them, they are on the registered unemployed list. We do try to find jobs for
them. In answering a supplementary question by the member for Avon I was able to
convince her that, in the New Zealand situation, we were coping with the problem of
married people who are unemployed and able to work more than the minimum full-time
working week of 30 hours. The policy, originally designed by the National Government and
furthered by the Labour Government, has been taken a great deal further by the National
Government in the last 18 months, and this Budget takes it further still, as I indicated a
minute ago.
Anyone can play with figures and suggest that they are higher than they actually are. I
have done that when in Opposition, but the register of unemployed in New Zealand has
been unaltered over the years, and it is no good someone saying that you can fiddle with the
figures and make the position look either worse or better than it really is. Certainly, we may
go on to change the basic criteria. Many people have suggested a different method of
calculation for the consumer price index, but in weighing one situation against another we
must accept that the figures are as reliable as we can make them and cover the field, as they
did during the terms of three different Governments. The Government has convened a
technical working party from the Department of Labour and the Department of Statistics to
investigate in detail the feasibility of a household labour force survey to measure employ-
ment and unemployment. I am hopeful that it will work. I cannot guarantee that it will, but if
it does it may lead us to a better set of statistics and an even better record than we have at
present; and I say unhesitatingly that I am not ashamed of the present record.
The National Government has achieved two significant employment trends. It has
restored confidence in the private sector and, in the year to April 1977, 11 023 more
jobs-an increase of 1.7 percent-were found. By comparison-and this is where the test of
the Government lies-the public sector employment, including Government and local
authority employment, decreased by 490, or 0.2 percent, to April 1977. The full effects of
this have yet to be seen. I concede that I am likely to be questioned about employing
temporary staff when we come to the estimates that follow on from this Budget debate. Yes,
we are employing temporary staff, but at no greater disproportionate level than have
previous Governments. Within the State sector, there has always been a degree of tempor-
ary employment, and when the statistics come out it will be seen that the position is no worse
and does not take away the credit due to this National Government for non-expansion in the
State sector.

Last year, the private sector subsidy scheme was introduced in Northland and Gisborne.
Yesterday, I answered a question by the member for Whangarei, and gave him the numbers
of those who ended up in permanent employment. As was said at the time, it was a pilot
scheme, a shot in the dark, but it was tried, and today I can tell the House, in praise of the
Budget, that it was successful, as those who listened to that answer would have accepted. We
have reintroduced the scheme this year. Finance is made available through the Budget to
extend the scheme to places such as Hamilton, Rotorua, Gisborne-which had it last
year-Napier, Hastings, New Plymouth, Blenheim, Greymouth, and Invercargill. Funda-
mentally, it is aimed at improving the situation for those who could become permanently
unemployed. We do not want to get into a situation such as is seen on the western seaboard
of the United States, where seven generations of a single family have never had a full-time
job. The aim of this scheme is to stop potentially unemployable people developing into a
state of living on social welfare, living on the State, and so on. The objective is to provide
productive and productive" is the key word-full-time employment, particularly for
younger people who would otherwise be unemployed.
As I indicated the other day, a most outstanding success story that comes to mind is in
the white work section, where young girls are taught to sew and are boosted up to a
productive level such that an employer can take them on without having to train them or
absorb training losses. The scheme can be used for persons with a real employment problem,
no matter what their age. It is aimed at creating further jobs in the private sector, thus
promoting production and balancing-and I use the word "balancing" deliberately-the use
of special work scheme employment in the public sector. We have no intention of subsidising
what the ratepayers should be doing, but I have already alluded to some special avenues and
might again if time permits. The scheme is also aimed at upgrading skills and attitudes, and
gives an employer the opportunity to train a worker to become fully productive. A 33
subsidy is offered on the weekly wage rate-a minimum of $25 and a maximum of $45. This
will encourage employers to take on trained apprentices-and heaven knows we are short
enough of those people-giving them an opportunity for a long-term commitment to engage
and train a skilled work force. I am sure the Opposition would agree that we need that.
Assistance is to be given to organisations operating voluntary and other work rehabilita-
tion schemes. There has been a growing concern for young persons with poor work records.

Through community rehabilitation the employment service is helping slow learners, the

I now want to turn to the vexed question of industrial stoppages, on which I answered a
question this afternoon. More than half the industrial stoppages last year were over wage
regulations or the wage freeze. I trust that figure will be reduced from next Monday. Three-
quarters of the non-industrial stoppages were in protest against the Government's fiscal
measures to restore the economy. Then by far the most significant effect on man-days lost
would have been the arrival of nuclear ships here. However, I do not wish to be sidetracked
into discussing the merits or non-merits of that issue. That is in effect the history of the last
12 months of our industrial relations. There are reasons why we have had these unenviable
difficulties. I wonder if members opposite would have lifted the wage restraints we had on
last year. I doubt it, in the light of their experience in 1973. Most sections of the community
have accepted and still do accept some degree of restraint. The statistics for the first quarter
of 1977 show a drop in the number of man-days lost last year. There has been a vast
improvement, which I trust will continue.
This Budget faces up to major short-term difficulties while building a better future for
all New Zealanders, but we need to have regard to some economic priorities. The Budget is
comprehensive and broad based. It is specific in priority areas so that we can re-establish a
basis for growth. I have mentioned some of those areas within my portfolios. We have to
stimulate efficient industries and promote the better use of resources. Those are almost
clichés, but we must bear them in mind. An overall strategy of economic development has
been recognised in the provisions of the Budget.
I want to deal now with some of the other aspects that have troubled me not only as
Minister but as a member of Parliament in my own electorate. I am thinking about farming. I
have already spoken about the rural water schemes. This Budget will help young farmers
acquire their first farms. There is a positive incentive for older farmers to get off the land so
that the young can come in. Thereby we will be improving working skills and the work force.
Inflation-adjusted savings bonds were sought by the Federation of Labour during discussions
about wages and restraints and what the priorities should be. I readily admit that the Budget
provisions are not as widespread as the federation would like, but some limitation was
needed.
The most troublesome issue that faces me, and possibly the country, today is the
industrial unrest in the freezing industry. I would be the first to concede that the level of
stoppages is far too high, but it is sporadic. It is confined to some works; there is no trouble
in others. The stoppages concern my department and me, and they certainly concern the
mediation service which we have established and extended. They concern the freezing
companies, Federated Farmers, and everyone else—including, probably, most members of
the House. Consequential upon a recent Federated Farmers conference I am delighted that
Federated Farmers, together with the Minister of Agriculture, have made a move that will
lead to a meeting in these buildings next week to look at the overall situation.
Apart from looking at transport, hygiene regulations, pelting machines, and other
matters, I propose to try to arrange a seminar of all interested parties to discuss one issue
only which we think is paramount in solving the problems in New Zealand's largest industry.
That would be a seminar of all involved in the freezing industry, and it must include some of
the members of boards of directors. It must not stop with personnel managers or general
managers. We must get the boards of New Zealand freezing companies more interested in
the human relations involved in the industry. I speak that way deliberately. I regret to say
that far too often we have found that an unsympathetic note from the board has spread
through to the management. That is what leads to a confrontation situation such as we have
in Southland, something I deplore but about which I shall be forced to take action,
unpleasant though it may be. I hope that that seminar and other moves being made will
assist. It would be idle for me to pretend that this would solve the problems facing us in the
coming freezing works season, but that is a major hurdle facing us all. I am delighted that so
far the problem has not become a political issue. I have had nothing but co-operation from
the unions which have visited my office. They quietened the situation early this year.

Bank. The bank was founded in 1867 and is expanding all the time. Twenty-five percent of
its depositors live in sawmill houses, and 15 percent of the bank's finance is with ancillary
industries-carriers or tradesmen-and doctors or scientists. The bank should have a big say
in the future of the West Coast. We have some good submissions here. I wish I had time to
read them, but I will say that the bank is also prepared to play ball in giving a small slice to
the national park down in south Westland. It played ball because it was decided to leave the
West Coast for some years, while the timber throughout the rest of New Zealand is being
cut. We are prepared to give that strip as a compromise-and also because it is mostly
swamp anyway. When the Cook River changed, nobody bothered to protect the white pine
trees. It was not the water that drowned them, it was silt. Trees will not stand silt around
their roots. There are dead and dying trees all over south Westland because of the silt left
around their roots. If the bank went it would be a terrific disadvantage, because I think
Canterbury would say no to taking the Westland Savings Bank under its wing.
I have another little point to clear up-the Maruia Declaration. That was another push-
over. According to the Beech Leaves organisataon, there were 344 000 signatures, including
six Rob Muldoons. They rubbed him out, however; as the Leader of the Opposition said, his
signatures depreciated the petition. They also had the signature of a joker called Denis
Holcroft, who has one of the mills on the West Coast. They forged his name. I believe they
had my name too, but somebody said, "No, he might use it in the House". The people from
the Beech Leaves office told the people gathering signatures to hold the Maruia Declaration
at the top so that nobody could read the small print. They were also told what patter to use.
They gathered signatures, and the result was a big bundle of paper, all made from timber,
that has come to the House. It will go before the committee that will decide whether we will
import timber with our overseas funds, or whether we will use some of the many millable
trees in Westland-5 percent of commercially millable trees. All we ask for in Westland is to
be allowed to continue cutting for 10 years or so until the exotics come up. There are enough
reserves in Westland to suit all the tourists from here to Hong Kong.
Many conservationists say that if you cut down the native trees you take away a lot of
the natural carbon dioxide. But for every acre of mature tree growth cut, the equivalent of 6
and sometimes 8 acres of trees is planted, mainly exotics. In a beech forest you could have 10
times the amount of trees with exotics. The exotics grow pretty fast if they are given a bit of
superphosphate. That is what we have to offer as a contribution to the health of the nation. I
ask members to remember that. I ask them not to let our coal mining or our timber industry
go down any further, otherwise they will have a Cinderella province on their hands, a
province that should be making an even bigger contribution towards the development of the
Dominion of New Zealand than it has in the last 100 years.

Mr Bruce Barclay: What would that contract be worth?

workers are producing very fine containers, better than those coming in from overseas.
Lloyds of London are overseeing the contract, the only one in New Zealand in which Lloyds
has an interest. The boxes are built to withstand a pressure of 81 tonnes on each corner,
assuming that they would be on the bottom of the hold. It is very important that these
containers are built to Lloyds' specification; if they collapsed, the ship could sink. Lloyds
have said that these Dunedin-built boxes are some of the best they have seen. That contract,
let by the Labour Government, was an example of practical regional development. The
Labour Government also let contracts for the building of buses by Emslie Consolidated Ltd
in Dunedin.

Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West): The member for Dunedin Central finished by saying

was nearly $1,450 million. For the 18 months following December 1975, the figure was
$1,004.4 million, a reduction of approximately 50 percent. Far from showing record
borrowing, as alleged by the member for Dunedin Central, the true picture shows that the
period of record borrowing is over and that this Government has done something to stabilise
what threatened to become a runaway situation. As for the problems in the balance of
payments, the deficit for the year ended March 1975 was $1,370 million, or 14.6 percent of
the gross national product. For the year ended June 1977 the figure was $850 million, or 6.6
percent of the gross national product. Opposition members ideas of what constitutes a
record need to be straightened.
In this debate I wish to traverse certain matters which concern our economic situation,
the true picture of which is brought home by the figures I have just quoted. We have a
chronic situation in our balance of payments, and the difficulties here stem very largely from
overseas. In the face of these problems, the Government has embarked on stable, sensible,
and progressive policies; it has been concerned primarily to ensure the most effective use of
New Zealand's resources. To achieve that, it has been necessary to adapt-quite radically, in
some instances-to the new situation in which we find ourselves. Some very positive
adaptation has been undertaken by the Government.
I propose to give some examples, the first of which concerns the adaptation in local
government, where the Government is conscious of the need to adapt to the new situation
we now face, particularly in the shortage of resources and the need to make the funds the
are available go as far as possible. We have turned back for the time being the wasteful and
extravagant ideas of the previous Administration on what the reform of local government

might be all about. The typical response of the previous Government was a bureaucratic
one, which saw the answer as the establishment throughout New Zealand of 20 new regional
bureaucracies. On the available facts, which are indisputable, these could be neither staffed
nor financed, but as a bureaucratic exercise in futility they were to be established anyway.
This Government has recognised that the real task is that of basic planning, whether in our
cities or in general land use, with the object being to avoid waste as well as to achieve the
positive gains that come from sound planning in those areas. This Government's progressive
initiative will facilitate the planning of land use, without the establishment of new bureau-
cracies, on an effective, co-operative basis using existing local body staff. I am positive that
the changes involved will be achieved not without some argument and some debate, but that
is characteristic of the democratic, as opposed to the bureaucratic, process.
This Government has made quite radical responses in the field of energy. We know
there is an energy crisis not merely in this country but throughout the world. There has been
a swift and effective response from this Government. Hitherto fragmented departments and
committees are to be merged in the interests of more co-ordinated and efficient utilisation of
resources. A progressive step has been taken with the massive injection of funds and effort
into establishing the true extent of our indigenous energy resources, whether they be oil, gas,
coal, geothermal steam, or hydro.
In social welfare, the Government has recognised the new circumstances in which we
live; the most significant development has been the recognition of the importance of
voluntary agencies. In my city, in particular, many people would be much poorer and in
much deeper trouble than they are already, were it not for these voluntary agencies. These

children's homes, geriatric homes, and emergency accommodation; their work could never
be achieved effectively by a Government department. It is a great credit to New Zealand
that we have men and women in our communities who are prepared to act upon the basic
precepts of Christianity: the extending of practical help to fellow men and women. I am
proud the Government has recognised the value of this work and is setting out to assist the
increasing involvement of voluntary agencies in social welfare.
I draw a sharp line of distinction between what this Government is doing and what the
Labour Government proposed. That Government saw social welfare in terms of bureaucra-
tic forms, and produced its now notorious white paper, which would have turned one sector
of social welfare into another massive bureaucratic agency that would have been quite
incapable of discharging the basic practical humanitarian concerns I have just mentioned.
On rather similar lines, it is interesting to see that the Government has agreed to the
establishment of nurses' training facilities at the Waikato Technical Institute. This is
practical recognition of the need for changes in nursing training as a result of changes within
the community and within hospitals. To their great credit, nurses themselves have been
powerful advocates of changes of the kind that will result from technical institute training.
As a further indication of its progressive response to changing times and circumstances,
the Government has proposed changes in commercial law to curb doubtful practices that
have become associated in recent years with those companies that function mainly in the
financial field. The collapse of such companies has meant very heavy losses to small and
trusting investors. The Securitibank collapse, and the collapse of other companies before
that, indicated a need for clearer laws governing certain commercial practices. The proposed
introduction of the Security Advertising Bill, announced recently by the Minister of Justice,
is a progressive, if but first, step towards introducing some standards and some new ethics
into a sector of commercial practice that, in the light of today's circumstances, has simply got
out of hand.
There is one area of continuing wastage, which neither this Government nor, I think,
any Government could reduce dramatically, although continuing efforts must be made to do
so. By the end of July, 390 people had been killed on New Zealand roads this year, and the
total number killed last year was 365. Most of those deaths were senseless and needless. Two
or three days ago five young people were killed in one accident that occurred on a straight
road at 2 a.m. Accidents of this kind, on the face of it, are inexplicable and can be attributed
only to some kind of human folly, against which no law nor regulation is likely to prove
effective. If human folly is to blame, our problem is to know how to diminish human folly;
that problem is likely to be with us for a very long time.
The sheer wastage of young lives involved in the present toll is beyond all sense, but I
still believe that we must make efforts, doubtful though we may be about the efficacy of
some of them, to reduce this wastage. Investigations are being made at present into the

removal of technicalities from the laws concerning blood alcohol prosecutions. The present

Having said that, I think it is fair to say that the sheer sweep and scope of present change
throughout the world, and its speed and thorough-goingness, have created a need to adapt,
which none of us is meeting very adequately, and that in some areas a positive response has
yet to be made. I believe that in this country, when all the nonsense has been put aside, when
all the statistics are laid aside and we look at the broad picture, we are living in the shadow of
radical world change. We are involved in problems that concern the price of raw materials,
the world's energy resources, the balance of power struggle, and the determination of poor
countries to achieve a better share of the world's wealth. We live in an age of multi-national
corporations, and in an age in which the contrary phenomena of inflation and unemployment
have reached new and seemingly insoluble dimensions. Tremendous problems exist in
international finance, and at the same time technological change seems to advance at an
accelerating rate, notably in the field of computers and electronics. I believe the world is in
the process of a revolutionary change as fundamental as that associated with the industrial
revolution, which, as we know, demanded totally new attitudes and responses and required a
radical movement away from ideas and institutions that had become traditional.
It also required a change of laws. We are faced with the situation of having not only to
use our known and established resources to the best advantage, but also to see that our laws
and institutions by and large become adequate to meet the demands these changes are
making. The need for what I would call institutional change should be apparent to all.
Recent developments in this House-and I say this with the greatest respect-indicate that
this institution is in need of change as an urgent response to totally new circumstances.
Parliament must respond, and it would be remarkable if it were not called upon to reform
and alter itself in response to totally new problems and situations.
Our procedures, methods, and the way we spend our time are in need of a comprehen
sive review, if for no other reason than that so many procedures and methods have bee
overtaken by a radically changed world, and Parliament has to function in terms of nev
demands made upon it. Changes affecting this institution can be accomplished only fron
within it, and I call upon the senior members of the House to make change of that kind
possible by setting up an appropriate and representative select committee to suggest the
practical changes the House should adopt. I urge the senior members to pause from their
quite understandable preoccupation with day-to-day tasks and to find reasonable time to
initiate a select committee to recommend effective and progressive changes that will allow all
who serve here to contribute their time and efforts more effectively and more intelligently in
the service of New Zealand. It is no use looking elsewhere, to the universities and the
outside institutions, for that change. The initiative must come from within the walls of this
institution, and it will come only when the senior members of the House recognise and act
upon the need for it. At the moment we are all stalled in this effort by our preoccupation
with party political matters and day-to-day concerns.

mile economic zone, I am certain we will see the fishing industry develop so that before
many years it will be at least equal to the dairy industry. That might seem a rather rash
forecast, but when one sees the way the industry is growing, I believe that this can be
achieved. I am sorry that the member for Eastern Maori, who spoke about fishing the other
day, had not taken the trouble to read the Budget. He obviously had not read it, or he would
have seen the details included in the Budget. The fishing industry received as much in the
way of ideas and assistance as any other part of our economy. It is worth mentioning that in
the 9 months of this year 20 500 tonnes of fish, valued at $37,000, have been exported; in
1975, 14 400 tonnes, valued at $25,000, were exported, so an increase of about 57 percent has
been recorded in just over a year. The main markets have been the United States, Japan,
and Australia, and in each case there has been a substantial increase in the value of fish
exports when compared to that of 1975.
The most important aspect of the fishing industry is not the achievements of the past
years, but what appears to be developing in the immediate future. I read in the Dominion of
9 August that nine countries are now interested in coming to New Zealand to take part in
combined operations, and in applying for special rights for fishing off the New Zealand
coast. This means that we could reach agreements for more space than is actually available.
One of the features of the Budget and the recently introduced legislation is that the 200-mile
off-shore zone will be the fourth largest in the world.
There will also be other benefits, and I should like to mention the other assistance given
to the fishing industry. Not only are there so many forms of financial assistance, but many of
these have not been envisaged in the past. The Minister is to be commended for the time, the
thought, and the preparation he has put into it. First, there will be loans for fishing vessels,
gear, and equipment. Suspensory loans of up to 40 percent of the cost of construction will be
made available through the Rural Bank, and loans of up to 80 percent will be provided for
the cost of a vessel. Legislation designed to control fishing activity in certain fisheries has
also been enacted. Interest rates are at Rural Bank rates. We have fishing vessel ownership
savings schemes in the same way as we have ownership savings schemes for farming and
housing. Details of a training scheme were announced recently.
We also have a fund for development, and there is no doubt that the fishing industry has
the potential to become a significant earner of export income. To assist the industry to
realise its potential, and to promote research into new fisheries or alternative techniques, a
development fund grant will be established, and an initial sum of $200,000 has been provided
in this financial year. There is also a taxation incentive for the fishing industry. Finally, the
Government grant to the Fishing Industry Board for 1977-78 has been provided on the basis
of $1 for every $2 received from fishermen's levies. In 1979 this will be increased to $1 for $1,
and will be a further incentive for development in what will become one of the major export
industries.
