CARRIAGE OF GOODS BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Carriage of Goods Bill
be introduced. This Bill consolidates and reforms the law relating to the carriage of goods
within New Zealand. The basis of the Bill is a report of the Contracts and Commercial Law
Reform Committee, presented in 1968. In addition, the Transport Advisory Council
considered an early draft of the Bill and the useful contribution of that body is evident in the
Bill to be introduced today. The Carriage of Goods Bill has been long in preparation, as the
many groups who have expressed interest in its progress will know. In deference to those
groups I should make it clear that the time taken over the Bill does not reflect Government
lack of interest in it. Rather, it reveals the concern of successive Ministers of Justice that this
Bill really should do substantial justice between carriers and their customers. The area of law


## p. 2128 (#584) ###########################################

2128
12 August
Carriage of Goods Bill
is not without its complexities, and their resolution in a manner fair to both sides in a
carriage transaction has necessarily been time consuming. However, I believe that the Bill to
be introduced today succeeds in stating the law on the carriage of goods in New Zealand in a
manner that will be satisfactory both to consumers and to operators.
The law on the carriage of goods within New Zealand is at present found in four
statutes. They are the Carriers Act 1948, the Sea Carriage of Goods Act 1940, the
Government Railways Act 1949, and the Carriage by Air Act 1967. Other rules are found at
common law. One problem with this situation is that the liability of the carrier to the
customer depends on the mode of transport used. As one example of the anomalies that
exist, I refer on the one hand to a common carrier by land who is absolutely liable for the loss
of or damage to goods up to $40 per package or unit, but who can exclude all his liability by a
special contract. On the other hand, a domestic air carrier is liable for loss or damage up to
$240 in respect of the cargo of one consignor only if he did not take all necessary and possible
measures to avoid loss or damage. He may not contract out of his liability except in respect
of certain goods. As recommended by the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Commit-
tee, the Bill replaces this confused situation by rules of liability that apply to all carriers,
whether by road, rail, water, or air.
The committee looked at the ground on which a carrier should be liable to a customer.
It saw the question as where the risk of loss or damage to goods should lie as between carrier
and customer. Its answer-and I quote from page 8 of the report-was: "We would prefer
that in a commercial transaction like the carriage of goods, the risk should lie where the
balance of convenience places it. Since the risk of loss or damage is readily insurable, the
question becomes one of which party should be expected to effect insurance." The
committee went on to recommend that up to a given money limit the risk should lie on the
carrier. That is, the carrier's liability should be absolute up to a certain limit, but should cut
out completely beyond it. Conversely, the customer should bear no risk up to the limit, but
should bear all the risk over it. The Bill implements the committee's recommendation. A
carrier is absolutely liable for loss of or damage to goods except where the loss or damage
results directly and without the carrier's fault from the fault of the consignor. The Bill also
spells out that the carrier is liable for delay-which is implicit in the report-except where
the delay results from dangerous weather conditions or an attempt to save life or property.
Consistent with an approach based on absolute liability, the Bill narrowly circumscribes
the circumstances in which contracting out is permitted. A carrier may exclude his obliga-
tions under the Bill only if it is just and reasonable for him to do so, having regard to the
special nature of the goods or the special nature of the route. The financial limit that should
be placed on a carrier's liability is of great interest both to customers and to operators. The
present limits vary from $40 per package or unit for a common carrier, including the
Railways, through $100 per package or unit for a coastal sea carrier, to $240 on the cargo of
one consignor for a domestic air carrier. The Contracts and Commercial Law Reform
Committee approaches the matter by asking, in respect of units, of what value it is
reasonable that the consignor should effect his own insurance rather than rely on the
carrier's liability. Realising that views were likely to differ on the answer, the committee
nevertheless felt able to recommend $1,000 per unit. That figure appears in the Bill. I expect
that transport operators and consumers might have opposing views on the suitability of that
sum, but I regard it as a reasonable starting point. The $1,000 limit applies whether the
carrier is sued in contract or tort. I should point out that the $1,000 was recommended by the
law reform committee 9 years ago, in 1968.
Standardisation and modernisation are also desirable in respect of the unit of goods on
which the liability is computed. The statutes dating from the 1940s used the terms "unit" and
"package", and the Carriage by Air Act of 1967 talks of the cargo of one consignor. None of
these terms is adequate to cope with modern developments in unitisation of goods. For
example, is a loaded container a unit, or is each individual package inside it a unit? Similar
questions arise about pallets. The Bill answers the questions in an exhaustive definition of
the term "unit", and also deals with the situation where the goods are repacked in transit.
Because the Bill provides common rules on liability for all carriers, it is able to provide a
uniform claim procedure when one consignment of goods is carried by several modes of
transport. The Bill recognises two systems by which carriers, including freight forwarders,
and their customers may arrange for the carriage of goods in stages. The carrier and the
customer may make a contract providing for the carrier to carry, or arrange for the carriage
of, the goods to their final destination. If the goods are lost, damaged, or delayed the
customer seeks his redress against the carrier with whom he contracted. This is a contract of


## p. 2129 (#585) ###########################################

12 August
2129
Carriage of Goods Bill
through carriage under the Bill. Alternatively, a customer may prefer to make individual
contracts with a series of carriers to get his goods to their final destination. If loss, damage,
or delay occurs, all carriers with whom the customer contracted are jointly and severally
liable to him. A carrier is not liable if he can prove the event did not occur while he was
responsible for the goods. This is a contract of successive carriage under the Bill.
The Bill completes its statement of uniform rules by providing rights for all carriers. At
present the rights of carriers against the owners of goods are found in statutes and in the
common law. The rights stated in the Bill include the right to sue for freight and to sell goods
held under a lien. I am convinced that this long-awaited measure effects desirable and
necessary reforms in the law governing the carriage of goods. I shall be asking the House to
refer the Bill to the Statutes Revision Committee.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): In his closing remarks the Minister of Justice said

the Opposition welcomes that move. As members know, the report of the Contracts and

has been continuing for a number of years-from memory about 8 years. The Bill's
appearance is welcome. For many years it has been obvious to everyone involved in the

have to be updated, and this Bill moves to do that. As the Minister said, the maximum figure
mentioned in the Bill-$1,000 per unit-will not please everybody. That is fair comment, but

The measure is a complicated one-a complex legal transport insurance matter, and for

be a right for the individual parents to withdraw their child; and there should also be the
right for a parent to be consulted about the introduction of material on human development.
But I think it, would be impossible to have this sort of public scrutiny of every book in every
part of the curriculum.
Dr Wall: Does the Minister think that the Texas method-where there is public
scrutiny is quite impracticable for New Zealand?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: We have two problems. One is the question of textbooks and
material used for, say, the teaching of mathematics, on which there is professional expertise.
In that field, there is no right for a parent to demand changes in textbooks. Parents may have
to be given reasons why a particular textbook is being used; I think they are entitled to that
explanation. But I think when we get to the more contentious fields, it is possible to devise a
system where parents have some rights along the lines I mentioned earlier.
Dr Wall: Since the Minister understands the problem, would he indicate what steps are
now available to parents to review the textbooks and any ancillary texts which may be
available in the schools?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Parents have no absolute rights in primary schools, but a greater
interest by parents in the school committees would lead to more information being
exchanged between teachers, principals, and parents to explain the purposes of the text-
books when there is some concern about them. Material used in primary schools is largely
that which is prescribed by the Department of Education. In the case of secondary schools,
the material is within the constraints of the curriculum and the requirements for examina-
tions. The actual material used is the responsibility of the principal, and he is responsible to
the school board or council, on which there would be a majority of parents. That is the
present route that parents have for examining that sort of material.
Dr Wall: I am still not clear what steps a parent can take, and what right a parent has to
go to a school and inquire what books are being used or are available for the children.
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The parent has the same formal right that any person has to
make an inquiry. Whether the information is given or not is, of course, a different matter. If
a parent is unhappy or dissatisfied with the results of the inquiry he may go through his
parent representative to the board, and presumably the board can instruct the principal to
give the information. But we are talking about a slightly different matter-the control of the
material going in. I am sure there is no reason why the information should not be given to
parents.

6. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Local Government: What steps does

Mr COMBER (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Local Government): I
reply on behalf of the Minister of Local Government. His answer is as follows: "The fact that

discussions with the Controller and Auditor-General on the situation. Local authorities
should be, and no doubt are, well aware of the statutory requirements which prohibit them
from having a deficit financial situation at balance date. However, due either to inadequate
budgetary procedures or to unforeseen increases in estimated expenditure, some local
authorities find themselves in overdraft beyond the legal limits at the end of the financial
year-a situation that very often rights itself over a short period. I should like to explore
possibilities other than the imposition of statutory penalities on either elected members or
staff of local authorities in breach of the Act in an endeavour to find a satisfactory way of
overcoming the problem. In my opinion, the issue raised by the Controller and Auditor-
General could be resolved if greater efforts were applied to the proper training and
qualification of senior local government staff, on whom rests the responsibility for guiding
their councils in these matters."

there well may be a need to look at the regulations that govern the situation referred to by
the honourable member. In the light of new evidence I am sure that the Minister will be
prepared to do that. However, when considering any changes I think we should always bear
in mind that local authorities deal with public moneys, in the same way as central
government. This means that the public interest must always be paramount.

DRUG SENTENCING AND PREVENTION OF MISUSE BILL
With the leave of the House, it was agreed that the speaking time of the member for
Sydenham be extended.
Mr KIRK (Sydenham): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Drug Sentencing and
Prevention of Misuse Bill. Í thank the House for the opportunity to introduce this Bill. It is a
very sobering thought that New South Wales, with a society similar to our own, is estimated
by the health authorities to have 10 000 heroin addicts in its 4 700 000 population. Time is
short, so I will concentrate on the technicalities of the Bill.
Part I seeks two modifications to the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. For a first offender
involved in trafficking class A drugs into New Zealand-for example heroin, LSD, and
cocaine-the sentence of imprisonment proposed in the Bill shall be not less than 10 years
and not more than 15 years. For a second trafficking involving hard drugs into or out of New
Zealand, the mandatory sentence proposed is a minimum of 15 years to a maximum of 25
years. These sentences will not be reducible unless special mitigating factors can be
established, which the judge must reduce to writing when he gives his decision.
Part II deals with the Customs Department, which can play an important role in the
reduction, if not elimination, of the supply of hard drugs in New Zealand. Many people feel
that sufficient information on drug trafficking is not available to New Zealanders who leave
for overseas countries. Some have been interrogated and actually charged with some kind of
narcotics trafficking offence through participating in what may have seemed to them to be a
completely harmless operation. It is time that a few of the basic techniques employed to
inveigle or involye unwitting tourists or travellers in a narcotic trafficking operation were
clearly explained. Also, travellers should be informed about the penalties they will be
bjected to if they become involved in such operations. To deter those who might become


## p. 2140 (#596) ###########################################

2140
12 August
Drug Sentencing and Prevention of Misuse Bill
involved in trafficking hard drugs into New Zealand, the penalties should be printed on the
customs arrival document, to be read by all people who arrive through normal passenger
channels.
Another facet that has given the Customs Department a certain amount of consterna-
tion has been the trafficking of drugs through the unannounced arrival of small ships such as
yachts. It would clearly be an advantage to the Customs Department to know the projected
date, and time and place, of arrival of a vessel or private aircraft. At present there is no onus
on the master of an aircraft or a ship on a non-scheduled journey to New Zealand to provide
this information. In terms of profiling the arrival of this type of vessel or aircraft, it would be
of help to the Customs Department to know of the previous three ports of call. It could also
be in the interests of marine safety to know the features of identification of a small vessel,
and its call sign, so that if it is overdue a search can be instituted with some fair estimate of
where it should be. I feel this section would go a long way towards removing the supply of
hard drugs into this country.
With the addition of section 268A to the Misuse of Drugs Act, the Minister will now be
bound to distribute to persons who provide information that leads to a prosecution a set
percentage of the street value of a drug that has been intercepted. At present, if somebody
provides information that leads to the successful interception of a narcotic trafficking
operation, it is up to the Minister to decide what amount of money will be paid by way of a
reward for the information provided. It is well known that a severe risk is taken by anybody
who provides information on drug trafficking. The recent murder in Australia of a person
involved in the anti-drug movement stands testimony to that fact. Knowledge of the reward
for imparting information to the authorities would be a real incentive to help stamp out the
drug problem. It has been stated that the amount of money assessed by the prosecuting
authorities as the street value of a drug has been inflated for the purposes of presenting a
more awesome case and securing a conviction. An accurate assessment of street value would
result in a fair deal for a person who provided information, and would mean that the
trafficker was charged with an offence that truly represented the extent of his operations.
Part III deals with the Police Act. It has become obvious that the American drug
enforcement administration, and other governmental bodies in countries concerned about
preventing the manufacture and trafficking of drugs, feel it is time New Zealand pulled its
socks up and did its fair share of the work. A good move would be the appointment of a
narcotics liaison officer in South-east Asia. He would have a very valuable role to play in
stemming the flow of narcotics from South-east Asia to New Zealand, and would also be
seen to represent New Zealand's international concern over the hard-drug problem, which
up till now has been minor. This would be very valuable, and many of the authorities in
South-east Asia, Europe, and America would like New Zealand to make this move. From
discussions I have had with people in the Police Department I know they support the concept
of beating the problem before it arrives. I commend this to the House as another reason for
supporting the Bill.
In terms of Part IV, the Minister in Charge of the Legislative Department-the Prime
Minister-would request Parliament to set up a standing committee to consider various
aspects of drug abuse, and to make reports from time to time. There is a need to adopt an
overall review of the drug abuse problem in New Zealand. I do not totally subscribe to the
belief that supply reduction in itself is enough. A balanced response to the problem of drug
abuse is needed, by the addition of a vigorous prevention and treatment component to the
existing law enforcement efforts. There is a need for a balanced programme.
The basic objective of supply reduction effort is to make drugs more difficult to obtain,
and more expensive and risky to possess, sell, or consume. When relatively pure heroin at
low cost became available to American servicemen in South-east Asia, use was widespread.
When those servicemen returned to the United States, where heroin is much more costly and
hazardous to obtain, use dropped dramatically. During 1972-73, a shortage of heroin on the
east coast of America coincided with significant reductions in the incidence and prevalence
of heroin use there. It is felt that successful supply reduction efforts can minimise the number
of new users, increase the numbers of old users who abandon use, and decrease the
consumption of current users. It goes without saying that no supply reduction effort can be
completely effective, but it would be a start on a growing and serious problem.
The Bill is an attempt to give Parliament the opportunity of expressing its concern about
the growth of drug trafficking in New Zealand, and an opportunity for parliamentarians as
individuals to express and prove their concern about a problem that no doubt in turn causes
concern in many of the constituencies they represent. A standing parliamentary committee is


## p. 2141 (#597) ###########################################

12 August
2141
Drug Sentencing and Prevention of Misuse Bill
called for, because there is a need to adopt at legislative level a strategy for containing drug
abuse. The key to the adoption of the strategy for containing drug abuse should surely be
that we must be realistic about what can be achieved and what the appropriate role of the
Government is in the war against drugs. The fact of the matter is that some members of our
society will seek to escape from the stresses of life through drug use. Prevention, education,
treatment, and rehabilitation will curtail their number, but will not entirely eliminate drug
use. As long as there is a demand, criminal drug traffickers will make some supply available
if the potential profits outweigh the risk of detection and punishment. This again enforces
the need for a harder line on sentencing and policing. Vigorous supply reduction efforts will
reduce but not eliminate supply. However, it is eminently more suitable to reduce the supply
of drugs into New Zealand to a level that can be policed and is of controllable proportions.
There is a need for an assessment of the current situation, to decide the principal drugs
of abuse and their ranking, taking into account their consequences to the individual—who
after all is a member of society—and to society as a whole. The second point of Part IV
covers this. Not all drug use is equally destructive, and we should give priority in our
treatment and enforcement efforts to those drugs that pose the greatest risk to compulsive
users of drugs of any kind. Our policy should reflect a concern about those drugs with the
highest social cost. This does not suggest devoting every resource to the highest priority
drugs and none to the lower priority drugs. All drugs are dangerous in varying degrees and
should receive attention. I emphasise that those drugs with the potential for causing the
highest social cost should be given priority.
The third part of this section concerns the examination of enforcement procedures
necessary to immobilise drug traffickers and enhance the capabilities of the Police and
Customs Departments to provide for better interception. Supply reduction is a broader issue
than law enforcement, and there are many aspects of supply reduction. Legislation should be
aimed at removing all aspects of illicit production and distribution of drugs. Activities should
range from recognising that New Zealand has international responsibilities in drug traffick-
ing, to interdiction of illicit shipments and removal of important traffickers from the supply
system through long prison terms. We require more effective regulations and monitoring of
the legitimate production and distribution of drugs, such as amphetamines and barbiturates,
that can be abused or used illegally, and this is one matter on which attention should be
focused.

Minister of Police that methods other than those set out in the Bill are being employed at
present and are believed to be effective. I believe that the clauses in the Bill, with the
exception of clauses 3 and 7, which are both operative clauses, are really administrative
matters. Clause 3 calls for heavier sentences, and clause 7 requires non-scheduled ships and
aircraft to give certain notice on entering New Zealand waters.
The first matter the select committee will need to consider is whether the title of the Bill
is appropriate. I find it a curious title and hope that the member, when he replies to the
debate, will give some background on how it came to be chosen. The reference to drug
sentencing is a little curious in itself in that it must surely be a reference to drug offenders
being sentenced. The second part of the title-the "Prevention of Misuse Act", as it would
become known-seems to run counter to the Act passed in 1975, the Misuse of Drugs Act.
So we would have two Acts on the statute book, one called the Misuse of Drugs Act and the
other called the Prevention of Misuse Act, and they would sound, at least, as if they were
mutually self-cancelling.
The main matter to which I want to direct my attention is that of minimum penalties as
set out in clause 3. Of course, that is not a novel suggestion; it is one that is raised regularly
about a number of offences in which the community becomes concerned-such as assaults on
police officers, hijacking of aircraft, and the like. However, we need to face squarely the
question whether the imposition of minimum sentences in fact creates a greater deterrent
than the flexibility provided by setting a high maximum and leaving it to the court to do
justice in any particular case. As has been pointed out, the Bill provides for a minimum
sentence greater than the maximum sentence for drug trafficking generally; so, no matter
how serious a case of trafficking in New Zealand may be, the maximum sentence the court is
empowered to impose is lower than the minimum that applies to the second offence of
importing.
The minimum set by the Bill is higher than the maximum that can be imposed for such
horrendous offences as kidnapping, hijacking, attempted murder, acid throwing, and
bribery and corruption at very high levels. Those are very serious offences, and the
committee will need to consider whether the importation of drugs alone stands above those
matters that are subject to a maximum sentence of 14 years' imprisonment and in fact should
have a minimum of 15 years. I believe that Parliament has been correct in its attitude over
the years in consistently rejecting the suggestion of setting minimum sentences as a
deterrent. There could be inconsistencies in the attitude of parole boards if one person had
been sentenced by a court to 10 years' imprisonment when there was no minimum, and
another offender had been sentenced to 10 years' imprisonment, not because the court felt
that was justified but because the law said he had to be given at least that sentence. It has
been mentioned recently, and some publicity has been given to the fact, that New Zealand
already has the longest sentences in the Western World. Against that recently publicised


## p. 2148 (#604) ###########################################

2148
12 August
Drug Sentencing and Prevention of Misuse Bill
background, one wonders whether we should set a further advance—and certainly a much
greater advance than we have ever contemplated before-in providing for a maximum
sentence of 25 years and a minimum of 15 years. A difficulty arises in differentiating between
a serious case of its kind and one that is perhaps not so serious or perhaps only technical. A
person might be caught by the narrow discretion given to the court, although the offence
committed was a venial one of its kind. Presumably a court having to impose a sentence of 10
year's imprisonment in the venial case would still not feel justified in imposing a sentence of
more than 10 years in the more serious case when that sentence, in comparison with the
sentence for crimes such as hijacking, is regarded as being a very lengthy one indeed. The
other major difficulty is whether a jury would be inclined to convict. No doubt defence
counsel would make the most of the fact that an individual, perhaps an adolescent, who was
returning to New Zealand had been caught up quite wrongly-in an illegal association and
had brought into New Zealand a small amount of controlled drugs.
Hon. David Thomson: Himself an addict.
Mr BRILL: Yes, he might be an addict himself, and he brings a small quantity into New
Zealand. If he is a person with a clean record and the jury is informed that he must be either
guilty or not guilty-there is no half-way house-and if he is guilty he will go to prison for a
minimum of 10 years, I believe the jury would be inhibited in arriving at a just decision. If
juries are left with the present situation and know that the offender can be sentenced for a
term of imprisonment up to 14 years, they realise that the judge will take any mitigating
circumstances into account in sentencing the offender. The Bill provides for a narrow
discretion, but I believe that the imposition of the minimum penalty would lead to a jury
being very reluctant to impose a conviction in cases such as the one I mentioned.
On the other matter-the imposition of a 15-year term of imprisonment on the second
offence I believe we need to have some evidence. I ask the member for Sydenham to
indicate the incidence of reoffending. My understanding is that those who have already been
sentenced under the Misuse of Drugs Act or its predecessor, the Narcotics Act, were given
fairly heavy custodial sentences. I do not know of many who have come back for a second
taste of that. Is there evidence that this is the type of offence that leads to heavy reoffending,
and therefore should be singled out as one with a very high minimum sentence?
My final point is a short question relating to clause 5, which states that in any
prosecution the street value shall be set by the Crown. It seems to me that no evidence could
be called and no guess of the prosecutor could be challenged, and, whatever the street value
set by the Crown, that shall be the value adopted by the court. That is a departure from the
mainstream of our jurisprudence. Would the member for Sydenham give consideration to
that question when he replies, or raise the matter in the select committee to which the Bill is
to be referred?
Mr LANGE (Mangere): I welcome the referral of this Bill to a select committee. First, I
shall refer to some points raised by the member for Kapiti. I agree that, on the face of it, the
provision for a minimum sentence might turn a jury from convicting. Unfortunately, the
reality is that in this area juries might be more prejudiced against an accused person by the
nature of the offending, because the jury through its various members would reflect the
abhorrence New Zealanders feel about drug trafficking. That is the concern I express about
Part I altogether. I acknowledge the strength that the argument of the Minister of Justice
must have with the House and, I am sure, with the member who introduced the Bill.
Notwithstanding that, it is possible to say that Part I provides for a system of sentencing
which, by comparison with other jurisdictions that allow hanging, shooting, or other
methods of dispatch, with or without trial, might make the proposal seem somewhat liberal.
That is the balance to be tested when the Bill is referred to the committee.
If it be said by the member for Kapiti that he has not heard of people who have
reoffended in trafficking, I can point to some spectacular examples, one of which was a
gentleman who received a life sentence for the crime of murder and shortly thereafter
indulged himself in purveying narcotics on the street. It is not necessarily so that people do
not reoffend. In fact, the recidivism rate in New Zealand is almost spectacularly high. The
committee should consider whether or not sentences do in fact deter, because the contention
I advance is that the other part of this Bill will give some strength to narcotics control. We
are not after the body, but after the prohibition of importation of narcotics that can be
harmful. That is why the reservation of the Minister of Justice about production of narcotics
is met within the Bill, because it is competent for the police in New Zealand to detect a
factory where heroin could be manufactured. To intercept heroin coming in from abroad is a
much more difficult task.

2149
Drug Sentencing and Prevention of Misuse Bill
The House ought carefully to gauge the feeling and concern of the community-a
feeling I share, having undertaken or been present at post-mortems and inquests on clients
who have been killed by narcotics abuse, and being mindful at the same time of the
wretchedness of drug addicts. Some, in the course of feeding their addiction, will sell some of
their narcotics to others to sustain the habit. I am grateful that the Bill does not set out to
impose penalties any different from those already on the statute book for people who are in
that plight. The Bill is directed at stopping or impeding the flow of hard drugs into New
Zealand from other countries and, by implication, stopping New Zealand from being used as
a laundering place for dangerous drugs for distribution to other parts of the Pacific.
Referring to specific parts of the Bill, the question of the street value of drugs has been
raised. I see no objection to the statement that the street value means the value set by the
Crown as being the value of the drugs involved in a prosecution. It must be an incentive to
some people to get involved in the illicit narcotics traffic when they hear and read of the
value placed by the prosecuting parties on the narcotics before the court. The provision is a
good one, and the later corollary allows the Minister discretion. If I might answer the
Minister of Customs on that aspect, it is not a mandatory payment, but a discretionary
payment to an informant of a proportion of the street value, as stated by the prosecution in
the proceedings.
Regarding information on ships and aircraft arriving in New Zealand, the fact that this
will involve masters of ships beyond the New Zealand jurisdiction is not an impediment, nor
should the fact that no specific penalty is provided for breach of the requirement be taken as
necessarily bad, because precatory legislation providing for standards has been with our
society for many years. If it can be done in the Public Bodies Meetings Act, surely it can be
done in an effort to stop heroin coming into New Zealand. A strength in that broad section
might cause the Customs Department a great deal more selectivity in its rumbling of ships
that arrive on the New Zealand coast.
A sensible and useful provision in the Bill is that people leaving New Zealand should be
furnished with information about penalties attaching to the use of drugs or the trafficking of
them abroad, and, in particular, that those coming into New Zealand should be advised of
penalties for misuse of drugs within New Zealand. Would the committee, when examining
that subclause, consider whether or not it is now time for people to be given immunity from
prosecution if, on arrival in New Zealand, they elect to declare that they are carrying
narcotics in their luggage? After all, what is the mischief this legislation is aimed against? It is
aimed against the importation of hard and deleterious drugs into New Zealand. It has always
seemed anomalous that a person, asked by a Customs officer whether he has any narcotics,
should be expected to say yes, because immediately there would be an arrest and difficulty.
The committee might look at extending the provisions of the suggested clause 6 to allow
a person immunity on declaration that that material is in his possession or luggage. People
are used by internationally financially unscrupulous people to convey to New Zealand
certain goods, and they might wish to take advantage of the air fare offered, and then to
hand the goods over to customs on arrival without their being prosecuted. While this House
might not necessarily be willing to endorse such a fraud, when one considers the character of
the person furnishing the air ticket it might be something of a deterrent.
I endorse the novelty of appointing an international narcotics liaison officer, but can say
from my experience in acting for people who are slaves of narcotic addiction that the best
part of their product came from areas in South-east Asia. I believe it would be useful for the
police to extend their competence in stopping this drug traffic by having someone on the
spot. I accept from what the member for Kapiti said that perhaps the department could do
this in any event, but the people of New Zealand might believe that more is being done when
an Act of Parliament gives a mandate to the police to create such an appointment.
I do not pretend to have a competence in how parliamentary committees are established
or what they can do. While I respect what the member for Petone said, I hope that the
committee on drugs, if established, will produce a better result than did the Road Safety
Committee. I endorse that the committee ought to be set up, not to direct police opera-
tions and I appreciate the concern of the Minister of Police that that suggestion might be
implicit in the Bill-but so that members of this House might exercise a continuing vigilance.
Bear in mind that the Narcotics Act was passed in 1965, and the Misuse of Drugs Act was
passed in 1975. If this House were to have a body charged with eternal vigilance, and not
merely responding to the bait of legislation each decade, the people might be preserved from
the onslaught of narcotics into this country, which is causing such social stress. I endorse the
referral of the Bill to the committee.

Drug Sentencing and Prevention of Misuse Bill
Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga): This is an important matter, but it should be realised that
this is not the first time the House has expressed concern about the misuse of drugs. On 28
March 1974 the Drugs (Prevention of Misuse) Bill was introduced into the House. It was
reported back in June 1975, over 12 months later. During that time the Social Services
Committee, of which I was a member, had heard 51 submissions. I am mentioning this so
that members will realise fully that there will not be many points, if any, in this Bill that have
not been thoroughly dealt with.
Various angles have been mentioned during the debate. One suggestion is somewhat
new that the Police should have rights to operate in South-east Asia-and its merit or
otherwise would require close investigation. The police brought the committee up to date on
the seriousness of drug trafficking in New Zealand and the way it is affected by the countries
of South-east Asia. It was pointed out that heroin is 12 times as potent as morphine, and that
a person can be hooked on a "smack", as it is called, after 4 or 5 inhalations or injections.
We were told about the enormous amount of money behind the trade. Authoritative sources
have stated that one of the largest exporters of illicit drugs is communist China. The outlet is
through Hong Kong, the money being paid in gold from the Western World.
There was also evidence that drug trafficking has touched our shores. The drug weapon
has been used by practically all countries. It was used extensively by Japan when it overran
China in 1937; during the war it was used extensively by the Japanese throughout South-east
Asia; and we have seen its very powerful use in South Vietnam. With this background, we
have a problem that cannot simply be pushed under the carpet, or easily dealt with. It is
ongoing, and we must at all times keep up to date with trends. I do not believe that altering
the punishment is in itself sufficient. Many countries have adopted the principle that it is not
sufficient merely to deal severely with the traffickers; they also deal very severely with the
victims. In communist China, drug victims are dealt with by capital punishment. Drugs there
are for export only, according to reports we have received.
The member for Sydenham probably realises that under the Misuse of Drugs Act the
Minister has the power to set up a committee, and in fact a committee is sitting at the
moment, so not a great deal of new material would come before a select committee.
However, as chairman of the Social Services Committee I should be glad to have an annual
review of the reports of the Police Department, Customs Department, and Department of
Health on drugs and their use. Undoubtedly that would have some merit. The Social
Services Committee has been set up more or less as a permanent committee, and it certainly
could be a permanent one. It performs functions beyond the scope of a parliamentary select
committee in that it is a specialist committee, and deals with specialist problems in this very
complex area. Most of the ground has been pretty well traversed.
The point has been made that although the Bill centres on the importation of drugs, we
are concerned about the increasing sophistication in the preparing and refining of illicit drugs
in New Zealand, and in their use. The committee would be constantly looking at that. Both
the Police Department and the Customs Department have kept a very close eye on the
problem. This Bill is an expression of the concern of the member for Sydenham, which I am
sure is shared by all members. As the chairman of the Social Services Committee I am quite
certain that all members would welcome any evaluation of the situation that would help with
the problem.
Mr KIRK (Sydenham): I have been very pleasantly surprised at the reaction from all
members in this Chamber, and I am very grateful to those who have contributed to the
debate on an issue that is of concern to us all. Before I answer some of the questions that
were raised, I point out that there are many matters I thought should be covered in the Bill,
but because I was not able to do everything I decided it was more important to deal with the
subject generally.
I am concerned about, and should like the committee to take up, the matter of books
such as the one I have in my hand. A person who will make submissions to the committee is
concerned about books such as this, which tell people how to cultivate the opium poppy. It is
illegal for people to be told how to make bombs, but apparently it is quite legal to sell this
type of book in New Zealand. Among others who will want to give evidence is Dr Fraser
MacDonald, who is involved in drug rehabilitation.
This Bill generated a lot of interest in the Labour caucus, as I am sure it did in the
Government caucus and with the general public. The Opposition spokesman on health, the
member for New Lynn, was very keen to take part in the debate, but was not able to do so
because of illness. I should have liked to hear what he had to say on this matter.
Today the problem is greater than it was when the misuse of drugs legislation came into

the House. In November last year there was a leading article in the Christchurch Star which

stiff sentences have been handed down under the existing law, but this matter will receive a

cost is compared with the recent $400,000 worth of heroin intercepted in Christchurch
recently, I think the expenditure would be justified. Our police and Customs Department
people need international experience, because, after all, they are dealing with an inter-
national problem.
The comments made by the Minister of Police were very relevant, particularly those

problem, which must be handled in a very special and stern way. The incidence of people

just want to be the catalyst to bring about better legislation. At the committee stage, I shall

provision applies also to widows and other solo parents with children under 10. It will be
equivalent to $4 a week.
There is more still. The existing wife rebate has been adjusted so that a wife may now
earn up to $520 a year before the rebate reduces, compared with $375 a year before the 1977
Budget. This means that the married taxpayer with a child under 5 who qualifies for both
rebates will pay no tax if his taxable income is less than $82.63 a week. I do not know
whether we have had such a position before, but before the 1977 Budget those people would
have paid tax if their taxable income exceeded $57.65. In effect, the Government has made it
possible for far more young low-income families to pay no tax at all. The tax reductions
amount to about $85 million for the 1977-78 year. Families eligible for the original young
family rebate numbered 90 000, and an additional 70 000 families are eligible for the
extended provision. In addition, 156 000 people are eligible for the new single-income
rebate. It is estimated that about 218 000 families will receive tax relief under these schemes
in 1977-78, or 128 000 more than were eligible for the original young-family rebate. Yet the
Opposition says this is a nothing Budget that does nothing for the young people on low
incomes. I take that as a grave insult to those who prepared the Budget.
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): I compliment the member for Hamilton

we have heard from the Opposition benches.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: You'll support the 10c on spirits, will you?

inflation of which they were the instigators. Inflation is the most hurtful thing that any
country can have, and the National Government is doing its utmost to control inflationary
trends. We have to convince the people of that before 1978.
Statements have been made about the additional money that should be allocated to
health, education, and the social welfare services. Members of Parliament accept the

These are factors that obviously we have to bear in mind, and accordingly the expenditure on
health, welfare services, education, and the like has to be kept to the bare necessities.
Another feature that has come out of this debate is that Opposition members absolutely hate

Another matter that has been discussed is the cost of national superannuation, and
the fact is that it has been implemented successfully with very moderate additional funds
being required. The total cost is $930 million, of which $165 million will come back to the
coffers of the State by way of tax, leaving a net cost of $765 million. When we subtract from
that the $598 million for universal superannuation and similar benefits paid before the
introduction of national superannuation, we have a net additional cost of $167 million. I wish
Labour members would keep those figures in mind when talking about the cost of national
superannuation, because Labour's superannuation scheme would have been costing the
taxpayers another $168 million at this stage, and about twice that amount by the time the
scheme came into full implementation.

Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: Ha, ha! It was going to come from the pay packets of the

I shall confine most of my remarks today to matters coming within my portfolios. The
important industry of tourism has been the subject of press comments from the Opposition's
spokesman on tourism. I want to put straight one or two comments about the present state of
the industry, and mention my hopes for its future. The National Government promised to
make tourism a top-tier industry, and although there has been a slowing down in the number
of visitors coming to New Zealand, I am sure this is temporary. In the Budget, $2.02 million
s allocated for the promotion of New Zealand overseas, and this will be done by the Tourist
ind Publicity Department throughout the coming year. I am hopeful that we will get our just
eturns from that investment.
In addition to the $2.02 million provided for the Tourist and Publicity Department,
private entrepeneurs, together with Air New Zealand, Mt. Cook and Southern Lakes
Airways, and the National Airways Corporation, are extensively advertising abroad. For
many years, the New Zealand tourist industry has maintained an exceptional growth rate
well ahead of the world average, both in visitor arrivals and in the foreign exchange earnings
therefrom. The world patterns are encouraging. Although the United States visitor intake
suffered a decline in 1975—which I believe reflected the economic conditions-there has
now been a notable recovery, with a rise of about 18.5 percent in the total number of visitors
to the United States during 1976. For the May year, New Zealand earned $162.5 million in
overseas funds from tourism-which is a considerable increase on the $143 million earned in
the 1976 March year. A greater promotion has been undertaken to encourage New
Zealanders to travel in the off-peak tourist season.
Mr O'Brien: Tell us about the fall-off from Australia.
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: I will tell the member about the Australian scene. We have
increased our promotion in Australia to try to encourage more visitors from that country.
Investigations have confirmed the desirability of establishing a travel office in Canada, and I
am hopeful that this will be achieved during the next 12 months, thus giving New Zealand
official representation in all its principal tourist markets.
The member for Island Bay referred to Australian visitors to New Zealand. Although
there has been some pessimism about the downturn in the number of visitors from Australia,
which for the year ended 31 May totalled 218 496—a reduction of 5.6 percent on the previous
year-it should not be overlooked that that number is nearly 40 000 more than the number
forecast at 1 April 1973. It is difficult to explain that extraordinary growth. In 1973-74, there
was a 35 percent increase in the number of Australian visitors compared to the previous
year; a further increase of 24.9 percent in 1974-75; and an 8.5 percent increase in 1975-76.
We must regard the total number of visitors from Australia as very satisfactory, although the
phenomenal growth rate in 1973-74 and 1974-75 cannot be expected to continue. The most
recent statistics on Australians travelling overseas during the month of February indicate
that, apart from one or two minor exceptions, the total number of departures to all
destinations has dropped. As the number of visitors to those destinations numbered no more
than a few thousand, New Zealand is therefore just one of many countries not being visited
by Australians in the same numbers as in the previous year. Despite this, New Zealand is

12 August

intensifying its tourist promotion in Australia, and, as I said earlier, the increased allocation
to the Tourist and Publicity Department is already being applied to maintain New Zealand's
competitive position on the Australian travel market.
The total number of visitors to New Zealand to 31 March 1977 was more than 380 000,
or only 4300 less than the previous year. The most recent figures to the end of May indicate a
satisfactory increase of 8.3 percent in the number of visitors from the United States. The
number of visitors from Western Europe has increased by 17.6 percent, and from Japan by
19.4 percent. The only market showing a decline is Australia, which is down by 5.6 percent.
The number of visitors from North America, Western Europe, and Japan has shown a very
satisfactory growth, particularly in the months of April and May. Indications are that that
trend will continue. A quarter of a million New Zealanders have travelled overseas in the
past year an increase of 3.3 percent. Coincidentally, the number of visitors from New
Zealand to Australia-112 800-was down 3 percent compared with last year. I feel that the
Australian market is sound, and that we will have a continuing good response from our
promotions there. Unfortunately, in May we had the Australian air traffic controllers' strike,
which disrupted the flow of tourists from both New Zealand and Australia-it is estimated
that between 10 000 and 12 000 visitors had their travel arrangements affected. I trust that in
May 1978 the progressive pattern of previous years will be maintained.
Recognising the desirability of conserving overseas funds and the importance of
expanding travel by New Zealanders within their own country, a very imaginative campaign
has been launched to promote travel by North Islanders to the South Island and vice versa.
Television commercials have formed the basis of the campaign, with specific incentives in the
form of discounts offered by some 28 tour operators, hotels, transport companies, and
souvenir shops. A revised tourist accommodation development scheme was introduced in
September 1976. The original scheme had proved most successful in helping to overcome
shortages of tourist accommodation in key areas during the period of the previous National
Government from 1962 to 1973, when the scheme was cancelled by the Labour Government.
It is interesting to note that during that period the TADCO scheme supplied finance or
guarantees for 3253 beds. The money involved was just on $4 million in cash advances and
$10.5 million in guarantees. The revised scheme has been introduced, and several applica-
tions have been lodged for accommodation in the Auckland area. One is well advanced with
its planning, and appears to meet the TADCO criteria. It appears that about 200 extra rooms
could be constructed in the Auckland area within the next 18 months to 2 years. I have
recently announced the establishment of a Tourist Advisory Council, and of four committees
to serve it. I am delighted that all those who have been asked to serve on the council have
graciously consented to do so. I look forward to serving with them in the coming months,
and have every confidence that they will make a very worth-while contribution to the
development of tourism in New Zealand.
The Tourist and Publicity Department has broken new ground in the motivation and
attitudinal surveys that it has carried out in the past 12 months. Australian and North
American holiday visitors have been examined as to their range of motivations and attitudes.
The information from the studies has been made available to the tourist industry, particu-
larly those concerned with promotion and marketing, so that they can carry out their
activities in overseas markets with maximum effect. Interestingly enough, the studies show
that personal communication with friends, relatives, and travelling New Zealanders is a
decisive factor in helping visitors to decide whether or not to come to New Zealand. Visitors
generally have high praise for our New Zealand way of life, our scenery, and our tourism
services. Most people questioned were particularly satisfied with our tourism facilities.
Provided that advantage is taken of the incentives offered by the Government for the
development of accommodation and other tourist facilities, and given healthy economic
conditions in our main tourist markets, there is a firm expectation that in 1978 the overseas
earnings from tourism will be more than $200 million.
Tourism is thus in the course of becoming established as a first-tier industry, in
accordance with the Government's election promise. Interestingly enough, last year we
amended the Tourist Hotel Corporation Act, and it is very gratifying to know that the
corporation has enjoyed a very successful year. I compliment the board of directors and the
general manager on their very fine performances.
Richard Walls: We have got rid of the red tape.
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: Yes, we have, and the corporation can now progress unfet-
tered. The fact that the corporation's profit increased by 241 percent last year was very
'pleasing indeed. The corporation has spent $3.3 million during the past 12 months on

The Budget presented this year is a good one. It is a hold-the-line Budget, and it is

Air Traffic Controllers, Auckland
3. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked Minister of State Services: Is it correct, as
reported in the Auckland Star of 29 June 1977, that 600 days' holiday were then owing to air
traffic controllers at Auckland International Airport, and that the only way of remedying
this was to transfer officers from secondary airports to Mangere, and, if so, what action has
been taken in the meantime?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): It is correct that a substantial
accumulation of leave has accrued to air traffic control staff at several airports. At Auckland
it is estimated that in excess of 600 days' leave will remain untaken at the end of November
1977. This situation is caused primarily because of a decision by the State Services Tribunal
in May 1976 on a claim by the Public Service Association, which gave an additional 8 days'
annual leave each year to all qualified air traffic controllers, and the introduction of a revised
shift cycle that increased rostered time off by 16 days a year. The extra leave was made
retrospective to 9 July 1975, creating a very large accumulation of leave at all airports. The
transfer of staff from secondary airports is not the only way of remedying this. This is not a
satisfactory solution to the problem because of the time required to give training in the
different procedures applicable to the major airports and centres, and to validate ratings.
The most effective answer lies in the recruitment of additional manpower. In December 1976
the Government authorised an increase of 23 staff for this purpose, but a normal air traffic
control cadet requires 3 years' training before being ready for full operational duties. The
training capability and capacity of the Ministry of Transport is at present fully extended. It
may still take up to 12 months to clear the present backlog of leave. However, I am satisfied
that all possible measures are being taken to enable as much leave as possible to be taken,
and that the transfer of secondary aiport staff to major units is unlikely to become necessary.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: If the amount of leave accrued at the end of November will be
more than 600 days, does that mean that it is increasing at present, and the problem is
gaining momentum rather than being reduced, and how many additional staff will be
required to make the impact on it that will get rid of all the accumulated leave within the year
forecast by the Minister?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: It is correct that 600 days will be accrued by the end of
November, and it will probably continue to accumulate until such time as the extra staff
becomes available for Auckland. I understand-and it is a cursory answer; I hope the
member does not hold me to it—that 8 extra staff are required at Auckland to change the
rosters and allow them to catch up with the leave over a relatively acceptable period.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: What is the overall figure required to reduce the total arrears for
all airports, including the secondary ones?

Regional Development-Suspensory Loans
6. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister of Regional Development:
What were the votes for, and the expenditure of, suspensory loans in the years 1975-76 and
1976-77, and what was the percentage of expenditure in relation to the vote in each year?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development): For the year ended 31 March
1976 the vote for suspensory loans was $4,277,000, and expenditure under the item was
$2,594,000. The percentage of expenditure in relation to the vote for 1975-76 was, therefore,
61 percent. For the year ended 31 March 1977 the vote for suspensory loans was $3,230,000,
and expenditure under the item was $1,867,700. The percentage of expenditure in relation to
the vote for 1976-77 was therefore 58 percent. The allocation for suspensory loans in 1975-76
and 1976-77 was underexpended because of a more cautious approach by business to new
investment.

regional development in 1975-76 and 1976-77, and what is the projected expenditure in

information if he would be good enough to ask another question. Obviously, the question
does not seek elucidation of the answer to the question posed by my colleague the member
for Dunedin North.
Mr Marshall: In view of the underexpenditure mentioned by the Minister, could he
confirm that some of the restraints placed by him on regional development expenditure last
year have now proved to be unnecessary, and that this is borne out by the fact that some of
the restraints have been removed in this year's Budget?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I cannot agree with the proposition advanced by the member for
Wanganui. Last year the Government was presented with the very real problem of trying to
solve the runaway Government expenditure which had been allowed to occur under the
previous Government. The expenditure for regional development, like all other departmen-
tal votes, had to be carefully studied to see where savings could be made. The qualifications
placed last year were to emphasise the true priorities for regional development. It was
possible, in this year's Budget, to remove some of the restraints placed last year.

Inflation-proofed Bonds
7. Mr KIRK (Sydenham), on behalf of Mr ROGERS (Onehunga), asked the Minister of

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): Investments in the proposed

Contractors' Plant
13. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) asked the Minister of Works and Development: Is
he aware that approximately 35 percent of contractors' plant is lying idle, and, if so, what
proposals are in hand to utilise this waste of resources?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I am aware that such a
claim has been made, but I am in no position to verify its accuracy. I am also aware that this
is the season of the year when, because of adverse weather and working conditions, plant
utilisation is always at its lowest. I am further aware that successive Ministers in both
National and Labour Governments have repeatedly warned contractors of the dangers of
overpurchasing. Despite these warnings, some contractors continue to acquire excessive
amounts of new equipment. Nevertheless, the Government has taken measures to make
more work available, and the recent Budget relaxed restrictions on local authority loans for
water supply, sewage treatment, electrical reticulation, hospital works, stormwater, and
natural gas reticulation works. The financial allocation for irrigation and rural water supply
schemes has been substantially increased, and considerable contract work will be available
on the multi-million dollar Upper Waitaki and Clutha hydro-electric projects.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: In view of the Minister's answer that some contractors are
overequipping themselves with plant, could he indicate the extent to which this is taking
place?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: I am not in a position to indicate in a general way, but I can say
that one contractor has placed an order for six pieces of machinery totalling $1.8 million,
which equals the total amount spent by the Ministry of Works and Development on plant
replacement programmes for a whole year. I can further indicate that when the department
had a sale of used machines in Mangere a month ago, contractors bought equipment to the
value of a further $250,000.
Mr Cooper: What restraints are being imposed by the Minister on his own department's
purchases of machinery and hiring of staff, in order to allow the private sector resources to
be more fully utilised?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: In keeping with Government policy, restraints have been placed
on my department, and a reduction in the total amount of machinery purchased this year as
compared with last year has been carried out. I think that the total expenditure for New
Zealand of $1.8 million speaks for itself.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that a higher proportion of contractor's plant and
equipment has been idle this year than is customary?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: I have no relative figures, but I have told a previous questioner
that this is the winter season of the year, when the use of contractors' machines is at an all-
time low. I have indicated to the House that the Government's policy, as outlined in the
Budget, will give increased work to contractors in several centres.

made by the lines themselves on commercial grounds. In addition, the harbour boards
themselves are actively promoting their ports both within New Zealand and overseas.
Mr Isbey: If there is a shift in trade from the container ports to the non-container ports,
will this mean a decrease in the volume of container operations?

Transport, one being a survey of coastal shipping and the other being an assessment of the
effect containerisation is having on non-container ports, with particular reference to the
reduced flows of wool through those ports. I repeat that I have no way of directing shipping.

## p. 2166 (#622) ###########################################

2166
16 August
Oral Answers to Questions
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): Although national archives has Sir
Walter's papers in its custody for safekeeping, it does not have control of them. Under the
terms of his will, control of access to the papers remains with his trustees and advisory
trustees. When the papers were deposited in national archives the trustees granted exclusive
access to the papers to Sir Walter's biographer for a period that has not yet expired. In the
memorandum of agreement at that time, they indicated that access should continue to be
restricted for at least 10 years—that is, until 1980-with the proviso that this period could be
extended to 1990, so that the papers can be properly sorted and recorded. On archival
grounds, the chief archivist strongly supports the view that the task of appraising, arranging,
and describing this vast collection should be undertaken before general access is allowed.
Most researchers who have expressed interest in working on these papers have accepted this
view.
Mr Marshall: Can the Minister confirm that an arrangement was made with Professor
Sinclair whereby, during the period for which he was responsible for compiling the
biography, he was to be consulted on requests for access to the papers, and that this
arrangement does not appear to be operative now?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: My department is not aware of any such arrangement, which
would naturally have been made with the trustees. I accept the member's word that such an
arrangement was made, but the matter has never been discussed with me.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Am I to understand from the Minister's reply that any restriction
binding on the body he referred to is not compulsory but arises simply as a result of a private
agreement made by it and Professor Sinclair, which could be abrogated by both parties if
they agreed?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I believe that is correct. We have actually asked the Crown Law
Office for an opinion on the matter.

APPROPRIATION BILL-FINANCIAL STATEMENT
Adjourned debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I have heard many expressions used
to describe the 1977 Budget. I shall call it a common-sense, caring Budget. I believe the
Prime Minister approached the Budget as a paternal GP, diagnosing the causes of our
economic troubles, coming to grips with the symptoms, and endeavouring to alter as gently
as possible the course the economy is taking, rather than resorting to panic measures or
indulging in major surgery. I call it a caring Budget because the Prime Minister has cared for
the single-income families, including widows and solo parents, by providing a new $4 a week
tax rebate for single-income families with a child under the age of 10. That shows his
understanding of the position the parents of young families are in at present.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: And I suppose you call that compassionate?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I believe it proves that the Prime Minister is compassionate, as
members on this side of the House have always known him to be. It is also a down-to-earth
Budget, underlining the fact that no one owes New Zealand a living, and that we must work
our way out of our present difficulties. It is a reminder that our future prosperity depends
largely on three factors: (1) a growth in our export production; (2) world demand for our
products; and (3) access to world markets.
World demand and access to world markets is largely beyond New Zealand's power and
influence, but the Prime Minister and his deputy have had considerable success in opening
new markets over recent months, and by hard work, greater efficiency, and planning, we can
expand our export production. Worth-while incentives have been given in this Budget to
encourage greater production, but in the final analysis it rests with our farmers, our
manufacturers, and our workers to make the extra effort needed for us to work our way out
of our economic troubles. That is the challenge in the Budget, and I have faith that New
Zealanders will respond to that challenge. I want to confine my remarks on the Budget to
matters that affect my portfolios, but before doing so I should like to say how pleased I am
that the inflation-adjusted savings bond scheme has been introduced, and how gratifying it is
to the many friends of the member for Piako, who has been advocating this type of bond for
many years.
The Budget shows the determination of the Government to come to grips with some of
the most troublesome aspects of local government finance. The tax rebate and the rates
rebate speak for themselves. The tax rebate for rates on owner-occupied homes gives $15


## p. 2167 (#623) ###########################################

16 August
2167
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
million in the first year, and coupled with the rates rebate, which will continue and will
amount to $8.3 million this financial year, it will give relief to ratepayers of more than $23
million. I hope the tax rebate is but the first step. Assistance to urban transport has been
very well received, and the director of transport in the Auckland Regional Authority said he
was delighted at the Government's moves. This is the second major area of assistance in the
urban transport sector.
The bus replacement programme, which is estimated to cost $50 million over the next 5
years, will be of tremendous help to urban local authorities; $6.8 million, and a further
$500 000 to assist smaller local authorities and private operators, will be given in this
financial year. I was pleased to hear this announced at the weekend. This assistance has been
directed primarily to the main centres where urban transport losses have become a matter of
major concern, but provision has also been made for the participation of the smaller centres.
I applaud that. Direct assistance from the Urban Transport Council will be given once the
council is established.
I should like to refer to interest rates, because the Budget increases the maximum local
authority interest rate from 94 percent to 10 percent. Increased rates for shorter terms have
since been fixed to assist the Local Authorities Loans Board. The intention behind these
moves is to help maintain the supply of money on the local authorities loans market, which
needs it so very badly. The relaxation of the Local Authorities Loans Board's general
determinations will also have marked effects. These are the restrictions relating to the raising
of loan money for essential works, of which the following have been removed: water supply,
storage, or reticulation; sewage treatment or sewage reticulation; electrical reticulation;
hospital works, subject to approval having been given after 22 July by the hospital works
committee and the Minister of Health; storm water reticulation or prevention; and natural
gas reticulation and installation. Removing these restrictions on the raising of loan money
will have quite a considerable effect on the money that will be available for the essential
elements of local bodies' works programmes, and coupled with the rise in interest rates it will
certainly help to overcome the major financial problem facing them at present.
I should now like to refer to local government generally, because besides the financial
moves already enumerated, there have been major developments in relation to local bodies.
As Minister I have strengthened the consultative processes of the Territorial Local Govern-
ment Council. Municipalities and counties are, through the efforts of their associations, now
taking practical steps to bring urban and rural interests closer together. Representatives of
catchment boards are now meeting regularly with the Territorial Local Government Coun-
cil. All these moves are in response to the Government's initiatives in bringing about a more
co-ordinated and effective system of local government through co-operation and assistance.
I should like to discuss briefly major legislation affecting local government that will
come into the House in the next few days. I shall be introducing the first instalment of
legislation designed to update and consolidate the Municipal Corporations Act and the
Counties Act, and other legislation relating to local government that is presently tucked
away in other Acts, in order to codify and simplify and bring into one Act all the major law
relating to the conduct of territorial local government. This Bill will not deal with the poll
provisions affecting local body reorganisation, which I know are of considerable concern,
but I give an undertaking that these will be looked at in a separate exercise in the very near
future. Coupled with the new Town and Country Planning Bill that my colleague the
Minister of Works and Development will be introducing shortly, and the current revision of
the Public Works Act and a proposed water bill, this legislation will bring local Government
legislative measures into line with today's requirements.
I should now like to say a word or two about the regional schemes under the Local
Government Act. The Local Government Commission is currently bringing down schemes
in order to establish united councils or provide regional groupings of local authorities for
essential functions such as civil defence, and such other functions as the region's needs may
dictate. These schemes are marked by progressive and responsible co-operation among the
major local authority associations, which are moving with the Government towards the
establishment of a better relationship between the two arms of government. With the co-
operation of the local authorities these regional schemes should be completed by the end of
the year.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: How are they being received?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Generally well; there is the odd spot where we are having a little
trouble, but I am certain that once these authorities have submitted their objections to the
Local Government Commission it will be prepared to alter the regional schemes to fit in as

I now wish to refer to gaming and racing, because within the next week I shall be
introducing a Gaming and Lotteries Bill. I am hopeful that it will bring a breath of fresh air
into what is presently an archaic and anachronistic body of law dating back to the conditions
prevailing in the nineteenth century, and perhaps even further. I know this will be welcomed
by the courts, the legal profession, and also the general public, which is confused and
worried about the present outdated laws. I also intend to introduce a Racing Amendment
Bill to deal with some necessary changes to the 1971 Act. This will give some recognition to
the greyhound racing industry. The Bill will introduce the concept of a restricted totalisator
licence for greyhound racing, and for racing and trotting if they wish to use it.
Relief of 0.5 percent on all on-course investments was given to racing and trotting clubs
in the 1976 Budget. This was well received, and the Government will continue to give
consideration to further taxation relief when economic conditions are right. On the recom-
mendation of the New Zealand Racing Authority the number of totalisator permits was
increased by 33, 21 of which went to trotting clubs and 12 to racing clubs. The trotting clubs
in particular were very appreciative of those extra days.
The allocation in the Budget to recreation and sport was the same as last year, but the
grant from the Lottery Board of Control has been increased from $250,000 to $400,000, so in
effect the Council for Recreation and Sport receives an additional $150,000 this year. The
council could use more money for this important social programme, but it has accepted the
difficult economic conditions and has agreed to make the best use of what it has. While
assistance for the major recreation facilities is not possible, more money is being spent on
developing school facilities for community use, and in my visits to those schools I have been
most encouraged at the work that is being done. National recreation and sports organisations
will receive $800,000 this year, and members will be interested to know that about half the
amount allocated last year was used for coaching schools and the like. I am pleased to see
that more cultural organisations are beginning to use the recreation and sports scheme, and
on the local level more cultural groups are now applying to and receiving recognition from
their local councils. Later this year a booklet on recreation will be published, which will
present some ideas and methods to help local authorities determine their needs and establish
their priorities.
I should now like to spend a few moments on sporting contacts. All sportsmen in New
Zealand, and in fact all New Zealanders, will have greeted with relief the very sensible
statement drafted at Gleneagles. New Zealanders do not like being pilloried as "racist”, and
we are the last of all people to justify such a label.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Used to be.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: And we still are. Perhaps the member for Timaru feels he can
speak for New Zealanders. I believe that I know the sportsmen of this country much better
than he does, and I know they feel as I do when I say that we do not deserve this racist label.
We must now hope that we will get fair play, and if the Commonwealth community decides
on a code of conduct on race relations, including sporting contacts with racist countries,
those rules will apply equally. Recently I feared that New Zealand would receive special
treatment and would be required to meet tougher criteria than that applied to other
countries. I am pleased that it now appears that our friends in Africa, including Mr Ordia,
appreciate the fact that this Government does not support apartheid and will apply the terms
of the Gleneagles declaration fully and fairly, but cannot and will not interfere with the basic
freedom of citizens. I congratulate the Prime Minister for the part he played in bringing this
about during his recent visit to the United Kingdom.
The Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council has been granted $2.2 million this year, which is
an increase of 18.9 percent on last year's grant, and with the additional sum that has been
made available recently represents the minimum the council said it needed. It gives me
considerable pleasure to be able to announce that the requirement set by the council has
been met. With the grant of $50,000 for the establishment of the Council for Traditional
Maori and Polynesian Arts and the $50,000 for the regional community arts councils, the
grants to the arts have been increased by 21 percent this year. No other vote has received a
bigger increase, and that is why it is most annoying for me to hear groups such as Downstage
complaining about this "niggardly" Government. I believe the Prime Minister and the
Cabinet have been very generous in the allocations made to the arts. During its election
campaign the National Party promised to give more recognition and support to Maori and
Polynesian arts, and the amount allocated in the Budget represents a very significant

the arts. The Government should not have to go it alone, and it is important to encourage a
