I received a report recently from the Arts Council recommending that the levels of
taxation exemption be raised, and I am pleased that the Prime Minister has increased the
amount of deductible donations for charitable and cultural purposes from $200 to $375. I
hope he might be able to increase those still further, but on behalf of the people interested in
the arts, I thank him. The Arts Council's working party on taxation is considering further
related matters. It is clear that our laws do not encourage the level of benefaction that exists
overseas. Gift duty, estate and death duties, and sales tax are all fields in which some
alteration to the tax laws might encourage the arts. I believe the idea of an arts development
foundation is well worth consideration.
I also believe that we should look seriously at a feature film industry. This morning I saw
the film Solo produced by Toni Williams, which I believe is the first New Zealand feature
film with a true New Zealand flavour, and I am confident it will succeed on the overseas
market. Local production has shown a marked growth with Blerta's Wild Man, Sleeping
Dogs, and TV1's production on the life of Sir George Grey. But there is a lack of co-
ordination, and we find several productions using the very limited resources of skilled
personnel and finance at the same time. A film commission could be a means of providing
more resources and better co-ordination. My department has almost completed a report on
the future development of the industry, and I shall be discussing this with my colleagues
shortly.
Last year the Government set aside $50,000 from lottery profits for the emergency
conservation of art works. This is only one of the many fields in which the nation's ability to
conserve its past is inadequate. Buildings, historical records, shipwrecks, costumes, Maori
artefacts, and old films are other fields where resources such as personnel, facilities, money,
and the necessary knowledge are in short supply. I intend to look into these matters so that
recommendations can be made to the Government when the economy allows.
Most members are interested in lotteries, and I shall now make a few comments about
them. The policy of constantly reviewing the Golden Kiwi lottery ensures that profits are
sufficient to help many worth-while organisations that rely on the proceeds. To meet public
demand, last year the Government introduced the $1 Golden Kiwi Jackpot Lottery, which
proved to be an instant success. The Lottery Board of Control, which is responsible for
lottery profits, is confident that a healthy increase of profits will be available next year for
community organisations. Four distribution committees were set up under the Gaming
Amendment Act 1962, and receive annual allocations. The four committees invest in
medical research, scientific research, welfare of the aged, and welfare services, and care is
taken to ensure that grants made in these areas do not conflict with the Government's
funding. The committees supplement that funding by enabling research to be undertaken,
and provide services that would not otherwise be available. The Lottery Board of Control
also makes a grant to the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council, the New Zealand Historic Places
Trust, and the Litter Control Council, as a supplement to the Government grants to those
organisations. The lottery board regularly funds the water and mountain safety councils and
makes an annual contribution to the recreation and sports programme. I have already
referred to the funds being given this year for the community use of schools scheme. The
board also funds the cultural facilities scheme for the capital cost of theatre and auditoria
equipment. I recently had the good fortune to open two art galleries, which are a credit to
their cities.

I turn now to the Budget, which spells out a message for New Zealand that the Labour
Government failed to tell the people when it was in office. The terms of trade have turned
right against us. It should now be clear that we must earn our living abroad in a world where
huge energy surpluses make it difficult for small countries like New Zealand to pay their way
and where we face tougher trade barriers against agricultural produce. The Budget sets clear
objectives in the face of continuing uncertainties in the world economic situation. It spells
out the necessity for New Zealanders to live within their incomes, for New Zealand to live
within its income, and that we must earn our living efficiently, both at home and abroad. If I

objectives, it has a regional emphasis and deserves the title, "a regional Budget".
The National Government came into office in 1975 firmly committed to strengthening
the regional development programme by placing firm emphasis on the development of
regional resources. The Government also promised to continue the previous Labour
Government's policy of incentives, which were directed largely at manufacturing industries
in the form of regional maintenance. The inherited programme was retained and examined
closely. This examination revealed fundamental weaknesses, which could be expected to
show themselves after an initial period. Those weaknesses included a failure to come to grips
with the underlying causes of regional development problems; and the approach was largely


## p. 2171 (#627) ###########################################

16 August
2171
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
one of treating the symptoms without treating the real ailments and a failure to reconcile
regional and national policies, and in particular a failure to take account of the severe
economic conditions the country faced and the need to reassess the regional development
incentives along with other policies.
Some changes were made to the existing programme-changes that were necessary in
view of the economic conditions. In the first full financial year of the National Government,
$5.27 million was voted for regional development under the Trade and Industry vote. This
was $1.16 million more than the Labour Government spent in its last year in office. It
covered suspensory loans, freight subsidies, railways unit rate, and the cost of running
regional development councils. It is not commonly understood that regional development
suspensory loans are intended to encourage new investment in plant, equipment, and
buildings, that they are interest free, and in essence are written off after 5 years. This
emphasis on investment has not changed. Every application is judged on its merits, including
the employment opportunities it will create and the degree to which local resources will be
used. No restrictions have been placed by this Government on the number of loans
available, although the maximum for any one loan is set at $100,000, which experience has
shown to be sufficient for most applicants.
Last year Otago took $367,200 in suspensory loans, 21.44 percent of the total for New
Zealand. Our neighbouring friend, Southland, took $432,360, representing 25.25 percent.
Southland was one of the four areas to receive increased advances, the other three being
Wanganui, the East Coast of the North Island, and Marlborough. Despite accusations, there
have been no restrictions on the number of loans available through the Development
Finance Corporation. Otago received 16 loan approvals from that source, a number almost
identical to the number of approvals given during the last 2 years of the Labour Govern-
ment. The 16 companies received $2.64 million.
It should be pointed out, however, that financial assistance from the Development
Finance Corporation does not always suit a company, and regional enterprises continue to
draw finance from the private sector with the full encouragement of the Government. The
reduction in total advances from the suspensory loans scheme and the Development Finance
Corporation simply reflects a lower level of economic activity resulting from our adverse
terms of trade and the economic mess that Labour landed us in. In this situation it was
entirely appropriate for business investors to adopt a stance of cautious optimism. It is also
the reason for the $4.19 million for regional development in the Trade and Industry vote this
year. Expenditure in the boom year of 1974-75 was only $4.97 million, and of that nearly
$500,000 went to the ill-fated Matai Industries. Given the current level of economic activity,
it is reasonable to assume that there will be sufficient funds this year for those who seek
regional development finance, but the councils know full well that the Cabinet will provide
extra funds in the supplementary estimates if they are needed. Only muddled socialist minds
would suggest that businessmen and entrepreneurs who take risks should ask for loans
simply because they are available—an arrogant socialist philosophy, as my friend the
Minister of Tourism would say.

Both Governments have preferred an investment commitment by regional manufactur-
ers. For Otago the freight subsidy scheme has been the most visible form of regional
assistance. Labour promised at the 1975 election that it would continue the freight subsidy
scheme, but it did not disclose the criteria, or its intention to review the subsidies. It was
subsequently revealed that the main criterion was to give industry a breathing space during
which it could rationalise production and become efficient in its regional location. However,
the breathing space was never defined. The election undertaking to continue the subsidies
was not put to the test. Before the election the Otago and Southland manufacturers claimed

Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
that Labour saw the subsidies as an instrument of inefficiency; and other sources added that
the subsidies were not a preferred form of assistance as they were administratively untidy.
Experience of the freight subsidy scheme during the 3 years of the Labour Government
revealed some interesting facts. First, three recipients ceased operation in the region, despite
the subsidies. Five companies' freight subsidies lapsed when they failed to apply for renewal,
and eight companies relinquished their freight subsidies in favour of suspensory loans. The
review also showed that, although distance from the market place was a common problem,
its effect varied considerably and freight cost as a percent of sales was very light in some
instances. Quite startling was the fact that some companies had a profitability record ahead
of the national average, and thus a subsidised advantage over their competitors even though
those competitors might also be at a regional disadvantage in relation to markets. The review
of the freight subsidy scheme and its continuation by the National Government recognises
that in the meantime the problem still exists for certain regional industries serving the
national market. While a statement in the 1976 Budget indicated that the general aim was to
phase out this form of assistance, a flexible attitude to renewal applications has been
adopted. Sixteen renewal applications were made, about half of them after considerable
personal urging by officers of the Otago Regional Development Council and the Otago
Manufacturers Association. Five companies have had their subsidy continued in full for 3
years, and eight will receive it on a diminishing basis for 3 years. Of the two immediate
terminations, one is under appeal to the Minister and the other has opted for a suspensory
loan. An assurance has been given, and is repeated, that if a company cannot be helped in
any other way the Minister can extend the range and the percentage of the subsidy. That
assurance was backed by the Prime Minister when he addressed the annual meeting of the
chamber of commerce in Dunedin last year.
The 1976 Budget confined the scheme to priority areas of Otago, Southland, and the
West Coast. In the first year of the National Government, Otago received $621,628, or 97.24
percent of the total payment for this form of regional development assistance. That was
$220,628 more than the payment made in the last full year of the Labour Government, and
honoured a promise given by the National Party during the 1975 election campaign. In
addition it is calculated that Otago received $146,500 in unit rate assistance through the
Railways Department. Advances by the Rural Bank to the agricultural sector increased in
number, and by almost $2 million to $11.73 million. Forest planting for the first full year of
the National Government increased from 2239 hectares to 2312 hectares in Otago, and a
similar programme is expected for the current year.
In Dunedin and its immediate environs such enterprising firms as Shacklock, Christies,

have expanded. The increased employment opportunities being provided, however, are
largely uncommented on. We have heard the member for Dunedin Central talk about

fact is that the AB Consolidated and St. George companies were both in receipt of regional
development assistance.

We in Dunedin are proud of our human skills, our investments, and our achievements,
and are grateful for the incentives and the assistance provided by the Government. What has
this Government done for regional development? Shortly after the election, it defined
regions to ensure that assistance was directed according to a region's needs. It set the
regional development councils the early task of identifying worth-while development oppor-
tunities in their regions through comprehensive resource surveys. Yesterday the Otago
Regional Development Council released a very well researched resource survey.
The important point is that that survey was carried out by the people in the region, who
have investigated their own resources, set their own priorities, and can now talk to the
Government, to each other, and to entrepreneurs, with a document which lists all the
advantages and some of the constraints applying to the development of the region. The
Holmes task force on economic and social planning was quickly established, and identified a
lack of administrative co-ordination as a major weakness in setting policies. As a result, the
New Zealand Planning Council was established, with Sir Frank Holmes as its chairman. As
members well know, the council is already working on long-term policies, especially those
connected with regional development, and will provide the secretariat and the co-ordination.
In its first Budget the National Government introduced a new regional development
investment allowance. Otago was designated a high-priority area, giving its manufacturers,
its fishermen, and its farmers moving into the export market a 5 percent advantage over their
competitors in lower-priority areas. The export incentives were increased following the
devaluation last year. Multimillion-dollar loan finance has been provided for the Port
Chalmers container terminal, which will be opened by the Prime Minister on 10 September.
Provision is made in this Budget for the introduction of the new pioneer status incentive
scheme, a new approach which provides additional capital assistance for qualifying expendi-
ture on new commercial resource development in priority regions.
The regional development councils are fully involved in assessing the advantages and
the use of this new scheme. The establishment grant scheme will make contributions towards
commercial feasibility studies, commercial development, and initial or pilot production in
marketing costs of manufacturing and processing projects in areas such as Otago. Together
with the pioneer status incentive scheme, it implements the specific proposals outlined in our
manifesto, and will give regional development councils a major role in highlighting the
development potential of their local resources and sorting out their priorities in conjunction
with the Government.

Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
The statement by the Minister of Housing telling young people how to save $12,000
caused a great deal of comment, and indeed consternation, bewilderment, and wonderment.
In late May he said that if a young couple on the average wage were prepared to put off
having a family for the first few years of marriage they could, if they saved regularly, save
$12,000 in 3 years towards their first home. He said also that if they decided to have children
their income would be reduced to a single one. He talked about the couple banking $1,300
each for 3 years, if possible, and so on. He said, however, that if the couple felt they could
afford to bank a little more each week, and if they had their accounts in a trustee savings
bank, they might qualify for some type of loan. If, however, accounts were held by the Post
Office, they would be in a different situation. He said that if the couple wanted to save for 5
years, their return would be even greater. One can only call that an “if-ing" policy.
It was no trouble for this Government to find an extra $180 million to put into the
pockets of many people who do not require it, but at the same time it robbed the Housing
Corporation of more than $68 million last year. The Labour Government had funded $200
million through the National Development Loans Account for housing loans. The National
Government said last year that the estimates for housing loans would be $132 million, but in
the Budget we find that only $118 million was funded to the Housing Corporatio.1 for loans.
Not content with that, the amount this year is reduced to $108 million. Within a space of 18
months, therefore, the Government has almost halved the amount of finance available for
lending through the Housing Corporation, and this at a time of inflation and a time when,
notwithstanding that New Zealand is suffering from emigration rather than immigration,
thousands upon thousands of New Zealanders are desperately in need of a home, whether it
be through ownership or by renting.
What is the National Government doing to assist people in this time of housing crisis?
What happened to the variable mortgage repayment scheme, one of the innovations
introduced in the 1974 Budget and, I believe, one of the most important measures taken at
that time by the former Labour Government to assist young people into home ownership
with a much greater loan than they now receive to reduce initial outgoings? That scheme
provided many people with a new opportunity to enter into home ownership-the aspiration
of most New Zealanders. However, owning a home is now called a luxury by the Govern-
ment's friends, and possibly also by one or two Government members. I did not hear the
Minister of Housing defend his policies strongly in the face of statements made by a
millionaire who appeared on a television programme recently.
As the Leader of the Opposition said not long ago, the people will remember the
statement made by the Minister of Energy Resources when he proclaimed that if the
National Government was elected it would produce a dynamic new housing policy. Let us
consider that dynamic policy. The Government has wrecked the private mortgage market; it
has allowed mortgagee sales to increase dramatically, and it has set about destroying the land
bank built up by the former Labour Government. What kind of foresight does that indicate?
Just as National members have never liked State housing, so they have always hated having a
land bank, and once again they have set out to rid themselves of it at the very time when they
'could use it to provide the greatest help to the greatest number in the greatest need by
adding to the number of State houses, and by encouraging builders to come forward with
their own home designs. That is another policy knocked out by the National Government,
although it was welcomed by the builders when it was announced, and would be very
welcome today. However, it has been tossed out despite the fact that I believe—and I know
that most of my colleagues also believe that a rental proposition is frequently the first step
to home ownership. Indeed, in present circumstances, it is an essential first step.
The National Government has made it much more difficult to obtain a home. Under the
former Labour Government one could buy a State rental house with a deposit of 5 percent,
but the amount required has now quadrupled and a tenant has to buy the house he has
occupied for 6 years, whether or not he wishes to do so, otherwise he will be tossed out. That
is another indication of the way the National Government cares for people! I can hear the
member for Palmerston North making loud noises. He should have his photograph placed in
the Palmerston North Art Gallery, which we have heard him boasting about, with the
following caption: "This is the man who in 1972 made the infamous statement that under a
National Government mortgage finance would flow more freely." We all know that private
mortgage interest rates are now higher than ever before. The current rate of 10.4 percent
represents an increase of considerably more than 2 percent over the rate that applied during
the term of the former Labour Government. The prime interest rate on a Housing
Corporation mortgage has been raised to 8.5 percent, which means that a person with a

account. Under the third scheme, which is not beyond the bounds of possibility, and comes
within the bounds of probability for many working couples, a couple able to save $2,000 a
year to a total of $10,250 could receive tax rebates of $4,500, or an effective return of 44
percent of savings after 3 years or 5 years.
Dealing with one of these schemes—and I am not trying to pick selectively that which is
most attractive, but that which is probably in most cases practical-with $1,550 for the first
year's savings and $1,300 for each of the remaining 4 years, the total will be $6,750, the
interest $800, the rebates $4,310, and the accumulated balance in the account at the end of
that time $11,860. That means that in return for savings of $6,750 over 5 years a depositor
could receive tax rebates of $4,310. That represents an effective return on savings of 64
percent after 5 years, or 60 percent after 3 years, in addition to the normal 3 percent interest
on all deposits.

1976 was terrifying. It amounted to $340,000 million, or, to illustrate it more graphically,
1300 times New Zealand's annual defence expenditure. In 1976 the world spent, in 1 year,
sufficient on arms alone—not taking into account defence salaries or other incidentals-to
maintain New Zealand's defence budget at the current level until the year 3277, far ahead of
any year depicted in the space operas we see on television. Put another way, the world's
armaments bill in 1976 was 66 times New Zealand's total budget in 1977-78. Research shows
that 70 percent of arms spending is divided between the NATO and Warsaw Pact countries,
and 30 percent is spent by Third World countries. The great tragedy is that much of the
spending is by countries that cannot afford it. In fact, it seems to me that some Third World
countries may almost be forced by the great powers into the purchasing of armaments.

a neutron warhead capable of killing more people by radiation than the conventional nuclear
warhead. In the name of God, has science gone completely psychopathic? The new neutron
warhead spares buildings and properties, and that seems to have a familiar political ring,
with property becoming more important than people. Even worse, there is the prospect of an
ultrasonic bomb being perfected, which destroys the human mind, making human beings
into maniacal idiots incapable of reason—and it is an irreversible process.
Although I paint a depressing picture of the world's race for arms-and it has been
described as the arms bazaar, although I would prefer to describe it as the arms bizarre—
there does appear to be some hope for survival. President Carter is committed to the
abolition of nuclear weapons, and President Brezhnev is committed to the achievment of
detente, although that seems to have become a little more difficult recently. In the name of
humanity, the arms race must be stopped. Governments should not be able to spend the
world's major resources to promote a nuclear war.

It may seem something of an irony that I speak about disarmament and then speak of
some of our defence needs, but there is no conflict whatsoever in my mind. I have often said
in the House that we do not yet live in that beautiful, perfect world where armed forces are
no longer needed; therefore the maintenance of armed forces cannot really be argued. What
can be argued, however, is the way in which those armed forces are maintained, and the
arms with which they are provided. I will-as will the Labour Party-always support the
need for the defence of our nation, and the need for supporting our defence obligations, but
I-support defensive means, not offensive methods.
I understand that members of the Government caucus committee visited the
Christchurch workshops of the National Airways Corporation yesterday and were impressed
with the capabilities and performance of NAC's flight simulator. For that reason I think I
might strike a sympathetic ear when I strongly recommend to the Minister of Defence that
he and the Defence Council consider the purchase of flight simulators for the Royal New
Zealand Air Force. I would like to claim that such purchases would mean an immediate
saving in fuel; I cannot really do that, but there is a potential for a vast saving in fuel bills
through the use of flight simulators by the RNZAF. No real savings would come about at the
moment, because I understand that the RNZAF's flying hours are currently at an irreducible
minimum. But I understand we could meet P3-that is, the Orion-and C130 flight
simulator training with co-operation from the Royal Australian Air Force.
The provision of flight simulators in New Zealand for the A4s, Strikemasters, and
Iriquois would have the following advantages: first, crews could reach an even greater
standard of efficiency; secondly, additional flying hours, even within current restrictive
hours, would become available for tactical training and flying; thirdly, the flying training
syllabus could be used to better advantage; and fourthly, potential accidents could be
lessened—although it is hard to determine as a result of simulated training just what
accidents would not have happened. For the A4s and the Strikemasters, $3 million to $4
million would cover the cost of flight simulators, and, for the Iriquois, $400,000. This is a
small cost indeed to provide greater efficiency and safety for our RNZAF crews.
The days when an aircraft could be diverted from a primary role to pure training without
biting into an air force's finances are long gone. The maintenance and operating costs of a
simulator are only 10 percent of those of an actual aircraft. In simulator flying training,
errors can immediately be detected by the instructor or by the pilot from an instant video
playback of the simulator training session. The instructor can stop the exercise in flight. He
can freeze the instrument readings and the visual representations of the scene outside the
cockpit. He can then discuss with the pilot just how the emergency arose, and they can
discuss the effect of every action the trainee took or should have taken to keep the situation
under control.
I want to discuss further electronic needs for our C130s and Andovers. I refer to flight
recorders and downed aircraft position indicators-DAPIs, as they are sometimes known, or
more commonly crash position indicators. It is an almost universal fitment for commercial
airlines, and should be a must for RNZAF aircraft. We could meet that requirement for
$500,000. The items I have spoken about this evening would cost about $5 million. I do not
think that is very much money to provide for the safety required in a modern air force.

granted.

Squadron Leader DRAYTON: Not one loan has been granted to any serviceman who

I want now to talk about my other portfolio, and first to pay well deserved tribute to the

efficient manner in which the police maintain law and stability. Everyone should be proud

## p. 2191 (#647) ###########################################

16 August
2191
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
thinking that some form of smear campaign is under way. Despite this, nobody could fail to
notice that there has been no flagging of the service given. Twenty-four hours a day, 7 days a
week the police continue to give a very professional crisis intervention service as well as a
wide range of specialised help.
In peak periods police patrols move from one human crisis to another, working in an
environment of lust, hate, greed, deceit, anger, and frustration. Unlike the ordinary citizen,
the police cannot step back behind the cordon lines. They do not have the luxury of walking
out, and they must go right in head first, often against very heavy odds. On our behalf they
must act to resolve whatever situation may arise. Policemen often find themselves on the
horns of a dilemma. One party is bound to be dissatisfied with the way the problem is
resolved. Logically the policeman must decide in favour of one point of view. He cannot take
sides, but in most cases must make a decision on the spot. Much later, in the peace of a living
room, the warmth of a hotel bar, or in the calm atmosphere of a court room the constable's
actions will be judged. Armchair critics, law abiding or otherwise, will draw their own
conclusions-objectively or subjectively. Others in more formal arenas armed with clear
hindsight, full statements, testimony, and expert opinions will subject the snap judgment to
the most searching post-mortem. Eventually the quick decision could be tested in the Court
of Appeal, or even the Privy Council, and it is perhaps surprising that most withstand such
withering scrutiny. That they do vindicates the training of the police and the quality of their
judgment.
New Zealand is very well served by its police service. To prove my point, I draw on the
1 100 000 cases that have been handled in the last 5 years by a national strength that has only
recently reached 4500. This volume of reported crime has kept the police very busy, yet not
only have they coped, but they have also recorded one of the highest detection rates in the
Western World. In considering this volume of crime, I ask members to reflect for a moment
on the potential for criticism of a service that functions day and night, day in and day out,
dealing with the world's worst vices. Consider also the risks policemen run of being assaulted
and insulted, and the number of enemies they make, however illogical that may be. Yet New
Zealand policemen have managed to function within the community for 91 years without
generating the real animosity that is obvious in some other countries. Work-load studies
show that some 60 percent of jobs attended by police patrols are of a social rather than an
enforcement nature. Recent attempts to discredit the police by those with one axe or another
to grind are cause for concern and do nothing to build up police morale.
Since taking office the Government has made several important legislative changes to
assist the police and the courts to deal with certain types of crime. These include authority
for the courts to confiscate motor vehicles used by people convicted of specific crimes. When
this measure was introduced the member for Auckland Central said, "It will never happen.
There is no way it can happen." I want to tell the member for Auckland Central that it has
happened, and it has happened in Christchurch. New offences relating to disorderly conduct
and the manufacture of explosives have been dealt with.
The Government promised to give particular attention to police pay and conditions.
That promise has been honoured, and this year the police have received a pay rise of
something like 20 percent. In addition, increases in the number of allowances have been
approved. Mobility and effective communications are vital to an efficient police service, and
the Government has approved a 3-year plan to provide vehicles for all country policemen.
This is a great move, and will give safer working conditions in rural areas. Telecommunica-
tions expenditure to the tune of $767,000—the largest amount ever allocated-will counter
the activities of criminals with very sophisticated electronic communications systems. The
use of sophisticated radio equipment of the type in the new Wellington operations room will
be extended to other areas. The critical role of dog handlers will be assisted by the
installation of repeater radio systems in cars.
In the very near future the Government will make a final decision on the number of
extra police and civilian staff needed to cope with increased demands. Meanwhile, to ensure
that the facilities at the police college are fully used, approval has been given for an
additional 44 admittances to the August intake. In the first few months after taking office the
National Government increased the police staff by 183. I am particularly proud to be
associated with the police college, which will cost $19 million and, when completed early in
1981, will be the finest police college in the Western World.
I move now to the subject of juvenile crime. Last year more than 26 000 offences were
committed by 20 000 youngsters. Youngsters are regarded as those up to 14 years of age, and
young persons as those between 14 and 17. Crimes committed by those youngsters included

robbery, serious assault, car conversion, and a variety of sexual and liquor-related misde-
meanours. Members might ask what is being done to deal with this problem. In the police
service we have formed what are known as J teams, made up of police officers, educational-
ists, and social workers. In addition, 93 full-time and 53 part-time police youth aid officers
have been appointed throughout the country.
Early this year the youth aid section tried an experiment. It chose an intermediate
school with a disproportionate number of pupils to whom police attention had been drawn.
The school had a roll of more than 800, a wider than usual cultural and ethnic cross section,
unusual language and attitude difficulties, and an unusually high proportion of pupils from
the lower socio-economic groups. Truancy was a real problem. The headmaster's co-
operation was sought and readily obtained, and the programme commenced with a teachers'
preparation day, when the various functions of the police were explained to the school staff.
In a 6-month period, 66 children had been referred to the police, thus putting the school's
rate of juvenile crime above that of all other schools in the region. The aim of the experiment
was to exert informal influences to promote a new respect for rights, responsibilities, and
rules among those young people. The pupils were divided into easily manageable syndicates,
and the police visited the school on each of the first 5 days of the new term.
Films about the police were shown, and groups were addressed with the object of
dispelling misconceptions and prejudices. Children were invited to examine police vehicles
and equipment and encouraged to talk openly with all the police officers. On the fifth day
the school assembled to watch a spectacular police dog demonstration. After a break of 1
month, J team and youth aid members and police from the general branch visited the school
regularly to maintain pupil contact. The programme continued for 3 months, and the results
were remarkable. The rate of offending dropped from well above the average to well below
half the average. We make no wild claims of unqualified success, but the results show that
time spent in this way can substantially lower juvenile crime. I am concerned that while such
activities are going on certain television programmes undo all the good that is being done.
That experiment in Auckland reduced juvenile crime and brought the police in personal
contact with the youngsters, who realised that the police were there to help them. But I feel
very upset that these "anti" people undo all the good that has been done.

MARILYN WARING (Raglan): It is a privilege to follow a colleague in this debate, for

This evening I should like to address myself to the traditional constitutional reason for a
wide-ranging debate on the second reading of the Appropriation Bill. The Budget debate
has traditionally been a means whereby Parliament and individual members of Parliament
have the opportunity to express and ventilate grievances before voting public money to the

I speak in the context of the following quote in the foreword of a book called The Death
of British Democracy by Stephen Hassler. It is sour grapes, perhaps, because Hassler was a

never-successful Labour candidate in many British general elections, and is by no means an
authority. I use his words not as an indictment of any member here, but as something for
every member to ponder. Mr Hassler said, "The modern politician becomes so enmeshed in
the administrative bureaucracy and party machine and so dependent upon them that to reach
out beyond the hollow political rhetoric that sustains and justifies his existence is to risk his
career and to sour his relationships. Consequently very few politicians will ever raise the
political debate to a level that will disturb the smooth running of the political machine. In
this environment ideas become awkward and indeed subversive. Rigorous application of
ideas to politics will for the practising politician often lead to a clash with the machine, which
he will normally lose. Today's successful politician works the machine irrespective of the
direction in which it is going and he effectively removes himself from politics. The man of
ideas removes himself from office."
It has seemed to me in listening to this debate that the problem is that while we all
intellectualise and philosophise very few members internalise. We all know the clichés and
expect to apply them to our neighbours and not to ourselves. The crux of the Budget and the
economic situation is the realisation that it means you and not the guy next door. A parrot
can be turned into a learned political economist by learning the words "supply and demand".
Ours is a mixed economy in which public and private institutions exercise economic control.
Our competitive price system uses supply-demand markets to solve the basic economic
problems of what, how, and for whom. The next decade will see no change in our nation's
subjectivity to the primary economic laws.
First, there is the law of economic scarcity that is so prevalent in the energy resource
field and the land use field where there is only a finite amount of human and non-human
resources. Secondly, there is the law of production possibility and of substitution, which
means so much in terms of an examination of our agricultural potential and diversity of
markets. Thirdly, there is the law of diminishing returns where, after a point, the extra
output resulting from the additional input becomes proportionately less and less. Fourthly,
there is the law of increasing relative costs.
Of crucial importance in all these laws is the relationship of population growth to fixed
resources. The Holmes task force report concluded that New Zealand is in a period of "high
turbulence", which makes it difficult for society or decision makers to understand fully the
changes that are occurring. In order to improve the position, those who have to think about
their direction and rate of adjustment in social policies will need to understand the dynamic
nature of the changes that are taking place. The foreword to the guide to the National Party
election manifesto in 1975, published as a pictorial manifesto, contained this sentence:
"Social progress can only be made in a healthy economy." I have no quarrel with that, but if
there is no appreciation of the nature of the changes that are taking place socially there will
be a tendency-and there is evidence of this in the Budget-to try to maintain the status quo
when it has been found wanting.
I refer in particular to the budgetary moves on the domestic purposes benefit. Questions
that must be tackled are, for example: are the closely related problems of educational
underachievement, truancy, vandalism, and juvenile offending primarily the concern of the
Department of Education, the Department of Social Welfare, the Police, or the Ministry of
Recreation and Sport; will the State Services Commission be able to clarify whether the
Department of Education or the Department of Social Welfare is primarily responsible for
the development of child care facilities? I said that our main resource, people, was one of the
chief factors in our economic future. Some projections can and should be made realistically,
no matter how much they offend the status quo. Although our potential labour force will
continue to grow for some years, our lowest ever fertility rate is heading quite seriously for a
zero population growth, with the average rate of increase now less than 0.3 percent. Our
population will have proportionately fewer young people and more elderly people.
There is a vital need to study the economic and social implications of an ageing
population; the possible re-allocation of resources between services-for example, from
education to geriatric needs. The pre-school component of the population is decreasing, but
it will increase again towards the end of the century. The expansion of the school-leaving
population and of those leaving the labour force will not be great in the next decade, but will
rise towards the end of the century. Expansion of the newly married age group will be high in
the next decade, but will fall off in the late 1980s and 1990s. The rate of expansion in the
dependent sector-persons over 60 years of age-will be extremely high. I have no desire to
enter the partisan bickering about the superannuation scheme, but at my age I must confess
to some fear that, projected 20 or 30 years, I and my generation will not be able to afford the

cost of the care and income-maintenance of all those over 60. I know my colleague the

The 1977 Budget presents many challenges for the development of potential in the

The coming decade presents many challenges to the farming industry: to increase
production, to diversify, and to compete for A1 arable farm land against the expanding
urban acres of reinforced concrete and glass. The farmers of the Raglan electorate will meet
those challenges because they are of the calibre of young Keith Holmes from Cambridge
who recently won the Young Farmer of the Year award, and who in his essay for that award
spoke more common sense on agriculture than I have heard for a long time. This Budget
challenges young men and women like him through the livestock incentive scheme, and
through the promise to look at the possibility of developing productivity incentives as an
alternative to incentives for increasing livestock numbers. Amounts available for lending to
young farmers have been increased, and 55 farms are up for ballot in the coming year.
Rural depopulation has been a problem in the Raglan electorate for some years for,
while we heartily invest money in agricultural production for the rurally isolated, we slowly
deprive them of their social needs. We close their small schools and their rural Post Offices,
and consequently the store and the garage go too. The access roads deteriorate, and morale
drops as the farm worker, 3 miles from the end of the school bus route, packs up and moves
to town. The innovation in the Budget to assist farm owners building or acquiring dwellings
in townships near the farms for occupation by the farm workers is most welcome.
I think the minds of most of us boggle at the possibilities opened up and the challenges
that confront us by the establishment of the 200-mile economic zone around New Zealand.
The next decade for fishing will be expensive, and courage will be needed to maximise
options. Suspensory loans equal to 40 percent of the cost of construction will be made
available to owners of fishing vessels built in New Zealand shipyards. To assist my
generation of young, well qualified fishermen to obtain their first fishing vessel, a special
lending scheme that will provide loans of up to 80 percent of the cost of a vessel will be
introduced. The loan limits on Rural Bank financial assistance for fishing gear are removed,
a fishing vessel ownership savings scheme is introduced, and a development grant fund for
research into new fisheries and alternative processing techniques has been established.
It has been said that knowledge is the only instrument of production that is not subject
to diminishing returns. Perhaps paraphrased in the light of the Budget it might be said that
research is one of the few investments that is relatively inflation-proofed. This Budget sees
an increase of 15 percent in the vote for agricultural science research, 22 percent in the vote
for fisheries science research, and 13 percent in the vote for the Department of Scientific and
Industrial Research, bringing expenditure on these areas of research to $37 million. We have
an increase of 29 percent on the amount expended in the last financial year for the National
Research Advisory Council, and a 31 percent increase in the Defence vote for science
research.
A new item of $500,000 is voted for energy research and development under the
Ministry of Energy Resources vote, $1,380,000 as a new programme in the Education vote is
provided for research purposes, and there is a 15 percent increase for research in the Works
and Development vote. In the New Zealand Forest Service, provision for research accounts
for 5.7 percent of the department's total expenditure, and an additional 18 percent is voted
for medical science under the Health vote. There is a 46 percent increase in Programme I
under the Treasury vote for economic and financial policy and planning. Grants under Trade
and Industry for assistance to industry for research have dropped, probably because the total
vote last year was not spent.
The underdeveloped state of social research and social statistics in New Zealand is
deplorable. In the same Budget in which $3,055 million, or nearly half the total amount, is
expended on three votes-Social Welfare, Education, and Health—the vote for the Depart-
ment of Statistics and for research in this area has been reduced. Certainly a drop was
expected because it is not census year, but the department is now being asked to handle pay
research, an economic census, and a profile of the New Zealand family for the Cabinet
committee on family affairs. For too long this department has had insufficient staff,
insufficient services, and insufficient attention. The poor state of social research is one of the
key impediments to the development of coherent social policies in New Zealand.

Budget, and it is the best compliment that can be paid to the Minister of Finance. The fact
that he was able to produce a Budget that pleased most New Zealanders, in spite of the
economic restraints that still apply, is a credit to his acknowledged economic expertise.
Of course, cne does not expect the Opposition to be pleased with anything the
Government does. I have been paying close attention to the sections the Opposition has
chosen to criticise, and when that criticism is analysed it is clear that Opposition members
have not been able to get their teeth into any particular section. Starting with the tedious
speech made by the Leader of the Opposition, we have heard the usual carping criticism that

were never matched by performance. The Budget was greeted enthusiastically in Southland,
and Mr Dougal Soper, Secretary of the Southland Drivers Union, is quoted as being
generally in favour of some of the Budget announcements.
I now want to talk about Southland. The continuing container port controversy has
brought to a head the struggle between Otago and Southland over which province should
service the region. Like many other Southlanders, I was disappointed that Bluff was not
given container port status. However, Southland has a lot more left going for it than it has
lost. I do not see Southlanders sitting around bemoaning the loss of the container port for
too long. The problem to be resolved is what kind of development will be best for Southland.
I foresee a major fish processing industry for Bluff, employing many hundreds of people. I
also foresee the Mataura lignite deposits being processed on a huge scale, and a major
business expansion to service the rapidly expanding tourist areas of Manapouri, Te Anau,
and Queenstown, because of the shift of allegiance towards Invercargill rather than
Dunedin. Invercargill's growth rate is already greater than that of Dunedin in absolute and
relative terms, and I am optimistic that Invercargill will continue to provide a solid base for
industry and commerce in Southland.
The recent announcement by the Minister of Energy Resources that the Government is
prepared to spend about $14.5 million to reopen the Wairakei mine at Ohai, both as an
opencast and underground mine, has assured the future of Ohai and Southland as a major
coal-producing centre-and I think I can take some credit for that. People in West Otago are
already doing business with Invercargill. In the last census, Queenstown reported a popula-
tion increase of almost 50 percent in 5 years. The big holiday crowds in that district must be
supplied and serviced from somewhere, and I predict that businessmen in Queenstown will
look more and more towards Invercargill to supply their needs. This trend will accelerate,
and I advise any business wanting to open a branch in Southland or Otago to look very
seriously at Invercargill first.
Southlanders are born optimists, but they are also realists, and they know that both the
good Lord and the Government help those who are prepared to help themselves; Southlan-
ders have a record of helping themselves equal to none. We built our own co-operative
freezing works, our own harbour, and our own co-operative fertiliser works, and I doubt if
there is one that is more efficient. Of course, we also have an aluminium smelter which,
although it has not brought to Southland the predicted boom in ancillary industry, is
Southland's largest single industry. I must confess that initially I did not support the smelter
if it meant raising and ruining Lake Manapouri and Lake Te Anau, and I actively
campaigned to save those lakes. As I saw it, Southland should have the best of both
worlds-and today it has. The lakes have been retained and are earning much needed tourist
dollars. The aluminium smelter is an integral part of the employment scene in Invercargill
and Southland, and about 9000 people are directly or indirectly dependent on it.
I am no longer interested in the politics of the original smelter agreement. But I am
vitally interested in the continuing security of the men who work there and of their families,
and also of the business enterprises based on the smelter. I have made my views known in
writing to the Prime Minister and, while I expect the owners of the smelter to pay for
Manapouri power at a fair and reasonable price on today's values, I do not expect the
smelter to be screwed down to pay an uneconomic increased price. I am completely
confident that the Prime Minister, who has received my representations on this matter, will
ensure that the price finally agreed upon will be accepted as fair and reasonable by both
parties.

number of Jeremiahs in Southland, led by the former Labour member for Awarua, Aubrey
Begg, have been making the most dismal predictions about what will happen to Southland in

I am acting as a sort of anchorman at the moment. There are a number of things I want
to say. I feel obliged to speak out on a subject I feel pretty strongly about-political
interference in sport. As I see it, the whole purpose of the National Government, and
certainly the whole purpose of this Parliament, is to safeguard the freedom of the individual
and the freedom of the family in a secure and just society. I do not mean complete and utter
freedom for any individual to say whatever he or she wishes; that sort of freedom leads to
anarchy. I mean the fundamental freedom the individual can expect to have in a democratic
society under a democratic Government.
For me, as an ordinary New Zealander, one of our fundamental freedoms is the
freedom to travel from our country to play sport with whomever one chooses. There are
people in this country who want so much to see one or two of our athletes competing at the
Edmonton Games that they are prepared to sacrifice the freedom of other sportsmen for
that. I want to say to All Black captain Tane Norton and his fellow All Blacks who have been
invited to go to South Africa to play rugby as individuals that they go with my personal
blessing. I want to say to them that I am proud of them for sticking to their guns, because by
sticking to their guns and fighting for their individual freedom they are also fighting for my
individual freedom and for that of every other New Zealander.
The political pressure again being brought against our country and our Government
because of our refusal to stop individuals from doing their thing is the same political pressure
that manifested itself against this country during the Montreal Olympics. At least 34 other
nations competing there—including the host nation-were continuing sporting ties with
South Africa. What was the reason for HART, CARE, and a bloc of 20 Afro-Asian nations
blackballing New Zealand? The reason was that they could hardly pick on their "red fed”
friends in the communist bloc nations.
I shall have to stop with this thought: the truth of the Montreal Olympics is the truth of
what is happening today. At Montreal, half the competing nations were governed in the
main by bloody-minded dictatorships. When one thinks of the living dead in their jails and of
the psychiatric prisons that brainwash their political prisoners, then, as far as I am
concerned, half of those countries that competed at the Montreal Olympics are an insult to
human dignity and freedom. And that is what we are talking about. We are talking about the
freedom of the individual, and that is what we will lose in this country if we give way to the
same political pressures that are now reappearing over the Edmonton Games. Instead of
directing criticism at Tane Norton and his fellow All Blacks, people should be directing their
criticism at the black African nations which are chopping their people to pieces, and should
be telling them to clean the dirt and stench out of their own kitchens before pointing the
bone at New Zealand.

It is appropriate, since these matters have been referred to throughout the Budget
debate, to tell the country how much of our short-term economic strategy has been carried
out in a little over 18 months. That is just one item. I read from the National Party's
statement of economic policy: "Immigration which, in the last two years, has required
resources of the order of $660 million, will be cut to the bone." That has been carried out.
We have heard the whingeing and the grizzling from Labour members, but we have done
precisely what we said we would do before the election. We have carried it out.
"Confidence will be restored to our export industries, particularly farming." It has
been. Manufactured exports have soared, and confidence has been restored to the farming
industry. Instead of stock numbers going down, as they were under the Labour Government,
they have started to come up again under the National Government. Spending on farm
development and maintenance is on an upward trend. Confidence, in fact, has been restored
to farming, so much so that the various institutions that lend to farmers are strapped for
cash, because the farmers are spending. They want to borrow more, and that is a sign of
confidence.
"Price and income control measures will be used as necessary counterparts the one of
the other." We have done that. We have now introduced flexibility into wage fixing—and we
did not hear much about that from the Opposition during this debate. We have had talks
with the representatives of the employees and the Federation of Labour. We have said, "All
right, you negotiate in a moderate way, we will give you the flexibility you want, and we will
see how it goes." We are retaining price control, because price control can handle
reasonable wage increases. If that policy is accepted and carried out in the spirit in which it
was negotiated, we will be taking a step that the Labour Government never took.
"The New Zealand content of the goods we require assumes an increased value and
local production will be encouraged accordingly." We have done that with import substitu-
tion, and we are taking further steps by means of incentives-taxation and otherwise-to
carry out that policy. "Profitability will be restored to private industry so that jobs will
remain available to the New Zealand work force." I remember the Leader of the Opposition
going around the country before the election saying, "You elect this lot and there will be
50 000 unemployed", and in his wilder moments he said that 100 000 would be unemployed.
Sure, we have some unemployed, but no more than when they, the workers' friends over
there, were the Government; and throughout the country today a good man can get a job.
There is no doubt whatever about that.
"The taxation system will be used to give incentives for desirable economic activity." It
is being so used. We have amended it, with new incentives and new ideas through the
taxation system. "Trade negotiations will be conducted on the principle that we will not
import the unemployment of other countries." We are not, because our unemployment is no
worse than when we took office. We do not accept unemployment as a balancing factor in
economic management. Labour members said we would, but they were wrong. "Continuous
attention to economic trends and problems will replace stop-go and panic measures." I well
remember the tax cry of the Leader of the Opposition when he was Prime Minister. "I am
not going to panic." We used to say, "We don't want you to panic, we just want you to
govern❞—and he did not, and was thrown out. Well, we have not panicked; we have
governed, and we are making progress.
"The trend towards State ownership and control will be reversed and the vast superan-
nuation fund which is designed to provide State ownership of industry will be abolished."
And it was. We carried out that promise immediately, and put national superannuation in its
place. Members opposite said we could not finance that scheme. However, in this Budget we
have financed national superannuation—the major impact of our election policy--without
any increase in the rates of taxation. There have been all kinds of talk in the debate about the
extra cost of national superannuation. The total amount of $905 million, before tax, includes
the old universal superannuation, the previous age benefit, and the increased rates,
including those for people between the ages of 60 and 65. Before national superannuation is
paid out, $140 million is deducted as source taxation, so the net amount is $765 million. The
cost of the age benefit and universal superannuation was $625 million, less tax of $25 million,
making a net total of $600 million. So the net additional cost this year is $165 million.
When we were in Opposition, the present Minister of Trade and Industry, the present
Minister of Energy Resources, the present Minister of Health, and I did some arithmetic,
with a little bit of outside help, and said that national superannuation could be financed
without an increase in the rate of taxation. The then Labour Government had the total

The National Government has adopted a more flexible interest rate, and the controlled
and uncontrolled markets have been brought closer together. The Leader of the Opposition
is now going around the country saying that they will be spread apart, that the controlled rate
should be brought down, which means that the uncontrolled rate will go higher. What
incentive is there to save if the return on what you save is just a tiny fraction of the rate of
inflation? That is the policy he is espousing, as he did when he was Minister of Finance and,
subsequently, Prime Minister. We said that savings would be stimulated and that thrift
would be rewarded, and that is exactly what we are doing. With an inflation rate of 14
percent, how do you reward thrift? How do you reward thrift if you cannot give a return
after tax that is equal to the rate of inflation?
"A committee of inquiry will be set up to examine work done on inflation accounting in
New Zealand and overseas and report on its application to the New Zealand taxation
system." That has been done, and we are working on the report; we are hearing representa-
tions to see whether we want to implement it. We have carried out that promise. "Savings
accounts limited as to amount will be established in which deposits of individuals receive an
interest rate at least equal to the annual rate of inflation, thus preserving the purchasing
power of a basic savings nest egg." That is the "Luxton clause" in the Budget. It will be
legislated for this year, and we shall see whether the Labour Party opposes it.
"The growth of Government spending will be curbed, thus enabling income tax
increases to be less than the 87 percent increase of the last 3 years." That has been done; it
has been curbed, and the rate of increase of income tax is lower. "Small and contractual
savings institutions such as building societies, credit unions, savings banks and life offices,
will be encouraged by appropriate incentives." In last year's Budget, and again in this year's
Budget, they have been so encouraged. We have carried out that promise. Finally, "Death
duties which have escalated rapidly with increased property values will be reviewed at an
early date." And they were in our first Budget.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Industrial Mediators
1. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Labour: How many cases have been
dealt with by industrial mediators in each of the last 3 years, and how many referrals resolved
the issues involved?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The latest available figures relate to 1976
referrals. In 1973 there were 117 referrals to the mediation service. In 1974 and 1975 the
figures were 170 and 270 respectively, and in 1976 referrals totalled 275. In the majority of
cases the parties resolved the issues themselves—with the mediator's assistance—or agreed
to accept the mediator's recommendations for settlement. The number of cases so resolved
in the years 1973 to 1976 were respectively 100, 144, 249, and 260.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: What proportion of cases were settled by the parties themselves,
without active participation by the mediator, he simply acting as a chairman?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The analysis would be correct. The mediator has got the parties
talking together, and the issue has been resolved without the mediator having to make a
recommendation. I do not have the breakdown requested, but I should be pleased to get it if
the member would ask a separate question.
Question Transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

On-shore Oil Prospecting Licences
6. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga), on behalf of Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone),
asked the Minister of Energy Resources: Do the on-shore oil prospecting licences which the
Government has issued to itself despite the provisions of section 47D of the Petroleum Act
contain the same conditions and terms as would have been required from any other licence
holder?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): It is unnecessary for petroleum
prospecting licences issued to the Minister of Mines to include conditions relating to the
payment of royalties or an annual licence fee. Nor is it necessary that the Minister, as the
holder of the licence, should deposit with the Secretary of Mines as security a deposit or
bond. This is because the Petroleum Act provides that terms and conditions which are
required to be included in licences issued to other licensees need not be included in licences
issued to the Minister on behalf of the Crown. I note that the question suggests that the
petroleum prospecting licences have been issued to me as Minister of Mines despite the
provisions of section 47D of the Petroleum Act. This section, however, deals with a
completely different and unrelated matter, and is itself subject to the section in the Act
under which these prospecting licences have been issued. The object of section 47D is to
prevent public servants who, on account of their position, may have access to confidential
information from using their position for personal advantage by acquiring an interest in a
prospecting or mining licence issued under the Act.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Commission for the Environment Legislation
10. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori), on behalf of Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central),
asked the Minister for the Environment: What progress has been made on legislation to give
statutory independence to the Commission for the Environment, and when is a Bill expected
to be introduced into the House?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Environment): The Government has considered
the issue and has decided not to proceed with legislation at present. I am happy to leave the
question in abeyance for the time being. The commission is operating very effectively
without a statutory base, and its independence is widely accepted.
Hon. M. Rata: Are we to take it that the Minister's reply, that the Government does not
propose to proceed with enacting statutory provisions to ensure the independence of the
Commission for the Environment, indicates the importance the Government attaches to
environmental matters?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: As I said, at present there is no proposal for legislation, but that in
no way interferes with the independence of the commission. The independence of the
Commission for the Environment is widely accepted.
Dr Shearer: Can the Minister indicate whether the Commission for the Environment is
hampered in carrying out its activities because of the fact that it lacks statutory independ-
ence?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: In fact, the reverse applies. The absence of a statutory basis for the
commission has placed no constraint on its activities. In fact, it can be and has been argued
that the absence of a statute has enabled the commission's role to develop and expand
according to its needs.
Mr SPEAKER: Before I call the next honourable member, I should say that we have
dealt with fewer than half the questions and used considerably more than half our time.
Hon. M. Rata: Can the Minister advise the House of the exact reason the Government
does not propose to proceed with legislation to give the Commission for the Environment
statutory independence?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The exact reason is that it is not necessary. The commission is
independent and it does not require to be established independently by statute. Its
independence is accepted. Let me say too that the presentation of audits by the commission
has not been interfered with by the Government in any way, as it was by the former Labour
Government.

Auckland International Airport-Rescue Services
18. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Civil Aviation and

Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services):
Marine rescue facilities have been maintained at Auckland International Airport during the
period that the hovercraft has been inoperable by the utilisation of two 16 ft outboard
powered inflatable rescue craft known as Z boats. These carry inflatable 10-man life rafts,
and it is normal practice for these to be used whenever the hovercraft is rendered
unserviceable during maintenance periods or for any other reason.

so, does the Minister intend to place primary reliance on a substitute craft or find some
better craft that will serve the real needs of the airport?

Nash Papers in National Archives-Removal by SIS

held by the National Archives?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): It is not correct to say that the SIS
removed certain reports from the papers of Sir Walter Nash held by the National Archives.
What did happen was that certain reports of a highly classified nature were returned to the
SIS, as the originating department, for safe custody.
Mr T. J. Young: Can the Prime Minister confirm that this action was voluntarily taken
by the trustees in charge of those papers?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I have no knowledge of whether it was an action
voluntarily taken by the trustees. The papers belonged in the custody of the SIS, and should
never have been elsewhere.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: If, as the Prime Minister says, they were not taken but returned,
does that not necessarily imply that there was an element of volunteering by the trustees who
gave them up without pressure?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: It could certainly mean that. It says here that this was done
following discussions, which is also compatible with the statement I made, but it was not
necessarily a question of volunteering.
Mr T. J. Young: Can the Prime Minister confirm that Sir Walter Nash was in possession
of these classified papers wrongly?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: That, in essence, is my impression. This matter was
discussed in public some time ago. The member will be aware of this and the position about
documents of this kind which is that they come to the Minister in Charge of the Security
Intelligence Service, myself at present, and my procedure is to peruse them, enclose them
immediately in an envelope, and return them by hand to the SIS. That is the proper
procedure, and that procedure has been carried out for as far back as I am aware. I think it is
well known that the old gentleman was an inveterate hoarder of paper, and on these
occasions these papers found their way into his archives. They should not have been there,
and that, I think, is the substance of the matter.

(28/7/77)
Sheep Measles Cysts
3. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Agriculture: Has
he or his department read the article in the Sunday News on 26 June 1977 in which, among
other things, Whangarei's chief hydatids inspector says he is ". . . . hot on the way carcasses
are tested for hydatids cysts. Carcasses that are found to have five or more taenia ovis cysts
are rejected for export. They are kept for the local market, we eat them, the cysts are those
crunchy bits of gristle you find in meat. . . it would be hard to buy a piece of mutton in New
Zealand today that didn't have taenia ovis cysts in it”, and will he state how much of the
article is true; what steps are being taken to obtain and publish all information about the
incidence of hydatids cysts in sheep meat; and what measures are necessary to counteract the
disease?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: I have seen the article, and the
major part of it is quite misleading. Written instructions to meat inspection staff require
inspectors to look for Cysticercus ovis (sheep measles) cysts. Those are the Taenia ovis cysts
referred to in the article. Where cysts are found the carcass must be retained for concen-
trated inspection. Cysts are counted and the judgment made depends on the count, but a
difficulty is that only those that can be seen or felt are noted. Obviously the carcass cannot be
mutilated in searching for C. ovis cysts that may or may not be there and which in any case
are not considered to affect humans. The article incorrectly states the fate of carcasses found
to have C. ovis cysts. If more than five cysts are found the carcass is condemned or sent for
pet food and not used locally as the article suggests. If not more than five cysts are found the
carcass is passed for human consumption-but only after cysts are removed. The judgment
for local-consumption meat is no different from that used for export meat. Some countries
prohibit the importation of those C. ovis carcasses retained for a concentrated inspection,
and those same countries prohibit the importation of any carcass retained for any disease,
whether it affects humans or not. Statistics on the incidence of C. ovis are available for
anyone to see. Such statistics are collected from all abattoirs and export slaughterhouses in
New Zealand and published in the annual reports of the Ministry of Agriculture and
Fisheries and the National Hydatids Council. These are readily available public documents.
The measures necessary to counteract the disease are described clearly in the annual reports
of the National Hydatids Council: e.g., dog control, dog dosing, offal and meat treatment
before feeding.

commission to do so.

Raupunga-Kotemaori Forestry Project
13. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Forests: Is it
proposed to sell by preferential procedure an area of State Forest Land Block S.F. 143 in the
Raupunga-Kotemaori district, and, if so, why is the normal procedure of advertising for
tenders not being used?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: It has not been proposed to sell any area
of State forest land in the Raupunga-Kotemaori district by preferential allocation. The land
in question was originally purchased for a grazing/forestry trial in association with the
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, but the project had to be abandoned because of the
difficulty and the cost of controlling blackberry. A neighbouring farmer, who also held a
grazing lease over a large part of the area, applied to purchase the land, but this was
declined. The farmer again applied to acquire it so that he could establish from it and his
adjoining land economic units for his two sons and himself. It was subsequently decided that
the most appropriate future land use for the property would be farming. To maintain the
area of land available to the Forest Service for afforestation, the possibility of exchanging the
Raupunga area for other land adjoining the Mohaka State Forest was explored, but without
success. It was then proposed that an exchange could possibly be effected for other land.
However, it has not proved possible so far to find suitable land for this purpose, and it is
therefore proposed that the Raupunga land will be declared Crown land in the Reserves and
Other Lands Disposal Act. As such it will be available for disposal in accordance with the
provisions of the Land Act 1948.

Linden Home-Admissions
17. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: In view of the fact
that there are at least 12 unsettled children from the Porirua area who already qualify for
admission to the Linden Home, which was set up for preventive care with a teacher as
supervisor, can he explain why only three of the seven places in the home have been
allocated to these children and the other four allocated to social welfare wards?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: Following the establishment of
the family home in 1975 it was found that the flow of referrals from secondary schools of
children who require the type of care envisaged was sparse and intermittent, resulting in an
uneconomic operation in so far as foster parents were concerned and it was necessary to
admit numbers of State wards to overcome this situation. After the departure of the previous
foster parents on transfer, difficulties were experienced in finding new foster parents and the
opportunity was taken to review the structure and the administration of the home. Under the
new arrangements the Department of Social Welfare runs the family home for State wards in
the normal way, but reserves three places for emotionally disturbed secondary school pupils.
In this way the bed-occupancy rate is maintained, thus enabling the home to operate
economically for the foster parents concerned. Under the new arrangements all referrals
from secondary schools should be made through the psychological services of the Depart-
ment of Education, enabling the family home foster parents to deal only with psychologists
of that department instead of guidance counsellors and other interested persons as occurred
previously. The new arrangements operate in accordance with an agreement reached with
the Minister of Education following the complete revision of the structure and administra-
tion of the home. My department has a responsibility to provide care for children as and
when necessary. On occasions this may require the urgent placement of children away from
their home to ensure their well-being. It is such a situation which has necessitated the
allocation of four places in the Linden home to State wards at the present time. Three places
are reserved for disturbed secondary school pupils, but more may be made available as
necessary and taking into account the needs of other children who may require urgent
placement.

US Naval Observatory-Use
18. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Is it intended
that the observatory which the US Naval Observatory is reported to be planning in the South
Island at either Black Birch or Mt. John should have a defence function either for New
Zealand or for the United States?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: Black Birch and Mt. John
are among a number of possible sites in the Southern Hemisphere that are being considered
by the United States Naval Observatory for the installation and operation of a 7 in.
astronomical telescope. Other sites under consideration are in Western Australia and South
America. The principal requirements are a high number of clear nights and as great a
distance as possible from the Equator. Two members of the observatory staff visited New
Zealand in April and May this year for preliminary discussions with the Carter Observatory
and the University of Canterbury, but no official approaches have been made yet to the
Government. The telescope would be used in a 10-year programme, to be called Operation
Southern Hemisphere Transit Circle, which it is hoped to start about 1980. It would be
concerned with fundamental goeodetic and astronomic positioning, and would be carried out
by up to 10 civilian professional astronomers from the United States, probably with some
local assistance. The results would be publicly available and would be used to improve the
astronomical data published in the Nautical and Air Almanacs. These are produced for use
in navigation by all mariners and air navigators, whether military or civilian.

Women on Statutory Bodies

Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: I am very much in agreement with
recommendation 2, chapter 3, from the report of the Select Committee on Women's Rights.
In making appointments to statutory bodies I am keeping in mind that women be appointed.
However, in the case of most of the statutory authorities to which I make appointments,
nomination for membership is also placed by statute in the hands of independent organisa-
tions such as the New Zealand Educational Institute, the Post-primary Teachers Associa-
tion, the University Grants Committee, education boards, the New Zealand Manufacturers
Federation, the Federation of Labour, and so on. In making these appointments I am
therefore largely in the hands of the organisations making the nominations, and it would not
be appropriate for me to suggest whom they should nominate. These organisations have
historically nominated people qualified in particular fields, irrespective of sex. All appoint-
ments to State services positions must, of course, be made in accordance with section 28 of
the State Services Act 1962.
