announce their intentions if a commercial judgment has been made to cease operations, or to
consult at an early stage if they wish to explore alternatives. Any such consultations would,
of course, be confidential. No complete lists are held of closures of manufacturing concerns
as there is no obligation on any company to inform the Government of such a move.
However, in the Wairarapa region since 1 January 1976 some 18 companies classified as
factories have advised the Department of Labour of their intention to close, while during the
same period some 20 new factories have been registered in the region.

Questions and Replies
Sawmills-Employment
29. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) asked the Minister of Forests: Does the Forest Service
have a policy to ensure that employment at sawmills around the country will not be affected
by cuts in sawlog allocation due to the implementation of the indigenous forest policy, and, if
so, could he supply it?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: In some instances where there are
reductions in the supply of indigenous logs from State forests there will inevitably be a drop
in sawmill employment. However, to minimise the effect the Government encourages the
substitution of exotic logs wherever this is practicable, and is deliberately planning such a
policy for the region most concerned, namely, the West Coast of the South Island. It is also
Government policy to extend employment by having the wood from the limited supply of
indigenous State forest logs processed to the greatest extent possible in the district in which it
is milled.
(4/8/77)
Forestry-Land Purchases
30. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) asked the Minister of Lands; Can he indicate how
much land has been purchased by the Government for forestry since this Administration
took office?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: Since the National Government took
office, the following areas of land have been purchased for forestry purposes: 1975-76, 1956
hectares; 1976-77, 5536 hectares; 1977-78, 742 hectares; to the end of July 1977 a total of
8234. The bulk of this land has been purchased to maintain land banks for exotic afforesta-
tion, to fulfil soil and water conservation functions in areas requiring erosion control
measures of protection, and to acquire areas of outstanding scenic or recreational value for
addition to State forest parks.

Regional Development Programme-Restrictions
34. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Regional
Development: Can he (a) indicate each of the restrictions that were placed on the regional
development programme by his Government in 1976, and (b) indicate which of these
restrictions will now be lifted?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development) replied: The following restrictions
were placed on the regional development programme on 29 April 1976: (a) New Plymouth
was removed from regional development priority classification; (b) the maximum levels of
assistance for Wanganui, Wairarapa, Taranaki (excluding New Plymouth), and Whangarei
City were altered as follows: (i) suspensory loans on plant and equipment were reduced from
30 percent to 20 percent; (ii) training costs assistance was reduced from 50 percent to 30
percent; (iii) suspensory loans on buildings were reduced from 30 percent to 20 percent; (iv)
suspensory loans on plant and buildings were reduced from 20 percent to 15 percent; (c)
small projects assistance was restricted to communities of up to 10 000 only, excepting
Gisborne and Invercargill; (d) regional development assistance was limited to priority
regions, except in exceptional circumstances; (e) a maximum of $100,000 was placed on
suspensory loans, except where a significant resource-based industry was being established;
(f) regional development assistance was put on a "once only" basis; (g) the maximum for
staff training costs was fixed at $20,000; (h) the maximum for transfer costs was fixed at
$10,000; (i) regional development assistance was to be declined if few employment oppor-
tunities were created by any proposed project. In conjunction with the Budget of 21 July
1977 the following relaxations to these restrictions were announced: (a) New Plymouth was
restored to regional development priority region classification with a maximum level of
10-15 percent of qualifying expenditure for suspensory loans; (b) Taranaki (excluding New
Plymouth), Wanganui (excluding Wanganui City), and Whangarei City were restored to the
top-priority level of up to 30 percent for suspensory loans; (c) applications for assistance in
slow-growth areas other than regional development priority regions will be considered on a
case-by-case basis; (d) the "once only" rule for suspensory loans is relaxed to permit
companies in priority regions to undertake development in phases where appropriate. These
relaxations of restrictions were supplemented by the 1977 Budget measures to introduce: (a)
a "pioneer" status incentive scheme; (b) an establishment grant scheme; and (c) a difference
between north- and south-bound inter-island freight rates.

Trainee Chefs-Travel Allowances
38. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Labour: What were the reasons that
prevented trainee chefs from gaining entitlement to travel and accommodation allowances
when attending courses, similar to those provided in many other trades?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: Apprentices contracted under the
Apprentices Act 1948 receive travel and lodging allowances while attending approved
courses of trade training. Trainee chefs are not contracted under the Apprentices Act, and
thus are not entitled to these allowances.
(5/8/77)
Massey University-Staffing
39. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: In view of the heavy
workload carried by those lecturers at Massey University who have more extramural than
full-time students, has he any plans to grant full staffing entitlement to extramural students?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The teaching of extramural, as
well as internal, students is a normal part of the duties of the staff of those departments at
Massey University which offer extramural tuition. Extramural students normally take a
smaller number of papers each year than full-time internal students. It is, therefore, usual for
some members of the staff to have responsibility for more extramural students than internal.
However, the numbers of students, internal as well as extramural, at present enrolled is
causing some concern to all the universities, and the chairman of the University Grants
Committee is at present discussing the matter with the vice-chancellors of the universities.
(9/8/77)
Industry Training Boards-Financing
40. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Education: Has he read the fourth annual
report of the Hotel and Catering Industry Training Board and the final comment made by its
chairman: "This board is now of the opinion that the operational expenses of the board
should be met totally by Government; the finance either being from direct taxation or by a
levy on all employers in the industry", and, if so, what action has he taken or will he take on
this matter?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The Vocational Training Council
is responsible for administering the finances of industry training boards, and has made
representations to the Government about the need for increased flexibility in managing the
administration expenses of boards. These proposals have been accepted by the Government,
and new and improved policies will be introduced this year. At present administration costs
of boards are met largely by grants from the Government. Alternative methods of funding
industry training boards are under continuing consideration by the Vocational Training
Council.
(10/8/77)
Secondary School Boards-Overdrafts
41. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: Has he seen the report
in the Manawatu Evening Standard of 21 July, in which it is stated, “The Palmerston North
High School Board has had a $32,000 overdraft for the past year", and, if so, can he indicate
how widespread this situation is in the country secondary schools?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: I have seen the report referred to,
but am unable to comment on it as the board has yet to submit its statement of accounts for
the year ended 31 January 1977. However, secondary school boards are required, under the
Education Act, to obtain the prior approval of the Minister of Finance to use overdraft
facilities, and no such application has been made. If the report is true the board has,
therefore, acted illegally, and no doubt the Audit Office will be investigating the position.
As for the general situation, I am aware of some cases where secondary school boards have
had recourse to overdraft facilities. Where my department has been informed of their
difficulties, additional advances have been made to assist them with what have been only
short-term problems.
(10/8/77)

been working on a statement of objectives and a detailed plan of action for the introduction
of a pilot scheme in Northland. This work is nearing completion, and the committee plans to
visit Northland later this year to begin discussions on its proposals with all interested parties.
(b) At present there are no proposals which will affect the employment of groups such as
local authority health inspectors. The Special Advisory Committee on Health Services
Organisation is hopeful, however, that under the pilot scheme for reorganisation it will be
possible for all who provide health services in one form or another to be involved in the
planning and review process.

Unions-Voluntary Unionism Ballots
60. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) asked the Minister of Labour: Has he read the following
remarks by Mr Bill Andersen, as reported in New Zealand Truth of 19 July 1977: "The
Government's proposals are for State-run ballots to include supervisors and non-union staff
in the ballot in any particular industry"; and, if so, do Mr Andersen's comments reflect
correctly the Government's proposals for ballots on voluntary unionism?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: I have read Mr Andersen's remarks as
reported in New Zealand Truth of 19 July. They do not accurately reflect the Government's
proposals for ballots on the unqualified preference provision. Voting rights are restricted to
adult workers who are, or will be, bound by the award or collective agreement that is the
subject of the ballot. Mr Andersen's reference to State-run ballots is emotive. The ballots
will be conducted by the Registrar of Industrial Unions, who has had a responsibility for
conducting ballots on union membership since 1961.

Oil Imports by OECD Countries
64. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: According
to International Energy Committee projections, how many barrels of oil are imported by
OECD nations per day, and how many is it estimated will be imported in 1985?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Energy Resources: In 1975 23.4 million barrels a day of oil were imported by OECD nations.
The secretariat of the OECD, of which the International Energy Agency forms a part, has
estimated that, assuming "present policies"—the estimates were prepared in 1976-for
supply expansion and conservation continue, OECD countries will be importing 35 million
barrels of oil a day in 1985. With accelerated development of indigenous resources and
increased emphasis on conservation this figure could, the secretariat considers, be reduced
to 24.4 million barrels of oil a day.

Indigenous Timber Price Increase
68. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) asked the Minister of Forests: To what extent has the
increase in the price of indigenous timber been reflected by a reduced demand for native
timber and an increase in the use of exotic woods?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: There have been two recent increases in
sawn timber prices. On 14 March 1977 increases in exotic and indigenous prices were granted
on the basis of economic submissions by sawmillers, and on 1 June 1977 further increases
were granted in prices for the decorative grades of indigenous timber, the objects of the
latter increase being to encourage maximum recovery of the higher grades, and greater
discrimination in the end use of indigenous timber. Apart from the effect of any price
movements, the volume of indigenous sawn timber has declined. In the year ended 31 March
1976 roundwood removals from State forests amounted to 4 360 000 cubic metres, with
530 000 cubic metres, or 12 percent, coming from the indigenous forests, and 3 830 000 cubic
metres, or 88 percent, from exotic. Provisional figures for 1976-77 show a marked drop from
indigenous forests to 433 000 cubic metres, or 9 percent of the total, and a substantial
increase in exotic wood removals, which reached 4 352 000 cubic metres, or 91 percent. At
present it is too early to be able to judge what effect the latest increase in the price of
indigenous timber will have on the future demand for native timber and the use of exotic
woods.

Electricity and Gas Users-Payment of Accounts
74. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Electricity: Has he read an article in the
Otago Daily Times of 12 July 1977 that "many electricity and gas users in the Dunedin area
are having to be pressured into paying their latest power bills by the Dunedin City
Corporation", and, if so, has he any information to indicate that this disturbing trend is
being reflected in other parts of New Zealand?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Electricity) replied: I have read the article referred to.
Following up overdue accounts is a normal part of a supply authority's operations, and
disconnection warning notices are necessary for late payers. If firm credit control is not
maintained, a consumer's indebtedness would continue to increase to such an extent that the
account could never be paid, and disconnection would be inevitable. The policy of a quick
follow-up does result in fewer disconnections. The point is that although the number of
warnings has increased, the article does indicate that the number of disconnections has
remained steady at six or seven a week. I would expect the position to be much the same
throughout the country.

Waiheke County Council Rates
76. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Local Government: Has he
seen the two Waiheke County Council rates notices in the New Zealand Herald of 20 July in
which the rate in cents per dollar varies inversely with the land value of the property, and can
he state whether such rating is in accordance with the differential rating provisions of the
Counties Act 1956?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government) replied: I have seen the public
notice referred to. In relation to differential rating, the Counties Act 1956 provides that a
council may divide the county into differential rating areas. Any one differential rating area
may be a combination of several individual properties not necessarily contiguous with one
another. A county council is empowered to make and levy rates of varying amounts in the
dollar as between differential rating areas. Subject to the maximum total rates prescribed in
the Act, a council in its own discretion may determine the rate to be levied in each such
differential rating area. If it comes to a contest as to whether or not the Waiheke County
Council has complied with the letter of the law, this must, of course, be left to the courts to
resolve.

Questions and Replies
Radio Single Sideband Equipment for Fiji
78. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Is it true that radio
single sideband equipment for supply to Fiji under aid was purchased in Australia, though in
fact made in New Zealand?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied on behalf of
the Minister of Foreign Affairs: The Fiji Authorities asked New Zealand to supply, under
the bilateral aid programme, 20 Australian-made radio transceivers for use in small marine
vessels. This request was considered as part of a programme of New Zealand assistance to
transportation for the outer islands of Fiji. The merits of similar New Zealand - made
equipment were naturally drawn to the attention of the Fiji authorities. However, Fiji
already employs the same Australian equipment, and the Fiji authorities were concerned
about standardisation of equipment and uniform training of maintenance officers. The issue
of standardisation and maintenance is a particularly difficult problem in all our Pacific aid
programmes, and the New Zealand Government has agreed to play its part in trying to
reduce the complications of too many different sorts of equipment. The Australian marine
transceivers were accordingly purchased for Fiji. In general, however, it remains the
Government's policy to provide New Zealand - made equipment under the aid programme
to the maximum extent possible.

Irrigation Schemes
90. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) asked the Minister of Works and Development: How
many major irrigation schemes are in existence in New Zealand, how many schemes have
been completed since the election of the present Government, and how many schemes have
been planned and remain in the pipeline awaiting approval?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: There are 24 major
irrigation schemes completed and in operation over an area of 103 740 hectares, and these
are all in Otago and Canterbury. They were established from the 1930s through to the late
1960s. With the approval by the present Government of the large Waiau Plains and
Maniototo irrigation projects, there will be 10 new irrigation schemes under construction this
year, and these have a total estimated cost of $27.7 million. They will irrigate a further
59 790 hectares. Maniototo and Waiau Plains represent 45 percent of this total area.
Although not yet completed, many of the schemes under construction are supplying water to
some of their area. A further 11 irrigation scheme proposals covering an area of 18 760
hectares are at various stages of the design and approval process. A further 21 potential
irrigation schemes are at early stages of investigation.

Pentachlorophenyl Poisoning
94. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Labour: Has he seen the
illustrated article in the July 1977 issue of Contractor indicating that a chemical applicator's
employee who contracted pentachlorophenyl poisoning in the line of duty was not entitled to
accident compensation, and will he take action to rectify the situation?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: Yes, I have seen the article. The
position is different from what is implied in the article. The fact is that a claim was lodged on
22 June 1977 alleging that the poisoning had first been sustained on 21 March 1977. It was
the first case of its kind received by the commission and required detailed medical
investigation. Following that the commission accepted the claim on 18 July 1977. Compensa-
tion payments were then commenced, backdated to the time of infection. It is to be regretted
that there has been no later publicity to correct the implications made in the article of a July
publication. I must point out that the Accident Compensation Commission effectively
handled a precedent-setting case in less than 1 month.

1977?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied: My department's training

formal training courses conducted by the Customs central training school—that is, some 53
in the year ended 31 March 1977-include sessions on narcotic identification, detection, and
current trends in importation and use. This system of education has been found to be the

officers requiring more in-depth knowledge of narcotics legislation and investigation tech-

between Police and Customs in these courses is excellent, and Customs staff play a full role
in providing both course members and instructors.

Custody Orders-Fathers' Rights
102. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the
Department of Justice statistics 1976 for domestic proceedings, which indicate that a total of
2397 custody orders were made, including custody orders to the mother in 2150 cases, and
does the Government propose any steps to overcome the inequality of fathers in such
situations?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: I have seen the figures referred to.
The honourable member will know that the existing law, as set out in the Guardianship Act
1968, focuses on the welfare of the child and does not discriminate against fathers. In many
cases, custody will be sought by the mother and not seriously opposed by the father. In other
cases the father will be unable to convince the court that he can make satisfactory
arrangements for the day-to-day care of the child while he goes out to work. The courts must
retain a discretion to act in what they see as the child's best interests, but it may be possible
to improve the practical application of the law in relation to fathers. This is currently being
studied in connection with the review of the law on matrimonial proceedings.

Freight Rates
107. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Transport: Can he
elaborate on the recently announced changes in transport pricing policy to allow freight rates
to reflect actual costs to a greater extent, and can he state clearly how and over what period
this new policy will be implemented?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) replied: The proposed restructuring
of inter-island freight rates has been designed not only to assist South Island manufacturers
but also to apportion the costs of freight services more equitably. As the predominant flow of
goods is at present from north to south, greater capacity and hence greater capital
expenditure must be provided to cope with this southbound traffic. The net result would be a
differential between northbound and southbound rates. Discussions have been initiated with
the Railways Department and the Shipping Corporation, who have agreed to implement
such a differential in their next review of freight rates.

tially with the introduction of the standard tertiary bursary at the beginning of 1976, and set
at an unabated rate of $24 a week. The Government has approved an increase of $2 a week
in all rates from the beginning of the 1978 academic year. Total tertiary bursary payments
per annum over this period are as follows: 1975-76, $13.7 million; 1976-77, $24.6 million;
1977-78, $25.9 million. In effect, therefore, this represents an increase of 88 percent in total
Government expenditure on bursaries in the last 2 years.

Education-Standard Tertiary Bursaries
114. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: Can he explain how
he arrived at the figure of $2 per week for the increase in the standard tertiary bursary and if
any weightings were used, in view of the fact that hostel fees for 1978 in Dunedin are to rise
to $38 per week?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The member will be aware that it is
the Government's policy to reform the tertiary bursary. It had a number of options available
to it to improve bursary conditions arising from the bursary conference held in December
1976. The decision was taken to increase the basic rate of the bursary, so that some benefit
would accrue to all students rather than to make significant improvements in more
specialised areas. No weightings were used, but I point out to the member that the $2 per
week represents an increase of 8 percent on the unabated bursary and 15.4 percent on the
abated bursary.

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied on behalf of
the Minister of Social Welfare: There is no reduction in national superannuation because of
hospitalisation unless the patient is unmarried and has no dependants. In those cases where a
reduction is applied, the provisions of section 75 (2) of the Social Security Act provide for a
reduction after 13 weeks in a public hospital. The amount of national superannuation which
would be paid in these circumstances depends on the individual situation of each case, taking
into account the superannuitant's income, family responsibilities, and capacity to appreciate
the payments.

Committee on Family Affairs have a watching brief on the censorship functions or duties of
such bodies as the Indecent Publications Tribunal, the Supreme Court, and the Department
of Education, and, if so, what are the committee's responsibilities?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied, on behalf of the Minister of Social
Welfare: The Cabinet committee does not see itself as having a watching brief on the
censorship functions or duties of such bodies as those mentioned by the honourable member.
It does, however, see itself as having a watching brief over legislation affecting the quality of
family life. It also has a responsibility, when the public expresses deep concern about a
matter, to look carefully at that matter in order to ascertain whether any measures are
required to safeguard the interests of family life. If the committee concludes that there are
deficiencies in the law, it will make proposals for change.

Rural Water Supply Schemes
131. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) asked the Minister of Works and Development: How
many rural water supply schemes are in existence in New Zealand; how many schemes have
been completed since the election of the present Government; and how many schemes have
been planned and remain in the pipeline awaiting approval?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: There are 31 rural
water supply schemes that have been completed with Government assistance since the late
1940s. Most of these schemes are in Otago and Canterbury. Three schemes have been
completed since the present Government took office, and a further 34 schemes are under
construction. Many of these are already supplying water to farms and they are well spread
throughout New Zealand. Eight new rural water supply schemes have been approved during
the term of the present Government, and a further 11 are programmed for approval and
commencement this financial year. Of the 11, 7 are in Otago and Southland. A further 49
proposed schemes are at various stages of planning and investigation, and 11 of these are in
Otago and Southland.

De Facto Relationships-Domestic Purposes Benefit
145. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Is it correct, as stated in
chapter 5.3 of the Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee's report, that guidelines
have been laid down by the Social Security Commission for those district officers with the
delegated authority to determine whether or not a de facto relationship exists, and, if so,
how does he equate this finding with his answer to a written question from the member for
Raglan, given on 6 October 1976, that "It is not possible to set down such criteria. It is
necessary for the particular circumstances of each individual case and of each relationship to
be taken into account?"
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: The guidelines referred to in
the report of the Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee are general procedural
instructions for the guidance of district officers. While they contain reference to particular
points concerning a relationship which should be known before a decision is reached, they do
not represent the specific criteria to be used in forming a judgment as to whether a de facto
relationship exists. As I said in reply to the earlier question asked of me by the member for
Raglan, it is not possible to set down specific criteria to cover all cases. The particular
circumstances of each individual case and of each relationship must be taken into account.

island freight rates will be introduced at the next freight rate review. The level of the
differential will depend on further analysis of the costs of the inter-island shipping
operators—namely, the Railways Department and the Shipping Corporation.

150. Mr BIRCH (Franklin) asked the Minister of Health: What is the average cost per

Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: Under the fee-for-service system applicable
in New Zealand the general practitioner is entitled to charge a fee that he considers is
appropriate to the time and skill in providing the service. Consequently, fees for consulta-
tions vary. The contribution by the State by way of general medical service benefits varies
from $1.25 to $7 a consultation, but averages out at $2.36. On an average gross fee of $5 the
State pays $2.36 and the patient pays $2.64.

Import Deposit Scheme
157. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Customs: In view of the
Government's professed concern for small businesses, can he explain why importers
received such short notice of the extension of the import deposit scheme, and can he give an
assurance that he will make his decision much sooner when the next review is due in 6
months' time?
Hon P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied: When the scheme was initiated in
January 1976 the Minister of Finance stated that the scheme "will be kept under review in
the light of the need for scheme restraint". Subsequently, the scheme has been reviewed on
three occasions, one of which resulted in the reduction of a number of goods subject to the
payment of deposit effective from 30 July 1976. There has never been any advance
commitment that the scheme will necessarily be terminated on any specified date. There are
obvious advantages in deferring reviews to permit maximum information to be available on

Car Pools-Insurance Contracts
159. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Transport: In view of his
interest in car pools, is he making recommendations to the Minister in Charge of the State
Insurance Office and the various motor insurance offices about clauses in insurance contracts
which inhibit or prevent such arrangements?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) replied: As long as any car pooling
scheme is based on the following three principles it is not envisaged that clauses in insurance
contracts of private automobiles would inhibit or prevent any car pooling arrangements: (1)
that the scheme be run on a cost-sharing basis; (2) that those involved do not make a profit;
and (3) that only commuters are involved. I am informed that these principles were set out in
the Transport Amendment (Motor Spirit Conservation) Regulations 1973 specifically for the
purpose of ensuring that those people wanting to establish a car pooling arrangement were
not prevented from doing so by clauses in the insurance contracts of their cars. These
regulations also exempted drivers and vehicles involved in a car pooling scheme from various
legislative constraints applying to passenger service licensing, including regulation 4 of the
Motor Vehicle Indemnity Surcharge Regulations 1974. This ensures that the status of the
vehicle would not be impaired by its involvement in a car pooling scheme, as long as the
scheme is run on the three principles mentioned earlier. I am also informed that no further
legislation is needed to ensure that clauses in the insurance contracts do not prevent or
inhibit any car pooling scheme.

Post Office-Effect of Subsidy Payments
162. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Postmaster-General: What was the effect
on the Post Office administration of financing its operations by subsidy payments during the
period of the last Labour Government?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: During the period charges were
frozen the Post Office incurred losses totalling $65.7 million for the 3 years. These losses
were met by the payment of subsidies at the taxpayer's expense. The massive subsidy
payments had the effect of distorting the demand for Post Office services, because charges
were held at unrealistically low levels. The unexpectedly high demand for services not only
placed a greater burden on available resources but also disrupted the Post Office's planning
processes. Furthermore, I am assured by my department that management staff morale
suffers when personnel know they are working for an organisation that is not genuinely
paying its way.

National Superannuation
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I move, That this House notes
with no surprise the question asked in the Evening Post of 9 August 1977, “Just how long can
New Zealand afford the huge Super handout?”, recalls the statement made by the member for

2275
Discussion of Motions
country could long sustain paying superannuation benefits to those who were still working, and
asked what justification there was for it", and calls upon the Government to come out in the
open and announce forthwith to the country when the first cutback in the national superannua-
tion scheme can be expected. This motion seeks a discussion of the cost and desirability of the
national superannuation scheme, which was introduced by the present Government with so
much trumpeting about its concern for the welfare of certain sections of the community,
while at the same time its members were attacking the Labour Administration for its
handling of the economy.
I want to put these two together and examine them in the light of the economic
situation, and to refer the facts that emerge to one or two members on the other side, who
have already indicated that they, too, are concerned about whether the country can afford
the cost of the scheme. I want to start off from the straight, logical assertion that, because the
Minister of Social Welfare claims that all those who are receiving national superannuation
are at least as well off as they were under the former age benefit or universal superannuation
and because more people are in the superannuation scheme than were in the other two
combined, it is clear that the system is costing significantly more than the earlier ones.
Mr McLay: Are you saying it is too much?
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: I am saying that the cost, in our circumstances, is far too much. I
refer the member for Birkenhead to others of his own party who have expressed concern,
and ask him where he stands in this debate, because we have been promised that the amount
for this programme will be increased next year. According to the estimates, superannuation
is costing $930 million gross. That represents 64 percent of the total Social Welfare vote. We
have heard a little about the billion-dollar Minister. The Social Welfare vote now stands at
over $1.5 billion, but the increase has gone to people who do not really need it. There are
much higher priorities for this expenditure, but the Government has blatantly sought to
influence the electors by its social welfare policy. It has not sought to meet the needs of social
welfare recipients.
I contrast this figure of 64 percent of the present Social Welfare vote with the amount
spent in the last financial year, when we had three systems, two for part of the year and one
for the rest. Under that arrangement, the total of the three benefits amounted to less than 56
percent of the total Social Welfare vote. In the preceding financial year, when we had only
the age benefit, which was subject to a means test, and universal superannuation, payable at
65 without a means test, the two benefits represented 54 percent of the total social welfare
expenditure. So the figures for those years reveal a very significant shift in both total
expenditure on social welfare and the proportion going to recipients other than those over 60
years of age.
Many people need greater consideration than they have received from the present
Government, but this Government, quite knowingly, has shifted the emphasis of its social
welfare programme, and in doing so has put a severe strain on our economic system. This
concern has been expressed by the member for Hamilton West in the statement given in this
motion. It has also been expressed by the Associate Minister of Finance, who has called
upon everyone to live within his income, but who is part of a Government that has quite
deliberately increased the income of a section of the population that already has an adequate
income. His call for those people to live within their income does not mean very much; it
rankles with other sections of the community who have to pay the taxes to pay these extra
benefits, and it rankles with those whose income is such that it is not adequate to meet their
needs.
The problem will grow. The member for Raglan referred to it last night. I want to allude
not to that debate, but simply to the fact that she expressed her concern, which is that,
against the known demographic trends, there will be an increasing burden on income
producers to satisfy the payments that are to be made at the level of 80 percent of the
average wage after next year. That increase will add about $153 million to the gross cost. It is
$930 million this year, allowing for inflation at the present rate, which will add $144 million,
allowing for the increase from 70 percent to 80 percent, which will add $153 million, and
allowing something for the additional cost arising from the greater numbers of people who
will be in the 60-year age group next year, we arrive at the figure of an extra $310 million
gross. In all, $1,240 million will be required for that scheme.
Hon. G. F. Gair: Gross.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: That is the gross figure. That must concern a Government that
pretends to have the secret of economic management, because it will have a disastrous
effect. Either it will increase taxes or it will prevent the reduction in tax rates, consequent

upon inflation, that the people of this country are entitled to consider their due. Inflation is

saving money has not been good. It was magnificent at spending. We have only to look at
Government spending while Labour was in office. In 1973, Government expenditure in

Hon. A. J. Faulkner: You wait until you see this year's!

Government reduced the deficit to $1,000 million. Treasury predicted a $1,400 million
deficit for the year ended March 1977, and the National Government managed to reduce it
to $500 million. That is a marvellous record of expenditure control. As a result, we have had
a certain amount of room in which to manoeuvre on taxation. The Labour Government did
not, and if the people are ever unfortunate enough to have a Labour Government in power
again it still will not have room to manoeuvre.
Labour cannot or will not reduce spending. Money slips through the fingers of a Labour
Government like water, so where would members opposite get the money to pay for
restructuring if by restructuring they mean reduction? They changed the tax rates in 1975,
and increased the maximum tax for those with higher incomes, who then paid more than
they had ever paid before. Do they have in mind an extension of the policy of making those
on higher incomes pay the most, pay the hardest, and dig deepest? If this restructuring does
mean reduction, will it be paid for by those who have the greatest interest and greatest
investment in the country? Is that what restructuring means? Or does it mean something
else? Does it mean altering the scale rates for companies? Labour members do not like
companies or the self-employed because they make things called profits. The Labour
Government always spoke about profits as if they were unpleasant and unpalatable. Are the

LEGISLATURE AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill gives statutory sanction to two well established practices of the House.
Clause 2(1) provides that the House may hold over Bills and other business from one session
to the next, even though a general election takes place between those sessions. Because the
practice of holding over can be seen as ignoring the common law effects of a prorogation or
dissolution, it is desirable that the position should be clarified by giving the House a statutory
power, rather than rely on Standing Order 74. Clause 2(2) provides the format by which an
outgoing Parliament can ensure that business held over will be considered by members of the
newly elected House in the recess following a general election. There is nothing new in this
practice, but the present situation is unsatisfactory. Neither the committees nor their
witnesses are protected by privilege. This matter is now rectified by clause 2(3), which
confers on any committee meeting before the new Parliament meets the powers and
privileges of a regular select committee.
I should clear up any misunderstanding about subclause (4). It does not, as some
members appear to have thought when the Bill was introduced, allow a member to sit or vote
either in the House or on a select committee before he has been sworn in. What it does is
remove any doubt about the right of a member to sit on one of these inchoate committees
before taking the oath. There is no question of nullifying the requirement of section 46 of the
Constitution Act.
Clause 3 simply puts the matter beyond doubt, just in case a latter-day Mr Simpson has
any ideas of challenging the validity of an Act which, when in Bill form, was held over.
Interested members may care to refer to the 1955 volume of New Zealand Law Reports to
read about Mr Simpson's challenge to the valid existence of Parliament itself.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): The main purpose, indeed the sole purpose, of
the Bill is to overcome the difficulties in which the Government has found itself by having


## p. 2284 (#740) ###########################################

2284
17 August
Legislature Amendment Bill
newly elected members serve on committees before they have taken the oath, which they are
required to do by our Constitution Act. Objection has been taken to that on previous
occasions, and sundry devices have been adopted to overcome the difficulty in a temporary
kind of way. The effects of these were to have a member serve as a member of a committee
without having taken the oath. The taking of the oath is not just a symbolic matter. It goes
really to the roots of a person's right to sit and act as a member of Parliament. I quote from
the current version of Erskine May to show just how significantly the matter is dealt with in
Westminster, and I read from page 270 of the nineteenth edition:
"By the Acts (of several different statutes going back through many years) severe
penalties and disabilities were inflicted upon any Member of either House who sat or voted
without having taken the oath. By the Parliamentary Oaths Act 1866, any Peer voting by
himself or his proxy, or sitting in the House of Peers without having taken the oath, is
subject, for every such offence, to a penalty of £500; and any member of the House of
Commons who votes as such, or sits during any debate after the Speaker has been chosen,
without having taken the oath, is subject to the same penalty, and his seat is also vacated in
the same manner as if he were dead. These penalties can be recovered by the suit of the
Crown alone. When Peers or Members have neglected to take the oaths from haste,
accident, or inadvertence, Acts of indemnity have been passed to relieve them from the
consequences of their neglect. In the Commons, however, it is necessary to move a new writ
immediately the omission is discovered, as the Member's seat is vacated."
So, as I say, referring to that eminent authority the taking of an oath is by no means just
a formality, but a requirement that must be discharged before a person sits in the House. In
Westminster, if he does so in the absence of having attended to that requirement, then his
seat is liable to be vacated. The remedy suggested in the earlier stage of the introduction of
the Bill was that a simple device and procedure was open to any Government, and that
would be for the summoning of Parliament very shortly after an election so that members
could be sworn in. There is no difficulty whatsoever in arranging that, and rather than adopt
this device to overcome what is simply a procedural difficulty I strongly recommend that that
procedure be adopted. Even if the session were only a formality, simply for the sake of
swearing in a member, it could be held, and it would add to the dignity of Parliament if that
procedure were followed instead of having a person who is only half a member entitled to act
as a member of a committee but not entitled to act in the fullness of his responsibilities as a
member of Parliament. For that reason, I think the Bill provides for a misconceived manner
of overcoming a self-imposed difficulty.
In the introduction debate I mentioned one other consequence of the move. It will
ensure that anything done by an unsworn member in a committee will not expose him to any
kind of penalties, and particularly it will afford him the protection and absolute privilege of
members of Parliament for words said not only in the House but also as a member of a
committee. It is unlikely, but possible, that some unsworn member who is a member of a
committee may have said something that would expose him to some kind of claim. I suggest
that clause 2(3) should provide for the retrospective operation of the Bill. As it stands now,
"Every such committee shall have, subject to the terms of any resolution under subsection
(2) of this section, the privileges, immunities, and powers of a select committee of the House
of Representatives, and shall be deemed to be a committee of the House of Representa-
tives".
I have suggested before, and I put it forward again for the Government's consideration,
that the following phrase should be added: "and shall always be deemed to have been a
committee of the House of Representatives". In that way the proceedings of those
irregularly constituted committees would be perfected by giving members of the committees
the protection members of Parliament and committees of the House, as well as the House
itself, enjoy in that regard. I believe it is a meritorious suggestion, and one the Government
might well take into account before the Bill reaches the Committee stage.
Dr WALL (Porirua): I am delighted that this Bill is before the House, but I consider it a
somewhat inappropriate measure as it raises all sorts of anomalies and will not correct those
it seeks to correct. It will enable people to enjoy the privileges of being members of
Parliament when in fact they are not members of Parliament; it will give people the

TRUSTEE SAVINGS BANKS AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. Its purpose is to enable trustee savings banks to implement fully the Budget
measures allowing them freedom to set the structure of and the interest rates on their
investment and other term deposit accounts. These measures represent a further develop-
ment in the flexible interest rate policy introduced in March 1976. This policy is designed to
strengthen the role of the major financial intermediaries, and thus to improve the efficiency
of the financial system so that it may make its contribution to an improved allocation of
resources. It will also enable the Government to operate a more effective monetary policy.
Before the Budget, the savings banks were the only remaining major institutions still
subject to full interest rate regulation. They have been at an increasing disadvantage with
other deposit-taking institutions, which are free to set their own rates, and in particular have
suffered relative to building societies, which enjoy the same tax exemption on interest as
savings banks. Because of this, the savings banks are now being given greater freedom in


## p. 2286 (#742) ###########################################

2286
17 August
Trustee Savings Banks Amendment Bill
setting the conditions and interest rates on their investment and other term deposit accounts.
In recognition of their Government-guaranteed status, trustee savings banks will need
the concurrence of the Reserve Bank to the rates and conditions they intend to apply. The
greater flexibility being given to the savings banks will enable them to offer more adequate
and attractive returns to savers. It will also enable them to fulfil an enhanced role in the
financial system in the future, and increase the availability of high quality mortgage finance.
The need for any increase in the mortgage lending rates of the savings banks as a result of
these changes will be minimised by an arrangement to redeem part of their present low-
yielding Government securities, and to invest the proceeds in holdings at the new higher
rates.
The changes in this Bill are complementary to those already implemented by amend-
ments to the Trustee Savings Banks Interest Orders and Regulations. The Trustee Savings
Banks Interest Order 1977/186 removed the controls on rates and conditions applying to
investment accounts and term deposits. Changes can now be made by the banks themselves
subject only to the consent of the Reserve Bank. This gives trustee banks flexibility in the
interest rates and types of deposits they wish to offer. The limit of 3 percent interest on
ordinary savings accounts is maintained, and the interest rates and conditions applying to
existing investment accounts remain as specified in the previous interest order.
The Trustee Savings Banks Regulations 1949 Amendment No. 18, 1977/187, removed,
with respect to investment accounts, the limitation that a depositor could have only one
account in any class of account, the requirement that deposits had to be for a minimum of
$200, and the regulations relating to the method of making interest payments. The clauses in
this Bill simply complement those amendments to give full effect to the Budget measures.
Clause 1 sets out the short title and commencement date. Clause 2 removes the interest-
bearing deposit limits on all accounts, except farm ownership accounts. The limit of $60,000
applicable to the farm ownership account is retained in this Bill as it now stands, but it is
intended to remove this exception by a Supplementary Order Paper because it is now
redundant; all provisions relating to the farm ownership scheme are covered in the Farm
Ownership Savings Act. The provisions limiting to one the number of accounts a depositor
may have in any one class of account, and the requirement of a trustee savings bank to give 3
months' public notice of a reduction in an interest rate payable, are also repealed.
Clause 3 repeals section 36B, which provided for the acceptance of deposits to
investment accounts, and the conditions relating to the breaking of those deposits. A new
section is substituted providing for deposits in investment accounts or term deposits, and
defining these investments. The new section provides trustee banks with the freedom to
accept deposits for terms of not less than 30 days on conditions and at interest rates they wish
to offer. The Trustee Savings Banks Interest Order 1977 requires the consent of the Reserve
Bank to changes in the interest rates and conditions offered.
Government monetary policy has been to move towards a more flexible and competitive
financial system, one which is better able to react quickly and efficiently to the changing
economic and financial environment. The trustee savings banks play an important role as
major sources of housing finance, and it is essential that they be given the opportunity to
compete on an equal basis to enable them to strengthen that role.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): As the Minister of Finance has
said, the reason for this Bill is to remove an anomaly between the trustee savings banks and,
basically, building societies. It is an anomaly of the Government's own creation. I am afraid
it is one of the ironies of our time that much of our parliamentary work consists of following
through the consequences of an action by putting in another plug or taking out another check
to balance out a mistake that has been made.
Hon. H. R. Lapwood: Why can't you laugh?
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: I can laugh very cheerily at the member. Members opposite may
recall that a significant part of interest on savings invested with savings banks was exempt for
income tax purposes. This Government saw fit to give that concession also to the building
societies, something they had been denied by the previous Labour Government because the
interest rates they chose to offer were substantially higher than those the savings banks were
able to offer.
I have always felt that we get nowhere by increasing interest rates to attract savings. I

PRIVATE SAVINGS BANKS AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill contains the amendments necessary for the full implementation of the
Budget measures giving private savings banks the freedom to set the structure of and the
interest rates on investment and other term deposit accounts. Since 1976.the savings banks
have been at an increasing disadvantage relative to other deposit-taking institutions, as they
have been the only remaining institutions still subject to full interest rate control. Amend-
ments have already been made to the Private Savings Banks Regulations, the Private Savings
Banks Interest Order, and the Private Savings Banks (Government Securities) Order. This
Bill simply complements those amendments to give full effect to the Budget measures.
Clause 1 sets out the short title and the commencement date. Clause 2 removes the
existing interest-bearing deposit limits of $40,000 for an institution and $12,000 for a non-
institution. The provision in the Act specifying that the method of computing interest on
savings accounts is not to apply to investment accounts is extended to exclude term deposits
as well. The section providing that no depositor may have more than one account of any class
of accounts is repealed. This Bill is supplementary to the previous Bill.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): This Bill is an inevitable
consequence of a Government decision, and the attitude of the Opposition is the same as for
the previous Bill. It is unreasonable to place one group at a disadvantage to others and
therefore, although the Opposition does not agree with the basic purpose of the Bill, it does
not object to it if it means that the same rules apply to all institutions.

the reduction of discrimination on various grounds that are no longer acceptable to New
Zealanders as grounds for discrimination. It should be made clear—and there has been some
misunderstanding about the effect of the Bill-that New Zealanders will still be entitled to
cherish their favourite prejudices. They can continue to discriminate against persons with
red hair, persons with certain mannerisms, persons without hair, and people who do not
appeal for one reason or another. It is not an overall abrogation of the right of people to
have likes and dislikes, to have prejudices, or to cherish their own views. A narrow range of
grounds has been proscribed in the Bill, which provides that discrimination be discouraged.
The first of the grounds is race. In 1972 the House passed the Race Relations
Act-although it was opposed by the Labour Opposition. The Bill takes the provisions of the
Race Relations Act a little further and adds national or ethnic origin. I believe the people
fully support the view that persons should no longer be discriminated against solely on the
basis of race.
The second area is more of an advance. It lays down that people will no longer be
discriminated against solely on the basis of their sex. This provision is a follow-on from the
recommendations of the Select Committee on Women's Rights and the policy brought down


## p. 2291 (#747) ###########################################

17 August
2291
Human Rights Commission Bill
by the National Party before the 1975 election, which stated that we must do away with the
traditional stereotyping that a man is a person of particular ambitions or abilities and a
woman is a person of different abilities and ambitions. Generally that type of stereotyping
has rebounded in the past against the interests of women, who have tended to be regarded as
baby producers and housekeepers and not given the same opportunities as men to advance in
their careers. Many women will want to adopt the traditional role adopted by their mothers
and grandmothers. That is perfectly permissible. There is nothing mandatory in the Bill
about this. Our society has a tendency to force persons to fit into a mould or stereotype. The
Bill ensures equal opportunity for both sexes.
The third area in which the Bill seeks to remove discrimination is that of marital status.
This area is allied to sex discrimination and proscribes actions taken against a person merely
because that person may be married, or on the other hand may not be married.
Finally, the Bill proscribes religious bigotry. In doing so it makes reference to ethical
belief, but it is made clear in the definition that ethical belief is no more than an absence of
religion. If a person is a humanist or a rationalist he obtains the protection of the Bill. The
Bill is not so much of an advance in that field, because there is very little religious bigotry in
New Zealand today, and there would be very few people who would not be perfectly happy
to see enshrined in the statute book that discrimination on the grounds of religion be
unlawful and subject to sanctions.
The committee heard representations that other areas should be included in the Bill.
One was political belief. I had some sympathy for the inclusion of political belief; that a
person should not be discriminated against on the ground of political belief. It became clear
that there would have to be many exceptions to the rule. One of the witnessess before the
committee, the Public Service Association, said that it would not be prepared to employ a
person whose political view was that people are not entitled to civil rights. If, for example, an
extreme fascist were to apply for a job the Public Service Association would not accept that
person. In the last week we have seen that the Public Service Association can be even more
pernickity than that. If a person has a political belief on broadcasting, that can be sufficient
to exclude him from the association.
Age was another subject considered. Discussion was held on whether to permit or
disallow discrimination on the ground of age. Major difficulties are experienced when
drawing boundaries. There must be different provisions applicable to minors, to apprentice-
ships, to career structures, and the like. That matter was left out. Another provision
originally in the Bill and now omitted was a requirement that we should not discriminate
between de facto marriages and legal marriages. I was strongly opposed to that. The
institution of marriage is at present under considerable strain and is at something of a turning
point in its history. It behoves the House to shore up and strengthen the institution of legal
marriage at every opportunity rather than attempt to adopt any practice that would
undermine the institution by legally requiring New Zealanders to consider that there is no
more merit in a legal marriage than in two persons living together.
Another viewpoint that was emphasised strongly to the committee was that sexual
orientation should be included as a proscribed ground. That was a case for which one could
have considerable sympathy. I do not believe that one should discriminate against a person
because of his or her sexual orientation, but I am not prepared to go so far as to say we
should pass a law forbidding people to have views on that subject and to act on those views. I
take that so far as to say we should not retain the discriminatory provisions of the Crimes
Act; this ought not to be a matter for the law, but a matter for individual views and morals.
As to the actual discrimination that occurs, I believe it can be established that although there
is some discrimination against homosexuals, that discrimination is not based on the fact that
they are homosexuals, but possibly on their style of dress, their mannerisms, or their general
appearance. Discrimination might arise from the impact they make upon an employer who
would prefer them not to be holding a particular position, not because they are homosexuals
but because of their mannerisms or their dress, or for other reasons. It would be very
difficult to establish that there is any widespread discrimination based on the mere fact of
homosexuality as opposed to the manifestation of it in one way or another.
The final point I make relates to advertisements, which are mentioned in the Bill. The
committee was under pressure to include provisions proscribing sexist advertisements. That
is a matter of considerable difficulty in definition involving value judgments, and was not
supported by the committee. The committee did make considerable advances in its amend-
ment to clause 29(2) in stating that the mere use of a term which might be considered to refer
to one sex shall not be a breach of the Act, and it gives examples. It lists such terms as

status where the position requires a married couple." If a couple of people are required, and
an unmarried couple qualify and could not be discriminated against because there is no
definition, where does a homosexual couple stand? That was one of the problems faced in
the committee, and there has been no resolution of it. The Bill remains uncertain and open
to argument and dispute, as there certainly will be before the courts when the Bill is put into
operation.
I can see some unavoidable difficulties of definition, or rather of description, in a statute
that breaks new ground in New Zealand, although it certainly is not unprecedented if we
look elsewhere. To try to overcome them, a novel drafting technique has been invoked: that
of exemplification. That is common in ordinary conversation: if you are trying to describe to
a person you are talking to an object that is strange to him, you commonly liken it to
something with which he is familiar. That technique is adopted in the Bill. Clause 14(3)
states: "Nothing in this section shall apply to preferential treatment based on sex where-(a)

Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori): With the term
"human rights" in the title of the Bill, the Government-inspired publicity about it has
created the illusion of action across the full range of human affairs or human rights according
to the United Nations Human Rights declarations, where none actually exists. I repeat that
Government publicity has created the illusion of action where none actually exists. The New
Zealand Law Society, to which the member for Marlborough has just referred, claimed that
the choice of title was unfortunate. In fact, the United Nations Association of New Zealand
was but one of several groups that made submissions suggesting the Bill ought to be
renamed. Those groups suggested that such names as the “Anti-discrimination Bill" or the
"Equal Opportunities Bill" would more accurately reflect its objectives. As the United
Nations Association claimed, the Bill's title tends to mislead people into thinking it covers
the whole field of human rights, and inasmuch as the title is misleading and suggests a
proposition contrary to received opinion it is a paradox, for of course the Bill does not cover
the whole field of human rights. In fact, it resembles a measure I personally advocated in the
House on 9 July 1971, although even then I suggested that the complete range of arbitrary
and prejudicial discrimination might be incorporated into legislation.
The fact is that the bulk of this Bill-Parts II, III, and IV-deals with discrimination,
not human rights, and as such it is an anti-discrimination measure, inasmuch as it deals more
with what cannot be done than with what should be done. The anti-discrimination aspects of
the Bill deal with discrimination on the basis of race, colour, ethnic or national origin, sex,
marital status, religious, or ethical beliefs, but one of the several notable omissions is that
discrimination on the grounds of political belief or opinion is not to be outlawed-in spite of
the fact that the United Nations conventions provide for the freedom of political opinion, as
did the Bill of Rights introduced by the late Mr Hanan. A significant number of the
submissions made to the select committee-15, in fact-asked for political opinion to be
included in the list of outlawed bases of discrimination.
On "Checkpoint" on 9 July of this year, the Minister in charge of the Bill spoke of very
strong evidence for removing de facto relationships from the protection of the Bill, which he
said had been requested in submissions to the committee. I do not recall more than three
people-Patricia Bartlett, Des Dalgety on behalf of the ANZ Bank, and the Gospel Radio
Fellowship representative-seeking the removal of de facto relationships from the protection
of the Bill. That was hardly strong evidence, and one would imagine that 15 submissions
suggesting the inclusion of political opinion might have moved the Minister in a similar
fashion.
The basic function of the so-called Human Rights Bill was stated by Professor Keith,
Professor of Law at Victoria University, to be the resolution of disputes. Like Professor
Keith, I too consider it should assert a positive rather than the proposed negative role. The
commission should not be solely in the business of investigating complaints and, where
appropriate, attempting to produce a satisfactory result. The broader positive powers to
promote human rights through education, publicity, and related programmes and activities
are of great potential significance. Furthermore, I have said that it should be the role of any
Human Rights Commission to examine and report on the New Zealand Government's
reasons for non-ratification of international covenants and propositions. I also see another
positve role for any Human Rights Commission-to monitor, as does the Treasury, all policy
proposals and legislation formulated by Government departments and Governments them-
selves. The community could only benefit if the Human Rights Commission publicly
reported on all aspects of Government policy-and I reiterate the words "publicly
reported", as that is not necessarily provided for in the Bill.

of last year's Commerce Amendment Act and Part VI-all introduced by this
Government-violate that international convention. I claim that it should be the role of the
commission, as I have said, to examine and report on the Government's reasons for non-

Part VI is an attack on the internal disciplinary powers and the solidarity of the trade

submissions from groups whose human rights are in no way protected by the Bill, and despite
the improvements that were undoubtedly brought about at the select committee, where 45 of
the original 87 clauses were amended, there are many groups whose human rights are in no
way protected. I am thinking first of children, of whom article 25 of the United Nations
Declaration on the Rights of the Child, adopted by the United Nations Assembly in 1959,
speaks so poignantly. That declaration is still unratified by this Government. Secondly, I
think of a sad new phenomenon, the youthful underachievers rejected by the education
system, who contribute to the community's unemployed. Thirdly, we have those subject to
learning difficulties, and fourthly, the physically and mentally handicapped, subjects of the
Declaration of the Rights of the Mentally Retarded, now in process of adoption by the
UNO, the aged, and people who are not heterosexual.
Nineteen submissions made to the select committee pressed for the inclusion of sexual
orientation or sexual preference as a human right for law-abiding citizens and as insufficient
reason in itself for discrimination. My personal conviction was for its inclusion. However I
gained the impression that most committee members were of a different opinion. I might
have been wrong. Yet any area not given protection by this Bill will be even more vulnerable
than it would have been had the Bill not been passed. I expressed thoughts on this subject in
this House on 24 July 1974 during a debate on the Crimes Amendment Bill. Today I want to
express the same concern, since I hold personally to the view that like sex, skin colour, and
nationality, homosexuality is not a matter of choice. Some may argue that homosexuality is
more prevalent in times of social stress and strain, such as during the decline of empires, but
such stress and strain is not a matter of choice for the individual, who merely reacts to them.
Homosexuality is not a matter of choice. If 4 percent of New Zealand's population are
homosexuals—and research suggests this to be so-then at least 128 000 New Zealanders,
male and female, are homosexuals. None has any choice over his or her orientation. Indeed,
almost all researchers agree that homosexuality is innate or inherent.
Legal systems ought to condemn specific acts which are seen as wrong chiefly because
such acts hurt other people, but should not condemn people simply for what they are and
because they do not hurt other people. I maintain that my attitude is totally consistent. I do
not consider it ought to be valid to condemn a person purely because that person is a woman,
a man, a pakeha or a Maori, a German, a Jew, a heterosexual or a homosexual. What I
condemn are specific acts that offend against humanity, and, in particular, perpetuate
unnecessary suffering. After all, some degree of stress is an inevitable consequence of
existence, and it increases when society is undergoing change. Conflicting social pressures
cause it, but cause it unnecessarily when these pressures result from prejudice and bigotry.
Good government should always aim to remove unnecessary pressures that cause unneces-
sary suffering to citizens. I speak for the law-abiding among the significant minority. A crime
is a crime no matter who commits it, and it is against such criminal acts that punitive
measures should be directed, not against law-abiding people simply because of an innate
characteristic. The child molester commits a crime whether he is a heterosexual or not.
Couples who have a stable and meaningful relationship, whose togetherness is not causing
suffering to others, particularly children, and is reducing not only their own individual

suffering but also the suffering of others, should enjoy the same protection under the Bill as
other law-abiding couples. These thoughts are expressed against a background of previous
experience as a counsellor in this field.
Perhaps the most significant amendment is the addition of the new clause 5c, which
gives the Human Rights Commission extra power to invite representations from members of
the public on any matter affecting human rights. This amendment makes it clear that the
commission's activities are no longer to be totally confined to the much restricted areas of
discrimination mentioned in Part II, and is contrary to the Bill as originally introduced. The

Miss DEWE (Lyttelton): I recall a comment made by Neil Armstrong when he stepped

forward taken by this or any other Government, because it ensures that women will have
equal opportunity and equality with men in all fields of endeavour. I am disappointed that
the Opposition has concentrated on one or two aspects and has completely ignored the
positive steps taken in this important social legislation.
It is interesting to reflect that much of our important social legislation has been
introduced by National Governments; for example, the Race Relations Act, and Equal Pay
Act, the Accident Compensation Act, national superannuation legislation, the Evidence
Amendment Bill, and the 1972 budgetary provisions incorporating many of the recommen-
dations of the Royal Commission on Social Security. The Opposition is always ready to say
that the National Government is concerned about money, not people, but history proves
that to be wrong. National Governments have a stronger social conscience than any Labour
Administration has ever proved to have had. The Bill is concerned with the equality of
people regardless of colour, sex, marital status, ethnic origin, or religious belief. The
member for Southern Maori said the Bill should embrace people with handicaps, and should
be extended into other areas. The Bill is concerned with the rights of people who are equal
before the law and who may have been discriminated against in employment, job opportun-
ity, advancement, and housing.
Having established that particular basis, and the principle embodied in the Bill, let us
look a little more closely to see what the Bill actually does. It covers employment, the
provision of goods and services, access to public places, and to land, housing, education, and
accommodation, and it treats people as equal, whether they are male or female, married or
single, irrespective of their colour, race, or religious belief. The Bill's principles are worthy,
and therefore I support them wholeheartedly. Human rights legislation is still in its infancy.
In his submissions to the committee the Chief Ombudsman, Mr Laking, pointed out that the
Bill was an experiment similar to the experiment of instituting the original ombudsman.
There were not very many guidelines, and we had to feel our way. In this Bill we are still
feeling our way. The Chief Ombudsman also pointed out that the Bill covered a very
sensitive area and, by its nature, would impinge on the rights of individuals, there being no
strong and clear consensus of what those rights actually are. So we have had to tread with
caution, while looking at the matter with determination and making positive comments and
decisions. The retired Chief Ombudsman recognised this when, in his submission, he
congratulated those who were responsible for the Bill and said—and this was a matter of
sheer delight to me that it contained not only some very fine drafting but some very
valuable cerebration. He said it was a very good Bill and the Government was to be
congratulated on its forethought in introducing it.
We are conscious that people's natural prejudices will have to be suppressed so that
there can be a greater consciousness of the need for concern for others, but how far can any
Government go in restraining and restricting people's prejudices? That is a matter I have felt
very troubled about, particularly in the context of sexual orientation. I could not have
supported the introduction of the sexual orientation clause into the Bill, despite the fact that
there were great pressures on me as a member of the committee and of the House to do so. I
have discussed this matter with many people, but I still feel that New Zealand society is not
yet ready to accept that kind of orientation, which is still alien to the way of life of most of us.
The Bill provides a proper framework for women to achieve true equality with men,
particularly in employment, access to goods and services-particularly mortgage finance and
hire purchase credit facilities—to public places-that will please some of the women in

The member for Henderson mentioned the jockey clause-clause 22. I do not quite

Comment has been made about Part V of the Bill, which deals with privacy and the
function of the commission. The member for Henderson said that clause 58 was ineffectual
window dressing, and the member for Southern Maori said that it should be deleted. I am
disturbed about those comments. New Zealand has no legislation to protect the individual's

Southern Maori when she spoke about the reports that would be made to the Prime
Minister. The commission has nowhere to go for guidelines. Today we are at the mercy of
technology. The Government is giving the commission power to investigate matters that

has the right to some privacy. Guidelines should be set, so that the commission can benefit
not only the average citizen but also the public figure. If that is the way it has to be done,
then more speed to its being done. I trust that the commission will take its function seriously
and give earnest thought to the privacy of the individual.
Members opposite spent much time criticising clause 59, which deals with industrial
unions and professional trade associations. They said the clause should not be in the Bill and
that the necessary powers are derived from industrial legislation, tribunals, and courts. If
that is so, why was it necessary for Mr R. K. Davison, Q.C., to investigate the troubles with
the union at Kinleith? The inquiry was set up by the previous Labour Government because
of reports that had been received. The union took no action. Why did the union or the
labour movement not clear up the problem? It became such a festering sore that a special
inquiry had to be conducted.
Each subclause of clause 59 relates to the kind of intimidatory practices and threatening
practices that were found to be proved in the report of Mr R. K. Davison. The member for
Kapiti mentioned some of the subclauses and quoted from Mr Davison's report, of which I
have made an analysis. Clause 59(1)(b) states that it shall be unlawful for any organisation or
anyone connected with the organisation or carrying on the affairs of the organisation to
threaten any other member of the organisation with the use of violence or with any loss or
detriment, or otherwise to indulge in any intimidatory course of action in order to induce
him to agree to a particular course of action. Mr Davison's report stated: "Certain of the
workers have attempted to use strikes and threats of strikes in an endeavour to force
management to take action against other union members." The Bill is a translation into law
of Mr Davison's findings.
Clause 59(1)(c) states that it shall be illegal for any member to be caused to suffer any
loss or detriment in order to induce him to agree to a particular course of action. Mr Davison
stated in his report that in Robb's case his employer was forced to suspend him for 7 days to
satisfy the union's demands that he be penalised. That is what subclause (c) is all about.

I suggest that some of the praise lavished on the Bill may mislead people in our society

I recall the words of the honourable member for Southern Maori. It is a long established
principle of our Christian tradition that, while we might be concerned about what we would

would describe as the sinner. In other words, there are people who would not accept that
people of other than heterosexual proclivity fall under the judgment of God. If we take that

conduct other than orthodox heterosexuality. It would not mean that we as a society were
endorsing molesting or bestial behaviour. We would not be passing a judgment on the acts,

a slight inch forward, but even then it has not been adopted in this statute.
