Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 2)
THURSDAY, 18 AUGUST 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT AMENDMENT BILL (NO. 2)
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That the Local
Government Amendment Bill (No. 2) be introduced. The Bill is the first of a series of
measures that will co-ordinate and update the laws under which the territorial system of local
government operates. It will not be a new body of law, but will reduce the volume of local
government legislation by revising and bringing together two major Acts—the Municipal
Corporations Act and the Counties Act. At the same time, it will remove the dead wood,
and bring the powers and responsibilities of municipalities and counties into line. It will also
include sections of law from other Acts that it is considered would be more appropriately
included in a local government Act. The whole idea is to bring into one Act as much of the
law under which local authorities operate as it is practicable and sensible to do, and so to
provide a ready reference for both local authorities and the general public to the laws that so
closely affect them.
I emphasise that the Bill is only the first instalment of this major revision and
consolidation of the law. For this reason, so as to make progress on what is a very major
task, it was decided to introduce this first section as an amendment to the present Local
Government Act. As other instalments are completed—and work has already commenced
on the second instalment—they will also be introduced as additional amendments to the
Local Government Act, until we have a completed Act that is modernised and up to date.
That is why I have not attempted in this legislation to make major policy amendments to the
existing law dealing with the structure of local government.
I am well aware that there has been considerable discussion on the poll provisions in the
previous Act. These, of course, accurately repeat what we promised in our election
manifesto, but I know there are some who now think we should go further. I assure the
House that this matter, and other issues concerning the role of the Local Government
Commission, will be examined over the next few months, and any changes will be dealt with
in a separate Bill. It is obviously quite impossible for me to describe to the House at this
juncture all the matters dealt with in a Bill of this magnitude and with this range of subjects.
All I can say is that, in general, it deals with the constitutional, electoral, financial,
accounting, administrative, and procedural aspects of territorial and regional authorities.
The next stage will deal with major functional responsibilities, such as land subdivision,
water and drainage, roading, and so on. The general approach has been to instil more
meaning into the term "local government" by giving local authorities more discretion to
decide their own affairs.
I shall move that the Bill be referred to the Local Bills Committee, so that there will be
ample time for everyone to study it thoroughly, and for those who wish to make submissions
to the committee to do so. Although the initial preparatory work was done by departmental
and local authority officers working together-and I can assure the House that between
them they brought a great deal of expertise to the technical matters involved-it may well be
that some further changes are needed. The major policy issues have been discussed with the
Local Government Council, and I believe I can quite confidently say that, in general, the
national associations-the Municipal Association and the Counties Association-support
the Bill.
Dr WALL (Porirua): The Minister said, quite rightly, that with a Bill of this
magnitude-I see it has 185 pages—it is impossible for him to make a significant review of all
its provisions at this stage. From a brief glance at the Bill, which has just been made available
to me, it is apparent that most of its provisions are re-enactments of measures that already
exist. However, there are some changes, no doubt. I think the Minister could have served
the House better by indicating briefly what changes have been made. Merely shifting
legislation from one Act to another is of no great significance, but such changes as have been
made are of concern not only to the House, but to the whole community, because they so
strongly affect local government and the life of the community. It is important that the

## p. 2311 (#767) ###########################################

18 August
2311
Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 2)
might become confused. He asked about the preparation of the roll. The Bill provides for no
change; it will be the same as in the past. The returning officer can certainly use the general
election roll to his advantage, and, if he likes, take names from that roll. That course is open
to him, and special votes can be allowed in that way.
Rating or taxing powers are certainly included in the Bill, as is a provision covering the
petroleum tax, as has been the case in the past. As the member well knows, I am awaiting a
report from the Local Government Finance Committee, and any new form of financing to be
made available to local government will be covered in separate legislation after we have
received the recommendations of that committee.
The Bill makes no change to the franchise or qualifications of voters. A voter must be a
ratepayer or have residential qualifications, and the residential qualifications have not been
altered: a voter must have lived in the district for 1 month and in New Zealand for 1 year. I
have some notes on electoral rolls that I shall make available to the member; I am sure they
will help him. Basically, the rolls will continue to be prepared by the territorial authority.
However, the Bill includes new provisions that will facilitate the preparation of more
accurate rolls. For example, the Bill removes the existing provision under which a principal
officer can remove the name of a residential voter only if he sends a notice to that effect and
the notice is returned unclaimed. Failure to return the notice will in itself be sufficient cause
to have one's name removed from the roll. Provision is also made for the principal officer,
when preparing a supplementary roll, to include in it a list of those from whom he has
received advice since the closing of the main roll that they have lost their voting qualifica-
tion.
At intervals of not more than 6 years, a roll must now be revised as far as residential
electors are concerned. The manner in which the purge is undertaken is left to the discretion
of the principal officer. Some of the older legislation still requires the territorial authority to
take part in hearing objections to electoral rolls. That role of the territorial authority has
now been dispensed with, and objections will be considered by the principal officer. It is
considered inappropriate today that the elected body itself should have any duties what-
soever in connection with the roll governing its own election.
Two important changes should also be noted. The Municipal Corporations Act, but not
the Counties Act, at present contains a very old provision that, where a single rateable
property extends into more than one ward, it shall, for the purposes of the owner's ratepayer
qualification, be deemed to be in one ward only. That provision has been omitted, as it
appears that it is redundant. Wards exist in only a few boroughs, and the manner in which
they are defined makes it unlikely that a single rateable property will extend across any ward
boundary. The provision in the Municipal Corporations Act that a person owning separate
properties in more than one ward can be on the roll in respect of one ward only is retained,
and has been applied to all territorial authority districts. This means that the present
provision in the Counties Act that enables a person to have a ratepayer qualification in more
than one riding by virtue of the fact that he owns separately rateable properties in more than
one riding has been omitted. I hope I have answered the questions raised by the member for
Grey Lynn.
The matter raised by the member for Porirua was a rather difficult one. I could spend
half an hour of the time of the House in going through the various provisions if the member
so desired, but I think possibly the best I can do is provide him with a copy of the notes my
department has prepared. If he has any questions after reading those notes, he can then ask
them a little later on.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): One small point has struck me since I last spoke,

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Trade Unions in United States and Canada-Penalties
1. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Labour: Do any figures available to his
department reveal either court fines or civil damages imposed on or awarded against either
United States or Canadian trade unions?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The Department of Labour does not keep
statistics on this. However, I personally know of a case involving a wildcat strike by members
of the United Mineworkers Union in 1975. Judge K. K. Hall in Kentucky found that the
union was making "feeble attempts" to end the strike. He ordered a return to work and
assessed a fine of $500,000 with an additional $100,000 to be paid for every day the strike
continued. The amount payable increased to $1.2 million before the dispute was resolved.
The fine was set aside on resolution of the dispute. However, the union was found in
contempt of court and ordered to pay $500,000 to the coal operators. A similar case
involving teachers in New York City has also been reported.
Mr Malcolm: Is there any truth in the statements often made in New Zealand that the
penalty clauses which this Government returned to the Industrial Relations Act in 1976 are
without precedent?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I can appreciate the tenor of the question. The answer could be
yes, but the circumstances are different. In the United States there is a contract agreement
under a 2-year award. There is a sanctity of contract, and I hope sincerely that the
Government's moves last Monday will lead to a similar sanctity in New Zealand.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui): A point of order, Mr Speaker. Perhaps I should have
raised this before the question was asked, but I should like to draw your attention to
Standing Order 75, which states, "Questions may be put to a Minister relating to public
affairs with which he is officially connected." We need to beware of creating a precedent by
allowing questions such as the last question, because members could then ask any Minister if
he has any information about any matter anywhere in the world. It seems to me that the idea
behind the question was in the supplementary question asked by the member for Eden and
that the supplementary question he asked should have been the original question. I cannot
see how the first question complies with the Standing Orders. We are running the risk of
creating a precedent which will open up an enormous field.
Mr MALCOLM (Eden): In many instances a Minister's department has access to
overseas information which could be of interest and value to members. The Department of
Labour could have information about ILO resolutions or figures, or comparative statistics
which could provide a real insight into a comparable situation in other countries. I submit the
question was in order, because the Minister could have information in his department which
could tend to indicate certain things here.

Roading Programme, Highway 2
2. Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori) asked the Minister of Works and Development: Can he
indicate what plans he has for the completion of the motorway on Highway 2 between
Hairini Bridge and the Maungatapu causeway which was commenced some years ago, and is
it correct that the roading programme for the Tauranga area for the 1976-77 year is confined
only to the Barkes Corner-Ruahihi section and no further roading programme is set down
for 1977-78?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Works and Development. The motorway link between Hairini Bridge and the Maungatapu
causeway has been planned for some time and is one of a number of projects under
consideration by the National Roads Board for inclusion in its forward programme. The
roading programme for the 1976-77 year for the No. 3A District, which includes the
Tauranga area, was not solely confined to the Barkes Corner-Ruahihi section of State
Highway 29, and for 1977-78 works totalling $1,026,500 have been programmed, including
$230,000 for bridging, $622,000 for reconstruction, and $174,500 for miscellaneous works.

Defence. His answer is as follows: "I have read the New Zealand Herald article of 4 August

also noted an article in the Canberra Times of 4 August in which Mr Peacock, the Minister of

confidently say that there has been no unauthorised landing on the New Zealand mainland.”
The supplementary information states that on 21 April 1973 a helicopter from a Soviet
whaling mothership made a brief landing on Raoul Island in the Kermadecs as the whaling
fleet passed on its way back to the Soviet Union. This incident was investigated and was
assessed as being nothing more than an innocent, if unauthorised, landing.

Agriculture-Economic and Production Statistics
11. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Agriculture: What steps has the
Government taken to improve the collection and usage of economic and production statistics
from agriculture in order to make decision making by the Government, using up-to-date
information, more effective?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The Government is very conscious of
the need for up-to-date and informative agricultural statistics as an aid to policy formation.
To this end efforts have been directed towards a greater degree of co-ordination in the task
of statistical collection and in the conduct of field surveys as well as the increased use of
sample surveys where appropriate. The same objectives can be secured in part by the more
rigorous analysis of existing statistics. An example is the work of the joint industry-
Government agricultural review committee, which examined the latest production, cost, and
financial information early this year. The results of its work have been valuable as a guide to
policy formation, in particular in the development of policies based on selective incentives
designed to stimulate production.

relating to the use of 1080 to protect adequately human health and non-target species such as
birds, and the adequacy of research into the use of 1080. This report will establish whether
additional research into any aspect of the use of 1080, including the use of lures with baits, is
needed.

Income Tax Rate on Incomes under $2,000
19. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) asked the Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department: What was the income tax rate prior to 1973 on incomes which did not exceed
$2,000, when did an increase take place, and by how much?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I reply on behalf of the Minister in
Charge of the Inland Revenue Department. His answer is as follows: "The actual tax rates
for taxable incomes up to $2,000 were as follows: 1972-73 tax year, the rates of income tax
were on the first $650, 7.85c in the dollar; on the next $1,050, 21c in the dollar; and on the
remaining $300, 24.5c in the dollar. The following changes were made in subsequent years:
1974-75 tax year-on the first $500, 18c in the dollar; on the next $500, 18.5c in the dollar;
and on the remaining $1,000, 19c in the dollar. In the remaining tax years, 1975-76 and 1976-
77, the rates were 19.5c and 20c in the dollar respectively. I should add that these basic rates
are subject to the deduction of special exemptions and rebates."
Mr Schultz: Would the Minister agree that these tax increases, imposed by the Labour
Government, for people on low incomes have since been more than offset by the concessions
in the Budget?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Yes, it is perfectly correct that at this level the last two
Budgets would have assisted a considerable number of taxpayers-but bear in mind that
these are very low incomes.

Legislative Department
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) said that the last Administration had instituted
the opening of select committees to the press, and that move had been followed, but not with
noticeable enthusiasm, by the National Government. Much valuable work was done in
committees. There had been a tendency recently to supplement the standing committees
with ad hoc committees. Committee members had increasingly made themselves available
outside Wellington, and so witnesses had not had to travel to Wellington; that was a step
forward. It would be a forward move if more work was given to parliamentary committees, if
their work was done in the open, and if they travelled outside Wellington. The work of the
subcommittees of the Public Expenditure Committee was of public interest.
He knew the Hansard administration had been hampered because of the installation of
the computer at the Government Printing Office, but did the hold-up lie with the computer,
25 Vol. 412


## p. 2322 (#778) ###########################################

2322
18 August
Appropriation Bill-Estimates
or its integration into the Government Printing Office? A colleague had reported a delay of 6
hours between making his speech in the House and receiving his Hansard typescript. The
delay was not attributable to the staff, but an early return of the Hansard typescript was
desirable, to correct any misapprehension if a member's words in the House were chal-
lenged. Could the Minister give an assurance that the delay would be reduced to a

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister) said there had been considerable delay
since the installation of the computer at the Government Printing Office. There had been
delays in the printing of the Order Paper and Bills, as well as of Hansard, although those
delays had recently been reduced considerably. Hansard copy was prepared in the building
and made available to members as soon as possible to enable minor corrections before it
went to the Government Printing Office. Any delay would be inside the building. The time
in receiving the Hansard copy had varied over the years, but was now longer than before.
Little could be done about that. The Hansard copy was usually received within a reasonable
time earlier in the day.
Select committees were first opened to the press in the 1960s, and more committees had
since been opened to the press. There were good reasons why some committees should not
be opened to the press, whose presence inevitably affected witnesses. It was undesirable that
some evidence be given in public, and to say that a committee could at any time exclude the
press was not sufficient, as it was not known what evidence would be given. The press should
not be present at hearings where some of the evidence was confidential, but committees
were now more frequently open to the press; that would continue when appropriate. It was
disappointing that the press often reported sensational aspects, rather than the substance of
the evidence. The order of reference for the Public Expenditure Committee had been set up
in 1961, and since then the effectiveness of the committee had increased markedly.

what reason? An economist who had joined the department from the banking system had
left, presumably to return to the banking system; had he been the architect of the
Government's higher interest policy? The Prime Minister had previously been unenthusias-
tic about such policies, and had stated in a book he had written: "Against the advice of most
of my advisers I clung to a low interest rate policy for New Zealand. I was never convinced of
the efficacy of interest rates as an economic regulator in our relatively unsophisticated
system, but I was very conscious of the effect of high interest rates on costs. I believe that our
savings performance in recent years proved my point." The country had recently suffered a
complete reversal of that policy, which had cost sections of the community very dearly. Why
had the economist who was reputed to be the architect of that policy left the department?
In the 1975 financial year, two members of the Prime Minister's Department had
travelled at a cost of $3,064. In the 1977 financial year, 14 had travelled at a cost of

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister) said that the permanent head of the Prime
Minister's Department and his immediate staff now numbered four, compared with two in
1975. The figures in each case included the official secretary to the Governor-General; so
that there were now three staff members who worked directly for the Prime Minister, instead
of one. The additional members were a secretary-typist and an investigating officer, who
were carrying out work that had previously been done in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and
who were presumably taking the same number of man-hours. In essence, their salaries
represented a transfer from the vote for Foreign Affairs to that for the Prime Minister's
Department.
Three more were employed in the Cabinet office, making an increase from 22 to 25.
Only one represented additional staff; the other two dealt with an increased work load. One
officer liaised with the State Services Commission-work previously carried out by the
Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Prime Minister's private office now had five members.
compared with three when the Leader of the Opposition had been Prime Minister. In the
previous Government, the Minister of Finance had had a full office staff; but, as Prime
Minister also holding the Finance portfolio, he now had two more personnel to service that
part of his administration.
The press office now had a staff of six, compared with a staff of four when the Leader of
the Opposition had been Prime Minister, but one of the positions had not been filled and
only one extra person was attached to the press office, which also carried out work for
Ministers who did not have their own press secretaries. He could not make a comparison
between the number of Ministers who now had their own press secretaries and the number of
Ministers in the former Labour Government who had press secretaries attached to their own
office. There had been an increase in the liaison group or, as it was sometimes called, the
advisory group, which now had a staff of seven and one vacancy compared with a staff of
four when the Leader of the Opposition had been Prime Minister. However, the Leader of
the Opposition had stated last year that he had intended similarly to revamp the Prime
Minister's office. The number employed in the External Intelligence Bureau had increased
from 31 to 32, and the bureau was also now carrying out a little more work.
The total staff of the Prime Minister's Department had increased from 66 to 79. One
officer had left the department several months ago, as his 1-year contract had expired; he
had been replaced by another officer who, although he had once been a departmental
officer, had come from private industry, again on contract. A second officer, who had been
the chief economist of the Bank of New Zealand, would be leaving the department to return
to that bank the next day, because his contract had expired.
The Government's interest policy had not been suggested by that man, but had been
included in section 20 of the National Party's 1975 election manifesto, which had stated that
a National Government would make interest rates more flexible and would bring controlled
interest rates closer to uncontrolled interest rates. The employment of the officer from the
Bank of New Zealand had been part of the Government's short-term strategy. A low interest
rate policy was ideal. However, if the country had an accelerating and probably permanent
rate of inflation, and if interest rates did not match that rate to some extent, its whole
financial system could break down. The rate of inflation had to be lowered, but, until it was,
it was not possible to accept returns that were so much out of line with the real rate of
inflation. Different remedies had to be applied to meet different circumstances, but those
remedies were certainly not the brain child of the officer who had been attacked by the
Leader of the Opposition. They had been contained in the National Party's election policy,
and had been carried out.
The item for travel had increased because an officer had been acting as liaison officer
with the Government of Bahrain. The concept of a free port at Bahrain was very imaginative
and envied by other countries. That officer had paid five or six necessary visits to Bahrain,
and was a member of the Joint New Zealand-Bahrain Committee that had set up the free
port. It was usual that a press officer travelled with the Prime Minister of the day, and each
time he had been abroad as Prime Minister he had taken a press officer with him, who had
been most valuable in putting New Zealand's point of view to the press in other countries.
On the last occasion, he had gone to the United Kingdom with the permanent head of the

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister) said he deplored the totally unwarranted

Intelligence Service before . . .", with an appropriate date given. It was no discredit to Sir
Walter Nash that he had had the habit of retaining papers. Such papers had included
documents from the Security Intelligence Service, and would no doubt have been eventually
returned. When given access to those papers, Professor Sinclair had signed an agreement
stating that before he used any confidential documents he would refer them to the
originating department, which happened to be the Security Intelligence Service. The service
had then stated that the documents should have been kept in its custody. Although it had
tried to have extracts from those documents removed from the book, the publishers had
refused, and no further action had been taken. Crown Law opinion had been that the
documents should be returned to the service for safe custody. The suggestion that the service
had taken anything to which it was not entitled was unwarranted. The papers had been
returned to the service.

Mr SPEAKER: I regret to inform the House of the death of Mr Eric Alwyn Roussell, a
former Clerk of the House of Representatives. Mr Roussell was Clerk-Assistant from 1947
until 1971, and Clerk until his retirement in January last year. Mr Roussell died this

and our sympathy with the relatives of the late Mr Roussell. I now ask members to stand
with me and observe a period of silence as a mark of respect to the memory of the late Mr

Honourable members then stood as a mark of respect.
FINANCE (INFLATION-ADJUSTED BONDS) BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That the Finance (Inflation-
Adjusted Bonds) Bill be introduced. This is what we call the "Luxton" Bill, after the member
for Piako. The Bill authorises the issue of inflation-adjusted savings bonds, as promised in
the Budget and, of course, in the National Party's election policy. The bonds may be issued
to individuals of or over the age of 7 years, and are not transferable. In addition to interest,
which under the terms of issue of the bonds will be set at 2 percent per annum, there will be
paid to holders of the bonds at the time of their redemption a premium that may be
calculated on the basis of the inflation occurring between the issue of the bonds and their
redemption. The terms of issue of the bonds indicate how the premium will be calculated in
accordance with movements in the consumer price index. Additional details in the terms of
issue provide that the bonds must be held for a minimum period of 5 years, although
superannuitants, executors of deceased estates, and administrators of bankrupt estates may
claim earlier redemption.
Income tax will be payable on the interest received on the bonds, but the inflation
premium will be exempt from income tax. Statutory authority to exempt the premium from
income tax will be contained in the Income Tax Amendment Bill. Clause 2(2) of the Bill
provides that Part III of the New Zealand Loans Act 1953 will apply to the bonds, and the
Reserve Bank will act as registrar of the issue.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): Many of the limitations now
announced by the Minister were mentioned in the Budget, but these limitations do not
appear in the Bill. I take it that it will be perfectly in order for the Government to vary in
future issues the terms announced by the Minister, that what he has said will apply to any
issue intended to be made at present, and that there will be a minimum term of 5
years—although from a quick reading I see no reference to 5 years in the Bill. Is the inflation
proofing to be the actual amount of inflation calculated to have taken place on top of the
interest that will be payable, or is it the difference between the interest and the calculation of
the rate of inflation over the period? The interest that is normally payable on the bond is
subject to income tax; the bonus is not. Clause 2 makes no clear statement as to whether part
or all of the inflation is to be applied. There is, of course, a very significant difference. If the
interest is to be something like the current rate on Government stock for 5 years, or 7 years,
or any other term, and if on top of that there is to be a bonus payable on the present level of
inflation, which would give, say, another 5 percent, about only one-third of the total interest
would be exempt from income tax and about two-thirds would be liable to tax.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The form of the Bill is somewhat
similar to present legislation for other forms of Government securities and, of course, as the
member will realise, the terms of those vary very frequently. This is in exactly the same
form. It is permissive legislation; the detail can vary from time to time. If the member read
clause 2 closely, I think he would find the answer to his second question. Clause 2 states: “in
respect of money borrowed under that Act upon terms that, in addition to any interest


## p. 2340 (#796) ###########################################

2340
19 August
Finance (Inflation-Adjusted Bonds) Bill
payable on them, there shall be payable to the holders thereof at the time the bonds are
redeemed a further amount that may be calculated on the basis of the inflation occurring
between the issue of the bonds and their redemption." The words "in addition" mean that
the interest on the issue of 2 percent is payable, but, in addition, that the rate of inflation
calculated according to the consumer price index will be paid; so that the amount payable for
inflation proofing, tax free, will be the whole of the rate of inflation, and no part of the
interest will be subtracted from it. Otherwise, the bonds would not be inflation proof. The
whole idea of the scheme is that the purchasing power of the bonds will be maintained, and,
in addition, a small rate of interest is paid, taxable as earnings; but the principle is that the
purchasing power of the bonds will be maintained.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I am happy to accept the
Minister's assurance, but I should have thought that, if it was intended that the amount
should be equal to the amount of inflation, the words "equal to that amount", rather than
the words "calculated on the basis of the inflation" would be used. "Calculated on the basis
of the inflation" does not mean that an amount equal to the inflation will be paid. The
calculations could be based on several factors, including a consideration of the interest paid.
However, the Minister has now assured us that that is not the position, and I am happy to
accept it. My other point is that when the honourable member for Piako, as he was at the
time-

Mr LUXTON (Piako): I should like to deal with one or two points raised by Opposition

because a home was provided with his ministry.

insurance against inflation. The scheme will cater for the small saver, and will help people

Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): I want to ask the Minister of Finance just one
question: Why was it decided not to follow the suggestions made by the member for Piako in

that the bonus for inflation in the following year would be not only on the original capital
invested but also on the inflation of the first year. That would make a substantial difference
to the amount.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: Oh, would it?
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS: Yes, very substantial. In other words, if a person invested

between $300 and $400 better off than he will be under the Bill before the House. Why has

inflation; savings accounts will be limited as to amount, but they will receive an interest rate
at least equal to the annual rate of inflation. Most people would interpret that as meaning
that a bonus for the inflation rate would be calculated each year and added to the original
capital investment, and, if the further money was left in, the bonus for inflation for the next
year would be added to the new capital value. Can the Minister of Finance outline the
reasons for the change?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I can do that very readily. The

number at the time of the investment-will be taken, and the index number at the time of
realisation will be taken, and the difference will be added to the original capital sum, thus
preserving the purchasing power of the original capital sum.

simple enough for the member for Manukau. In addition, you will get 2 percent per annum
interest, on which tax will be payable. That is simple enough, is it not?

INCOME TAX AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That the Income
Tax Amendment Bill be introduced. The purpose of the Bill is to give legislative effect to the
Budget tax proposal for family assistance. The first proposal is to extend the existing young
family and wife rebates, and the second proposal is to introduce a new single-income family
rebate. At present, the young family rebate is allowable at the rate of $6 a week if the income
of the principal earner does not exceed more than $100 a week or $5,200 a year. The rebate
diminishes by 15c in each dollar when the claimant's income exceeds $100 a week, so as to
extinguish when the income reaches $140 a week or $7,280 a year. From 1 April 1977, the
rebate will be increased to $9 a week on incomes up to $150 a week or $7,800 a year. It will
then be reduced by 10c for each dollar of income in excess of that figure, and completely fade
out when the claimant's income reaches $240 a week or $12,480 a year.
The main change to the wife rebate is to the allowable income a wife can earn in any
year before the rebate is affected; that income will be increased from $375 to $520 a year.
The rebate will be reduced by 30c instead of the present 40c for each dollar of income
derived in excess of the allowable amount, and will extinguish when the wife's income
reaches $1,040 a year instead of the present $763 a year. To permit this extended fade-out,
the wife rebate has been increased by $1 to $156—that is a technical point. Consequentially,
the housekeeper rebate has been increased to $156 a year. These increased rebates, which
will apply from 1 April 1977, will be incorporated in the new PAYE tables that will come
into effect from 1 October this year.
The new single-income family rebate of $208 a year will also be allowable to the
principal income earner, but the qualifying criteria differ in three aspects from those
applying to the young family rebate. First, it is allowable if there is a child in the family under
the age of 10 instead of the age of 5 at any time during the income year. Secondly, there is no
limit on the allowable income of the principal earner, but the rebate will be reduced after the
income of the spouse exceeds $1,040 a year. The rate of reduction in this case will be 30c for
each dollar of income the spouse derives in excess of $1,040, so that the rebate will
extinguish where that income reaches $1,734. Thirdly, the rebate will be allowed in the
annual assessment; it will not be incorporated in the PAYE tables. For practical purposes, it
was decided not to incorporate this rebate in the PAYE tables because of the complexities
that the increased number of tax codes would cause for taxpayers and employers.
The remaining subject of the Bill is the requirement to furnish annual returns of income.
It provides that those persons whose only assessable income is from national superannuation
will not be required to furnish annual returns.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): The Opposition realises that
this is the maximum the Government is prepared to do for sections of the public, on that

do not have such an ambition. The families who will be helped would be much better helped

Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I am delighted that the

all. The Deputy Leader of the Opposition was not quite correct when he said that these
measures would not help many people, because 200 000 families will be affected. Under the

additional 70 000 will be eligible for the expanded young-family rebate, making a total of 160
000 families.
This new single-income family rebate, which we think an important measure, will lift the
figure to well over 200 000. It endeavours to remedy the growing disparity between those
with only one income, who are bringing up children, particularly children under the age of
10, and those who have two incomes now that more wives are working. We do not pretend to
be able to cope with a major sociological change of this kind by a tax measure, but we have
aimed to help, that is why we fixed the age at 10 years. Once their children have passed that
age, women who can work will find it easier to resume employment. The measure will affect
about 156 000 families, and we estimate that 98 000 which are eligible for the single-income
rebate will also receive the expanded young-family rebate. A large number of people are
affected by this Bill. We certainly wish to assist people by using the fiscal system, adapting it
to suit social conditions; that is what these measures are designed to do.

INCOME TAX (ANNUAL) BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That the Income
Tax (Annual) Bill be introduced. The Income Tax (Annual) Bill is the normal annual
measure fixing the rates of income tax, excess retention tax, and bonus issue tax. The rates
for the year are assessed from 1 April 1977, and are the same as those fixed for last year.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): Although this Bill fixes rates at
the same level as before, there is a much stronger objection to it from the Opposition than
there was to the Land Tax (Annual) Bill, which had much the same effect. We believe very
strongly that the rates should have been changed. As I understand it, the Government was
quite unable to make any adjustments to this Bill and to the rates established, because it was
committed to very heavy expenditure in limited areas. As a result, the general taxpayer did
not get any adjustment, although inflation has increased his income insufficiently to
compensate him in most cases for the higher prices he has had to pay for everything. In
addition, through the operation of this Bill, he will in fact pay more as a proportion of his
income, as well as in cash terms, in income tax.
Although the Minister was silent on this point when moving the introduction of the Bill,
I do not think the public will be misled by that silence. I think the public is very appreciative
of the fact that the Government, despite its utterances at election time, has failed in this Bill
to live up to its promises. It is one thing to hold the rates of taxation. It is a vastly different
thing to hold the amount of taxation levied on an income paid in return for the same amount
of work, for the same time at work. I wonder whether the Minister would be prepared to
comment on the reasons it was considered there should be no adjustment in the annual
income tax to compensate for inflation, when the Government felt it was necessary earlier to
bring in a special Bill to compensate a small section for the effects of inflation on their
savings. I suggest to all members that it is far more important in the fight against inflation to
do something in this Bill, rather than elsewhere, because this Bill affects every income
earner in the country.
In the past, it has been customary to adjust the rebates, the exemptions, or the rates of
tax, but as far as I can see the Bill does none of those. In other words, the Bill expresses the
Government's determination to increase the proportion of the taxpayers' earnings it takes
for its coffers. There has been a lot of talk about the ability of a Government to finance its
expenditure without changing the rates of taxation. Of course, that has meaning only if the
rates of taxation and the levels of income relative to effort remain the same, but we know
that if incomes go up in purely monetary terms the combination of the same rates and the
same exemptions produces a higher return to the Inland Revenue Department. This has
been a regular feature of our society, unfortunately, but normally a Government makes
some adjustment to the rates, to the steps at which they apply, or to the rate rebates—but
none of them is there.
We are going to go into very much greater depth because, according to Budget figures,
these provisions are going to obtain $742 million more this year than the same provisions
obtained last year. There will probably be fewer people at work because of emigration and
unemployment. I do not think that more overtime hours will be worked, but the calculations
by the Treasury and the Inland Revenue Department presented in the Budget indicate that
there will be a return of $742 million more from these provisions. I think the Minister would
have to agree that that is almost the total return from income tax in the 1970-71 year. One
year's increase at this stage is equal to 1 year's total take only 7 years ago, yet we are being
asked to accept that this is just in the normal course of events, and that the Government is
not doing anything serious at all. The Bill is designed to take $742 million extra in 1 year,
without changing the rates of taxation. That is a comment on the level of inflation, as well as
on the Government's need to take that money for its other policies without giving any relief
to income-tax payers.

Bill introduced and read a first time.
NOXIOUS ANIMALS BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): I move, That the Noxious Animals Bill be
introduced. This Bill of 42 clauses consolidates and amends the Noxious Animals Act 1956.
There are 19 new clauses, and all of the 23 clauses carried forward from the present Act have
been amended to some degree. The major changes are to be found in clauses 9 and 13 of the
new Parts II and III. These changes cover ownership of noxious animals, powers of forest
officers, noxious animal recovery using aircraft on Crown-owned land, and recreational
hunting.
There are five parts to the Bill. Its purpose is to make better provision for the control of
introduced wild animals, and to regulate helicopter hunting on all Crown-owned land,
including national parks. Complementary legislation to amend the Air Services Licensing
Act 1951 to require helicopter operators to obtain a new type of licence—a noxious animal
recovery licence-is in draft form. A new system of permit control over entry to Crown-
owned land for helicopter hunting is to be administered by the Forest Service. Some changes
are also proposed to allow wapiti, red deer, wapiti-red deer hybrids, and fallow deer to be
held outside their feral range for deer farming purposes.
What is commonly known as the safari tourist industry was looked at to see if any
regulation of such activities was necessary at this time, but no such need was established.
However, the Bill provides for this by regulation should it become necessary. It is thought
timely to recognise, provide for, and supervise, recreational hunting, so as to achieve
concerted action and more effective noxious animal controls. Welcome clauses of the Bill
will be those which strengthen the trespass legislation and, to some extent, remove the
incentive for a person to trespass and unlawfully take noxious animals. Those provisions are
linked throughout the Bill, and have the support of Federated Farmers.
One definition in clause 2 which has been changed from that in the existing Act is that of
"noxious animal". The sixth schedule to the Wildlife Act 1953 lists the noxious animals.
Wild animals can be added to the schedule only by the Governor-General by Order in
Council on the recommendation of the Minister of Internal Affairs. The new definition in
the Bill lists the existing species of noxious animals. It specifically excludes such animals
when they are held under a permit for farming, research, or in zoological gardens. It allows
for the Governor-General to declare any land mammal a noxious animal by Order in Council
on the recommendation of the Minister of Forests. The interpretation of "noxious animal
recovery service" includes aerial hunting for deer for the purpose of selling the carcasses,
and the live capture of noxious animals using aircraft. It also includes the servicing of both
the above types of operation, plus opossum poisoning or trapping using aircraft.
Part I is titled "Noxious Animal Control" and commences with a new clause outlining
the purpose of the Act. The Act is for the control and, where necessary and practicable, the
eradication of noxious animals. This clause in effect spells out what has been the accepted
policy of the Government since 1965. In that year a select committee reported on noxious
animal control. That report was later accepted as the basis of policy by the Government of
the day, and by successive Governments. Other new clauses provide that the Director-
General of Forests can delegate certain of his powers, and also that forest officers have
authority to enter on to land and to search vehicles, sheds, and so on, where they have


## p. 2352 (#808) ###########################################

2352
19 August
Noxious Animals Bill
reasonable cause to suspect that some breach of the Act has occurred. There are also new
clauses stipulating that lessees of Crown-owned land have an obligation to ensure that
noxious animals on their properties are controlled. There are also clauses ensuring that
special consultation and appeal provisions are to be available for farmers where entry on to
their land is required to control goats. These are goats which are not branded and farmed, or
held behind effective fences, and which stray on to neighbouring critical erosion areas.
Clause 6 allows the Minister to delegate certain of his powers-for instance, to national
park boards and park rangers. Clause 8 clarifies the point that noxious animals can only be
hunted or killed by lawful means—that is, with the permission of the person in control of the
land. This provision supports clause 9, which clearly states that all noxious animals belong to
the Crown. Noxious animals may become the property of the person who captures or kills
them only when that person is lawfully on the land where he takes the animals. These are
quite important clarifications of existing law which will make trespass an unprofitable and
unlawful means of taking noxious animals. The prohibition on the liberation, and the
restriction on the keeping, of noxious animals remains, but the Bill allows, in exceptional
circumstances, for fallow deer, red deer, wapiti, and wapiti-red deer hybrids to be held
outside their feral range for deer farming purposes. Completely deer-free areas of the
country, however, are not to be so used; for instance, North Auckland, areas of Taranaki,
and the Chatham Islands.
Clauses 13 to 16 contain the main authoritative provisions of the Bill. Forest officers,
who hold powers under the present Act, are already provided with powers of entry on to
land to assess the impact of noxious animals. The Bill gives new powers, where they have
reasonable cause to suspect an offence, to seize animals unlawfully held or, as stated earlier,
to detect or prevent offences and to search vehicles, and so on. The powers are similar to
those of wildlife rangers under the Wildlife Act 1953, Agricultural Pest Destruction Board
personnel under their Act of 1967, and inspectors under the Animals Act 1967. To obtain
entry to a dwellinghouse, the usual procedure for obtaining a search warrant-authorisation
by a magistrate-is required. This is not a new power; it is included in section 8A of the
present Act. Likewise, the powers of entry on to land in clause 16 are virtually the same as
those in section 10 of the present Act. There is the important difference however that the Bill
now allows for an appeal to the Minister.
Two new provisions relate to the obligations of lessees of Crown-owned land to ensure
that noxious animals are controlled. The Minister of Forests has discretionary power to
charge a proportion of the cost where this duty has to be carried out by the Forest Service.
These provisions give Forest Service officers the power to inspect Crown-owned land held
under lease. Of the three remaining clauses in Part I of the Bill, the fencing clause is
amended to clarify the roles of the adjoining occupier and the Minister as regards the fencing
of a common boundary or other land. The special provision relating to goats is completely
new. This clause provides that where a farmer has goats on his property he may brand them
as prescribed in Part V of the Animals Act 1967. Providing he keeps them behind effective
fences they are legally farm animals and not noxious animals. If they stray, the usual
procedures for giving notice to the owner to remove his trespassing stock apply. However,
where the goats are unbranded and not effectively fenced they are classed as noxious
animals. Consultation and appeal provisions have been worked out with the assistance of
Federated Farmers. They are designed to protect the interests of farmers who wish to keep
goats as farm animals.
Part II of the Bill is extremely important. Briefly, it provides that there be one permit
issuing authority, the Forest Service, for all helicopter hunting on Crown-owned land. This
includes national park and maritime park land. It also provides for consultation with land
controlling authorities on conditions of entry on to land, with appeal and adjudication
powers provided. Land may be zoned for the purposes of this part of the Bill. Permits to
enter on to land to hunt may be issued, varied, or revoked by the Director-General of
Forests. The holders of such permits must accept certain obligations. Neighbouring farmers
who may wish their land to be hunted along with any nearby Crown-owned land may request
that the director-general arrange for such hunting under special conditions that the occupier
may lay down. Officers of the civil aviation division of the Ministry of Transport have
collaborated in the drafting of some of the provisions so that this Bill and the proposed Air
Services Licensing Bill will be complementary. It is intended that helicopter hunting on
Crown-owned land should be better regulated and more effectively used as a noxious animal
control measure.


## p. 2353 (#809) ###########################################

19 August
2353
Noxious Animals Bill
Part III of the Bill allows the Director-General of Forests to publicly notify areas to be
used for recreational hunting. That will be done under noxious animal control plans to be
drawn up and administered by the conservator of forests within whose conservancy any
recreational hunting area may lie. Provision is also made for a National Recreational
Hunting Advisory Committee, whose powers would be solely advisory to the Minister of
Forests. All recreational hunting areas will be monitored by Forest Service staff. Forest
Service staff will advise on the effectiveness of recreational hunting in keeping the number of
noxious animals under control and in protecting the land and vegetation. The director-
general will have power to reimpose more effective noxious animal control at any time
should that be necessary. No high erosion risk areas will form part of any recreational
hunting area. No national park or reserve for the protection of flora or fauna will be
considered for inclusion.
Part IV is a much reduced part of the present Act, which has been rarely used in the last
21 years. Quite simply, the power for the Minister to agree to noxious animal control
proposals of local authorities and to approve of them operating using their own funds is
retained. All the procedures for appointing inspectors and other non-essential matters are
removed. A local body may wish to control opossums within its borough on land not covered
by any county agricultural pest destruction board. In such a case the Minister of Forests
would ensure that the proposals were practical, and agree to the local authority having such
powers.
The general provisions of Part V of the Bill are largely machinery clauses, little changed
from those in the present Act. There is a new provision, clause 32, on the definition of
notices given under the Bill, and two other provisions, clauses 34 and 37, which mainly seek
to plug inadequacies in the present Act. Clause 34 provides that offenders may be liable for
the payment of expenses arising from the act which constituted the offence. The provision in
clause 37 is similar to one in the Wildlife Act. It provides that where a person is found in
circumstances where a reasonable presumption can be made that he has committed or
intends to commit an offence, the liability rests on that person to establish that he has not
offended or does not intend to offend. In practice, where a person is found on land where
noxious animals are present with, for instance, a loaded firearm and he has no permission to
be on the land, it can be assumed reasonably safely that unless he can produce evidence to
the contrary he does intend to hunt noxious animals. That clause complements clause 9,
which deals with the ownership of noxious animals. All remaining clauses are purely
standard provisions.
As stated in my opening remarks, the Bill is designed to make better provision for the
control of noxious animals and to regulate commercial helicopter hunting and recreational
hunting. The need for legislative changes has been evidenced by the number of official
inquiries into noxious animal administration over recent years-for example, the select
committee inquiry in 1965; a further report in 1968, which dealt with some aspects of noxious
animal administration; the National Government's re-examination and re-affirmation of its
noxious animal control policies in 1970; the former Labour Government's caucus committee
report on noxious animal control and related matters in 1974; and, during the past 18
months, the review of noxious animal administration carried out by the present Govern-
ment, which has led to the drafting of the Bill. In addition to inter-departmental consulta-
tion, there has been consultation on the clauses that materially concern them with Federated
Farmers of New Zealand, the Fiordland National Park Board, and the National Parks
Authority. At the appropriate time, I shall move that the Bill be referred to the Lands and
Agriculture Committee.

NEW ZEALAND PLANNING BILL
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of National Development): I move, That the New Zealand
Planning Bill be introduced. The Bill gives a statutory basis to the New Zealand Planning
Council and to the Commission for the Future. The establishment of these two organisations
is in fulfilment of manifesto promises. The Planning Council represents the promised
revitalisation of the planning mechanism set up as the National Development Council by the
previous National Government. It was also promised in the manifesto that a Commission for
the Future would be established by Act of Parliament, and this is now being done.
The National Government pioneered consultative planning in New Zealand. The
26.


## p. 2356 (#812) ###########################################

2356
19 August
New Zealand Planning Bill
establishment of the National Development Council was a milestone in the country's
development. For the first time people came together from the public and private sectors,
and from the universities and the farms, to share their views on the desirable path of future
development. Soon after it took office in 1975 the present Government asked Sir Frank
Holmes to direct a task force on social and economic planning with the aim of recommending
how the planning machinery could be revitalised. I must pay tribute to the efficiency and
thoroughness with which Sir Frank and his group went about their task. The structure of the
Planning Council set out in the present Bill incorporates most of the recommendations of the
task force, and the Government has asked Sir Frank to be the first chairman of the new
organisation.
The New Zealand Planning Council will enjoy certain advantages over the previous
National Development Council. In the first place, it is to have a statutory basis which confers
on it a greater authority in its work of consultation. Secondly, it is to have its own
independent secretariat able to devote its energies to the work of planning. Thirdly, the
Government has agreed that Sir Frank Holmes, as its first chairman, will devote his full time
to the work of the council. The Minister of National Development is to be a member of the
council to ensure that its work is brought into consideration in the Government's decisions.
The Secretary to the Treasury is also a member, to ensure close co-operation between
departments and the council.
The principal function of the New Zealand Planning Council under the present Bill will
be "to advise the Government on planning for social, economic, and cultural development in
New Zealand". The Government intends that the council should play a role in co-ordinating
planning of all types and act as a focal point for a process of consultative planning for New
Zealand's medium-term development. This is spelt out in the Bill. The Bill gives the council
the power to prepare reports on any matter affecting the economic, social, and cultural
development of New Zealand, and to publish documents on planning topics which, in its
view, merit wide consideration and public debate. The Government is, therefore, setting up
the council as an independent organisation and has given it the right to express its views. The
appointed members are to serve as individuals and not as representatives of any interest
group.
The council will, I hope, provide a source of advice to the Government and increase
public understanding of issues relating to New Zealand's development. The Government
expects it to illuminate such issues, and the constraints on resources within which decisions
must be made. At the same time it is to be hoped that the council will stimulate Government
departments, local bodies, and private agencies to consider the long-term national interest as
well as their short-term aims. The council should increase the opportunities for constructive
consultations about how the goals of different groups can best be harmonised. There should
be no doubt, however, that when the advice of the Planning Council and of the Govern-
ment's other official advisers has been received, it is the responsibility of the Government to
make decisions.
I turn now to the Commission for the Future. This organisation is an innovation which
reflects the Government's desire to ensure that it and the public have an early warning of the
major issues looming up in the future as a result of long-term changes in the social,
technological, and economic environment in which New Zealand's development will take
place. The commission is to give special attention to the implications of new or prospective
developments in science and technology. It is generally accepted that such changes have had
a major effect in shaping our society, and will continue to do so in the future. The
commission will be concerned with identifying issues rather than resolving them, and the
time span that it is considering is much longer than that of the New Zealand Planning
Council. It is intended that the commission will initiate public discussion on the possibilities
for the long-term economic and social development of New Zealand. Special emphasis is to
be placed on ensuring that members of Parliament have opportunities to inform themselves
of the issues discussed in the commission's reports.
A significant feature of the commission is that it is to be a bipartisan body, including in
its membership a member of Parliament appointed on the nomination of the Leader of the
Opposition. The commission is already in operation, with a member of the Opposition
participating fully in its deliberations. A Minister of the Crown and the Director-General of
the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research are also to be members of the
commission, and provision is made for an independent chairman. The first chairman is
Professor James Duncan of Victoria University, and I appreciate the work he is putting in

New Zealand Planning Bill
during the initial stage of the commission's development.
The introduction of this Bill demonstrates the Government's commitment to three
important objectives. The first objective is to increase general awareness of key issues
relating to New Zealand's development; the second is to ensure that a sound basis for long-
term policy is arrived at by a process of wide consultation; and the third is to bring long-term

Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill be introduced. The Bill fulfils the Government's undertaking
to put before Parliament legislation that, if enacted, would implement those recommenda-
tions of the royal commission that can be implemented only by legislation. I take the first
opportunity of thanking Mr Roger Barker, parliamentary counsel, for the care he has taken
with its drafting.
The Bill should in one sense be regarded as Parliament's Bill rather than a normal
Government Bill, because Cabinet members and all Government members—and, I believe,
Opposition members as well-will be exercising their individual judgment on its merits. We
will be assisted in that exercise by reference to the carefully discussed arguments of the royal
commission and, to help honourable members and the interested public, the explanatory
notes to the Bill indicate the page and recommendation numbers of the report relevant to the
provisions in the Bill.
The Government is concerned to see that, whatever the House agrees as to the content
of the Bill, the end result should be clear and effective law. To that end I invite honourable
members who wish to offer amendments to any of its clauses to seek the assistance of the
Parliamentary Counsel Office in their drafting. Needless to say, the longer the notice that
can be given of such amendments the more likely it is that careful consideration can be given
to them. I have already had notice from my colleague the Minister of Education of his
intention to put forward amendments to the Education Act to give parents the right to be
consulted about and to withdraw their children from classes and courses which deal with sex
education. As the assurance of that right is given in the National Government's policy,
Government members are committed to it.
I need to refer now to the form of the Bill. If the Bill is read a second time I shall move
at the appropriate stage certain procedural motions designed to split the Bill into its
component parts for final enactment. I shall propose that Part I be enacted as a separate Act.
It deals with those matters that cannot be dealt with by amendments to existing Acts. Part II
comprises the various amendments to the Crimes Act 1961 recommended by the royal
commission. I shall propose that it be enacted as a separate Crimes Amendment Act. Part
III comprises a number of amendments to various Acts. I shall propose that the clauses be
enacted as separate amending Acts along the lines of the procedure followed for the Statutes
Amendment Bill.
Within Part I the various provisions are grouped under the headings “Contraception",
"Sterilisation", and "Abortion". It is not necessary for me to detail the clauses of the Bill.
As I have said, members will find reference in the explanatory note to the particular
recommendations of the royal commission to which each clause relates. I should, however,
comment on one matter. The royal commission recommended on page 293 of its report that
the decision about whether or not an abortion should be performed should be vested in
panels. As a second-best alternative the commission recommended that the decision be left
to two doctors. My Cabinet colleagues and I felt that—without in any way adverting to the
respectful merits of the proposals-we should provide for the commission's first choice, and
the Bill so provides.
To sum up, the Bill is a faithful attempt to set out in legislative form the recommenda-
tions of the royal commission. The ultimate fate of the Bill and each of its provisions rests, as
it must, with the honourable members of Parliament. I commend the Bill to the House.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I thought I should speak very briefly at

The royal commission set up by the Labour Government sat for 2 years. Its membership
was widely accepted at the time it was set up and was not criticised. That is one of the reasons
the Government does not propose to recommend that the Bill be referred to a parliamentary
select committee. If the Bill went to a select committee one would assume that the
committee would be made up of 10 members, and any further evidence heard would be
heard by only the 10 members. All members of Parliament have to make an individual
decision on each aspect of the Bill. If the Bill went to a committee 10 members would be fully
informed and the remaining members would be in a less favourable position.

Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The Minister of Justice has informed the
House that I will introduce a Supplementary Order Paper on clause 56, and the Prime
Minister also mentioned it. I take this early opportunity to explain why. The Prime Minister
quite rightly said that the Bill is entirely one of conscience. Any member may introduce
amendments at the appropriate time. However, our election policy contained promises on
the introduction of education on moral issues. The commission's report made some
recommendations that are included in clause 56, but did not go as far as our policy
statement.
Clause 56 implements the first recommendation on page 91 of the royal commission's
report. If the House agrees to clause 56, and this would be done entirely on a free vote,
primary and secondary schools would be required to include in their curricula courses and
studies on human development and relationships. The clause would provide the legal
authority for the Minister of Education to prescribe syllabuses of study and would implement
the principal recommendation of chapter 3 of the report. Clause 56 as it now stands—and
this is entirely in line with the commission's recommendations-refers to courses and
studies. I shall move that the word "studies" be deleted and replaced by "classes".
My reason for the proposed change is that the royal commission recommended that sex
education form an integral part of courses in human development and relationships and not
be treated in isolation. This could be interpreted to mean that courses and studies in human
development and relationships might become so integrated either as a separate course or
with other studies in the school curriculum that it would be difficult or even impossible for
parents to know what was being included and how the school intended to teach it. Such a
possibility has worried some people. The Supplementary Order Paper proposes that the
phrase be amended to "courses and classes", and "class" will mean a group of pupils or
students under instruction for a specified timetable period.
Mr Hunt: Will it include groups of classes?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It could include groups of classes, but it will be specified. The
other two proposed amendments have a different justification. Clause 56 of the Bill now
before us will be decided on a conscience vote. It will be voted into the Bill as it finally passes
through the House, or it will be amended in some way, or it will be voted out. If it is voted in
it will have implemented the recommendations of the royal commission for human develop-
ment and relationships courses in schools so far as legislation is required, but it will not have
satisfied the Government's policy as set out in its policy statement at the last election. The
Government is committed by its policy to do two things not recommended by the royal
commission-to ensure consultation with parents by schools before the introduction of
courses in human development and relationships, and to ensure that parents who object to
courses in human development and relationships given in local schools have the right to
withdraw their children from those courses, or from parts of the courses if it is their wish.
Clauses 56A and 56B, which will be incorporated in the Supplementary Order Paper,
ensure that each year before courses and classes in human development and relationships are
taught in a State primary, intermediate, or secondary school, parents and guardians have the
right to be given a clear indication of the proposed content of the course and the nature of
the classes. It would also give a legal right to parents and guardians to withdraw, if they so
wished, their children from attendance in courses and classes on human development and
relationships. This right would apply to all or to any specified part of each course, and there
would also be a power of withdrawal that a parent or guardian could revoke or vary at any
time.
I again remind members of the status of the amendments I have proposed under clauses
56A and 56B as set out in the Supplementary Order Paper. I shall move them if clause 56 of
the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill is passed by the House on a conscience
vote. If clause 56 is approved by the House it will be necessary for clauses 56A and 56B to be
moved as Government policy in order to carry out our manifesto promise. As far as the
Government is concerned, therefore, clause 56A and clause 56B would not be a matter of
conscience. For this reason the Supplementary Order Paper has been introduced at the same
time as the Bill, and I hope that whenever the Bill is being discussed it will be borne in mind
that the Supplementary Order Paper may form an integral part of it.

of Education, because they clarify a matter that would otherwise. be confusing-a Bill
introduced, and a Supplementary Order Paper introduced with it. I know it is customary to
question the Minister concerning matter contained in a Bill on its introduction, but on this
occasion I ask to be allowed to advance a certain argument because of the provision
announced by the Minister of making assistance from the departments and parliamentary

and wording of amendments. As members have been asked to consider the amendments
they might move in advance, some argument concerning the advisability of those amend-
ments might be appropriate at this stage, whereas it might not be appropriate at a similar
stage in the introduction of any other Bill.
In particular I am concerned about the highly emotional argument about the provisions
of panels that has already become public. The confusion is indicated by the headlines in the
local papers yesterday, stating that the New Zealand Medical Association rejected panels.
However, on reading the body of the articles, one found that the recommendation by the
NZMA involved more practitioners in the decision-making process than the commission had
recommended to be on the panel. A totally erroneous impression is thus being created by the
headlines when compared with the body of the articles. At this stage we should look at the
fundamental principles behind the panels and ignore the emotional aspects in the argument.
The reason that this matter is before the House is that it is thought proper-and I think
everyone in the House would agree that this procedure should be under some sort of public
control. We must then look at the possible ways of exercising that public control. In the
absence of a publicly administered body making the individual decisions, the woman may go
to any doctor-and nothing in our laws forces anyone to go to any particular doctor-and the
two of them may make a decision, either for or against the abortion. It is not difficult to see
what will rapidly develop in practice. Some practitioners will be known to be reluctant to
agree to abortions in cases where there is slight justification for it. Others will be known to
follow the principle now subscribed to by some practitioners: that the indication for abortion
is that a woman wants one, and that she be not more than 12 weeks pregnant. In that
situation there is no control, yet the whole purpose of the measure before the House is that
there should be some control.
The only way to exercise any form of control is to ensure that those making the decisions
do so in accordance with the principles laid down by the House. If it is to be left to any
woman and any practitioner to make the decision, those making that proposal should
advance to the House in legislative form, properly drafted, the machinery to restore control,
because unless there is some such machinery, which is not yet envisaged in the Bill,
Parliament, by advancing any amendment that would hand over to individual women and
individual practitioners the decision, in fact totally surrenders its control of this procedure.
Panels have been given a bad name simply because those who wish to see no control
whatever in our community over this procedure have chosen to campaign against them. For
at least 40 years the medical profession has used the panel system for a problem that is just as
distressing and urgent, and in which debate as to the right method of treatment is just as
diverse as that in decisions on abortion. I refer to the panels that are run in most
metropolitan hospitals on the treatment of cancer. The problem is similar, there is urgency
of treatment, there is disagreement about the appropriate treatment, and decisions may be
required about where the appropriate treatment should take place. Yet these panels have
given almost universal satisfaction for more than 40 years, and I am sure some of my fellow
practitioners, who condemn the use of the panel system for making decisions on abortion,
would be reluctant to see the panels on the treatment of cancer removed.
We must therefore ask ourselves why a different attitude is taken towards the two
problems. Is it because they want no control in one, but are happy to accept proper and
expert professional advice in the other? Most members have received a letter from Dr
McLean in Invercargill outlining the practice of panels over some years and the degree of
satisfaction given. The evils associated with the panel system, canvassed so widely by the
Abortion Law Reform Association, are not evident in practice. In Invercargill it has been
shown that the delay has not been great-at the outset about two weeks, and often less than
that—and that the referral rate to outside agencies away from Invercargill has been remark-
ably small, even under present conditions, if one goes to the right quarters in New Zealand,
no form of legal sanction is likely to be applied in the decision making on abortion.
The problem is whether or not Parliament intends to maintain any public control over
this procedure. If it does, then those making the decisions must be accountable to some
