Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): Because of the unusual nature of the
Bill and the free vote situation, the various steps in the passage of the Bill through the House
can be expected to assume a different significance in relation to each other. The introduction
comes as no surprise. The Government and the Minister have done what was publicly
announced and fully understood some months ago—namely, introduced a Bill as close as
possible to the recommendations in the royal commission's report, which called for legisla-
tive response.
The second reading debate is normally seen by the House and the country to give a clear
picture of members' attitudes towards the principles contained in a Bill. The procedures of
the House make possible only three types of response at the second reading stage: approval
of the Bill in principle; postponement of further consideration of the Bill, but only as a
totality; or rejection of the Bill. It is not possible to approve some parts, and postpone or
reject others. We should ask those unfamiliar with parliamentary processes to understand
that, with this Bill, the traditional summation of the outcome of the second reading debate
cannot be relied upon, because the prospects for change, which can only be made at the later
Committee stage, will, or could, do much to change the character of the Bill, even in its
fundamentals. I expect, therefore, that the second reading "aye" vote will include many
members whose only reason for support is to have the opportunity to amend the Bill
according to their wishes during the Committee stage. I, for one, will be in that category.
I know the Minister hopes that those members with amendments to propose in the
Committee stage will make their intentions known during the second reading debate.
However, there is a limit to the degree to which this can be done, because the need, or
otherwise, to propose amendments in some of the later clauses will depend directly upon the
success or otherwise of certain amendments in earlier clauses. This clearly means that the
Committee stage becomes very important, except that by the nature of things the debate on
the short title can have no more importance than the second reading debate in trying to
establish the true mood of Parliament and the will of members. This cannot be determined
until all clauses have been put and individually considered, and assessed in the light of such
amendments as the House may at various stages agree to. To me, therefore, the approval in
principle or otherwise must lie with the decision of the third reading debate. Then, and not
until then, will members know what they are being asked to commit themselves to in terms
of the total legislative package.
I am sure the House and the country will want to use the next 4 weeks or so between the
introduction of the Bill and the second reading to study the Bill carefully and to prepare
those amendments that are considered necessary. To my mind, the House must abandon the
idea that there is any chance of placing restrictions on either side of this issue. It is important
that the end result be a practical measure that can be made to work, and that must-and is
seen to meet the essential needs of those who are themselves directly involved. The Bill is
full of potential red herrings. An example is the royal commission's recommendation on how
to cope with cases of rape. No matter what the commission might recommend, or this Bill
might propose, 99 doctors out of 100 would see it as their duty to recommend an abortion for
a woman made pregnant by rape. Let us not imagine that we can make a token gesture to the
liberal conscience by removing the rape clause and leaving some of the more serious and
quite unacceptable features which, to me, are obvious throughout the Bill
I take this opportunity of informing the Minister and the House that I believe there is a
credible alternative to the abortion proposals in the Bill. I will undertake, with the help of a
committee of doctors and social workers who have associated with me in this study, to have
the alternative ready for the House by the time of the second reading. Whatever the answer
finally selected, three elements in the Bill as introduced deserve our special attention. First,
there is a need to remove the provision for panels, and, instead, rely upon members of the
medical profession acting in good faith; second, there is a need to remove the supervisory
committee, or certainly render it beyond the reach of the influence of abortion politics, if
that is indeed possible, by a most careful redefinition of its role; and, third, there is a need to
bring back into focus the fact that the real answer must lie with the integrity of the medical
profession, and any question of the doctor acting in good faith being required to prove his
blamelessness or defend his actions taken in good faith must be removed.

should agree to act until he is satisfied that his patient has had proper and adequate
counselling, and come to a firm and responsible conclusion.
Counselling, or advice, as we simply used to know it, should not be merely medical and
social-or, if you prefer it, sociological, or to use the term adopted by the New Zealand
Medical Association, psycho-social-but should encompass spiritual aspects and values.
When I use the word "spiritual" I do not necessarily confine it to religious or sacred
concepts. In my judgment it extends, or should extend, into the secular realm, and involve
an honest contemplation of the inner self, and the intangibles that go to make up what we
call ideals.
But it is said that there is another interest to be considered, and another voice to be
heard. Indeed, there is. If we want to put an emotional gloss on the argument we call it the
unborn child; if we want to be rather more dispassionate we refer to it as—and I prefer to
adopt the term-the foetus. Who is most attuned to that voice, and can best hear and
translate into sounds audible to us just what it is saying? Some people—I am bound to
describe them as pressure groups-have appointed themselves as spokesmen, and even as
advocates, claiming a clear mandate to demand on its behalf a right to be born. But is it not
conceivable that if the foetus were able to weigh up all relevant factors, and able to express a
preference, it might have a different, perhaps a contrary, view? Which is likely to be the
more accurate channel, the more reliable interpreter-a self-appointed committee, or the
woman actually in physical contact with the life not yet in being (and I say that with personal
conviction)? She alone is capable of making it live. Who, above all else, is capable of
assessing not only the fact of that life, but its likely quality?

A headline in this morning's paper states that the committee on women knocked panel
abortion, and the article states that the committee on women felt that proposals for a
statutory committee to develop abortion law constituted a vote of no-confidence in the
medical profession. It does not, of course, and the view of the New Zealand Medical
Association, which speaks for the medical profession, is that there should be this supervising
body. The NZMA recognises that it can no longer be assumed that all members of the
medical profession have equally high standards, equal moral attitudes, or an equally ethical
approach to the day-to-day problems they are faced with. The NZMA must clearly recognise
that that is not the case, and I think that anybody who has studied the subject in any depth
has recognised that it does not take many medical men with low ethical standards to
absolutely break any system we might try to introduce, and allow abortion on demand and
abortion on request to develop immediately.
I spoke some time ago to a division of the NZMA which had passed a resolution that it
would accept abortion on demand or abortion on request in the first 12 weeks. In my address
I mentioned the Hippocratic oath and the Helsinki Declaration. At question time, somebody
from the floor said to me, "Why do you refer to the Hippocratic oath and the Helsinki
Declaration? We in this division do not subscribe to that at all." I said: "I am surprised and
concerned and so will 90 percent of New Zealanders be concerned-to know about that. I
believe it to be of very great concern that a large body of doctors"-I did not take a head


## p. 2365 (#821) ###########################################

19 August
2365
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
count, but between 50 and 100 doctors were present—"can say that they do not subscribe to
the Hippocratic oath or the Helsinki Declaration. What ethical standards do they have?"
That worried me very much, and it still does. I have inquired into the position more closely,
and have asked the Medical Council-the body that registers doctors-to examine it. The
council's letter to me contained something like this, "We are very glad you have drawn that
question to our attention." I have also spoken with the chairman of the Medical Association,
and it was news to him that doctors no longer take the Hippocratic oath or an oath of any
kind. We require estate agents who join the Real Estate Institute to conform to a code of
ethics. Indeed, we require that of members of most professions, and I stress that it was a
great surprise to me that members of the medical profession are no longer interested in or
required to conform to any ethical code at all. In the medical handbook one finds the
Hippocratic oath, the Helsinki Declaration, and an admonition to abide by them, but
apparently nobody gives any undertaking to do so. That would be a danger, if there were no
panel system.
Panel systems have been operating very successfully for many years in New Zealand.
However, it appears that "panel" has become a very nasty word, like "racist". One can
always conclude an argument by saying, “That is racist.” Anyone to whom that statement is
put will be horrified that what he or she has said can be associated with racism, and will
immediately duck for cover and run away from the argument. These days one can stop
almost any argument in some circles by speaking about panels, as that word too has been
made to appear nasty. A previous speaker referred to Kew Hospital, where for 10 years Dr
McLean has been running panels which have exercised all the compassion, restraint, and
patience necessary. Certainly, they are run very successfully and efficiently.
In the Bill I find no suggestion that under the panel system three or four, or maybe even
two, beady-eyed doctors have to interview a patient who is distraught and worried about a
medical condition. The suggestion that the patient's own doctor cannot be associated with
the panel is nonsense. As the Bill is written, a panel can review the case of a patient only
when she has been referred by her doctor or a family planning clinic. Therefore the patient's
doctor is involved at the very earliest stage, and the panel can call on the doctor at any time.
Clause 34 provides that, "The function of every panel is to review every case referred to it
... by a registered medical practitioner or family planning clinic". Therefore, nothing can
happen without a recommendation from the patient's doctor or a family planning clinic,
which has a doctor on its staff.
The next point I make may be of importance when discussing panels. They have been
described as overriding and overbearing. I was surprised to hear the Leader of the
Opposition say a panel was inhuman, or something of that sort. I was surprised, because I
regard such a statement as a terrific insult to the many very good people who have carried
out excellent work as members of panels over very many years. The Leader of the
Opposition should have inquired into the position a little more closely before making such a
sweeping condemnation of existing panels. Clause 36(5) provides, "As soon as practicable
after receiving such written notice, the Panel shall consider the case and shall, unless it
considers it unnecessary or undesirable to do so, interview the patient." That provision could
have been worded the other way round, and might have been more explicit if it had been,
but the Bill clearly provides that panels shall interview patients unless they consider it
unnecessary or undesirable to do so. Does any member of the House consider that two
doctors who constitute a panel-and it has been suggested that two doctors will make the
decision should not, if they feel it necessary or desirable, interview the patient and ensure
that they have all the answers? Of course they would do that; they must. How could they
carry out their responsibilities as doctors on a committee or panel-call it what you like—if
they did not make a responsible decision? Unless they consider it unnecessary or undesirable
to interview the patient, they will certainly do so. I am sure the patient, and everyone else for
that matter, would consider that desirable, and the Bill provides for it. However, they will
not interview patients unless they consider it necessary or desirable.
I do not want to speak at great length. It was intended to introduce the Bill and give
members the opportunity to study it and make comments, but because debating material was
brought into the first reading I felt I should reply to it. I was denied the right of reply on the
Bill I introduced earlier, and I am taking this opportunity to express some of my views. I
hope people will study the Bill seriously and not accept at face value what is said by the
Leader of the Opposition, the member for Henderson, or myself. I reiterate that I hope that
most people, if they are really opposed to abortion on demand or abortion on request, will

consider the situation seriously, and recognise the position that would be reached very
quickly if a panel of doctors was not required to make the decisions. The doctors appointed
will be known for their integrity, not for their bias one way or another.
Some suspicions have been voiced about the status of such committees. They will be in
exactly the same position as the Chief Ombudsman, and will report to Parliament, not to the

Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon): First I should like to thank the Minister for ensuring that
copies of the Bill were available to us for a longer period than is normal on the introduction
of a Bill. I do not intend to deal with the Bill clause by clause at this stage, but in fairness to
the royal commission and to the legislation itself we should look at some of the positive
aspects. Therefore I should like to refer to the part dealing with contraception and
education. These may go some way towards ensuring that future generations of women will
not have to make a choice on whether or not they will have an abortion.
However, I find that I am not in agreement with the commission's report on some other

I have thought seriously about this, but from the information we have received from the New
Zealand Medical Association, the New Zealand Law Society, a group of Wellington women

this makes me realise that that provision is not suitable for women in New Zealand and is not
wanted. That is something we tend to forget. What we are really talking about is something

legislation, yet, this House, made up predominantly of males, will have its say in enforcing
what it believes is right. This matter was covered fairly well in a comment made by the

Government to interfere and legislate to enforce one side of the argument on pain of
criminal sanctions on members of society who do not hold that point of view." In other
words, what we tend to do is stop the freedom of choice. Those who do not want an abortion
are not compelled to have one, while those who do want one are stopped from having it.
The previous speaker spoke at some length about ethics, but frankly I wonder just what

when, according to the Minister, somebody misled the House. That the panel recommenda-
tion requires review has come through very clearly from the people whose views should be
most respected—the doctors. Social workers and women lawyers are also against that
recommendation. Surely doctors, who are experienced in health matters and particularly the
health of women, should be listened to with some respect. The proposal in the Bill will
separate a woman from her own doctor, at a time when she most needs him.
I know that some women in our society-I believe a very small minority-are
completely and utterly selfish and think of nothing but themselves and their own wishes, but
that type of woman would probably make a very poor parent, anyway. We seem to spend
our time insisting that women have children when perhaps we should be thinking about
quality rather than quantity in parenthood and teaching people to be good parents. That
would make for a better society.
When a women has to decide whether she will carry on with an unwanted pregnancy or
seek an abortion she finds herself in a very difficult situation. She is in need of assistance in
making this decision, and that assistance can best come from someone she trusts and has
faith in. Who better than her own doctor? An appearance before a panel of people she does
not know would be extremely humiliating, and I cannot understand why it is necessary. It is
all very well to talk about other panels in the health service, but this particular panel cannot
be likened to anything else.
The Minister of Health said that clause 33 stated that the supervisory committee shall

coloured by their personal views in relation to abortion generally. I wonder how the
supervisory committee will achieve that. This is one subject on which it has been proved that
people have definite views.
I believe the Bill should go to a select committee, and I say that recognising what the
Prime Minister has said about interested parties having had the opportunity to make

Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori): Under clause 3, the
law relating to the availability of contraception to people under the age of 16 is not
appreciably changed. I believe there is scant recognition of the fact that New Zealand has the
third highest teenage pregnancy rate in the industrialised world, and that adolescent mothers
face a 60 percent higher maternal death risk, as well as a higher rate of toxaemia and
anaemia. It should also be realised that little is done about the needs of the rejected child,
although much is said about the rights of the unborn child. Society has not yet provided
acceptable alternatives to the compulsory carriage to full term of an unwanted pregnancy.
Following a mother's decision that she cannot care for the expected child, society must step
in and provide acceptable and adequate alternative care if it compels her to bear that child.
The Bill would stop the work of the Aotea clinic, which performs 4000 legal abortions a
year. Under a new section in the Crimes Act these abortions would still be legal, and the
House, therefore, should not proceed with this measure until an assurance is given by the
Department of Health that facilities to perform a similar number of abortions with the same
speed and safety can be guaranteed in the public sector. It would be irresponsible to do
anything to impede the work of the Auckland clinic until such an assurance is given,
assuming that abortions will still be needed and sought by women.
The Bill creates a conflict between the statutory functions of the Department of Health
and the new supervisory committee, in that the duty to license institutions for certain
purposes would overlap and possibly be contradictory. The Bill is in direct contradiction to
the spirit and the provisions of another Bill at present before the House-the Human Rights
Commission Bill, which states in clause 22(1)(b) that it shall be unlawful to supply facilities
or services on less favourable terms by reason of a person's sex. I believe that the Bill we are
discussing violates the human rights of those women who believe they cannot cope with
carrying a pregnancy through to full term. Must we, as women, be compelled to accept that
we are carriers of life, despite our private will and all our intellectual comprehension that we
do not wish at a given time of our lives to accept this role?
The Bill has clauses that contravene a woman's personal liberty, because freedom from
unwanted reproduction is the very essence of women's equality. The Bill does not acknow-
ledge a woman's right to determine her own maternity—that is, to control her reproduction
potential. The oppression of woman is derived from her womanness. Her biological
difference has been used to build social structures and a supportive ideology of female
submission—an ideology so entrenched that woman herself has come to believe it. This is a
pity, for women are themselves divided on this issue because of that. So this issue alone has,
unfortunately, created and sustained division among women at a time when, through the
thrust of the feminist movement, they are striving for complete emancipation of themselves
as individuals. Abortion is a woman's issue, and it is fundamental to a woman's ability to
participate equally in society. New Zealand women must have the right to choose.
The Bill introduces a panel system that is likely to result in those who successfully
manoeuvre this maze being ultimately too far along in gestation to be legally aborted. Nor
does the panel system respect a woman's right to the privacy and the confidentiality of
counselling sought of her own volition with people of her own choice. Instead, she will be
compulsorily directed to a group of people she may never have met or known, and though
under considerable stress, will be forced to accept their decision even if it is diametrically
opposed to her own. This violation of the human rights of women is probably my strongest
reason for opposing many provisions in the Bill; and I give notice that I shall be seeking to
introduce amendments.
The measure is based on a royal commission report, which has a fatal flaw-it sought a
compromise despite the impossibility of compromise on this issue. Either the foetus is a
human being and there can be no justification for abortion, or it is not and there can be


## p. 2368 (#824) ###########################################

2368
19 August
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
justification. It is totally unjust for any one group in our community to invoke the power of
the State to stop those of a contrary view from using their own judgment. This Bill,
therefore, makes it possible unjustly to compel people against their own decision. There is
really no manoeuvre in the Bill, as I see it, for both views to be accommodated. Over 40
women legal graduates and practitioners, meeting for the first time in Wellington, consi-
dered any law based on the royal commission's report to be repressive. Inasmuch as the Bill
is repressive-and I believe it is-it removes the liberty of choice of the individuals who do
not subscribe to the rationale behind it. Thus it ignores the reality that abortion is a fact of
life practised in all cultures and civilisations from time immemorial; and Maori culture is no
exception.
The need for abortion has long been demonstrated, and women will continue to seek it
outside the provisions of this Bill, if necessary. It will revive the traffic in back-street
abortions. The State should not have the power to place people in this situation at risk. It is a
law that the rich can very skilfully circumnavigate, because they are wealthier than others.
New Zealand women who cannot afford a trip across the Tasman will find themselves in a
new discriminated-against group. For the rich, the whole system can be sidestepped by a trip
to Australia, as everyone knows.
The Bill is unworkable as it is. There are not enough qualified social workers to service
our present social services, let alone the new role introduced for them in the Bill. Therefore,
the Bill is unworkable with our present resources, and should not be introduced until we
have adequate social service resources. Furthermore, it requires the co-operation of the
medical profession. A significant proportion of both groups has publicly dissociated itself
from the report on which the Bill is based. How, then, will Parliament provide the resources
for it?
The panel system, which I consider is unnecessary, expensive, unsuitable, unworkable,
and cumbersome, will cause delays and be degrading for the women concerned. The system
is degrading because the woman has no part in the final decision, and neither does her
doctor, her counsellor, or her social worker, unless one happens to be chosen as a panel
member. The system also interferes with the tradition of confidentiality between doctor and
patient, which ethos is as important to social workers as the Hippocratic oath is to medical
practitioners. That is one of the reasons members of the New Zealand Social Workers
Association have dissociated themselves from the report of the royal commission.
What is the legal status of the panel envisaged in the Bill? Can a woman be represented
by her solicitor? Will a woman have the right of appeal against the decision of the panel? Is
the decision to be absolutely final? Will a panel of three people not known to the woman be
able to make a final decision on her case despite her subjective awareness of the acute stress
that that decision will exacerbate? As I have said, bureaucratic systems are liable to cause
delays, which in relation to an abortion would mean a later and less safe operation for the
woman. We would be wiser legislators if legislation such as this were more thoroughly
considered. Compulsory counselling is contrary to the development of good counselling
relationships, but that is one of the basic devices employed in the panel system introduced in
this Bill. Compulsory attendance at State-approved counselling services removes the free-
dom of choice. The panel system is not only unworkable, but is unjust and inhumane to the
extent that any woman under stress has to go before an anonymous group of strangers.
Opposition members have not had the Bill long enough to consider it in depth. The
provisions relating to contraception are inadequate. As we all know, no method of
contraception other than total abstinence is guaranteed to be totally effective. The essential
tools by which a woman can determine reproduction are not available, and are not made
more acceptable in the Bill. Therefore, the injustice is entrenched at a time when it could
have been removed. The existing laws relating to contraception should have been amended
to make it possible for contraceptives to be available to all.
Rape is not regarded in the provisions of the Bill as an adequate reason for granting a
woman a legal abortion. Rape is a crime. The woman victim who wishes to disgorge from her
body the repugnant results of her molester's lust is not able to do so, and therefore the Bill
makes the woman as much of a criminal as her rapist. Where is the justice in that? It is
contradictory and inhumane. After a violent brutal rape a woman may become pregnant,
and for 9 months she must not consider any alternative to carrying through the pregnancy
and bearing a criminal's child, a molester's child. The rapist probably introduced the woman
to the greatest trauma of her life-but rape is not to be regarded as sufficient reason for an
abortion.

2369
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
The Bill is based on the report of the commission, which considered that the morning-
after pill or the IUD was all that was needed for the victim of a rape. The report notes
correctly that neither method is effective if given after 72 hours. Studies indicate that the
morning-after pill is not 100 percent effective. Nor did the royal commission's report inform
New Zealand women that the drug in the pill, diathylstilbestrol, is the same drug that,
administered to women in America to prevent miscarriage, resulted in an unprecedented
epidemic of vaginal cancer in their female offspring, and a higher than normal incidence of
sterility in their male offspring. Yet that was the drug recommended in the commission's
report. Given the rate of pregnancy from a single act of unprotected intercourse as estimated
by the population council as being between only 4 percent and 10 percent, this degree of
risky overkill of offering the morning-after pill is highly questionable; yet the royal
commission's recommendation is contained in the Bill.
So is the practice of inserting an IUD in an already traumatised woman in the vain hope
that a little piece of plastic will end her anguish. That I consider to be equally questionable—
and all this when a simple menstrual extraction or early suction abortion procedure could be
performed by a competent medically qualified person without any great risk. Instead, we
have a bureaucratic creation which, to my mind, constitutes a violation of the human rights
of those women who do not wish to carry a pregnancy to full term. I speak as a woman, as a
mother, and as one who subjectively experienced soul-searching anxiety about my third
pregnancy. Under this Bill, women beyond the normal child-bearing years have no right to
seek an abortion no matter how much anxiety they may feel about the dangers and risks
involved; nor have those of teen or sub-teen age. We are third in the industrialised world in
our incidence of teenage pregnancies, yet, unless excepted by the panel, those pregnancies
must go through.
My final observation is that if every child were a wanted child—and the Bill does not
provide for that-society would be transformed. We would see the positive effect in our
criminal statistics and in statistics relating to many other phenomena arising in our social
scene-the unemployable, unemployed youth, and others who contravene our laws. I
suspect that many of those younger people were unwanted children. I look forward to
participating again in the debate on this Bill and to introducing some amendments along the
lines of my criticism.
Mr COOPER (Otago Central): I find myself at a disadvantage, as I can speak only as a

great extent it will lead to the woman's right to choose, which is what people in many
sections want. There is absolutely not one whit of difference between the woman's right to
choose and abortion on demand.
